text:
Breckenridge is joining a legal effort to challenge the federal government’s repeal of longstanding greenhouse gas regulations , citing concerns about the potential impacts of climate change on the town’s ski-dependent economy and mountain environment.

Breckenridge Town Council unanimously agreed Tuesday, Oct. 27, to sign onto a legal brief supporting a multistate lawsuit objecting to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s decision to rescind a 2009 scientific finding that greenhouse gas emissions threaten public health and welfare.

The Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding established the legal basis for federal regulations limiting greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles under the Clean Air Act. The EPA effectively axed the finding in February, eliminating federal emission standards for cars and trucks.

Colorado Attorney General and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Phil Weiser has joined attorneys general from 22 other states in challenging the decision , arguing that the rollback undermines efforts to combat climate change and protect public health.

In a legislative committee memo presented to Breckenridge council members, sustainability director Jessie Burley outlined several ways the federal ruling could affect the town, referencing increasingly volatile winters, heightened wildfire risks and additional costs for local governments.

“Climate change is already producing shorter, warmer and less predictable winters, directly threatening Breckenridge’s ski-dependent economy, local businesses and tax base,” the memo states.

The memo also warns that reduced snowpack and earlier spring snowmelt could lengthen wildfire seasons, driving up costs for emergency preparedness, insurance and infrastructure protection.

Town officials additionally expressed concern that the rollback could undermine investments in clean energy , electrification and climate resilience made under longstanding federal protections.

Breckenridge will participate by signing an amicus curiae , or “friend of the court,” brief, which allows organizations and municipalities to submit arguments supporting a legal challenge without becoming plaintiffs.

The law firm WilmerHale is preparing the brief on behalf of Aspen Skiing Company and a coalition of ski industry representatives and mountain communities, according to the memo.

Global Electric Vehicle Transition: A Multi-Speed Transformation

| Global EV adoption continues to expand, with annual sales projected to reach 23 million vehicles, representing nearly 30% of new vehicle purchases worldwide. Europe is emerging as a key growth engine, China remains the dominant manufacturing and sales powerhouse, and North America faces slower adoption. Advances in battery chemistry, vehicle range, and charging infrastructure are helping EVs mature into a resilient, global transportation ecosystem.

The $100 Flight

| Joby Aviation's recent electric air taxi flight across Tampa Bay retraced the route of the world's first scheduled airline service, highlighting the promise of eVTOL aviation. Yet the real challenge is economic, not technical. With four seats, pilot costs, insurance, maintenance and infrastructure expenses, fares near $100 may be necessary initially. Long-term success will depend on aircraft utilization, network growth, passenger demand and eventually automation.

Read Full Story

The Second Life of EV Batteries: A Billion-Dollar Opportunity Meets a Reality Check

| Millions of EV batteries will eventually retire from automotive service, creating an opportunity for a second life in solar storage, grid support and commercial backup power. But reusing old batteries isn't as simple as connecting them to a new application. Testing, refurbishment, safety certification and falling prices for new batteries are challenging the economics. The emerging industry must prove that reuse can compete with recycling and newly manufactured storage systems.

Electric School Buses Didn't Fail. Washington's Rollout Did

| The $5 billion federal Clean School Bus Program has encountered delivery delays, manufacturer bankruptcies, reliability concerns and serious EPA oversight failures. But these shortcomings do not establish that electric school buses are a failed technology. They expose Washington's inability to manage a complex transportation transition. The real lessons involve procurement, infrastructure, manufacturer accountability and the need to measure actual results rather than simply announce ambitious spending targets.

| As Waymo enters Canada, cities face a crucial choice between passive tech adoption and proactive urban stewardship. Navigating northern blizzards, black ice, and hidden road markings requires rigorous local safety standards over corporate assertions. To avoid gridlock and public transit decay, municipalities must deploy congestion pricing and curb management, integrating robotaxis as last-mile complements. Safer driverless tech enables cities to reclaim asphalt for pedestrian plazas and bike networks, setting a sovereign playbook where civic priorities govern the algorithm.

description:
Joby Aviation has been working to bring its electric air taxis to Texas, and, in September, the company started flying them around Dallas-Fort Worth.
The long-term goal of Project Nexus is to have air taxis make regional flights between Dallas, Austin, San Antonio, and eventually Houston.

Even if air taxis were to expand the same way that Waymo has been to major U.S. cities like Las Vegas and San Diego, you wouldn't be able to call an air taxi as easily.

text:
Joby Aviation has been working to bring its electric air taxis to Texas, and, in September, the company started flying them around Dallas-Fort Worth. The flights started at Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport on September 10 and went on for about a week. During that time, Joby flew its air taxis into DFW Airport, as well as out to Arlington and along a route to Toyota's North American headquarters in Plano.

None of the flights carried any passengers, though. Instead, Joby says the test flights are designed to give the FAA the real-world data it needs to build safety rules for commercial air taxi service. However, Joby's CEO JoeBen Bevirt says the flights are "just the beginning of what Texas and Joby can build together," and it does seem like the company is planning to stick around in Texas.

Back in August, Joby signed a lease at Alliance Air Trade Center, which is part of Perot Field. The company says it will use the space as a base for its air taxi operations in Dallas-Fort Worth. That was about a month before Tesla launched its self-driving Cybercab in Austin, so there has been a lot going on in Texas when it comes to innovative ways to travel.

The flights Joby made in Dallas-Fort Worth are part of Project Nexus, which is TxDOT's piece of the FAA's eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The FAA's program is set to run for three years, and Texas isn't the only state involved. TxDOT is working with Oklahoma, Louisiana, and the Choctaw Nation on the project, so the FAA will be able to test air taxis in cities as well as in rural areas.

The long-term goal of Project Nexus is to have air taxis make regional flights between Dallas, Austin, San Antonio, and eventually Houston. There's no date specified for when that could happen yet, though. Project Nexus isn't just about passenger flights, either. TxDOT also wants to test medical and cargo flights with these aircraft, and we've already seen a medical flight happen in another part of the FAA's program. In July, BETA Technologies and United Therapeutics flew a genetically modified pig heart between airports in Virginia and Maryland using BETA's electric aircraft, and that flight was actually the first one in the FAA's entire program. Getting an organ where it needs to go is highly impactful.

Joby still needs the FAA to certify its air taxi before it can start flying passengers. The company says it is currently in the fifth and final stage of the FAA's type certification process, but Joby hasn't revealed when people in Texas will be able to actually book a flight.

Getting to an air taxi might also be a problem for some people. The FAA says that early air taxis will use existing helipads where they can, and that they will operate a lot like helicopter services do today. The system will operate very differently from a robotaxi service like Waymo, where the car comes to pick you up. Even if air taxis were to expand the same way that Waymo has been to major U.S. cities like Las Vegas and San Diego, you wouldn't be able to call an air taxi as easily. Instead, you'd have to go to a helipad or landing site to catch your flight.

Air traffic at DFW is another thing that Joby and the FAA will have to deal with, too. DFW had the third-most takeoffs and landings of any airport in the world in 2025. NASA and Joby ran simulations of air taxi flights at DFW and Dallas Love Field back in 2023 to test procedures that could help reduce the workload on air traffic controllers. NASA researcher Ken Freeman said the simulation "validates the idea that we can find a way to safely integrate these vehicles into the airspace at scale." Still, a simulation isn't the same as flying real passengers over Dallas, and Joby hasn't done that yet.

text:
Companies should understand the significance of a June 21, 2021 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ("EPA" or "Agency") memorandum entitled "Strengthening Environmental Justice Through Criminal Enforcement." Addressed to EPA personnel, including Senior Management and Special Agents with EPA's Office of Criminal Enforcement, Forensics and Training, and Regional Criminal Enforcement Counsel with EPA's Office of Regional Counsel, the memorandum outlines how EPA will work with the U.S. Department of Justice ("DOJ") and use existing resources to more aggressively identify and prosecute environmental crimes committed in "overburdened communities." A directive to focus investigative resources on particular communities and affirmatively consider criminal enforcement is unprecedented. Companies need to understand both their environmental justice risk profiles and the unique challenges associated with criminal investigations.

EPA's most recent memorandum should be seen in the context of the Administration's "whole of government" approach to environmental justice and also in conjunction with Attorney General Garland's statements regarding environmental crime victims. EPA makes clear that while the Department of Justice ("DOJ") retains prosecutorial discretion over environmental crimes, the Agency is taking steps to achieve environmental justice in criminal cases by strengthening tools for the detection of environmental crimes in overburdened communities, enhancing outreach to the victims of environmental crimes; and ensuring that EPA investigations are structured to maximally support the DOJ.

Enhanced Communication between EPA Civil and Criminal Staff - EPA recommends that civil and criminal staff maintain regular and open communication regarding increased facility inspections in overburdened communities. Historically, communication between the civil and criminal components of EPA has been discouraged, and it was rare for a civil case to "turn" criminal. This directive will increase the likelihood that civil enforcement matters in overburdened communities will be referred for criminal investigation.

Impact of Early Outreach to Environmental Crime Victims - EPA advises case teams to use crime victim data and other relevant information to ensure the proper identification of individuals harmed by purported environmental crimes in overburdened communities.EPA is also considering creative avenues for directly communicating with environmental crimes victims, such as use of social media platforms, with the intent, in part, to integrate environmental crime victim concerns into every investigation and prosecution and identify first-person testimony of harm to bolster enforcement outcomes.

Cross-Training of EPA and DOJ Staff on EJSCREEN and Other Tools - EPA will form an Environmental Justice Workgroup for EPA and DOJ staff focusing on the use of EPA's EJSCREEN mapping tool and the identification of crime victims. Training will be provided to EPA environmental justice staff on the criminal enforcement process to enhance cross-referrals. Historically, environmental criminal investigations have arisen in the context of catastrophic events, or in the face of blatant violations of the law. The use geospatial mapping tools in conjunction with criminal enforcement training of EPA civil personnel will almost certainly lead to broader categories of conduct being at risk for criminal investigation.

Focus on Environmental Justice Remedies - EPA has directed that investigations be conducted in a manner that facilitates the identification of remedies that meaningfully protect overburdened communities and victims of environmental crimes.Notably, the memorandum emphasizes that "EPA recognizes that punishment for environmental crimes must be sufficient to achieve the goal of deterrence." Further, EPA's Environmental Justice Workgroup will develop guidance for agency attorneys and prosecutors to ensure restitution, community service payments, and other court-ordered projects supporting overburdened communities are considered in all cases identified as having environmental justice concerns.Historically, investigations have focused primarily on identifying misconduct and proving the elements of the alleged crime. Expanding the scope of the investigation to include information relevant to potential remedies may significantly increase the duration of the investigation and make it even more difficult to discern the potential charges at issue.

Now, more than ever, it is important for companies to understand their risk profile with regard to environmental justice issues. We urge you to consider the ACELAS environmental justice resource, which provides a convenient framework for analysis. Equally important is understanding the unique risks associated with criminal enforcement and importance of having a crisis response plan in place.

The content of this article is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter. Specialist advice should be sought about your specific circumstances.

In autonomous and self-driving vehicle news are Waymo, Toyota, Baidu, Lyft, Freenow, WeRide, Allianz, Ping An, Marti, CalmCar, TIER IV, NTRO, May Mobility, Rivian, Aurora, Roush, , Kodiak, Hyundai and Innoviz.

Waymo Scales Toward 20,000 Vehicles as Witherite Law Group Flags Stalled First-Responder Bill

Witherite Law Group founder Amy Witherite has pointed to safety vulnerabilities in autonomous vehicle operations as federal legislation addressing first-responder interactions remains stalled in committee without cosponsors. The delay coincides with Waymo advancing plans to scale its commercial robotaxi deployment to a 20,000-vehicle fleet while conducting active roadway testing across Philadelphia.

The push follows incidents involving autonomous fleets and emergency personnel, including a May 28, 2025 event in Dallas in which a stalled, unoccupied Waymo obstructed fire apparatus responding to a fatal gas explosion. Rep. Kevin Mullin introduced H.R. 10033, the AV Emergency Response Coordination Act, which would mandate 30-second hotline response thresholds for commercial operators, two-minute scene clearance timelines, and explicit manual-override protocols for emergency responders. Oversight remains contested at the state and local level, with PennDOT maintaining preemptive regulatory authority over autonomous deployments and thereby restricting municipal intervention in Philadelphia. Safety advocates and NHTSA leadership have emphasized that autonomous vehicle integration cannot compromise emergency response corridors, and have urged congressional delegations to establish enforceable federal operating mandates.

Waymo Adds Nearly 250 Square Miles Across Five U.S. Metros

Waymo announced an expansion across five commercial deployment zones that adds nearly 250 square miles of operational design domain coverage over the coming week. The additions extend commercial ride-hailing deeper into existing territories in Los Angeles, Nashville, Orlando, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

The new perimeters add suburban and intermodal connectivity, including a coastal push south to Torrance in Los Angeles County and southern coverage to the Berryessa BART transit hub in the Bay Area. Service also extends north to La Jolla in San Diego, with expanded southern corridors in Nashville and doubled service density across eastern sectors and downtown Orlando.

Toyota and Waymo Move From Memorandum to Factory Production of Level 4 bZ4X

Toyota Motor Corporation and Alphabet subsidiary Waymo have expanded their autonomous mobility collaboration from an exploratory memorandum of understanding to factory-level production and deployment. Toyota will build purpose-built bZ4X electric vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, integrating Waymo’s Level 4 sensor and compute hardware on the assembly line rather than through post-production retrofitting. Initial validation operations begin in Japan in 2027 and are intended to form the foundation for high-volume driverless ride-hailing before expansion to the United Kingdom and other territories.

The right-hand-drive bZ4X platform includes power-actuated doors, an automated liftgate, optimized rear-seat legroom, and integrated ambient interior lighting. In parallel with commercial robotaxi operations, Toyota, Waymo, and Toyota software subsidiary Woven by Toyota will use operational telemetry and real-world edge cases to develop safety-critical driver assistance architectures for privately owned vehicles and vehicle-to-infrastructure safety networks.

Baidu and Lyft’s Freenow Debut Apollo RT6 Robotaxi in London

Baidu’s autonomous driving division, Apollo Go, and Lyft subsidiary Freenow have publicly debuted the sixth-generation Apollo RT6 electric robotaxi in London, targeting driverless testing in 2027 ahead of full commercial deployment. Closed and safety-operator trials began in the London Borough of Brent in July, and the partnership plans to scale to tens of vehicles over the next 24 months. The RT6 features a purpose-built passenger cabin with a detachable steer-by-wire assembly and a manufacturing cost of approximately $37,000.

The deployment places London among the Western testbeds for Chinese autonomous vehicle stacks at a time of regulatory scrutiny and proposed vehicle hardware and software bans in the United States. Operating amid 20 mph municipal zones and traffic-calming infrastructure, the Baidu-Freenow service enters a competitive field that includes Wayve and Uber, Waymo, and Pony.ai. Beyond Transport for London licensing and Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency driverless permits, long-term commercial scaling remains contingent on international trade policy, specifically whether upcoming UK electric vehicle tariff structures will impose penalties on China-assembled automated vehicle hardware.

WeRide Builds a Global Insurance Program With Allianz and Ping An

WeRide has launched a global insurance partnership program with Allianz Insurance Singapore and Ping An Property & Casualty Insurance as founding underwriters. The program is designed to support the commercial rollout of tens of thousands of Level 4 vehicles across East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, and establishes standardized underwriting frameworks covering motor liability, commercial general and product liability, data privacy, and vehicle cybersecurity risks. Through centralized risk pooling and long-term contracts across high-volume deployments, the framework aims to lower per-mile insurance premiums and improve unit economics as driverless operations grow.

The program builds on existing deployments with each carrier. In Singapore, Allianz underwrote WeRide’s Sentosa Robobus service and its Ai.R robotaxi fleet operated with Grab in Punggol, which has surpassed 135,000 autonomous kilometers and 13,000 unique passenger trips. Ping An covers commercial robotaxi operations across Guangzhou, Beijing, Abu Dhabi, and Dubai, with trips dispatched through both the WeRide Go app and Uber’s platform. WeRide’s active global fleet totals approximately 3,600 automated vehicles, including more than 1,800 robotaxis.

Marti Partners With CalmCar on Level 4 Deployment in Türkiye

Marti Technologies has partnered with China-based autonomous driving software developer CalmCar to bring automated driving to its Turkish mobility platform. The first test vehicle running CalmCar software has arrived in Türkiye to begin closed-course validation and local operational testing in Istanbul, pending regulatory test permits. After track validation, Marti plans to offer autonomous vehicle hailing through its core application across a ride-hailing footprint spanning 40 cities.

CalmCar supplies L2 to L2+ advanced driver assistance stacks, Level 4 software, driver monitoring systems, and integrated smart cockpit solutions, and currently powers commercial robobus operations in Chongqing and Chengdu. The agreement supports Marti’s multi-partner autonomous driving strategy, which evaluates perception models, sensor suites, and drive-by-wire software under local infrastructure and operating conditions.

TIER IV and NTRO Bring an Autonomous Electric Bus to Australia and New Zealand Trials

Australia’s National Transport Research Organisation has procured a mid-sized autonomous electric bus from open-source autonomous driving software developer TIER IV to accelerate automated transit deployments across Australia and New Zealand. The 15-passenger vehicle, designated Rita, carries a TIER IV automated driving system calibrated for regional operating domains on a dedicated test track. It is built to support conditional automation with onboard safety operators as well as fully driverless operation, and is intended to progress to public road demonstrations and revenue-service trials with municipal councils, airport authorities, transit agencies, and fleet operators.

The deployment responds to projected driver shortages driven by late-2020s workforce retirements and to safety mandates aligned with Australia’s National Road Safety Strategy, which targets zero roadway fatalities by 2050. Drawing on deployment architectures established in TIER IV’s Japanese pilots, NTRO plans to validate the low-floor electric platform for first- and last-mile connectivity, specialized routes for riders with mobility impairments, and high-frequency off-peak circulators to replace underused heavy fleet assets.

May Mobility Adds Third-Party Safety Review With Edge Case

May Mobility has made third-party safety validation a mandatory gate for driverless deployment following an initial safety case assessment by safety assurance consultancy Edge Case. The milestone extends a technical evaluation partnership begun in 2022 and measures May Mobility’s end-to-end safety argumentation against recognized assurance standards, including UL 4600 and the Open Autonomy Safety Case framework. Edge Case applied its proprietary DevSafeOps methodology to audit the logical hierarchy, structural completeness, and clarity of the operator’s safety claims before commercial expansion.

Following the findings, May Mobility is streamlining its safety case architecture to keep it manageable as driverless transit fleets grow across municipal networks. The operator is benchmarking safety metrics against verified human-driving performance and expanding automated telemetry processing to resolve edge-case fleet anomalies. The next phase of the assessment will move from structural review to empirical verification, with individual autonomy and behavior-planning claims subjected to evidentiary auditing.

Rivian’s Scaringe Frames Autonomy as a Market Share Driver

Rivian Automotive CEO RJ Scaringe described autonomous driving technology as an industry inflection point during the company’s third-quarter 2026 earnings briefing, projecting that automated driving capabilities will reshape automotive market share. Addressing analysts, Scaringe positioned self-driving features not only as optional subscriptions but as core system software whose development costs will increasingly be built into base vehicle pricing to drive competitive volume.

The emphasis aligns with Rivian’s vertically integrated, software-defined vehicle strategy, which includes a proprietary zonal electrical architecture, in-house compute hardware, and a vision-centric Large Driving Model foundation stack. Rivian reported higher-than-expected adoption of its Autonomy+ package on the newly launched R2 platform and recently acquired Third Dimension AI to scale closed-loop neural network simulation ahead of its scheduled Autonomy and AI Day. The autonomy program serves as a foundational layer across consumer vehicle lines and commercial fleet integrations, including a multi-year fleet supply agreement with Uber.

Aurora Targets 20 Trucks Weekly Through Roush as FMCSA Approves Beacon Exemption

Aurora Innovation announced plans to scale production of its autonomous driving system to 20 Class 8 trucks per week beginning in early December through contract upfitting partner Roush. The run rate implies annualized build capacity above 1,000 Level 4 commercial vehicles and positions the company to surpass 200 operational driverless trucks by February 2027 and to target more than 1,000 deployed trucks by the end of 2027. The ramp bridges near-term carrier delivery timelines ahead of factory-integrated assembly with Volvo Trucks and PACCAR.

The scaling follows a five-year Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration exemption that allows Level 4 commercial vehicles to use cab-mounted, flashing amber warning beacons rather than physical roadside warning triangles or flares during highway stops, resolving a key operating constraint for driver-out interstate freight. Supported by cash reserves above $1 billion, Aurora also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with asset-based carrier Charger Logistics covering up to 500 autonomous Class 8 trucks powered by the Aurora Driver, with deliveries slated for 2027 and 2028. The agreement expands on an initial operational contract begun in July 2026 across Texas cross-border corridors.

Aurora and Charger Logistics Outline Ownership and Software Model

Under the proposed structure, Charger Logistics will purchase and retain ownership of the autonomous trucks while subscribing to Aurora’s Driver as a Service software model. The framework is designed to optimize total cost of ownership for fleet operators and supports Aurora’s capital-light path toward a targeted 30,000-truck footprint by 2030.

Charger plans to deploy the second-generation hardware platforms across domestic long-haul corridors and high-volume cross-border freight routes linking the United States and Mexico. The deployment connects the Aurora system directly to Charger’s internal transportation management system to scale unmanned middle-mile capacity across key commercial lanes.

DTL Transport Signs Binding Agreement for 75 Driverless Kodiak Trucks

California-based refrigerated long-haul carrier DTL Transport has entered a binding commercial agreement to deploy 75 driverless Class 8 trucks running the Kodiak Driver autonomous platform. Under a recurring Driver-as-a-Service framework, DTL retains ownership of the tractors and pays Kodiak AI a per-mile software utilization fee. The deployment is described as the first publicly announced, binding driverless fleet commitment by an interstate long-haul carrier. Initial rollouts target Sun Belt corridors, specifically Interstate 10 between Dallas and El Paso, Texas, and Interstate 20 between Dallas and Atlanta, Georgia, designed to bypass Hours of Service constraints in high-tempo refrigerated grocery distribution.

The contract expands on a September 2026 commercial pilot in which Kodiak-equipped trucks hauled temperature-sensitive produce 225 miles on California State Route 99 and Interstate 5 between Fresno and Los Angeles under state autonomous vehicle testing permits. It also extends Kodiak’s Driver-as-a-Service model beyond industrial energy transport, where partner Atlas Energy Solutions operated 35 driverless trucks in the Permian Basin as of mid-2026 toward an objective of 100 autonomous units by mid-2027.

Stoneridge and Kodiak AI Integrate MirrorEye Into Autonomous Trucks

Stoneridge and Kodiak AI have established a technology collaboration to integrate Stoneridge’s MirrorEye Camera Monitor System into commercial vehicles running the Kodiak Driver. Newly deployed Kodiak trucks feature the digital vision system, and both engineering teams are evaluating deeper integration of Stoneridge hardware and onboard edge processing to support autonomous operations.

The integration relies on Stoneridge’s Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration exemption, renewed in 2024 for a five-year term, which authorizes commercial vehicles to operate without conventional rear-vision mirrors. Kodiak’s proprietary SensorPods previously retained standard glass mirror assemblies to meet regulatory requirements alongside perception sensors. The compact, door-frame-mounted MirrorEye camera wing allows Kodiak to develop next-generation SensorPods with reduced mass, optimized aerodynamic drag, and simplified modular field serviceability. Stoneridge reports cumulative production above 200,000 MirrorEye units across six global commercial OEM platforms and more than 40 North American retrofit fleets.

Hyundai Motor Group Demonstrates Residential Parking Robots in South Korea

Hyundai Motor Group, through a consortium including Hyundai Motor Company, Hyundai WIA, and Hyundai Engineering & Construction, has demonstrated autonomous parking robot technology at the Hillstate The Wave City apartment complex in Siheung, Gyeonggi Province. Operating under South Korea’s Smart City Regulatory Sandbox, the pilot marks the country’s first residential deployment at a facility with more than 50 vehicle spaces. The demonstration covered simultaneous vehicle intake and dispatch, temporary retrieval, and automated double-parking relocation, with robots moving vehicles to designated staging zones within three minutes of a request from an in-home wall terminal.

The system combines facility access barriers, in-unit smart wall pads, and an AI-based automated vehicle inspection system with Hyundai’s Smart Parking Control System 2.0, which plans trajectories for up to 200 robots at once. Hyundai plans to use data from the Siheung pilot to establish safety and operational benchmarks, while consulting the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport on regulatory revisions to extend automated valet robotics to commercial office towers, airports, and public transit nodes.

Innoviz Positions Perciz LiDAR for Counter-UAS Defense Work

Innoviz Technologies reported rising engagement for its defense-focused Perciz brand following the Association of the United States Army Annual Meeting and Exposition. System integrators and defense prime contractors are prioritizing high-resolution 3D spatial sensing to counter low-cost first-person-view and fiber-optic tethered uncrewed aircraft. According to the company, legacy radio-frequency detection and jamming suites struggle against non-emitting guidance, while active optical point-cloud data provides the centimeter-level localization needed for kinetic and directed-energy interception.

The Perciz platform adapts Innoviz’s automotive-grade solid-state LiDAR, currently deployed with Tier 1 automotive programs including BMW and Volkswagen, to defense and perimeter security applications. Combining hardware returns resilient to environmental occlusion with perception software for positive target identification, the system is meant to address effector cueing gaps in heavy clutter. Innoviz aims to convert recent pipeline engagements into formal system-level evaluations ahead of C-UAS Technology USA in late 2026.

HIROSHIMA, Japan, Nov 1, 2026 - (JCN Newswire) - Mazda Motor Corporation (Mazda) is advancing initiatives based on three pillars-energy conservation, shifting to renewable energy, and introducing carbon-neutral fuels-with the goal of achieving carbon neutrality at its global manufacturing facilities by 2035. As part of its renewable energy initiative, Mazda will expand the use of on-site power purchase agreements (PPA)(*1) to the Mazda KD Center, scheduled for completion in November, and to the Miyoshi Plant, which includes an battery energy storage system.(*2)

At the Miyoshi Plant, ORIX Corporation (ORIX) will install solar power generation equipment as the PPA provider. The generated electricity will be consumed on-site, and any excess solar power will be stored in a battery energy storage system that uses new automotive lithium-ion batteries. This will allow Mazda to effectively utilize surplus solar power and reduce peak electricity demand.

At the Mazda KD Center, ORIX will also install solar power generation equipment as the PPA provider. Toyo Kohan Co., Ltd., a steel sheet product manufacturer, will utilize the environmental value(*3) associated with surplus electricity. These efforts will contribute to the increased use of renewable energy throughout the region's total supply chain.

Mazda aims to contribute to the region's sustainable development and enhancement of the industrial competitiveness by working with its partners to demonstrate and implement a range of carbon-neutral technologies, drawing on their respective strengths.

Mazda will continue to collaborate with like-minded partner companies to advance initiatives toward carbon neutrality. These initiatives include expanding the use of renewable energy and creating a positive impact on communities, the environment, and society.

(*1) A system in which a power producer installs solar power generation equipment on a customer's premises and supplies them with electricity generated from renewable energy, along with associated environmental value.

(*2) A system that stores surplus solar power and other electricity in batteries for use during periods of high electricity demand, thereby enabling the effective use of renewable energy and reducing peak electricity demand.

(*3) The environmental value of electricity generated from renewable energy sources, such as solar power, including the value of reducing CO2 emissions.

(*4) A system in which the environmental value of electricity generated from renewable energy sources, such as solar power, is traded separately from the electricity itself.

text:
This article was originally published on Construction Law International and is republished here with permission as it originally appeared on October 9, 2026.

Introduction

The global imperative to decarbonise energy production has emerged as a significant driver of infrastructure development. Climate change concerns and energy security considerations, heightened by geopolitical instability, have prompted governments to pursue ambitious renewable energy targets while grappling with the challenges of maintaining reliable power supplies to meet domestic demand. This tension between sustainability and energy pragmatism has produced a complex, rapidly evolving regulatory landscape, creating opportunities and risks for infrastructure projects across the energy sector.

Progress towards decarbonisation has been neither linear nor uniform. Jurisdictions have pursued strategies based on their distinct geographic characteristics, existing energy infrastructure, political considerations and available natural resources. For example, Italy utilises solar and biomethane technologies that can be integrated with its agricultural sector; Germany and the European Union have invested in wind energy; and the United States has witnessed a remarkable resurgence of interest in nuclear power, driven by strong energy demands from data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The US is experiencing a nuclear renaissance – not so much to meet energy self-sufficiency as to serve the extraordinary energy requirements of data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure

This article arises out of a panel presentation at the International Bar Association Annual Conference in Toronto in November 2025.[1] It examines how the regulatory shifts across these energy technologies and jurisdictions are shaping infrastructure project development. We identify key regulatory shifts and their impact on projects, including evolving social licence and financial considerations.

Emerging issues in regulating energy technology

Solar and biomethane in Italy

Italy has recently implemented legislative and regulatory changes to accelerate the development of renewable energy, particularly solar and biomethane. These measures are driven by EU targets and the country’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza or PNRR).[2] Key focus areas include simplifying authorisation procedures, introducing new incentives and defining rules for end-of-life management of these plants.

One important driver is the need for energy independence, which became critical with the Russia–Ukraine War, when Italy’s dependence on Russian gas had been approximately 43 per cent.[3] To strengthen local sources, Italy has developed technologies integrating energy production and agriculture, which combine agriculture and solar plants in ‘agri-photovoltaic’ projects, fuel biomethane plants with digested agricultural waste and reuse bio-products as fertiliser.

Wind energy in Germany and the EU

Wind energy stands at the heart of the EU’s energy and climate agenda. After nuclear energy, which provides 25 per cent of the EU’s electricity, wind is the largest energy source, providing 20 per cent of all electricity consumed across Member States.[4] It is indispensable to decarbonising the European economy. However, despite stable long-term output, the pace of producing new capacity falls short of what is required for the EU’s 2030 binding targets. Only 13 gigawatts of new wind capacity was added in 2024 and 19.1 gigawatts in 2025, making it necessary to increase capacity by more than 30 gigawatts annually in the coming years.[5] The need to double the growth in capacity heightens both the regulatory urgency and the commercial stakes in the wind energy debate in Europe today.

The challenges are threefold: navigating new EU permitting requirements, overcoming persistent delays in grid connection and stimulating demand-side uptake of renewable electricity among end-users. Each dimension has distinct legal requirements and commercial logic. All have generated regulatory issues at the EU level and in the German domestic regulatory framework that enforces EU standards.

Nuclear power in the US

The US is experiencing a nuclear renaissance – not so much to meet energy self-sufficiency as to serve the extraordinary energy requirements of data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure.[6] Technology companies operating large language models require enormous quantities of reliable, baseload power, with large data centres consuming as much electricity as a small city.[7]

Nuclear power is uniquely attractive to this industry. Unlike solar and wind, nuclear plants produce consistent baseload power, regardless of weather conditions. This reliability is essential for data centre operation, which cannot tolerate service interruptions caused by intermittency. Moreover, nuclear power produces no direct carbon emissions during operation, allowing technology companies to satisfy operational requirements and corporate sustainability commitments – although nuclear waste storage remains a politically sensitive issue.[8]

The US nuclear regulatory environment has been very stringent, particularly after the Three Mile Island disaster in 1979, when the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission implemented extensive safety requirements significantly increasing construction and operation costs. Recent policy shifts signal meaningful change, with the current administration aiming to significantly expand capacity by 2050.[9]

The current nuclear resurgence departs from the traditional approach of constructing massive new plants like the Vogtle nuclear facility in Waynesboro, Georgia.[10] Rather, driven by commercial interest in increasing available electricity, the industry is proceeding along two tracks: recommissioning previously shuttered plants and developing small modular reactor (SMR) technology.

The immediate path to increased capacity involves recommissioning plants closed for economic rather than safety reasons. This eliminates the lengthy process of site selection, environmental review and initial licensing of new construction. Technology companies have entered power purchase agreements (PPAs) with nuclear operators, providing the revenue certainty needed to justify investments.[11] However, SMRs are also being introduced. The output of SMRs is typically below 300 megawatts, in contrast with traditional plants, which exceed 1,000 megawatts.[12] Their modular design allows factory fabrication and transport to installation sites, potentially reducing costs and timelines. However, SMR technology remains largely unproven at commercial scale and regulatory procedures designed for large light-water reactors do not translate seamlessly to novel designs.[13]

Impact of regulatory changes

Having identified several trends in the development of carbon-reduced energy sources, we now turn to some emerging regulatory issues that shape that development.

Wind energy in Germany and the EU

The Renewable Energy Directive (RED), the primary legal instrument governing the EU’s approach to wind and other renewable energy, has undergone successive revisions. The core logic – that Member States bear individual responsibility for achieving national targets through support schemes and mechanisms – has remained constant.

However, the current generation of the framework, RED III,[14] sets a binding target of 42.5 per cent renewable energy in the EU energy mix by 2030, with an aspiration to reach 45 per cent. To increase available renewable sources rapidly, RED III has raised the headline target and introduced binding permitting timelines and streamlined procedures. It designates renewable energy deployment as ‘overriding public interest’ – a classification of direct consequences for weighing competing interests in planning and environmental impact assessment (EIA) proceedings. This resonates with the German approach, where the Renewable Energy Act 2023 (Erneuerbare-Energien-Gesetz) declares electricity generation from renewable sources to be of ‘overriding public interest’ and a matter of ‘public security’, with renewables to be treated as a priority consideration.

RED III also introduces provisions on ‘Renewable Acceleration Areas’ – pre-designated zones where simplified, time-limited permitting applies and where environmental assessment is carried out at the planning stage rather than for individual projects. According to Article 15(c)(1) of RED III, by 21 February 2026, Member States should have ensured that competent authorities adopted one or more plans to meet at least their national contributions towards the overall EU 2030 target.

Solar and biomethane in Italy

Similarly, Italy has introduced legislative and regulatory changes to boost the development of solar and biomethane projects. These measures are driven by EU targets and the PNRR. As in Germany, the key focus areas in Italy include simplifying authorisation procedures and introducing new incentives. Italy has also regulated end-of-life management in solar and biomethane projects.

Solar energy

Italy has streamlined the administrative processes for solar photovoltaic (PV) plants to accelerate their deployment. The recent Renewable Energy Consolidated Act (Testo Unico per le Energie Rinnovabili)[15] reorganises the legal framework to reduce bureaucratic hurdles. For large-scale plants, Single Authorisation[16] consolidates all necessary permits into a single process with stricter deadlines. For smaller-scale projects, the Simplified Administrative Procedure[17] streamlines approval. Further, authorities are defining ‘Suitable Areas'[18] for renewable energy installations to simplify permitting.

Three incentives support solar projects from utility-scale to small residential systems. The ‘Bonus Fotovoltaico’ (Photovoltaic Bonus) provides a tax deduction of up to 50 per cent on installation costs for residential and commercial systems, including storage batteries. The temporary FER X Decree (Transitional) provides incentives for electricity from renewable sources, including solar, with a focus on market-competitive projects. Finally, PNRR Measures[19] allocate significant funds to the development of solar energy, with a focus on agrivoltaics, and the deployment of PV panels on agricultural and industrial buildings, often through capital contributions.

Nuclear power remains significantly more expensive than solar, wind and natural gas generation

To address solar panel end-of-life management, the EU’s Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Directive has been transposed into Italian law.[20] The Gestore dei Servizi Energetici (GSE),[21] Italy’s energy services manager, manages the financial aspects of decommissioning. For plants that receive incentives, the GSE may retain a portion of the incentive payments to cover future disposal costs.

Biomethane energy

Biomethane regulation in Italy incentivises production from agricultural, livestock and organic waste, promoting a circular economy. The Ministerial Decree of 15 September 2022[22] incentivises the production of biomethane for transportation, heating and industrial processes, and simplifies the complex regulatory requirements related to energy, agriculture and waste management, creating a ‘Single Authorisation’ or similar procedure that involves multiple public entities.

The PNRR also targets the development of biomethane infrastructure. PNRR investments are designed to streamline the administrative process and allocate funds, including capital contributions of up to 40 per cent of eligible investment costs, to convert existing biogas plants and construct new ones. The PNRR also has an incentive tariff on net biomethane production for 15 years. The tariff amount varies based on the plant’s production capacity and feedstock type. Incentives are granted through competitive procedures managed by the GSE, with specific deadlines for plant commissioning aligned with PNRR goals.

The decommissioning of biomethane plants follows general environmental and waste management regulations. Key concerns include the safe disposal of all materials and equipment, anaerobic digesters and any associated waste products. The closing and dismantling of biomethane plants must comply with environmental permits and authorisations, and ensure proper soil and water protection. Operators must ensure the safe and environmentally sound disposal of all plant components, and restore the site to its original condition.

Nuclear power in the US

Nuclear power remains significantly more expensive than solar, wind and natural gas generation.[23] This cost disadvantage reflects high capital costs; lengthy construction timelines; and extensive safety systems, redundant components, specialised materials and documentation required by the regulations governing nuclear development and operation – compliance burdens that competing technologies do not face to the same degree.[24]

The capital requirements for traditional nuclear projects create financing challenges. Large plants can cost tens of billions of dollars and take over a decade to construct. The Vogtle expansion in Georgia, originally estimated to cost US$14bn, exceeded US$30bn as regulatory changes forced expensive modifications.[25]

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s licensing process imposes substantial costs, with the average licensing timelines historically extending well beyond those of other countries.[26] More significantly, the US approach lacks fixed timelines and permits requirements to evolve during construction, creating uncertainty that compounds project risks.[27] The central question is whether the regulatory framework can adapt quickly enough to support the current window of opportunity created by the surging commercial demand.

Evolving social licence considerations

Despite the powerful drivers to develop carbon-neutral energy sources, every infrastructure project has the potential to affect the local community in which it is built. This section examines features that require community engagement and support, and their corresponding effect on the regulatory environment.

Wind energy in Germany and the EU

Permitting remains the primary bottleneck for wind energy deployment across the EU. Although RED III introduces binding timelines and an ‘overriding public interest’, implementation at national and subnational level is uneven. EIA requirements,[28] directives for species protection obligations[29] and habitats,[30] and the integration of wind turbines with spatial planning frameworks – all products of the regulatory interest in sustaining social licence – create procedural complexity and lead times of five to ten years for large-scale projects.

In Germany, the Onshore Wind Energy Act 2022 (Wind-an-Land-Gesetz) shifts from a negative exclusion planning model to a positive area target system, requiring each state to designate minimum percentages of territory for wind by 2027 and 2032, with a sanction of full outer-zone privilege applying automatically if targets are missed. Priority zones[31] must simultaneously be designated as acceleration zones, with streamlined environmental rules under the Federal Spatial Planning Law (Raumordnungsgesetz).

These initiatives have boosted onshore wind expansion, leading to record-level licensing in 2024 and 2025. Designating two per cent of Germany’s land for wind and streamlining environmental assessments has reduced bureaucratic hurdles and accelerated project planning, but challenges remain at the state level.

In 2024, approximately 14 gigawatts of wind power was approved, a record exceeding the combined approvals of 2017–2020, signalling that acceleration measures are reducing red tape. In 2025, this increased to 20.8 gigawatts. Projects in designated acceleration areas have benefited from reduced EIAs, with authorities conducting reviews using existing data. This has reduced average approval times by 10–20 per cent as of early 2025. Nevertheless, grid connection delays are a structural commercial risk for wind energy operators across the EU. In Germany’s offshore sector, the obligation to connect lies with the transmission system operator. Failures to meet the agreed connection date trigger compensation claims.[32]

Litigation over the calculation of compensation – including the measurement of wind speed for estimating lost generation, the treatment of shadow effects between turbines and the scope of the grid operator’s duty to minimise damages – has generated substantial German case law.[33] More broadly, the pace of onshore grid reinforcement and extension – required to transport wind-generated electricity from production-intensive northern regions to consumption-intensive southern regions – lags behind both onshore and offshore wind installation rates.

A third challenge is demand: despite the need for expanded sources of carbon neutral energy, industrial and domestic energy users are transitioning their consumption to electrified, renewable-sourced supply chains slower than anticipated. This dampens the commercial incentive for accelerated wind investment and makes it harder to justify infrastructure costs.

PPAs between wind energy developers and large corporate buyers have emerged as a partial market-based solution, reducing dependence on public support schemes and creating long-term revenue certainty. However, PPA markets remain underdeveloped in several EU Member States due to regulatory barriers and the difficulty of pricing long-term renewable risk.

Solar and biomethane in Italy

Any new energy infrastructure, including solar and biomethane plants, must face the so-called ‘not in my backyard’ (NIMBY) syndrome. For permitting procedures involving local communities, whether towns/municipalities or regions, community support often requires ‘mitigating measures’, including allocating a budget for public works, renovation of streets, public buildings, schools, public gardens or hospitals, including energy efficiency initiatives.

By designating renewable energy infrastructure projects as projects ‘of public interest’,[34] the need to make these commitments for additional public infrastructure to secure the necessary permitting has developed from maintaining community goodwill to essential requirements for project planning.

Nuclear power in the US

Nuclear power has historically faced the most severe social licence challenges of any energy technology. The Yucca Mountain experience illustrates how social licence issues can derail initiatives, even when technical and regulatory requirements are satisfied – despite billions invested in the Nevada waste repository, political opposition prevented the facility from ever opening.[35]

Nuclear power has historically faced the most severe social licence challenges of any energy technology

Despite this history, recent polling indicates increasing public support for nuclear power, reflecting growing recognition that decarbonisation requires zero-emission baseload generation, concerns about grid reliability and increased confidence in the safety of nuclear energy.[36] Corporate endorsements from leading technology companies may also be influencing attitudes, as prominent firms announce nuclear commitments to power data centres. SMRs may offer further social licence advantages through reduced footprints, enhanced passive safety features and the possibility of locating facilities on former coal plant sites.

Financial implications

Regulatory shifts and evolving social licence considerations have contributed to a complex environment for the design and delivery of renewable energy projects, thus increasing the complexity of the financial foundation on which they must proceed.

Wind energy in Germany and the EU

In Germany and the EU, wind energy has grown from a niche technology into a core power generation sector. Offshore wind involves some of the largest infrastructure investments in Europe. The commercial model for onshore and offshore wind in most EU Member States now is based on competitive auctions: developers bid for a support rate (contract for difference or premium tariff), receive a grid connection entitlement upon winning and must commission the facilities within a defined period or face penalties.

In Germany, EEG auctions impose 24-month commissioning deadlines and 30-month deadlines for the lapse of subsidy entitlement, with penalties (Pönalen) accruing for delays. Commercial viability remains exposed to risks beyond auction outcomes: supply chain disruptions, grid connection delays causing outages and compensation claims, and costs from complex environmental and planning procedures.

EU wind energy investors must contend with frequently and abruptly changing regulations. In Germany, fundamental legal reforms pose systemic challenges.[37] In Spain, Italy and Czechia, retroactive reductions in renewable energy support schemes led to a wave of investor-state arbitrations under the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT). Following the Court of Justice’s judgment in Achmea (C-284/16) and Komstroy (C-741/19), intra-EU arbitration clauses in the ECT were deemed inapplicable as between EU Member States and EU investors, resulting in another shift in the prospect of a secure basis for financing projects. The German Constitutional Court has confirmed this position from a domestic law perspective.[38]

Solar and biomethane in Italy

In Italy, regulatory changes have resulted in recalculations of incentives to be awarded on certain plants, and permit and authorisation requirements, disrupting business plans on which investors and their financers have relied. This has prompted investors and financing banks to consider the risk and mitigate the related disruption to timelines and other features of the project.

Nuclear power in the US

Regulatory uncertainty drives the cost of capital for US nuclear projects above comparable jurisdictions, reflecting perceived risks, including regulatory changes during construction, licensing delays and political shifts that could undermine project economics.[39] SMRs face the compounded regulatory uncertainty of unproven technology. The cancellation of the NuScale Carbon Free Power Project – which would have been the first utility-scale US SMR – illustrated these difficulties when cost estimates rose from US$55 per megawatt-hour to US$89 per megawatt-hour, undermining the economic case and leaving the project without sufficient subscriber support to proceed.[40]

Achieving financial viability is likely to require regulatory reform; policy support through mechanisms like production tax credits or loan guarantees; and innovative commercial arrangements that transfer risk to creditworthy offtakers. The current environment of strong demand, corporate buyers, political support and reform momentum presents unusual conditions favourable to nuclear expansion. However, whether those factors are sufficient to overcome historical financial obstacles remains an open question.

Conclusion

The drive to decarbonise has produced a complex regulatory landscape for energy infrastructure projects worldwide. Across the three jurisdictions examined, regulatory uncertainty emerges as a central concern – when rules can change during development and construction, investors demand risk premiums that increase costs and slow deployment.

Energy transition will continue to generate novel challenges for infrastructure developers, regulators and host communities. What remains constant is the fundamental tension between the urgency of decarbonisation and the practical difficulties of transforming the systems that power modern economies – a tension that will shape infrastructure development for decades to come.

The energy industry has long been associated with a tremendous number of hurdles that developers have to overcome if they want to pursue certain projects. However, ever since the clean energy transition started, various nations, including the United States, have reduced the number of restrictions that companies are facing because they understand the importance of achieving their clean energy targets. This explains the abundance of projects that have materialized after companies became aware that there is a path of less resistance that they can take to ensure that electricity is made available. As of late, T1 Energy secured a federal waiver to keep Texas solar manufacturing moving.

T1 Energy maintains momentum in executing groundbreaking projects

One of the keys to success in the energy industry lies in a company’s ability to capitalize on any momentum that it is experiencing because there are no guarantees that the environment will always allow it to generate revenue and execute captivating projects, especially considering the rapid pace at which the industry evolves.

T1 Energy Inc. is an energy solutions provider that is currently focused on establishing an integrated U.S. supply chain for solar. The solar sector was once regarded as a very risky investment because developers knew there was no way to guarantee the consistent availability of sunlight throughout the year, but nowadays, technology allows them to overcome all challenges.

In 2025, solar power generation across the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grid officially overtook coal-fired generation for the first time.

In December 2024, T1 completed a transformative transaction, positioning the company as one of the leading solar manufacturing companies in the United States, with a complementary solar and storage strategy. Based in the U.S. with plans to expand its operations in America, the company is also exploring value optimization opportunities across its portfolio assets in Europe.

A plan to further advance Texas’ solar sector: T1 Energy secures federal waiver

A press release from T1 Energy Inc. announced that the company has received a waiver from the Department of Commerce that supports its advanced photovoltaic manufacturing activities and plans to expand U.S. solar cell manufacturing. One of the biggest advantages for the United States during the clean energy transition is that there are various governmental bodies that are actively involved in ensuring that projects can be executed with ease.

T1 is a company that industry experts believe is in the process of shaping the future direction of the solar energy sector, as the company heavily incorporates technological innovation in its projects. T1 is the largest American-owned manufacturer of silicon-based TOPCon solar modules. In this particular instance, the company asked for the expedited waiver to import up to 1.725 GW of solar cells to facilitate uninterrupted manufacturing at T1’s G1_Dallas solar module facility in order to meet existing and expected contract demand.

Analyzing T1 Energy’s decision to execute the project in the state of Texas

Texas has become the national leader in utility-scale solar energy production, surpassing California in 2025. In 2025, solar power generation across the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grid officially overtook coal-fired generation for the first time. Texas accounts for an estimated 19.8% of total U.S. utility-scale solar generation.

According to reports, the cumulative utility-scale solar capacity has surged past 55,000 MWdc, with Texas projected to lead the nation in new additions. The abundant open terrain in West Texas combined with high solar insolation is known to make large-scale farm development fast and cost-effective.

name: American Energy
title: The Datacenter Backlash Goes Bipartisan: Next Week's Midterms and the 2028 Buildout
authors: Maya Barkin, Wayne Ma, Reyk Knuhtsen, Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros, Dylan Patel
description:
Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model That leaves a 2028 pipeline still working through approvals, power projects and construction schedules as the rules change.
We already flagged to Datacenter Model subscribers which companies are most at risk from the current pause.
If the candidate proposing a datacenter pause won in every state where one is running, those states would together contain roughly 30 GW of planned capacity scheduled for 2028.
Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model Which states are the most impacted depends on which companies are building.
We made the same point from the other direction in Stop Saying Half of 2026 US Datacenter Capacity Is Canceled.
text:
The 2027 datacenter boom is already being built and next week’s midterms won’t stop it now. Roughly three-quarters of the 33.8 GW due across our top 20 states is already under construction, which is why we remain comfortable with the global +50 GW year we laid out in our Oct. 16 article. The campuses are taking shape. The election will change the rules around them, but much of the 2027 pipeline already has a substantial head start.

The fight is over 2028. Our model has 62.2 GW of US net additions that year, most of which hasn’t started construction. Most of it sits in states electing a governor on Nov. 3. This piece tracks the 13 states with the largest 2028 net additions in our model, setting aside Virginia and Mississippi, which don’t hold state elections this November. Together they account for 43.5 GW, or 70% of what we expect nationally, and 10 of the 13 elect a governor.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

That leaves a 2028 pipeline still working through approvals, power projects and construction schedules as the rules change. In September, we argued that datacenter moratoriums weren’t killing the US buildout: of roughly 20 GW inside local restrictions, we estimated only 1.5 GW faced delay. Most exposed capacity already had protections or did not need the affected approval until after the pause expired. That broad conclusion has held up. What is changing is the reach of the restrictions given the growing anti-datacenter backlash.

Three things have worsened since. Texas, the largest US market, froze Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) permits on Sept. 21 on top of the interconnection-queue audit begun Aug. 3, bringing onsite power into the hold. Oregon expanded its earlier state-land freeze to air and water-discharge permits on Oct. 9, through July 1, 2027. And midterm candidates have campaigned on more restrictive positions: nine of the 20 nominees want a pause on new construction and the other 11 want conditions, and the split is about even by party. Both parties want developers to accept stricter conditions. The main difference is whether a developer can meet the new terms and keep building, or has to wait for the state to reopen approvals.

The biggest risk to our buildout forecast right now is a prolonged permitting freeze at the TCEQ. Texas alone adds close to 30% of US GW in 2028. A few months of lost time in that market can move the national number. We already flagged to Datacenter Model subscribers which companies are most at risk from the current pause. The question now is how long the pause lasts.

Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who is running for re-election in Texas, could reopen permitting once the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the state’s grid operator, finishes its audit and the Texas Water Development Board completes its water-use review. ERCOT is targeting Dec. 10 to file its report, which does not by itself reopen permitting. A restart around then would leave developers dealing with a relatively short interruption, which some projects can absorb within their schedules. The audit still has to lead to a decision to resume issuance, and each permit still needs approval.

By contrast, Gina Hinojosa (D), his challenger, presents a more bearish approach: She would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice and protects household utility bills, as well as ends the tax incentives for datacenters. The regular legislative session in Texas takes place from Jan. 12 to May 31, 2027. By keeping approvals on hold throughout that session, the freeze would last about eight months from September. If you wait for the new rules to come into effect in late summer, it will be close to a year, that is five to nine additional months compared to restarting in December. A deal or a special session might happen sooner. However, a campus racing toward delivery in 2027 may not have that much time to spare.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

This is the risk posed by the pro-moratorium candidates: a project cannot carry out work if it still requires an approval which the state has ceased to issue. If the candidate proposing a datacenter pause won in every state where one is running, those states would together contain roughly 30 GW of planned capacity scheduled for 2028. How much actually slips depends on the permits each project still needs and how long the pause lasts.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

We are less concerned with the candidates who support conditions only. Most of their demands change the price and terms of development. A developer can fund the grid upgrade, change the cooling design or negotiate the community agreement and then move forward. That can be expensive and time-consuming, but it gives projects a route to approval. Several of the main conditions were already coming:

Submitting thorough water-usage studies: manageable for many projects, but the answer depends on cooling design and the local water supply.

Paying the infrastructure costs they create: We expect this to come anyway, with datacenter developers now offering credits toward household electricity bills

More environmental transparency and dropping non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) – Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google have already started down this path

If the less restrictive candidates win, that exposure falls to 5.7 GW, mainly because Ohio and Oregon have proponents of a pause on both sides. That is a much smaller pipeline to test for delays. It would still be a tougher development environment: fewer tax breaks, more upfront commitments and less room to leave infrastructure costs with the utility’s other customers.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

According to race ratings and available polling as of Oct. 30, from multiple sources (Cook Political Report, Multistate, and The New York Times), the conditions-only candidate is favored in Texas, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and Iowa, and Georgia is a toss-up. Here we take candidates’ positions at face value. It will be up to whether these promises are turned into actual policy and whether the resulting pause intervenes in a project at the wrong stage in its timeline to determine the extent of the delay.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

As noted in our September moratoriums article, these positions are overwhelmingly bipartisan now, with many campaigning on the following three points:

Make datacenters pay their own grid costs (15 candidates)

End the tax breaks (12 candidates)

Limit or report water use (11 candidates).

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

Which states are the most impacted depends on which companies are building. We interviewed six current and former employees of hyperscalers, including people who worked at Amazon, Microsoft and Google and are involved in datacenter development. Several said that hyperscalers can afford to pay the higher costs of new rules and can more easily bring or pay for their own power.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean they will be able to deliver capacity on time. These projects still require their own permits and equipment. And having the money to pay for power transmission doesn’t make it available immediately. A moratorium can block any project that still needs approval, and it won’t be easy to shift development to another state: anywhere else would still require power, permits and construction schedules that can meet the same delivery timeline.

We made the same point from the other direction in Stop Saying Half of 2026 US Datacenter Capacity Is Canceled. Many projects being described as 2026 delays were speculative announcements that never belonged in a credible 2026 forecast. Here, the task is to identify which real campuses still need the approval a candidate wants to stop. A governor’s campaign platform is the start of that work. The permit, power phase and construction schedule tell us what happens to the megawatts.

The Growing Anti-Datacenter Sentiment Shaping US Politics

The datacenter backlash has moved faster than the industry expected. The AI boom has made these campuses visible, and candidates are tapping into concerns about jobs, noise, power rates and local resources. Those concerns now shape the terms on which developers can build.

The local candidates we interviewed all said that non-disclosure agreements that hide who developers are while they negotiate with local governments are a concern. “The public gets to know about all of this last,” said Rex Meyer (R), who is running for a seat on the Linn County Board of Supervisors in Iowa, which has datacenters and power projects being developed for Google and QTS within its borders. Meyer opposes the proposed Morgan Valley natural-gas plant at its Fairfax site, which would support the nearby Google and QTS datacenters.

Pam Marsh (D), who is up for re-election as a state representative in Oregon, said voter anxiety over AI is part of the problem. “We are starting to hear stories about people losing their jobs to AI. We’re looking at our kids, going: What can they train in? What should we be offering at our universities that will give people the best chance to make it in an AI world? And we don’t have clear answers to that yet.”

Marsh is open to a brief pause on datacenter construction in her state while tougher policies are written but doesn’t support the three-year moratorium recently proposed by her fellow Democrats, which she sees as effectively a ban.

In Georgia, Josh Tolbert (R), who is running for the Georgia Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, believes datacenters should pay their own way. “If a datacenter causes a cost, that datacenter should pay it. Existing customers’ bills should not go up because of datacenters. It is that simple,” he said.

Development Risk at the State Level

State and local authorities control many of the decisions that determine where and how quickly datacenters get built, including land use, permitting, and access to power. Federal policy also plays a role via its transmission rules, environmental permitting, infrastructure costs and oversight.

Politicians at the federal level have occasionally pushed for measures that would require state action. In Michigan, both Senate candidates, Mike Rogers (R) and Abdul El-Sayed (D), have called for datacenter moratoriums, but neither would have the power to enact one from the Senate.

In our analysis, state elections, governors, legislatures and utility commissions have the most influence over policy. Although governors can at times delay certain approvals, more extensive restrictions or changes to taxes generally have to go through legislation, as we explained in our September newsletter article on moratoriums.

Governors can act quickly by halting permits an agency hasn’t issued, changing review priorities and directing agencies to impose conditions within their legal authority. Abbott’s TCEQ freeze and the environmental-permit hold imposed by Tina Kotek (D) show how quickly that can affect a schedule. Existing permits protect the work they authorize, but a campus can still need approval for its next power phase. Appointments also matter: in Texas, Ohio and Pennsylvania, governors appoint utility commissioners, subject to Senate review; Ohio’s governor also shapes the Power Siting Board.

Legislatures hold the money and the statute. The equipment sales-tax exemption is one of the biggest levers they wield, potentially worth billions of dollars per gigawatt, as it eliminates the sales tax on the servers, GPUs, networking gear, cooling systems, transformers and backup generators that fill a datacenter. Legislatures also write the statutory moratoria that outlast executive orders, which can be quickly repealed or reversed.

Utility commissions decide what datacenters pay for power and the terms of service, including deposits, minimum bills, upgrade costs and exit fees. Commissioners are elected in Georgia, Arizona and Oklahoma and appointed in many other states. Staggered terms and confirmation requirements mean a governor’s victory doesn’t immediately change a commission’s majority. In states where the nation’s largest power transmission organization, PJM Interconnection, operates, governors don’t have much power over it.

Across the largest datacenter markets with state elections this November, we ask whether Nov. 3 can change the relevant decision-makers (governors, legislatures, and elected utility commissions), how much policy differs between the possible outcomes and how much capacity still depends on an affected decision. Local approvals remain a separate source of project risk. Our analysis focuses on state-level elections.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

We divided states into three tiers based on their unstarted capacity exposure in 2028 and how directly the Nov. 3 midterm results could change the policies affecting that capacity. In this analysis, we distinguish existing restrictions from changes the election could bring.

Tier 1 includes states with large unstarted capacity exposure (>2 GW), where further restrictions are likely whoever wins. Texas, Ohio, and Arizona have restrictive candidates on both sides, while Georgia has a toss-up governor’s race and a Public Service Commission (PSC) majority on the ballot.

Tier 2 includes states with meaningful unstarted capacity (1.5-2 GW) where additional restrictions depend on a change in political control, through Pennsylvania’s Senate race or a Democratic win in Oklahoma’s governor’s race.

Tier 3 covers smaller unstarted capacity exposures (<1.5 GW), where more restrictive datacenter policies are highly likely: Illinois, Oregon and Iowa may face tighter policies whoever wins.

We’re leaving out Indiana, Missouri, Wyoming, and West Virginia from these tiers. Indiana and Missouri have large Republican majorities and supportive governors staying in office. Wyoming is likely to retain Republican control of both branches, while West Virginia’s governor and dominant Republican legislature remain aligned on datacenter development

text:
The US Department of Energy (DOE) has released a national battery strategy and launched the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator (BattMan), a consortium intended to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing and supply chains.

The strategy sets DOE's priorities: building a fully integrated domestic battery supply chain by 2030, achieving US leadership in battery technology and manufacturing by 2035 and accelerating the commercialization of energy storage. According to DOE, US battery demand across transportation and energy-storage applications is projected to nearly quadruple, from 179 GWh in 2025 to 707 GWh in 2035.

The strategy identifies six pillars:

targeted investment in upstream and midstream supply chain steps

faster commercial deployment of laboratory discoveries

manufacturing process innovation

mission-driven deployment for grid modernization

coordination with international partners

investment in American talent

BattMan is designed to lower manufacturing costs, speed the transition of new battery technologies from laboratory discovery to manufacturing deployment and develop battery materials made from more abundant domestic elements. The accelerator's work will use "Super Intelligence" and manufacturing capabilities to identify challenges earlier and improve production processes.

BattMan is led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) and supported by the Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office in DOE's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation. Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the National Laboratory of the Rockies are partners, along with five universities. Organizations interested in collaborating can find details on the BattMan site.

"From transportation and power grids to medical devices and consumer electronics, batteries are essential to modern life," said Audrey Robertson, Assistant Secretary of Energy. "DOE's national strategy demonstrates the Trump Administration's commitment to accelerating American battery innovation, onshoring manufacturing, and securing the supply chains we need to power our economy and maintain American energy dominance."
