When the moderator (former TRDer Joe Lovinger) asked if anything could stymie Texas' growth story, Crow Holdings' Michael Hyun pointed to data center regulation: "If there is a significant slowdown in that development, it affects so many areas of the Texas economy."

It's something of a double-edged sword for someone like Hyun, who also noted that the frenzy has drawn real estate's finite resources to the buzzy asset class.

"You're competing for many of the same contractors to develop your site and guess who can pay more?" he asked.

Still, he characterized a crackdown on data center development as "economic suicide."

In the lead up to the midterm elections, Gov. Greg Abbott, facing a viable challenger in Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, veered from his typical pro-business stance and responded to community outrage over data development. He directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt approvals for data center projects and ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas to audit pending projects.

Even so, at least $9 million or 13 percent of the money he's raised since July 2025 came from data center developers or entities tied to data center development, the Texas Tribune reported.

Hinojosa has characterized Abbott's actions as temporary moves in service of attracting voters. She says she supports strict legislative guardrails for data center development to protect water supply and grid capacity and curb tax breaks.

Laura Hines-Pierce, the co-CEO of Houston-based Hines, was also on the Bloomberg Invest panel. She said the issue isn't as binary as being for or against data centers. According to Hines-Pierce, part of the gray area is in the domain of developer responsibility.

"Data centers don't need to be a Star Wars ship that landed in the middle of a community," Hines-Pearce said.

DFW tops real estate markets to watch list … again

North Texas topped the list of markets to watch for the third consecutive year in a report from the Urban Land Institute and PricewaterhouseCoopers. The report points to robust industrial development — including data centers — as well as corporate relocations and the rise of Y'all Street.

North Texas attracts billions in semiconductor investment

DFW continues to rake in billions of investment from semiconductor chip manufacturers and testers. In the latest news on this front, King Yuan Electronics selected Fort Worth as the location for its Nvidia chip testing plan. The Taiwanese company purchased 27 acres near Everman for $79 million for the project. It's planning to build a $1.3 billion facility there.

Up in Sherman, near the Oklahoma border, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is considering a $45 billion expansion. Sherman is already home to semiconductor facilities for Texas Instruments and GlobalWafers.

Tech giants slough off Austin office space

It became clear that Austin's tech blitz went overboard when companies like Meta started putting huge chunks of Class A office space on the sublease market a few years ago. The effort to chip away at that space hasn't abated. Job search company Indeed listed its entire 308,000-square-foot lease at namesake Indeed Tower after offering chunks of unused space at the Downtown Austin building in 2023.

Meanwhile, Meta has been slowly chipping away at subleasing the 589,000-square-foot space it never occupied in the Sixth and Guadalupe building. It's down to 456,000 square feet after InKind took 32,000 square feet of the building.

title: Energy Costs Dominate Midterms; Climate Battles Play Out Down Ballot - Capital & Main
description:
Energy is everywhere on the ballot — as heating oil, diesel, power bills and water — but almost always as a question of price.
Data centers have scrambled the usual partisan lines.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers agree on little except data centers: Both back moratoriums in some form.
In Georgia, 46.3% of climate voters had cast ballots by the time of the report, compared with 21.2% of all registered voters, Stinnett said.
“We often see that climate concerned voters are more likely to vote early than on Election Day,” he said.
text:
In the final stretch of the 2026 midterm campaigns, the most potent climate issue in American politics arrived by delivery truck across the country.

The average price of heating oil hit $6.23 a gallon for the week of Oct. 26, up from $3.60 a year earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration. At that price, filling a 250-gallon tank cost about $1,557 — roughly $657 more than the year before. As cold weather settled over the Northeast, Democrats turned that bill into an attack on Republican candidates.

In New Hampshire, where about 43% of residents heat with oil, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Chris Pappas said energy costs and heating oil prices were “the beginning and end of every conversation I’m having on the campaign trail.”

That is the pattern across the closest races in this cycle. Energy is everywhere on the ballot — as heating oil, diesel, power bills and water — but almost always as a question of price. The argument over what actually powers the country — fossil fuels or renewables — surfaces mostly down-ballot, in low-profile contests for the commissions that regulate utilities and drilling.

“If you talk to voters, they are upset about their energy bills and they’re upset about data centers,” Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, which backs climate-focused candidates in state and local races, told Capital & Main. “People want to hear from politicians about their plans on their energy bills and their plans on their data centers.”

The consequences reach far beyond any one state. Control of the Senate will determine whether Congress revisits the clean energy tax credits Republicans rolled back in last year’s budget law. And the governors and regulators elected Tuesday will approve the gas plants, transmission lines and data center deals that shape the grid for decades to come.

The U.S. Senate

More than $191 million was spent on political ads referencing utility and energy bills in the first nine months of 2026, plus another $96.3 million from Oct. 1 to Oct. 16, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Climate Power, a Democratic-aligned advocacy group.

In Maine, heating oil defined the final weeks of the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democrat challenger Troy Jackson. Jackson said Mainers were paying 80% more for heating oil than a year earlier. Collins countered with an announcement: a release of 315,000 barrels from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, which she and her counterpart, Sen. Angus King, had requested of President Donald Trump. Climate itself registers here, too: In the Environmental Voter Project’s polling of eight U.S. Senate battlegrounds, Maine had the highest share of voters naming it a top-three priority at 22%.

In the farm belt, the price that matters is the cost of diesel. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek released a closing ad on fuel prices against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson. Both candidates said data centers shouldn’t receive tax breaks — in a state that already gets more than 60% of its power from wind and solar. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, yet Adam Hamilton built his challenge to Republican Sen. Roger Marshall around energy and utility costs, while Marshall said Kansans were “on fire” over data centers. High fuel and fertilizer prices have strained the farm economy in a state that generates roughly 50% of its electricity from wind.

Data centers have scrambled the usual partisan lines. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown branded Republican Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers,” and WinSenate, the country’s main Democratic Senate super PAC, ran an ad implying corrupt dealings between Husted and an energy company, though Husted was never charged. Kelcy Warren, executive chairman of the pipeline giant Energy Transfer, gave $3,500 to Husted’s campaign in late September.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers agree on little except data centers: Both back moratoriums in some form. El-Sayed’s framework would bar utilities from using data center demand to weaken Michigan’s clean-energy laws, while Rogers holds up to $250,000 in a Blackstone real estate trust that backs data centers. The climate stakes are concrete: Surging data center demand could trigger a provision in the state’s climate law that lets fossil fuel plants stay online during a capacity shortage.

In Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for a critical U.S. Senate seat, the backdrop is Gov. Greg Abbott’s audit of every data center seeking to connect to the ERCOT grid — a review that won’t be finished until December, long after the midterm votes are cast.

In Alaska, the fossil fuel question barely registers. Both Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola support oil and gas expansion, so the fight is over who will deliver it and who is to blame for Iran war-driven fuel costs. Sullivan has made the Alaska LNG pipeline, backed by a $54 billion South Korean investment, a centerpiece of his campaign.

The Statehouses

Thirty-six states will elect governors this November, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report considers 12 of those contests competitive — including Alaska, Iowa, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, Florida and Texas, where Republicans now hold the office. In 39 states, utility regulators are appointed by governors or legislatures rather than elected — which means many of those governors become energy policymakers whether they campaign on it or not.

Climate surfaces more openly in Alaska’s overlooked governor’s race, where Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has pressed the state to address climate change and said it relies too heavily on natural gas — rare talk from an Alaska politician. Republicans Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson are also on the ballot. Nathaniel Stinnett, founder of the Environmental Voter Project, called Kreiss-Tomkins “probably the favorite” but said the race is “extraordinarily close.” In the group’s polling, 21% of likely Alaska voters identified climate as a top-three priority, second only to Maine. “I don’t wanna pretend like this is a climate election,” Stinnett said. “But certainly thousands and perhaps tens of thousands of Alaskans are going to vote with climate change top of mind.”

In Nevada, the main climate focus is water. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo sued the Trump administration over cuts to the state’s allotment of water from the Colorado River, and Arizona has since joined the suit. Nevada Conservation Voters gave Lombardo a C+ grade, crediting his support of clean energy while faulting his backing of fossil fuel projects. Because Democrats already control both chambers of the legislature, a win by his challenger, Attorney General Aaron Ford, would give the party a trifecta. Stinnett noted that Ford has talked up the clean energy transition in a state that “is kind of like the Saudi Arabia of solar energy, or it can be.”

Kansas offers Republicans their best chance to flip a Democratic-held governorship. Republican Ty Masterson is more moderate on energy than many in his party, and both he and Democrat Cindy Holscher voted for a 2025 data center tax exemption. Holscher has since said she would freeze data center development until stronger guardrails are in place.

Georgia’s open governor’s race between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson will shape the state’s energy direction too — but the most direct fight over Georgia’s power sits further down the ballot.

Legislatures may matter as much. Spears, the Climate Cabinet director, is focused on five states where Democrats could win full control — Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. “If they were a country, they’d be the world’s ninth largest climate polluter,” she said. “But 22 flipped seats stand between five trifectas and none.”

Minnesota and Michigan both passed 100% clean energy laws the last time Democrats held full control. In Pennsylvania, where Republicans control the state Senate but not the House, Spears was blunt: “The Pennsylvania State Senate is where clean energy bills go to die.”

The Regulators

This is where fossil fuels and renewables actually collide. Spears called these “weird statewides” and said that as utility bills have become a defining issue, the culture war is “getting involved in utility elections as well.”

Control of the Georgia Public Service Commission, which oversees Georgia Power, is on the ballot. Democrat Peter Hubbard, who won a special election last year, faces a rematch with Republican Fitz Johnson, while Republican Josh Tolbert and Democrat Shelia Edwards vie for an open seat. Republicans hold a 3-2 majority; if both Democrats win, Georgia would join Illinois’ commission as the nation’s only ones that are Democratic aligned. Hubbard argued the state is “oversubscribed on fossil fuels.” Johnson said data centers will pay their fair share because of protections he put in place.

In Texas, the race for the Railroad Commission — which, despite its name, regulates an oil and gas industry that supplied nearly half the country’s oil last year — tightened after Republican Bo French drew widespread condemnation for a racist post on X. The Texas Oil and Gas Association, which represents ExxonMobil and Chevron, left him off its latest endorsement list. French has been bankrolled largely through PACs funded by billionaires Tim Dunn and Farris Wilks. His opponent, Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, is a former oil-field mechanical engineer. A Democrat hasn’t held a seat on the commission since 1994.

Rosenthal traced the split to a rule backed by Jim Wright, the incumbent French ousted in the Republican primary, requiring liners for shallow oilfield waste pits so they don’t “leak noxious poison into the surrounding land and water, which I think most people think is a reasonable precaution.”

Rosenthal, who said he has taken almost no money from oil and gas operators, has proposed banning industry donations to commissioners. “If we actually had ethical campaign finance laws, you wouldn’t want these people’s campaigns to be wholly or majorly funded by the people they’re supposed to regulate,” he said. “But that’s just how it is in Texas.”

French did not respond to Capital & Main’s request for comment.

In Arizona, Republicans Kevin Thompson and Ralph Heap face Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill for two seats on the Corporation Commission as electricity provider the Arizona Public Service seeks a roughly 14% rate increase — and the decision is not expected until after the election. Heap’s platform, endorsed by right wing group Turning Point, reportedly centers on prioritizing coal. Even if both Democrats win, Republicans keep a majority, since only two of five seats are up.

Colorado voters face the most literal version of the question. Amendment 82 would add a right to buy and sell natural gas to the state constitution and could limit state and local governments’ ability to enforce natural gas regulations. It needs 55% of the vote to pass. It is one of eight measures funded by the conservative group Advance Colorado — and the state’s own oil and gas industry opposed it, wary of upsetting its 2024 truce with Gov. Jared Polis.

The Turnout

Who shows up may matter as much as what’s on the ballot. A report from the Environmental Voter Project, which works to turn out voters who prioritize climate, found that as of Oct. 26, more than 3.7 million climate voters in 21 states had already cast early ballots, including more than 400,000 voting in a midterm for the first time.

In every Senate battleground the group tracked, those voters were turning out faster than the electorate as a whole — often at twice the rate. In Georgia, 46.3% of climate voters had cast ballots by the time of the report, compared with 21.2% of all registered voters, Stinnett said. In Iowa, the figures were 22.8% and 9.5%.

In Michigan and Nebraska, Stinnett said, the ratio was 2.5 to 1. “We often see that climate concerned voters are more likely to vote early than on Election Day,” he said. “But we’re not used to seeing margins like this.” His explanation: “Just because politicians aren’t talking about something doesn’t mean that voters aren’t concerned about it. Climate concerned Americans know how important these midterm elections are, and they ain’t gonna miss it come hell or high water.”

Whether they are voting over a heating oil bill or a warming planet, the result lands in the same place. The senators elected this fall will decide what Washington does about clean energy, and the regulators will decide what gets built. The harder conversation starts after Nov. 3, Spears said, when the winners realize, “Oh, now I have to actually figure out what to do.” The bills will keep arriving long after the ballots are counted.

text:
Porter County Clerk Jessica Bailey and Chesterton management consultant John Schick are challenging Indiana State Comptroller Elise Nieshalla, who is seeking her first election to the office after being appointed in November 2023.

Jessica Bailey, who is winding down her second term, is the Democratic nominee, while Schick is running on the Libertarian Party ticket.

Nieshalla, a Zionsville resident, was president of the Boone County Council when she was appointed to the post by then-Gov. Eric Holcomb. She previously spent two decades in economic development and real estate acquisition for what is now the Indiana Economic Development Corporation.

The name of the office was originally the State Auditor, but the Indiana General Assembly changed its name in 2023 to more closely align with its duties, including managing the state's finances, making sure state employees are paid, and distributing tax dollars.

On her campaign website, Nieshalla states her leadership is rooted in faith, family, fiscal responsibility, and freedom. She touts her work as Chair of the National Debt Crisis Task Force for the State Financial Officers Foundation to advocate for leaders in Washington, D.C. to restore America's fiscal stability. Nieshalla has also worked to remove state investments from funds with entities aligned with the Chinese Communist Party and those that focus on Environmental, Social and Governance factors while serving on the Indiana Public Retirement System (INPRS) Board and as Chair of the Indiana Deferred Compensation Committee (IDCC).

Nieshalla touts the state's transparency portal and is seeking to include more data on federal grant money coming to Indiana, but her opponents both point out that the portal isn't very workable for members of the public.

Schick said when he tried to find information specific to Porter County's finances, around 60% was labeled as "settlements" and lacked specificity.

"It's not transparent," Schick said in a Friday interview. "And the account structures between counties aren't comparable. Just look up LaPorte County and it's all different."

According to Bailey's campaign website, she wants the office's transparency portal to actually become a tool Hoosiers can actually use, by improving the search capability, explaining what visitors are looking at in plain language, as well as staying current. Those improvements would help taxpayers see how their money is being spent.

Bailey is also critical of how open State Board of Finance meetings — on which the Comptroller sits — actually are. The meetings, which concern the movement of millions between state funds, last about three minutes with little discussion, Bailey said on her website.

"Jessica will be the independent voice in the room: asking questions, requesting documentation, and making sure the record shows a real review before the money moves," Bailey's website stated. "No money should move without an independent set of eyes on it."

Bailey cited her nearly eight years in office as the Porter County Clerk as preparation — from helping to run clean elections, helping residents access public records and managing payroll. The Porter County Elections office won a National Clearinghouse Award from the Election Assistance Commission and Bailey was named Clerk of the Year from the Association of Indiana Counties in 2023 and Election Board Member of the Year in 2021.

Schick is running for the office for the fourth time. He has a masters degree in business administration from Indiana University and works as a professional management consultant.

Schick said party polarization is souring voters on both Republicans and Democrats.

"They both have agendas to try to influence public in their direction," he said. "We want people do things voluntarily and not direct them to do it."

As the state comptroller isn't a policy making role in Indiana, a comptroller can bring more transparency to the table but the the office is not incentivized to do so if they are of the same party as the majority of the Indiana General Assembly.

"No one wants to be accountable, but people want to know where's something is coming from and who did it," said Schick, who said he would he issue more press releases to communicate what the office does to assist the public.

title: Everyday Economics: The U.S. economy is undergoing a structural shift | National
description: (The Center Square) – The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady last week. But borrowing costs remain elevated, making homes and cars less affordable. Meanwhile, higher energy prices are eroding
text:
A pile of U.S. fifty-dollar bills is displayed. Photo: Emilee Calametti / The Center Square

(The Center Square) – The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady last week . But borrowing costs remain elevated, making homes and cars less affordable. Meanwhile, higher energy prices are eroding purchasing power, and weak hiring is limiting workers' opportunities to change jobs.

The bond market's reaction suggests there's more to the story.

According to Treasury data , short-term yields fell while longer-term yields rose. Inflation-adjusted yields accounted for half the six-basis-point increase in 10-year yields and roughly 71% of the seven-basis-point increase at 30 years.

Higher real yields can signal stronger growth expectations, tighter monetary policy or greater compensation for risk. The market moves alone cannot tell us which.

But several major economic shifts are happening simultaneously, and their effects are becoming increasingly visible.

America is aging. Immigration and trade policies are reshaping labor supply and production costs. The U.S.-Iran war is pushing energy costs higher. And businesses are investing heavily in artificial intelligence, even as hiring remains weak.

Policymakers face difficult tradeoffs: interest rates can restrain demand, but cannot create workers, lower tariffs or produce more energy.

According to Federal Reserve researchers , aging and slower immigration could bring labor-force growth close to zero this year. The economy may need very few additional jobs to maintain stable unemployment.

Aging also changes the balance between production and consumption. Retirees generally work less, draw on savings and consume more healthcare services. When consumption remains strong while labor supply grows slowly, prices can face upward pressure.

A 2018 Bank for International Settlements study found that inflation has historically tended to be higher when a larger share of the population is too young or too old to work.

For decades, international trade helped businesses access cheaper inputs and more efficient supply chains.

Now, tariffs are raising import costs, immigration restrictions are constraining labor supply, and the U.S.-Iran war is disrupting energy markets.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration , Brent crude averaged $121 per barrel in the week ending Oct. 23, up roughly 70% from $71 before the U.S.-Iran war began in February.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) data showed annual PCE inflation increased to 3.6% in September from 3.4% in August. Yet the GDP report shows prices rose at a 2.1% annualized pace in the third quarter, down from 5.0% in the second. That slowdown wasn't enough to lower annual inflation.

Meanwhile, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reports private-sector wages rose 3.1% over the past year, but benefit costs increased 3.9%, including a 6.4% rise in health benefits. Total compensation growth barely slowed, to 3.4% from 3.5% a year earlier.

Inflation-adjusted private-sector wages fell 0.6% over the year. Workers' purchasing power is shrinking even as businesses face substantial compensation costs.

According to the BEA , real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter. Underlying private domestic demand expanded 4.9%.

Yet according to BLS , employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, while unemployment edged up to 4.2%.

The labor market remains stable but fragile. According to BLS labor turnover data , the hiring rate was just 3.3% in August and the quits rate stood at 1.9%. Workers are staying put as job opportunities remain limited.

Slower labor-force growth helps explain low unemployment. Productivity may also explain why output is growing much faster than employment.

According to BLS , productivity increased 2.2% over the year through the second quarter, as output rose 2.5% with just 0.2% more hours worked.

Economist Gad Levanon argues AI may already be contributing to this divergence. The evidence is intriguing but not conclusive.

Business investment is supporting growth, though part of the third-quarter acceleration came from inventories, which can fluctuate considerably. Equipment investment also increased, led by computers and information-processing equipment, according to the BEA.

Construction spending reveals another shift.

According to the Census Bureau's August estimates, total construction spending declined 1.7% from a year earlier. Residential construction fell 4.8%, and manufacturing construction dropped 19.2%.

Yet office construction, which includes data centers, increased 24.6%, while power construction rose 8.5%.

As I reported in July , data-center construction is surging even as the factory construction boom fades.

AI could eventually expand production with fewer resources. But building that capacity requires energy, specialized workers, materials and capital, potentially adding to near-term cost pressures.

This week's productivity report, and especially Friday's jobs report, will offer another look at how these shifts are appearing in the data.

The policy mix matters. Tariffs and immigration restrictions can constrain supply and raise production costs. Meanwhile, the investment boom is creating additional demand for energy, materials, skilled labor and capital, potentially adding to near-term price pressures and keeping interest rates elevated. Technological advances, however, could expand future productive capacity.

For households, the stakes are high. If these forces keep inflation elevated, borrowing costs could remain high even as hiring slows, leaving families facing higher prices, fewer job opportunities and little relief on mortgages, auto loans and credit cards.

Can productivity growth expand America's productive capacity fast enough to offset the upward pressure on prices from these structural changes?

Orphe Divounguy, PhD, is chief economist for The Center Square and founder and chief economist of Quantitative Research Group, the co-host of the Everyday Economics podcast and a former economist at Zillow. He has briefed the White House Council of Economic Advisers, testified before state legislatures, and delivers more than 30 speaking engagements annually. Orphe also has a large media footprint, typically 300-400 media mentions per quarter. He specializes in housing, labor markets, and the broader economy. More at orphedivounguy.com

text:
Nearly 15 years worth of hard-won pollution reduction efforts are set to be undone in the United States, as a wave of data centers powered by gas plants enters construction.

That’s according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club, first reported by Bloomberg, which notes that the US energy grid is expected to belch out 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, assuming the country’s currently-planned AI developments enter operation as scheduled.

That’s a massive rise compared to even 2025 — itself a near-record year for US carbon emissions. If the AI industry and its data center developers get their way, the analysis found, emissions will likely skyrocket by 42 percent over the five-year period, an expected increase of 618 million tons compared to 2025.

“The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” the Sierra Club’s principal advisor for climate and energy Jeremy Fisher told Bloomberg.

Due to major bottlenecks in the electrical grid, many data center developers have opted for on- or near-site power plants, which are overwhelmingly fueled by noxious fossil fuels. Projects like Elon Musk’s 1.2 gigawatt data center near Memphis are already choking out residents with fleets of methane generators, which legal experts say flaunt all kinds of local permitting and federal environmental regulations.

Still, for anybody banking on having clean air to breathe, there is some hope. The number of data center projects at risk of cancellation is rising precipitously as time goes on — driven by grass roots organizing and increasing financial pressures.

So if you’re one of the many activists mounting opposition to data centers in your community, just know that the benefits of a cancelled hyperscale facility extend far beyond your backyard.

text:
The U.S. effort to reduce its dependence on China for critical minerals has led to a boon for U.S.-related critical mineral stocks, including copper, lithium, silicon, and neodymium and praseodymium, which are used in permanent magnets, as well as companies that produce rare-earth elements.

One of the key drivers for these stocks is government support in the form of price supports, grants from the Department of Defense (DOD) and the Department of Energy (DOE), low-cost loans, tax credits, and fast-tracked permitting.

Freeport-McMoRan(NYSE: FCX), MP Materials(NYSE: MP), TMC The Metals Company(NASDAQ: TMC), and USA Rare Earth(NASDAQ: USAR) are expected to be the key U.S. beneficiaries of the increasing need for U.S.-based critical minerals. However, they present wildly different investing situations.

Freeport-McMoRan is showing solid growth

Freeport-McMoRan is a Phoenix-based mining company and one of the world's largest producers of copper, a critical mineral used in electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), wind and solar infrastructure, national defense systems, and artificial intelligence (AI) data center infrastructure. The company also produces molybdenum, a critical mineral used to strengthen steel, and gold.

The company reported third-quarter revenue of $7.5 billion, up 8% year over year, and earnings per share (EPS) of $0.81, an increase of 76% over the third quarter of 2025. Its shares are up more than 29% so far this year.

The miner's Grasberg minerals district in Papua, Indonesia, has one of the world's largest single copper and gold deposits. Freeport also operates significant copper mines in Arizona, New Mexico, Peru, and Chile. Freeport-McMoRan received an $80 million grant last year from the DOE's Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations for its MILESHIGH Project.

MP Materials is ramping up production

MP Materials owns and operates the Mountain Pass mine in California, the only active, large-scale rare-earth mining and processing site in the United States. The processing part is key because there are few alternatives outside China for processing rare-earth elements.

The stock is down more than 19% this year, but the company is making progress in increasing its production of neodymium & praseodymium (NdPr), critical elements for ultra-strong permanent magnets used in EV motors, wind turbine generators, and military guidance systems.

In the second quarter, MP Materials reported revenue of $108.4 million, up 59% year over year, and trimmed its net loss by 34% over the same quarter last year, to $20.3 million. More importantly, it is raising its NdPr production and sales, with production of 840 metric tons, up 41% year over year, and NdPR sales of 1,006 metric tons, an increase of 127% over the same period last year.

MP Materials has received both grants and loans from the DOD, including a $35 million grant from the DOD in 2022 to build the first heavy rare-earth element separation facility in the U.S. and a $150 million loan in August, 2025 from the Office of Strategic Capital to build its separation facility at Mountain Pass.

USA Rare Earth is boosting its processing capabilities

USA Rare Earth focuses on an integrated mine-to-magnet supply chain, through producing heavy rare-earth elements (HREEs) and neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) permanent magnets.

The company holds the mining rights to the Round Top deposit in Hudspeth County, West Texas, which contains significant heavy rare-earth elements and other critical minerals. It also spent $2.8 billion to purchase the Serra Verde Group, which owns the Pela Ema rare-earth mine and processing plant in Goiás, Brazil. The acquisition secures the only large-scale producer of vital HREEs outside Asia.

USA Rare Earth operates an NdFeB magnet production facility in Stillwater, Oklahoma, and is expanding its metal-making and magnet production facilities, having just broken ground on a second site in Blacksburg, South Carolina, and is finishing a hydrometallurgical facility in Wheat Ridge, Colorado.

While the company's extraction capacity is expanding, it isn't profitable and produces little revenue. It also has to demonstrate operational efficiency once all its facilities come online. It does have roughly $1.6 billion in funding from the U.S. Commerce Department. The stock is down more than 12% this year

TMC The Metals Company focuses on underwater mining

TMC is a deep-sea exploration and mining company focused on harvesting polymetallic nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific Ocean. The nodules are rich in critical minerals, including nickel, copper, cobalt, and manganese.

Because TMC isn't producing minerals yet and is still awaiting permits to begin production, it is the riskiest of these four critical minerals stocks. Its shares are down more than 55% so far this year. In the second quarter, it reported having $143 million in cash but lost $60 million. Its shares are down more than 55% so far this year.

The company said it expects to receive an undersea mining permit from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) before the fourth quarter of 2027.

TMC isn't yet receiving direct governmental financial assistance, but it benefits from regulatory fast-tracking through NOAA and strategic prioritization by Congress and the DOD for future critical mineral supply chains.

Your investment depends on your risk tolerance

All four stocks are in an emerging industry. However, the safest bet of the four is Freeport-McMoRan, which is why it is the only company whose shares are up so far this year. The other three have varying levels of risk. MP Materials is ramping up production and seeing improved financials, while USA Rare Earths and TMC The Metals Company are still in the development stages.

It's difficult to see who the winners will be in critical minerals at this point, but it makes sense to invest in companies that already have an early mover advantage, such as Freeport-McMoRan and MP Materials.

title: Sodium-ion vs. lithium-ion: Tracking the battery race in 2026 - Interesting Engineering
description:
Lithium-ion batteries use lithium, while sodium-ion batteries use sodium, which is widely available in seawater and common salts.
Sodium-ion cells can also use aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, potentially reducing their reliance on copper.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that sodium-ion battery production remains heavily concentrated in China, despite the potential for more geographically diverse raw-material supplies.
According to the IEA’s 2026 assessment, the latest sodium-ion cells can reach around 175 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg).
CATL’s 60 GWh agreement with HyperStrong reflects this opportunity, while its TENER sodium-ion storage system, unveiled in June 2026, points to growing interest in commercial-scale stationary applications.
text:
Lithium-ion batteries have become the backbone of electric vehicles and energy storage. But a rival chemistry built around one of the world’s most abundant elements is now becoming more and more viable.

Sodium-ion batteries are entering commercial production, with major manufacturers betting they could make energy storage cheaper, more resilient, and less dependent on lithium.

In February 2026, China’s CATL and automaker Changan unveiled what they described as the world’s first mass-production passenger vehicle equipped with sodium-ion batteries, with sales planned for the middle of the year.

In April, CATL also signed a major agreement to supply 60 gigawatt-hours of sodium-ion batteries to energy storage company Beijing HyperStrong Technology over three years.

These developments suggest sodium-ion technology is approaching a new stage. But it still faces a fundamental challenge. Lithium-ion batteries have a considerable head start in energy density, cost, and manufacturing scale.

Sodium is abundant, but that doesn’t automatically make better batteries

Both technologies work on the same basic principle. During charging and discharging, ions move between a positive electrode (cathode) and a negative electrode (anode), with an electrolyte allowing them to travel between the two.

The main difference is the element carrying the charge. Lithium-ion batteries use lithium, while sodium-ion batteries use sodium, which is widely available in seawater and common salts.

That abundance could reduce dependence on lithium mining and price fluctuations. Sodium-ion cells can also use aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, potentially reducing their reliance on copper. Some designs avoid lithium, cobalt, and graphite altogether.

More from Energy

See All

However, sodium-ion batteries are not automatically free of critical minerals. Certain commercial cathode chemistries still use materials such as nickel and manganese, while their hard-carbon anodes require specialized manufacturing. The supply chain for these components is also much less mature.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that sodium-ion battery production remains heavily concentrated in China, despite the potential for more geographically diverse raw-material supplies.

Lithium-ion still has the energy-density advantage

For electric vehicles, one of the most important measures is energy density. It measures how much energy a battery can store relative to its weight or volume.

Here, lithium-ion remains ahead. According to the IEA’s 2026 assessment, the latest sodium-ion cells can reach around 175 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). By comparison, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells can reach approximately 205 Wh/kg, while nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries can reach around 265 Wh/kg.

A less energy-dense battery needs to be larger or heavier to store the same amount of energy. In a vehicle, this can mean less driving range or less space for passengers and cargo. The IEA estimates that an average SUV equipped with sodium-ion batteries could achieve up to 350 kilometers (217 miles) of range, compared with approximately 400-600 kilometers (249–373 miles) for lithium-ion vehicles under average weather conditions.

Sodium-ion batteries do have an important advantage in colder environments. The latest cells can retain around 90 percent of their nominal capacity at temperatures as low as -40°C (-40°F), outperforming conventional lithium-ion chemistries, particularly LFP. This could make them useful in cold-weather vehicles and equipment.

The competition is shifting toward specific applications

Sodium-ion’s strongest near-term opportunity may not be replacing the battery in every electric car. Instead, it could find a place in smaller vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, urban delivery fleets, and stationary energy storage, where weight and volume are sometimes less restrictive.

The grid-storage market is particularly interesting. Batteries used to store electricity from solar and wind installations do not need to fit inside a vehicle or maximize driving range. Cost, safety, durability, and reliable performance can matter more than energy density.

CATL’s 60 GWh agreement with HyperStrong reflects this opportunity, while its TENER sodium-ion storage system, unveiled in June 2026, points to growing interest in commercial-scale stationary applications.

Still, the economics are not settled. Lithium-ion manufacturing has benefited from decades of investment and enormous production volumes. In particular, LFP batteries have become highly cost-competitive, making it difficult for sodium-ion to win simply because sodium is cheaper and more abundant.

The IEA says global sodium-ion production in 2025 was less than 1 percent of lithium-ion output. Even announced projects for 2030 represent only a fraction of planned lithium-ion manufacturing capacity.

A second battery chemistry, not necessarily a replacement

The arrival of sodium-ion batteries is important, but it does not mean lithium-ion is about to lose its dominant position. Lithium-based cells continue to improve, while sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine materials, and demonstrate consistent performance.

The more likely outcome is a battery industry with multiple chemistries serving different needs. Lithium-ion will remain attractive where range, weight and energy density are priorities. Sodium-ion could become increasingly useful where cold-weather performance, material availability and supply-chain diversification carry greater value.

Right now, sodium-ion’s biggest achievement may be giving battery manufacturers another option. And in an industry increasingly shaped by the demand for electric vehicles and grid storage, having more than one viable chemistry could prove just as important as developing a better battery.

title: China's hydrogen strategy offers new industrial opportunities for Oman
description:
For Oman, which is developing a green hydrogen industry with a strong export focus, China’s approach offers a potential model for building domestic industrial demand alongside overseas sales.
The initiative addresses one of the industry’s biggest obstacles: hydrogen production capacity is expanding faster than the development of customers willing to purchase the fuel at commercially viable prices.
The Hydrogen Council’s Global Hydrogen Compass 2026 report identifies the country as the world’s largest market for committed renewable hydrogen capacity, accounting for more than half the global total.
These possibilities are particularly relevant as China expands its domestic hydrogen manufacturing base and develops larger projects supported by industrial demand.
Although no specific hydrogen agreement arising from the visit has been confirmed, China’s changing energy strategy creates potential areas for collaboration in technology, manufacturing, industrial investment and future trade.
text:
MUSCAT: China’s growing investment in renewable hydrogen and its latest efforts to stimulate industrial demand could open new opportunities for Oman to deepen energy and manufacturing cooperation with Beijing, as His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik begins a two-day state visit to China.

The visit comes at a time when China is strengthening its position in the global hydrogen industry, not only through large-scale production and technology development but also by encouraging factories, transport operators and other businesses to use hydrogen.

For Oman, which is developing a green hydrogen industry with a strong export focus, China’s approach offers a potential model for building domestic industrial demand alongside overseas sales.

Beijing recently approved four-year hydrogen development programmes covering five regional city clusters, with central government incentives of up to 8 billion yuan, equivalent to approximately $1.1 billion.

The programme, announced by Chinese authorities in October, links government support to the expansion of hydrogen applications, including industrial processes, fuel-cell vehicles and related infrastructure.

Each participating cluster can receive up to 1.6 billion yuan over four years, with funding intended to reduce the cost of hydrogen use and encourage commercial adoption.

The initiative addresses one of the industry’s biggest obstacles: hydrogen production capacity is expanding faster than the development of customers willing to purchase the fuel at commercially viable prices.

China’s position is already substantial. The Hydrogen Council’s Global Hydrogen Compass 2026 report identifies the country as the world’s largest market for committed renewable hydrogen capacity, accounting for more than half the global total.

Globally, committed investment in clean hydrogen has reached $130 billion across more than 570 projects, representing 6.9 million tonnes of annual production capacity.

However, only around 1.7 million tonnes of that capacity is operational, while binding purchase agreements cover approximately 4.2 million tonnes annually.

The difference between committed production capacity and contracted demand illustrates the commercial uncertainty facing developers, particularly those planning projects dependent on future export markets.

For Oman, the challenge is especially relevant.

The Sultanate has allocated substantial land resources for green hydrogen development, seeking to use its renewable energy potential, industrial infrastructure and access to international shipping routes to establish a competitive export industry.

Yet producing hydrogen at scale is only part of the equation. Developers must also secure financing, build infrastructure and negotiate long-term agreements with buyers prepared to pay the cost of cleaner fuels.

China’s strategy suggests another potential direction for cooperation.

Rather than viewing Beijing solely as a future destination for Omani hydrogen exports, Oman could explore opportunities to attract Chinese investment into industries that use hydrogen as an input, including low-emission steel, chemicals and other manufactured products.

Such investments could help create demand within Oman while generating higher-value industrial exports.

Chinese companies could also contribute technology, equipment and manufacturing expertise to Oman’s hydrogen supply chain, including electrolysers and related infrastructure.

These possibilities are particularly relevant as China expands its domestic hydrogen manufacturing base and develops larger projects supported by industrial demand.

However, China’s growing production capacity also presents a competitive consideration for Oman.

A country increasingly capable of meeting its own hydrogen requirements may offer fewer opportunities for imported hydrogen than its industrial growth alone would suggest.

Meanwhile, Europe’s hydrogen industry faces a different set of challenges, including project delays, high costs and uncertainty over the implementation of demand-support policies.

Europe remains a potential destination for hydrogen and its derivatives produced in Oman, but the pace at which buyers enter binding contracts will influence the commercial outlook for export-oriented projects.

These contrasting developments highlight why future investment decisions cannot rely solely on projected international demand.

China is using public incentives to encourage consumption, while European policymakers are seeking to translate regulatory requirements into commercially viable demand.

For Oman, a balanced approach could involve securing overseas customers while encouraging industries at home to use hydrogen and its derivatives where economically justified.

The timing of His Majesty’s visit provides an opportunity to examine how the longstanding energy relationship between Oman and China could develop beyond conventional hydrocarbons.

The two countries established a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2018, and the current visit is expected to explore wider economic and investment cooperation.

Although no specific hydrogen agreement arising from the visit has been confirmed, China’s changing energy strategy creates potential areas for collaboration in technology, manufacturing, industrial investment and future trade.

For Oman, the longer-term opportunity may lie not simply in exporting hydrogen to China, but in attracting the industries and technologies needed to turn hydrogen production into broader economic value.

text:
Australian drivers could lose 3,000 to 5,000 Australian dollars ($2,095 to $3,493) in annual savings if the Liberal-National Coalition wins in 2028 and follows through on its plans to eliminate an electric vehicle tax break.

Here's what to know

The Electric Car Discount is the tax break the Coalition intends to abolish, Shadow Attorney-General Michaelia Cash said, according to The Driven.

The program exempts qualifying EVs priced at AU$89,332 ($62,488) or less from fringe benefits taxes.

The proposal is part of a package the Coalition says would cut spending by AU$31 billion ($21.7 billion) over four years beginning in 2028-29. Funding for the Australian Renewable Energy Agency would be reduced, and home battery rebates would end.

Parliamentary Budget Office modeling prepared for the Coalition estimated that immediately eliminating the EV exemption would save AU$2.1 billion ($1.5 billion) over the following three financial years. That estimate applies to an immediate rollback, not one beginning after the 2028 election, The Driven reported.

More background

According to the Electric Vehicle Council's midyear State of EVs report, sales from January through June totaled 103,716 battery-electric vehicles and 54,241 plug-in hybrids. Combined, those sales marked a 117% increase over the same period in 2025.

EVs accounted for 25.8% of new car sales, bringing Australia's EV fleet to 612,000 by June. Buyers also had more options: 125 battery-electric models and 71 plug-in hybrids, according to The Driven.

The council's CEO, Julie Delvecchio, cited the EV Ownership Survey from March, noting that yearly fuel spending fell by over 60% for most EV drivers.

What's being done?

The federal government plans to narrow the discount.

It has committed to lowering the eligible vehicle price ceiling from AU$89,332 to AU$75,000 ($52,470), with further reductions planned for 2029.

Cash didn't commit to EV infrastructure when asked during an appearance on 7News. Labor environment and water minister Murray Watt, meanwhile, argued in favor of retaining the subsidy.

The Electric Vehicle Council has urged officials to retain the discount, arguing it makes EVs more affordable. Aman Gaur, who leads the organization's legal, policy, and advocacy work, told The Driven the program had enabled thousands of Australian suburban families to obtain EVs, with yearly savings reaching AU$3,000.

"Removing the discount now would only keep Australians hostage to expensive, imported petrol and diesel," he said.

Where can I learn more?

Vehicle prices and charging access also influence what Australian drivers pay to go electric.

• Australian power bills rose AU$1 annually to help fund curbside EV charging infrastructure.

• Ampol acquired 1,030 EV charging bays for AU$225 million.

• BYD's Atto 2 remained Australia's cheapest electric SUV, though competing models narrowed the gap.

• GWM's Ora 5 hatch could start under AU$30,000 as EV options expand.

• A Sydney commuter considering a used Bolt faced charging without a home plug.

text:
Brazilians send 215 million messages to ChatGPT messages per day, according to OpenAI, making the country the chatbot maker’s third biggest market for weekly users after the U.S. and India.

Google said it plans to double its cloud infrastructure there by 2030 in response to growing demand, and even signed a sponsorship deal with the Brazilian Football Confederation in March to integrate Gemini across the country’s men’s, women’s, and youth national teams.

Other tech giants are investing too. Amazon Web Services has spent more than $3.8 billion on data center infrastructure there since 2011 and pledged another $1.8 billion through 2034, while Microsoft committed $2.7 billion to cloud and AI infrastructure over three years.

Local demand, rather than American companies moving operations abroad, has driven much of Latin America’s data center growth. But Carlos Barrera, CEO of Atlas Renewable Energy, thinks that could change.

“We do see the region as actually an attractive release valve for some of the U.S. capacity constraints that you see now,” he said.

With a population of almost 214 million people spread out across an area larger than the contiguous 48 U.S. states, Brazil makes sense as a country for hyperscalers to court.

Its electricity supply is also a major draw and costs less than half what it does in the U.S. According to a report from its Ministry of Mines and Energy, the country generates nearly 87% of it from renewable sources, and its rapid growth of wind and solar power has also led to a surplus.

“U.S. backlash isn’t pushing hyperscalers out of the country so much as pushing them toward wherever power shows up first,” James Mercer, a principal at data center advisory firm Metro Colo Advisory, told Fortune.

But Brazil’s cheap electricity could also become more expensive. Barrera said Brazil will need more transmission lines to connect large data centers to the grid, and government officials are split on whether electric bills will go up or not.

Another obstacle to Brazil’s AI growth is the tax code. High federal import taxes made building big data centers more expensive compared to other countries in the region.

To fix that, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed a law on Sept. 15 cutting taxes on qualifying data center equipment. This contrasts with some U.S. lawmakers proposing taxing data centers’ electricity use and output.

“If Brazil wanted to be a player in the data center space, it had to do this tax law change,” Christopher Torto, the CEO of Latin America’s largest data center and connectivity service provider Ascenty, told Fortune.

Data sovereignty

Lula’s government hopes that the tax break, by bringing more computing capacity into the country, will help Brazilian businesses develop AI products and rely less on foreign services. Currently 60% of Brazilian digital data is processed abroad, according to the country’s Ministry of Development.

Under the legislation, called REDATA, companies must offer at least 10% of their qualifying computing services to Brazilian customers and invest 2% of the value of the tax-benefitted equipment in Brazilian research and development.

“It’s to improve the data sovereignty of Brazil, so we won’t rely so much on foreign services, especially in a time with Trump,” Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes, a Brazilian anthropologist and data center researcher at nonprofit policy institute Data & Society, told Fortune.

Nunes pointed out Brazil wants to depend less on foreign technology but is giving tax breaks to the same companies that dominate the industry

Torto admitted Brazil is unlikely to develop its own Google or Microsoft. Still, having local data centers in the country could improve latency and keep more data in the country.

“It’s not just the model or the data center themselves; it’s everything that goes around them that will be really the larger investment long term,” he said.

Potential for backlash

While Brazil hasn’t seen the same scale of backlash to data centers as the U.S., some resistance has emerged. Days before REDATA became law, Brazilian federal prosecutors went to court over a TikTok-linked data center project. They wanted an environmental impact study and consultation with the Indigenous Anacé people prior to the data center becoming operational.

Nunes said opposition to data centers in Brazil isn’t as politically united as in the U.S., where they’ve drawn criticism from the left and the right. She said foreign investment still carries prestige in parts of Brazil, especially for people who see it as a chance to join the global economy.

“For people who are so marginalized and pushed away from global systems, it’s just like ‘oh, Google is coming here, that’s great,’” she said.

Growing up in Goiânia, in central Brazil, Nunes lived near a Unilever factory that made tomato paste. She recalled how proud her mom was of the connection to a global company, even as others worried about the factory’s use of local resources.

“It felt like we were part of something big because we lived close to that company,” Nunes said.

The new Alliance for the Future unveiled by Canada and the European Union at the end of their two-day summit in Montreal Friday anchors the countries’ future economic cooperation in clean growth and climate priorities, according to one of the lead observer groups following the talks.

“Canada and the European Union have sent a clear and unwavering signal that closer cooperation on decarbonization and climate resilience will be central to their new strategic alliance,” declared Canadian Climate Institute President Rick Smith, in a statement Friday afternoon. “The task now is to turn talk into action.”

The seven-page joint statement “calls for more industrial collaboration and supply chain integration” in areas like digital trade and artificial intelligence, and includes an undertaking to keep the conversation going on Arctic and border security, The Canadian Press reports.

“Our Alliance with the European Union is built on shared history, common values, and mutual respect,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. “They are the foundation on which we move ever closer together to give our citizens more choice, more opportunity, and a more affordable future. That is what sovereignty looks like.”

“The time has come to build a broader and deeper political and institutional partnership, one that reflects the major partners, strategic allies, and close friends we have become,” said European Council President António Costa. “That’s why we are starting an ever-closer association. Our relationship is so special that we want to create something new: to go beyond a simple association, everything short of full EU membership. Our association will be the closest, deepest, and most unique of its kind.”

During the summit, the European Investment Bank announced a “new chapter” for its presence in Canada, beginning with accelerated investment in critical minerals.

“At a time when both sides of the Atlantic are working to reduce strategic dependencies, we want to turn our partnership into investment in real projects, from mining and processing to recycling,” EIB Vice-President Nicolas Beer said in the statement. “That is how we build supply chains that are not only more secure, but more competitive too.”

Joanna Kyriazis, director of policy and strategy at Clean Energy Canada, praised the EIB announcement as a “bright spot of the summit” and “one of the few tangible actions” detailed in the joint statement. But “as the EU and Canada seek to advance a partnership anchored in ensuring mutual security and navigating an uncertain world, it is essential that electrification remains a north star,” she said, “one of the greatest ways we can advance both short- and long-term affordability, competitiveness, and energy security.”

An EIB spokesperson did not reply to an email asking whether the bank expected to either invest or help leverage investment in Canadian energy transition priorities like grid infrastructure, renewable energy, battery storage, or mass energy retrofits and heat pumps, and whether the institution had any intention of helping to finance Canadian fossil fuel infrastructure.

A Foundation for Action

While some observers expected the summit to be steeped in the doctrine of “minilateralism”, where small coalitions of countries form around shared interests rather than overarching principles, Canada and the EU maintained that they were forming “an alliance of values”, with an “unwavering commitment to effective multilateralism, democracy, and to the rules-based international order” at its core. The statement recognizes “the existential threat of the interdependent crises of climate change, biodiversity loss, ocean and land degradation, and pollution,” and includes language on geostrategic cooperation, democratic resilience, citizen engagement, investing for job creation, reliable supply chains.

The Canadian Climate Institute statement interpreted that outcome as a foundation for Canada to take more decisive action on climate change.

The existential threat that climate change poses for both jurisdictions “is increasingly impossible to ignore as the impacts of extreme heat, wildfires, floods, and other disasters become more disruptive and expensive,” Smith said. The statement “reaffirms existing commitments established by the Canada-European Union Green Alliance, which both parties recognize as the ‘compass for advancing decarbonization while also strengthening competitiveness, affordability, and economic security’. And it provides a number of avenues to accelerate investment in Canada’s critical mineral supply chains,” supporting “substantial economic opportunities in the global energy transition.”

With language on investment, innovation, job creation, industrial carbon markets, decarbonization technologies, working with Indigenous peoples to strengthen Arctic sovereignty, and pushing together for “ambitious outcomes” at this year’s UN climate summit, COP 31, “Canada can take action now to follow through on this high-level agreement,” Smith added. He cited electric vehicle and heat pump safety standards, modernized and strengthened industrial carbon markets, and compatibility between Canada’s and the EU’s sustainable finance taxonomies as “practical steps that make life more affordable and better for Canadians, while smoothing the road for closer ties with Europe.”

‘Long-Term Feasibility’ of LNG Exports

Alongside the emphasis on critical minerals and raw materials, the statement calls for a “joint long-term feasibility study on liquified natural gas (LNG) exports to Europe”, but no immediate investment in that direction. It cites continued joint efforts on nuclear technologies and pledges enhanced cooperation on sustainable grids and energy sources as well as battery storage.

A media briefing circulated in advance of the summit had warned that the call for a long-term feasibility study would play into Canada’s efforts to rebrand a high-polluting fossil fuel as a reliable, low-carbon energy source. But the eventual announcement was read by some observers as a concession on Canada’s part, after more than a year of overheated rhetoric predicting a boom in Canadian exports to the EU and elsewhere. In August, 2025, with Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson touting LNG exports to Germany in “as little as five years”, The Energy Mix and Berlin-based Clean Energy Wire jointly reported on mounting doubts that serious demand for additional gas supplies would ever materialize.

On Friday, the Globe and Mail’s European Bureau Chief Eric Reguly reached a similar conclusion. “The EU’s gas demands are falling fast,” he wrote. “If the trend remains intact, its appetite for imported LNG will fall with it. LNG projects—financing and building the pipelines, the gas liquefaction sites, the export terminals, the insulated ‘Thermos’ ships—can take a decade or longer. By then, the EU’s gas consumption could be half or less of what it is now.”

“What is clear is that the EU is reducing its gas consumption drastically,” Adrian Hiel, director of the Brussels-based Electrification Alliance, told Reguly. “The long-term trend is clear and by the middle of the next decade, Europe should be out of the LNG game.”

text:
PLYMOUTH TWP, MI -- A Metro Detroit technology company is expanding its battery storage facility to test energy systems designed to support data centers and other businesses.

The Plymouth Township Planning Commission unanimously approved the final site plan for Delta Electronics on Oct. 14, clearing the way for the company to move closer to construction at its facility in Metro West Technology Park.

The project includes a new 12,500-square-foot microgrid installation, additional battery storage equipment, a transformer and a natural gas generator.

The expansion is expected to add approximately 10 megawatt-hours of battery storage capacity and 5 megawatts of power capacity, according to details presented during the meeting.

Delta Electronics already operates a microgrid at the Plymouth Township facility, where it tests technology designed to help businesses manage electricity consumption, reduce energy costs and maintain power during disruptions.

Mike Standing, a Delta Electronics representative, told commissioners the expansion will allow the company to demonstrate its latest technology to potential customers.

"We have new products," Standing said. "The microgrid components we have on site now are a 5-year-old design."

The company plans to install two new battery systems that can transfer energy between them, allowing engineers to conduct testing under different conditions.

Standing said Michigan's changing weather makes the Plymouth Township location particularly valuable for testing technology that may eventually be used elsewhere.

The expansion also comes as data centers and other energy-intensive businesses look for ways to manage growing electricity demands.

Standing said Delta's technology could help data centers reduce their impact on surrounding electrical infrastructure while providing backup power capabilities.

The Plymouth Township project is not itself a data center. Instead, the facility serves as a testing and demonstration site for energy technologies that businesses could eventually install elsewhere.

Delta Electronics unveiled its existing microgrid system earlier this year in partnership with DTE Energy.

The system combines solar panels, battery storage, electric vehicle charging equipment and advanced power management technology.

Delta Electronics said its existing microgrid has reduced the facility's reliance on electricity from the power grid by approximately 50% annually, according to a May report by DBusiness.

The facility also allows the company to test how different energy sources interact with the electrical grid under real operating conditions.

The latest expansion would significantly increase the site's battery storage capabilities.

According to construction documents submitted to Plymouth Township, the expansion is planned for Delta Electronics' 4.98-acre property at 47659 Halyard Drive.

The project includes new equipment foundations, drainage improvements and landscaping intended to screen the installation from nearby properties.

During the October meeting, Standing said the company hoped to begin concrete work before the end of the year, although delivery of the new battery equipment could be delayed until spring 2027.

The project also includes landscaping and screening requirements intended to reduce the visual impact of equipment installed near the front of the property.

Planning officials said the company would remove 23 trees, including one heritage tree, and replace them with 40 new trees on the property. An additional 44 arborvitae would help screen the equipment from view.

Commissioners approved the project with several conditions, including additional vibration documentation, updated landscaping information, lighting adjustments and irrigation for screening plants.

The approval allows Delta Electronics to continue working toward obtaining the necessary building permits.

Delta Electronics did not respond to an MLive request for additional information about the project's investment cost, potential job creation and construction timeline.

By Independent columnist Simon Chorley

Welcome to the Sustainability Corner where each week we’ll look at a global issue making a local impact.

These issues are based on the 17 Sustainable Development Goals, which were set by governments, including Canada, in 2015, with the aim of achieving them by 2030. The aim is not to provide all the answers, but to spark constructive conversations about our role in addressing these challenges.

Week 7: Clean Energy?

Growing up in East Africa, long periods without electricity were a weekly occurrence. That has helped me to be patient when we get the occasional power outage here in Northumberland County.

Yet, the United Nations reports that 655 million people around the world still remain without regular access to power. The pace of electrification has slowed significantly as the population without access dropped by only 11.5 million. Those remaining without access are increasingly concentrated in remote rural areas, low-income households, and conflict-affected regions.

At our current pace, an estimated 645 million people will still lack electricity by 2030, and 1.8 billion will continue to rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking.

But a major shift is underway. Low-income countries are now growing their renewable capacity faster than wealthier nations, recording a 13 per cent annual growth rate over the last five years, compared to eight per cent in high-income countries. Renewables now provide more than 30 per cent of global power generation, led by solar and wind.

Global primary energy intensity improved by 1.5 per cent in 2023, but this was down from 2.4 per cent in 2022. Several major economies have outperformed this global average though. One of these was Canada.

According to the Government, total energy consumption per capita was unchanged from 2023 and at its lowest level since 2015. Although total energy consumption has risen, population growth has outpaced that increase, reducing energy consumption per person.

But Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operator has forecast that electricity demand in the province could increase by 65 per cent by 2050. Nuclear energy has provided half of the province’s power for many decades, and in 2026, Ontario Power Generation (OPG) signed a partnership agreement with Port Hope for new nuclear energy generation at Wesleyville.

OPG cites a Conference Board of Canada study estimating that the project could contribute $65.7 billion to Port Hope’s economy over the estimated 95-year lifespan, as well as generate $10.5 million in annual municipal tax revenues, boost overall employment levels by 15 to 20 per cent, and provide up to $30 million for associated infrastructure investments.

However, others are not so sure. Blue Dot Northumberland, a group of local citizens advocating for sustainable economic development in the county, have been making multiple presentations to municipal councils and others on the potential impacts. These include the potential for a sudden influx of thousands of construction workers to overwhelm the local labour market, pull workers away from local businesses, and create wage pressures that many existing employers cannot sustain. Local infrastructure and social services may have to absorb the sudden increase of thousands of workers. And it could also absorb scarce rental housing, push up rents and home prices, and make life harder for residents who are not sharing in project wages.

When construction ends, Blue Dot also believes that many of those jobs and workers could disappear. The community could be left with overbuilt infrastructure, inflated housing costs, weakened local businesses, and stretched municipal systems. Some residents will have benefited; others will have suffered.

What do you think? The Impact Assessment Agency of Canada is currently conducting an impact assessment on the project. You can view and submit comments at https://iaac-aeic.gc.ca/050/evaluations/proj/89802.

text:
C. M. (Cathy) Rubin and The Nest Campus CEO Peter Gilmer explore AI's growing environmental footprint, billions in climate investment, and the technologies that could help accelerate climate action.

NEW YORK, Nov. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- NEW YORK, NY — November 1, 2026 — As artificial intelligence rapidly expands, its enormous energy and water demands raise a critical question: Is AI worsening climate change—or could it become one of our most powerful tools for fighting it?

In the latest episode of Planet Classroom's AI for a Better World, host C. M. (Cathy) Rubin speaks with Peter Gilmer, CEO of The Nest Campus, to examine how AI intersects with climate technology, clean energy investment, conservation, and youth environmental action.

Key Takeaways from the Discussion

AI's Climate Dilemma: AI infrastructure consumes substantial electricity and water, yet its extraordinary processing power could accelerate climate solutions. Can its environmental benefits outweigh its growing footprint?

Billions Flowing Into Climate Solutions: Gilmer explores why clean energy, energy security, and climate innovation are attracting major investment—and how these investments could help accelerate the transition to a more sustainable future.

How AI Is Already Helping the Planet: From smarter electricity grids and Climate TRACE emissions monitoring to satellite technology tracking deforestation and illegal fishing, AI is creating new opportunities to understand environmental threats and respond faster. Advanced weather forecasting offers another promising application.

From Climate Anxiety to Climate Action: Gilmer encourages young people to turn environmental concerns into practical local solutions—from expanding urban tree cover to improving air quality—and build on what works.

"AI isn't there to replace the great work that scientists, engineers, and conservationists are doing. It's there to make them even better," notes Gilmer. "We have to hold two things in our hand at the same time—scaling AI's benefits while addressing its environmental footprint."

title: I went to Mexico to test-drive the luxurious cars Americans can't buy - PressReader
