title: BAAJA Blast Part 3: Data Centers and Large Loads Under the Senate Permitting Bill
description:
What Makes a Data Center Under BAAJA BAAJA uses more than one definition of a data center.
Concerns that data centers drive up household electricity bills have helped to fuel local opposition and proposed moratoria in many jurisdictions.
A separate customer class gives state regulators a transparent, durable way to show that data centers are paying their own way.
Data centers in regions without an RTO or ISO, including much of the Southeast and West, would not see the same benefit.
Looking Ahead BAAJA would create binding federal rules for data center cost allocation backed by expanded state tools.
text:
This is the third post in our four-part “BAAJA Blast” series covering the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, released on September 30, 2026. Check out our earlier posts on the bill’s provisions on transmission and offshore wind.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) contains three provisions that, if adopted, would meaningfully shape data center development in the United States. Section 2107 would introduce binding protections for ratepayers. Section 2108 would create new market access for behind-the-meter energy resources, including batteries and other storage. And Section 2114 would require new reporting on data center load.

Whether a data center gets built remains, first, a question of community support and, second, a state and local question of zoning, siting, and permits. But BAAJA would significantly shape how that data center is powered and who bears the cost. As discussed in our earlier series on sustainable data center growth, the projects most likely to succeed pair speed with responsible energy, water, and community practices. The bill's framework tends to reward that approach.

What Makes a Data Center Under BAAJA

BAAJA uses more than one definition of a data center. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) transmission pricing provisions in Section 2107(a) apply to a “computational load site.” That term covers one or more buildings or installations at a single location that primarily contain IT infrastructure for software applications and services, artificial intelligence training and deployment, cryptocurrency mining, or other data center computing. The site must also connect to the bulk-power system. That definition has no size threshold.

The ratepayer protections in Section 2107(b), by contrast, apply only to a “covered load,” meaning electricity demand from one or more data centers or “high-density computing facilities” that reaches 20 megawatts or more. A load can meet the threshold at a single site or across multiple sites under common ownership or control. Phased projects count if they can reasonably be expected to reach 20 MW at full buildout. Qualifying facilities include those used for AI training or inference, cloud computing and data hosting, and cryptocurrency or other digital-asset computation. The definition excludes computing equipment that is merely ancillary to a facility with another primary commercial or industrial purpose.

Section 2114 uses a similar definition for its data reporting requirement. It defines a “data center entity” as an end-user, or group of co-located end-users, whose primary purpose is to house computing, networking, or data storage equipment used to process, store, or transmit digital data. The covered uses and the exclusion for merely ancillary equipment mirror the covered-load definition.

A given project could fall within one definition but not another, so a project-by-project analysis will matter.

Section 2107: Ratepayer Protection

The core principle running through Section 2107 is “cost causation,” the idea that the customer whose demand creates a cost should be the one who pays it. The section applies that principle to large computing loads at both the federal and state levels.

Section 2107(a): FERC Transmission Pricing

Within 270 days of BAAJA's enactment, FERC would have to revise its 1994 transmission pricing policy statement. Under the revised policy, utilities would charge costs for transmission service to data centers, whether the data center buys that service directly or through a utility or other entity acting on its behalf.

The provision also contains formal findings by Congress. In them, Congress finds that transmission rates are not “just and reasonable” if they charge computational loads less than both embedded costs and incremental expansion costs. “Just and reasonable” is the legal standard FERC applies to rates. Embedded costs reflect a customer’s fair share of the existing grid. Utilities already recover the cost of the lines, towers, and substations they have built through the standard rates all customers pay, and a new data center that plugs into that system would have to pay its share too. Incremental expansion costs, by contrast, cover new equipment that would not exist but for the data center, such as a new substation or an upgraded line built specifically to serve it.

Further, the bill guards against double-charging. Each year, a utility collects a set total amount to pay for its transmission system and spreads it across customers’ rates. Under the bill, payments for a data center’s own new equipment would count against that total, lowering the amount the utility collects from everyone else.

The revised FERC policy would also have to offer a lower rate for loads that elect non-firm, interruptible transmission service. FERC would be required to propose a rule within 270 days after publishing the revised policy statement and finalize it within one year after that, meaning that the final rule could be issued as late as roughly two and a half years after BAAJA’s enactment.

Section 2107(b): The Ratepayer Protection Floor (New FPA Section 228)

Section 2107(b) would add a new Section 228 to the Federal Power Act focused on data centers and high-density computing facilities that meet the 20 MW covered-load threshold. The Federal Power Act is the primary federal law governing the interstate transmission of electricity and wholesale power sales. It is also the source of FERC’s authority over those markets.

For covered loads, the bill sets a “ratepayer protection floor.” It starts with a utility’s “incremental cost” of serving a covered load: everything the utility must spend only because that data center connected. Unlike the FERC transmission provisions in Section 2107(a), this definition covers the full cost of supplying the data center, including new generation, storage, transmission, and local distribution. The bill would bar utilities from passing any of that incremental cost on to other customers. That is the “floor” because a data center’s payments could not fall below what it costs to serve it. The floor is a minimum, not a cap. Regulators could charge a data center more than its incremental cost and return the excess to other customers as a rebate or a rate reduction.

Cost recovery would also continue if a data center terminates its contract or stops buying power early, so stranded costs would not land on everyone else. Before building or upgrading facilities to serve a covered load, utilities would have to require financial assurances or contributions sufficient to cover the cost. They would also have to credit any amounts the load already posted for the same upgrade.

Section 2107(b): New Tools for the States

If BAAJA is enacted, the new Section 228 would also preserve state authority over retail service to covered loads. States could set rates for covered loads above both average and incremental cost and apply the excess to reduce other customers’ rates. The bill would also give states the option to allocate the opportunity to obtain service through an “open season” or competitive solicitation. Awards would go to the projects offering the greatest benefit to other ratepayers, rather than on a first-come, first-served basis. States could also require a data center to procure or build new generation sufficient to meet its demand. Or they could require it to accept a transmission service that limits how much energy it can withdraw from the grid, or when.

A subsection of proposed Section 228 titled “Protection of American Industry” would let states treat covered loads as a separate customer class. That class could face less favorable rates, terms, and interconnection or service priorities than other large industrial, manufacturing, or commercial customers. The ratepayer protection floor and the state rate-setting and open-season tools described above would apply only to loads that interconnect on or after enactment, and arrangements that FERC or a state approved before enactment would remain in effect. The bill does not expressly extend that forward-looking limit to the “Protection of American Industry” subsection, however. Read literally, states could apply less favorable treatment to existing data centers as well, an issue owners of operating facilities should watch closely as the bill moves forward.

At first glance, less favorable treatment may sound like bad news for developers. But it could also clear a path forward. Concerns that data centers drive up household electricity bills have helped to fuel local opposition and proposed moratoria in many jurisdictions. A separate customer class gives state regulators a transparent, durable way to show that data centers are paying their own way. That can make it easier for communities, existing customers and regulators to understand that they would not be subsidizing new projects.

Projects that bring their own clean generation and storage, commit to flexible operations, and engage early with host communities will be best positioned to benefit, both in open seasons that weigh benefits to other ratepayers and in the local approval processes that have stalled projects elsewhere.

Section 2108: Market Access for Behind-the-Meter Resources

The bill pairs Section 2107’s cost-allocation rules with new options for flexible supply. Section 2108 would open wholesale energy, capacity, and ancillary services markets to aggregations of “qualifying behind-the-meter distributed energy system” facilities. These include batteries, fuel cells, and generators on the customer’s side of the meter that can come online within 15 minutes and that the grid operator can dispatch on signal. Individual facilities would have to be at least 5 kilowatts and aggregations at least 100 kilowatts.

The market-access requirement would take effect 18 months after enactment and would apply to markets run by Regional Transmission Organizations (RTOs) and Independent System Operators (ISOs). Data centers in regions without an RTO or ISO, including much of the Southeast and West, would not see the same benefit.

For data centers, Section 2108 could change the economics of on-site clean energy. Under Section 2108, a data center could join an aggregation and sell energy and grid services from battery system into wholesale markets. That new revenue stream could make on-site storage more attractive. It could also help data centers meet the state conditions described above, such as a requirement to bring their own generation or to accept limits on how much power they draw from the grid. Data centers can strengthen these benefits by pairing storage with on-site renewables.

Grid access matters here as well. When new grid connections take years, some developers turn to on-site fossil generation simply to get power sooner, with lasting emissions consequences. Faster interconnection, which we discussed in our earlier post on transmission, combined with Section 2108’s new market access, would incentivize cleaner, grid-connected options at data centers.

Section 2114: Data Center Load Reporting

Section 2114 directs the Energy Information Administration (EIA) to revise Form 861 to include load from “data center entities.” EIA is the independent statistical and analytical agency within the U.S. Department of Energy. Form 861 is EIA’s annual survey of electric utilities and other electricity providers. It collects data such as retail sales, revenue, and customer counts.

The deadline for the revision is no later than 90 days before the first April 1 after enactment. The bill places the obligation on EIA to revise the form, which electricity providers complete. It does not, on its face, impose a new reporting requirement directly on data center owners or operators. Still, the change should give policymakers and the market a clearer picture of how much load data centers are adding to the grid.

Points to Watch

The ratepayer protection floor, the new state rate-setting tool, and open-season tool would apply only to covered loads that interconnect on or after enactment. The provision allowing states to treat covered loads as a separate, less favorable customer class is not expressly subject to that limit. How states read that gap could determine whether operating facilities face new rates, terms, or service priorities.

States could award service to covered loads through open seasons or competitive solicitations that favor the projects returning the greatest benefit to other ratepayers on a present value basis, regardless of when requests for service were received. If states use this tool widely, an early place in line could matter less than the strength of a project’s ratepayer value proposition, including on-site generation, storage, and flexible operations.

The 20 MW covered-load threshold can be met across multiple sites under common ownership or control, and phased projects count if they are reasonably expected to reach 20 MW at full buildout. Developers planning smaller or staged facilities should not assume they fall outside the ratepayer protections.

FERC’s final transmission pricing rule could arrive roughly two and a half years after enactment. The behind-the-meter market-access requirement would take effect after 18 months and only in RTO and ISO markets.

Looking Ahead

BAAJA would create binding federal rules for data center cost allocation backed by expanded state tools. For developers and buyers, that means higher and more predictable cost exposure, more financial assurance requirements, and a greater premium on flexibility and on-site supply. For utilities and commissions, it offers a framework for protecting other customers while still serving new demand. The bill itself does not address sustainability or community engagement directly. But its approach is compatible with a sustainability-focused version of data center policy. Data center development paired with sustainability and genuine community engagement is the growth most likely to move forward.

Stay tuned for the final installment of our BAAJA Blast series.

title: What Will Transportation Look Like In The U.S. In 2050? - Jalopnik
description:
We'd certainly be in flying cars by the 21st century, right?
With all the turmoil, what will transportation look like in the U.S. in the year 2050?
Here's how I see it: In the year 2050, if Detroit's automakers survive, they'll barely be hanging on.
You won't need public transportation if you're at home all day, everyday, putting in time to help power the Amazon grid.
With that nightmare now out in the world, it's your turn to tell us what you think transportation will look like here in the U.S. in 2050.
text:
Depending on who you ask, the motor car was brought to life in Europe, but it was Henry Ford that brought it to the masses from the U.S. By the Jet Age, technology had already advanced so quickly, humanity's dream was a place in the stars and with flying cars, reflected in jet-inspired, futuristic designs on everything from cars to toasters. We'd certainly be in flying cars by the 21st century, right? But we're 26 years into the 21st century and still flying on the same planes that revolutionized the skies almost 70 years ago. The technology operating those aircraft and vehicles is different, but the cars aren't flying. And thank goodness, because a good portion of the population can barely drive. Can you imagine them also flying?

Humanity has been inching closer to that future, but there are still big hurdles to clear. We are clearly struggling through the growing pains of possible driverless technology, and no matter what Florida does when it comes to flying VTOLs and e-VTOLs, regular commuters won't have flying transport in their future any time soon.

The future feels a bit murky right now, too, as the gas crisis caused by the U.S. and Iran war has sent consumers towards adopting electric cars, all while the U.S. continues to eliminate fuel economy restrictions. With all the turmoil, what will transportation look like in the U.S. in the year 2050? That's what I want to know.

The romantic optimist in me dreams of a future where leaders come to their senses and realize investing money in public transportation (extended to rural areas) and high speed rails will improve accessibility and affordability for everyone. Can we really change that much in 24 years, though? After the last 10, it's difficult to say.

Here's how I see it: In the year 2050, if Detroit's automakers survive, they'll barely be hanging on. And to my mind, the biggest threat to the automotive scene is now Amazon. Obviously, by that point, it will have beaten out SpaceX-Tesla because Amazon already delivers anything the American people need at a moment's notice. With grocery delivery, drone delivery, and drivers that deliver seven days a week, why not also figure out a way to deliver people too? Jeff Bezos invested in the Slate truck and quickly brought it back into the fold as an Amazon Basics product.

Amazon's autonomous vehicles (because it has those too) will deliver you to your Amazon factory job, because we still won't have nailed down robots. Otherwise, people won't need to leave the house much because everything can be brought to your Amazon-made home. You won't need public transportation if you're at home all day, everyday, putting in time to help power the Amazon grid.

With that nightmare now out in the world, it's your turn to tell us what you think transportation will look like here in the U.S. in 2050. Maybe your vision is a bit more optimistic. Seeing as the biggest things we've gotten in the last 25 years are massive home offices on wheels, electric cars, and some hands-off driving, a realist might predict improvements in those sectors, and possibly the death of some auto companies. Let us know what you think in the comments below.

text:
Should you keep driving the old car or swap it for an EV? The question gets louder every time a registration renewal or a repair bill lands. A report on e: The Environmental Magazine, dated Oct. 24, 2026 in search results, gives a short answer: an EV’s emissions “payback period” usually takes about three years, and after that the EV delivers a net environmental benefit over a “gas guzzler.” The same piece adds a caveat for people who rarely drive.

That framing matters more now because the market around EVs is shifting under buyers’ feet. Our earlier look at EV sales falling 23.8% without tax credits showed how price pressure reshapes the decision. This analysis separates what the e: report actually says from what it leaves open, then lays out a practical way to test your own situation.

·

Add Now

What the Report Says About Keeping an Old Car or Buying a New EV

The e: Environmental Magazine story, titled “What’s Greener? Keep An Old Car Running Or Get A New EV?”, poses a question millions of drivers face. It asks whether holding on to an aging gasoline vehicle beats replacing it with a newer, more efficient or electric model. The answer it gives has three parts.

First, it says an EV’s emissions payback period usually runs about three years. Second, it says that once that period ends, the EV gives a net environmental benefit compared with keeping a gas guzzler on the road. Third, it says keeping an old vehicle can make sense for someone who rarely drives, because manufacturing emissions take longer to offset when the vehicle sits idle most of the time.

Those three claims are the entire verified core of the story. The search result does not name an author, an EV model, an automaker, a battery size, a purchase price, a study title, or the method behind the three-year figure. We treat the numbers as a reported rule of thumb, not a measured fact about any specific car.

That distinction shapes how to read everything below. A rule of thumb helps you frame a decision. It cannot replace your own driving pattern, your local power grid, or the actual car sitting in your driveway.

The Three-Year Payback Claim, Explained

A payback period is a simple idea. Building a new car releases emissions before it ever turns a wheel. An EV usually starts with a bigger manufacturing footprint than a comparable gasoline car, largely because of the battery. Then, mile after mile, the EV emits less than the gas car does while driving. The payback point is the moment when the running savings erase that head start.

The e: report puts that point at about three years for typical use. That is a short window against the many years a modern vehicle can stay on the road. If the figure holds for your situation, the EV spends most of its working life ahead on emissions.

Three variables move the number. Annual mileage drives it most directly, since more miles mean faster payback. The carbon intensity of your electricity matters next, because a cleaner grid shrinks the EV’s running emissions. The efficiency of the car you are replacing comes third, since a thirsty old truck gives the EV a bigger gap to close than a frugal compact does.

The report does not say which assumptions sit behind its three years. Treat it as a typical-case marker. If you drive far more than average, your payback likely arrives sooner. If you drive far less, it arrives later, and that is exactly the exception the story makes.

Why Manufacturing Emissions Sit at the Center of the Debate

Most arguments about green cars fixate on the tailpipe. The e: framing shifts attention to the factory. Every vehicle carries an emissions bill from mining, refining, assembly and shipping before its first mile. A car you already own has already paid that bill. A new car has not.

That is why the keep-or-replace question differs from the question of which new car to buy. When you compare an EV against a new gas car, both start with a manufacturing debt. When you compare an EV against the old car in your garage, only the EV carries one. The EV must earn that debt back through cleaner driving, and the e: report says that usually takes about three years.

The battery is the hardware piece that drives this. It is the part that makes an EV’s build heavier on emissions at the start, and it is also the part that determines how long the car stays useful. Our report on Tesla’s Model Y structural battery and Cybercab modules shows how pack design can change repair and reuse. Those choices affect how long a pack lasts, and a longer life spreads the manufacturing debt over more miles.

Seen this way, the greenest vehicle is often the one that stays in service longest. An old car that runs for years more avoids a fresh manufacturing debt entirely. A new EV that runs for a decade beyond its payback point piles up savings. Both can be right, depending on how many miles each will cover.

When Keeping the Old Car Makes Sense

The e: report names one clear case for holding on: the person who rarely drives. If a vehicle mostly sits parked, the cleaner running of an EV has little distance to work with. The manufacturing emissions take far longer to offset, and the payback period stretches well past three years.

Think of a retiree who makes a few short trips a week, or a city dweller who uses transit and keeps a car for occasional weekend runs. For them, buying new swaps a sunk emissions cost for a fresh one and recovers little of it at the tailpipe.

Beyond what the report states, a few practical points support the same logic. A paid-off car carries no payment. Maintenance on a well-kept older vehicle may cost less than a new loan. Those are general considerations and not findings from the e: story, so check them against your own numbers.

The takeaway for low-mileage owners is straightforward. If your car runs reliably and you barely use it, the greener move may be to keep it going and spend the effort on routine upkeep instead.

When Switching to an EV Pays Off Sooner

The flip side covers everyone who drives a lot. Commuters, rideshare drivers, and families with long daily routines put on miles that let an EV recover its manufacturing debt quickly. For them, the report’s about-three-years figure is a typical case or even a cautious one, and the net benefit that follows can last for years.

Home charging also changes the picture. Owners who plug in overnight avoid a good deal of the friction people associate with EVs. Our comparison of the EVDANCE $254 charger and Tesla’s $585 wall unit shows that home setup costs vary widely. Those costs belong in the personal math even though they do not change the emissions result.

The efficiency of the old vehicle matters here too. The e: story uses the phrase “gas guzzler,” and the logic favors replacement most strongly when the car you drive burns a lot of fuel per mile. A large old truck or SUV gives an EV the widest running-emissions gap to exploit.

Keep one caution in view. The report does not claim that replacing every old car with a new EV is greener in every circumstance, and neither do we. It gives a typical payback and a clear exception. Your own mileage decides where you land.

Old Car vs New EV: A Decision Table

The table below maps common driver profiles to the direction the e: report points. It uses the report’s logic only and adds no new figures.

The last two rows go beyond the report and reflect straightforward reasoning from its logic. Check them against your own mileage and repair estimates before you decide.

What the Report Leaves Unconfirmed

Good news analysis flags gaps, and this story has several. The available search result names no author. It cites no specific EV model, automaker, battery size, or purchase price. It does not identify a study title or explain the method behind the three-year payback figure.

It also contains no on-record quotation from a named speaker, so we have none to share. We will not invent expert voices to fill that space. Readers should weigh the story as a framing piece and not as primary research.

Why the missing methodology matters

Payback estimates swing with their inputs. Change the assumed grid mix, the assumed annual mileage, or the assumed battery size, and the answer shifts. Without those inputs, the three-year number is a headline and not a calculation you can reproduce.

What a stronger version would show

A stronger analysis would publish its mileage assumption, its grid assumption, and the vehicle pair it compared. Until a source does that, treat three years as a reasonable ballpark and verify it with a calculator that lets you enter your own figures.

The Battery Pack as a Hardware Question

For a hardware site, the battery pack is the interesting part of this story. It is the single component that most explains why an EV starts behind on manufacturing emissions. It also sets the car’s useful life, its repair cost, and its resale value.

Battery health works much like the cells in your laptop or phone. Capacity fades with age and use, and monitoring it tells you how much life remains. Our guide to checking laptop battery health in 13 steps covers the same idea at a smaller scale. When you shop for a used EV, a battery health report plays the role that a compression test plays on an old gas engine.

Pack design also affects what happens at the end of a car’s life. Modular packs can swap failed sections, while tightly integrated designs may complicate repairs. The more repairable and reusable the hardware, the longer the manufacturing debt gets spread. Browse more of our hardware coverage for deeper looks at the components behind these trade-offs.

Market Context: EV Demand and Pricing Pressure

The environmental math sits inside a market that has turned choppier. We have covered several data points on this site that frame what buyers face. The table lists them with the headline figure from each story.

Taken together, these items show a market where price and incentives matter as much as environmental logic. Our look at Rivian’s Q3 deliveries and revenue gives one view of supply, while the Blazer EV lease-end story shows one owner who chose to stay electric.

Keep, Lease or Buy: Three Paths Compared

The e: story frames a two-way choice, but drivers actually face three. Keeping the old car avoids a new manufacturing debt. Buying a new EV takes on the debt and aims to repay it through cleaner driving. Leasing sits between them, because the car still gets built, though the lease ends and the vehicle moves on to another driver.

The report does not rank leasing, so we hold back on a verdict. We do note that a leased EV’s manufacturing debt does not vanish at lease end. Someone else drives the car afterward, which can spread the debt over more total miles. That is a reasoned point and not a figure from the source.

The comparison below summarizes how each path interacts with the payback idea.

Keep the old car: no new manufacturing debt, but you keep the higher running emissions of a gasoline vehicle.

Buy a new EV: takes on manufacturing debt, then repays it, usually in about three years per the e: report.

Lease an EV: same build debt, with total miles possibly spread across more than one driver.

Used EVs, Hybrids and Other Middle Paths

The headline question presents a binary, yet the real market offers more options. A used EV carries a manufacturing debt that someone else already started to repay. A hybrid cuts fuel use without a full battery pack. A simple tune-up on the old car can trim its running emissions at almost no manufacturing cost.

The e: report does not analyze any of these, so we cannot attach figures to them. As a general principle, options that extend the life of existing hardware tend to avoid fresh manufacturing emissions. That principle is why many analysts favor repair and reuse. It is a direction to explore, not a verified result from this story.

If you are leaning toward an EV, a used one may shorten your effective payback because the build emissions are already in the past. If you are leaning toward keeping your car, simple maintenance such as proper tire pressure and timely servicing keeps it running efficiently.

Historical Context: How the Green-Car Argument Shifted

For years, the green-car debate centered on tailpipe output. Early EV marketing leaned on the zero-emissions label for driving. Critics answered that factories and power plants still emit, and the lifecycle argument grew from that pushback.

The payback-period framing is the mature form of that debate. It accepts that an EV starts with higher build emissions and asks how long the cleaner running takes to cancel them. The e: report’s about-three-years answer fits that framing and gives drivers a single comparison point.

What has changed recently is the weight of cost and policy in the decision. Incentives, prices and charging access now shape purchases as heavily as emissions math. Our coverage of the Bahrain EV purchase-intent survey found that range had no effect on intent among 320 respondents, which hints at how much non-technical factors steer choices.

Predictions: Where the Old Car vs EV Debate Heads

These are our own analytical expectations, not reported facts. We hold them loosely.

Payback calculators spread. Expect more tools that let drivers enter mileage and grid mix, since a single three-year figure leaves too much open.

Used EVs gain attention. As new-EV prices and incentives shift, used models with proven batteries look more attractive on both cost and emissions.

Battery health becomes a sales document. Buyers will ask for pack health reports the way they ask for service records today.

Low-mileage drivers get clearer guidance. The keep-the-old-car exception will earn more space in mainstream advice.

Repairability becomes a selling point. Pack designs that allow section swaps will carry an environmental argument as well as a cost one.

How to Test the Claim for Your Own Driving

You can pressure-test the about-three-years figure in an afternoon. Start with your annual mileage from the last two service records. Next, find your utility’s published electricity mix, which many providers list online. Then check your current car’s fuel economy rating and compare it with the EV you are considering.

With those inputs, a lifecycle calculator can show a personal payback point. If it lands near three years, the e: report’s rule of thumb fits you. If it lands far later, you may belong to the rarely-drives group and keeping your car could be the greener call.

Write down the assumptions you used. That habit turns a vague feeling into a decision you can revisit when your commute, your grid or your car changes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does an EV take to pay back its manufacturing emissions?

The e: Environmental Magazine report says the payback period usually takes about three years. It does not publish the method behind that figure, so treat it as a typical-case estimate.

Is it greener to keep an old car or buy a new EV?

It depends on how much you drive. The report says an EV gives a net benefit after the payback period, while keeping an old car may make sense for someone who rarely drives.

Why does low mileage favor keeping the old car?

A vehicle that is mostly unused offsets its manufacturing emissions more slowly, according to the report. The EV’s cleaner running has little distance to work with.

Does the report say every old car should be replaced?

No. Nothing in the available result establishes that replacing every old car with a new EV is greener in every circumstance.

Which EV model or study does the three-year figure come from?

That is unconfirmed. The search result names no specific EV model, automaker, battery size, price, study title or methodology.

Where does the battery fit into this debate?

The battery pack is the main reason an EV starts with a larger manufacturing footprint. Its lifespan also decides how many miles the car can cover to repay that footprint.

Are there quotes from experts in the report?

No on-record quotation from a named speaker appears in the available result, so this article carries none.

What should I check before switching to an EV?

Check your annual mileage, your local electricity mix, your current car’s fuel economy and your home charging options. Those inputs decide whether the three-year rule of thumb fits your case.

name: Detroit Environment
title: Voices: Imagine Ann Arbor beats DTE. Why Prop E is worth fighting for. - Planet Detroit
authors: Jackson Koeppel, Rev. Dr. Calvin Glass, Tepfirah Rushdan, Daniel Wiggins Jr
description:
It’s because of this history that I am so profoundly disappointed by Ann Arbor City Council’s recent resolution and lawsuit against Ann Arbor for Public Power, or A2P2, which contradicts the values I once thought we shared.
Rather than stepping forward to lead with ambition in the face of crisis, Ann Arbor City Council is telling its citizens that solving these problems at their actual scale is not their responsibility.
Rather than stepping up to assert local control, Ann Arbor City Council is placing hope in a regulatory process in which it has little power.
Imagine instead: Prop E passes, and Ann Arbor elects a municipal utility board.
Unimaginable, that is, before Ann Arbor proved the cartel is not as all-powerful as they want us to believe.
text:
Fifteen years ago, I started my journey fighting for community-led solutions to the climate, affordability, and infrastructure crises as the founding executive director of a frontline energy justice organization in Highland Park.

In that time, I’ve participated in dozens of electricity rate case, resource plans, and working groups at the Michigan Public Service Commission. In more cases than not, I did so alongside staff from the city of Ann Arbor, whom I regarded as allies in efforts to address racial and economic inequities in infrastructure quality, collections practices, and clean energy access caused by DTE Energy.

It’s because of this history that I am so profoundly disappointed by Ann Arbor City Council’s recent resolution and lawsuit against Ann Arbor for Public Power, or A2P2, which contradicts the values I once thought we shared.

The resolution formally opposes Prop E and the formation of a board that would consider steps toward forming a municipal utility. Further, it commits public money to sue A2P2 over the proposition, which they have done days before the election. Beyond the resolution’s alarmist inaccuracies, it sends a troubling message about the priorities of city leadership at a time when questions of democracy and the role of government are sharper than they have been in a generation.

The question before Ann Arborites is about big problems facing the whole country: skyrocketing utility bills, a spiraling climate catastrophe, and decrepit electric infrastructure.

I’m a fan of Ann Arbor’s work with the Sustainable Energy Utility, but let’s be frank — solar panels and geothermal for a couple hundred homes in a city with over 50,000 households does not come close to the needed scale of action. Rather than stepping forward to lead with ambition in the face of crisis, Ann Arbor City Council is telling its citizens that solving these problems at their actual scale is not their responsibility.

It’s reasonable for city leadership to be concerned about taking on these big challenges, but they remain unclear on who actually will. DTE Energy, whose neglect got us into this mess? Donald Trump and a runaway AI industry that are stripping the EPA for parts and undoing decades of climate action? The resolution states the city will “strengthen oversight and regulation” of DTE, but they don’t have that authority to do that — the MPSC does.

I’ve spent more than a decade in those trenches, alongside the city of Ann Arbor. We’ve no doubt averted some of the worst of DTE’s proposals, but the bills keep going up, and DTE keeps grinding forward to build data centers and gas plants.

Rather than stepping up to assert local control, Ann Arbor City Council is placing hope in a regulatory process in which it has little power. The council is giving up in advance at a time when we need boldness from political leadership at every scale of government.

The resolution cynically projects only the worst possible outcomes of attempting to municipalize, and envisions doing so as being in fundamental tension with the city’s other strategies. But there’s another way it could go.

Imagine instead: Prop E passes, and Ann Arbor elects a municipal utility board. Alongside the Sustainable Energy Utility and City Council, the board lead a second phase feasibility study and has the knock-down, drag-out fight with DTE, alongside community organizers and activists.

Against the odds, they win. All those years of hard-earned lessons from regulatory intervention and program development suddenly take on a newfound value. Ann Arbor buys out DTE and launches a municipal utility with the vision, strategy, and financial capacity to deliver affordable, clean, and reliable power to its residents. The city is longer appealing to an agency where it has no real authority, and is the decision-maker building the future Ann Arbor needs.

Alongside this groundswell, public power campaigns spring up across DTE’s service territory. Suddenly on the back foot, seeing threats on all sides, DTE is forced to negotiate with the communities it has most harmed. Progressive leaders win, and keep winning, up and down the ballot. They advance state and federal legislation to fund affordability, climate action, and local control that would have been unimaginable. Unimaginable, that is, before Ann Arbor proved the cartel is not as all-powerful as they want us to believe.

A vote for Prop E doesn’t guarantee any of this. It’s a commitment to fight for a future that coming generations deserve. It’s a future worth fighting for.

title: 6,300 see-through solar panels now stand over 5.2 acres of apple trees on a German ...
description:
It put solar panels over them instead, and on Sunday, October 25, about 200 people showed up at Obsthof Bernhard in Kressbronn to officially switch the thing on.
If agrivoltaics is a new word for you, it just means farming and making solar power on the same piece of ground.
Basically, the solar farm sells electricity straight to a neighbor over its own wire, instead of pushing it into the public grid and letting the utility sort out who gets what.
The company’s slogan for the project is “from apple to apple.” It’s a little cheesy.
Solar panels make most of their power around midday, which is when pretty much every other solar farm in Germany is doing the same thing, so prices drop.
text:
Hail nets are basically car covers for apple trees. Growers stretch plastic mesh over the rows, the ice bounces off, and the rest of the time the net’s pretty much just there.

But one fruit farm on the German shore of Lake Constance (the big lake where Germany, Switzerland and Austria meet) has decided to skip the netting on its newest block of trees. It put solar panels over them instead, and on Sunday, October 25, about 200 people showed up at Obsthof Bernhard in Kressbronn to officially switch the thing on.

The system’s rated at 2.4 megawatts peak, according to pv magazine, and it covers about 5.2 acres. The developer, a young company from nearby Lindau called Sonntag Energy, says it’s the largest agrivoltaic system over apples in Europe, based on data from Germany’s Fraunhofer research institute. I haven’t seen anyone outside the company check that ranking, so I’d treat it as their claim rather than a settled fact.

If agrivoltaics is a new word for you, it just means farming and making solar power on the same piece of ground. Most of the time that involves lifting the panels high enough that the crop, the tractors and the people picking the fruit all still fit underneath.

So what does the roof actually look like?

Pretty industrial, judging by the photos. By mid-June, crews from the Maschinenring Tettnang, a local farmers’ cooperative, had already driven about 4,000 steel posts roughly 13 feet into the ground, according to Kressbronn’s town newsletter. The newsletter described the pile driving as loud and heavy on the vibration, which I’d guess the neighbors could confirm.

About 6,300 semi-transparent panels were due to go on top. That count comes from the same July newsletter, written while the frame was still bare, and I can’t find a final number published since. Nobody’s said how high the new roof sits above the trees, either. That’s a bit of a strange gap when the whole pitch is what happens underneath it.

Semi-transparent panels like these are usually glass on both faces, with gaps left between the solar cells so some of the sunlight falls through to the leaves. Think of a tinted sunroof rather than a sheet of steel. Here, the panels are supposed to let enough light through for the trees while keeping off hail and heavy rain, pv magazine reports.

That second job is the one the farmer actually cares about. “For us, the key thing is that we keep growing apples successfully,” Hubert Bernhard said at the opening, as quoted by pv magazine. The solar income, he added, gives the farm a second leg to stand on.

So where does the power go?

About a third of it can go down a direct cable roughly 1,640 feet long (a bit more than a quarter mile) to a BayWa Obst site in Kressbronn, where the fruit company runs big sorting and cold-storage lines. The rest gets sold on the power exchange.

That setup is called an on-site power purchase agreement. Basically, the solar farm sells electricity straight to a neighbor over its own wire, instead of pushing it into the public grid and letting the utility sort out who gets what.

Why bother running your own cable? Because the grid isn’t free to use, the same way your power bill has delivery charges stacked on top of the electricity itself. Mark Kugel, one of Sonntag Energy’s founders, said at the June groundbreaking that both sides skip grid fees and surcharges this way, so the farm earns more and BayWa pays less. He called it a perfect win-win, which is the kind of thing founders say, but I’ll admit the logic holds up pretty well here.

The company’s slogan for the project is “from apple to apple.” It’s a little cheesy. It’s also a pretty complete description of the whole thing.

Then there’s the battery. It stores 3.4 megawatt-hours and is about the size of a 20-foot shipping container, per the town newsletter.

So why does an orchard need a battery?

Solar panels make most of their power around midday, which is when pretty much every other solar farm in Germany is doing the same thing, so prices drop. A battery lets the farm hold some of that power back and sell it later when it’s worth more. If you’ve got time-of-use rates at home, you already know the idea. Farm magazine top agrar describes that timing trick as central to making the project pay.

Honestly, I’d argue the battery is doing more to make this pencil out than the panels are. Sonntag Energy spokesperson Timo Gass told Photon pretty much the same thing: the company adds a battery to every one of these farm systems because that’s how it gets the economics to work.

Kugel also used the opening to lobby the state politicians who showed up. He wants batteries allowed to charge from both the solar panels and the grid without more delays, plus more flexible grid connections and workable rules for selling power directly to the business next door. It’s safe to assume none of that is easy in Germany right now, or he wouldn’t have spent part of a party asking for it.

The farm tried this on a much smaller roof first

Bernhard isn’t new to this. Four years ago, his farm got about an acre of panels over a working apple orchard as part of a state research program, opened by Baden-Württemberg’s premier at the time, Winfried Kretschmann. According to the program’s project page, it was the first power-producing agrivoltaic system built into an active apple orchard in Germany, and the state covered half the cost.

That test roof used two kinds of panels that let through different amounts of light, roughly 40% and 51%. Researchers from Fraunhofer and the regional fruit-growing research center have been watching how the trees handle the shade ever since. Bernhard shared some of what he’s learned at the June groundbreaking, according to the town newsletter.

Yields under the panels usually ran about 10% lower at first, he said, but these days the covered trees are more likely to come out ahead. Gala and Elstar apples didn’t do so well in the shade. Kanzi, a cross between Gala and Braeburn, has done best.

I’m most interested in the spray figure. Bernhard said the farm never got crop-protection sprays down to zero, which was the original goal, but it did cut them by about 70%. As I understand it, a lot of orchard sprays wash off in the rain, so growers have to go back out after a storm and spray again. A roof keeps the rain off the leaves, so the spray stays put.

I’d love to point you to a published study with that 70% in it, but as far as I can tell it comes from Bernhard talking at a press event, not from a paper. Treat it as one farmer’s experience, and a pretty encouraging one.

The new block also fixes an annoyance from the pilot. On the test roof, hail nets still had to be strung between the panels. The new section uses wider panels, so Bernhard says the nets aren’t needed anymore.

Apparently the test roof turned into a bit of a tourist attraction, too. Bernhard said more than 3,000 visitors from every continent have come to look at it. I’m choosing not to ask about Antarctica.

He isn’t the only German apple grower trying this. We’ve looked at an organic orchard in the Rhineland that’s been growing apples under solar glass for five years, and at a Bavarian farmer who put panels over his hops and got fewer cones out of the first version.

This one went up without a subsidy

Here’s where the two roofs really differ. The state paid half of the pilot. The new 5.2 acres went up without any subsidy, according to top agrar and the town newsletter.

Germany’s renewable energy law actually includes a bonus for agrivoltaic power, 2.5 euro cents per kilowatt-hour, but it still doesn’t have the European Union’s sign-off, Photon reports. EU state-aid rules basically stop member countries from handing out subsidies Brussels hasn’t approved. So for now the bonus only exists on paper, and Sonntag says none of the seven agrivoltaic systems it has switched on this year uses it.

That’s not a small thing in a year when, according to top agrar, some of the leading companies in German agrivoltaics have gone through insolvency. Building one of these without the bonus is either pretty confident or a little stubborn. Given what the battery brings in, I’d lean toward confident.

The ownership setup is a bit different too. Leander Hengge, who runs the Maschinenring Tettnang, told top agrar that the farmer ends up owning the system, so the money it makes stays on the farm. What the whole thing cost hasn’t been made public.

On paper, the roof makes enough electricity for about 600 households, or roughly 14% of what Kressbronn uses, according to the town’s estimate. Keep in mind German homes use a lot less electricity than the average American one, so that’s not 600 houses in suburban Texas.

Sonntag Energy says Kressbronn is the seventh agrivoltaic system it has switched on this year. About a week before the apple roof’s opening party, it started building the next one on another Lake Constance farm, a 1-megawatt array of solar panels that tilt to follow the sun over strawberries, paired with a 5-megawatt-hour battery.

title: Who is standing up for Eugene's future? | Letter to the editor
authors: Letters to the Editor, Owen Murray, Jaime Adame, Tyson Alger, Nick Rohlman
description:
Why have more than 100 businesses, organizations, unions and community leaders endorsed Measure 20-388, the Eugene Clean Energy Fund?
The Eugene Clean Energy Fund offers a practical solution: Ask the wealthiest corporations doing business in Eugene to contribute just 2% of their local gross profits to fund clean energy, home energy upgrades, climate resilience and good local jobs.
More than 100 endorsements demonstrate the breadth of support for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.
These are people and organizations who care deeply about Eugene and are willing to invest in its future.
Look around town and see all the signs for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.
text:
Why have more than 100 businesses, organizations, unions and community leaders endorsed Measure 20-388, the Eugene Clean Energy Fund? Because they recognize that the climate crisis is already here, and that Eugene needs real resources to protect our community and build a more resilient future.

Now is the time to take a stand. We can no longer afford the status quo to address the climate crisis. This is an existential challenge. Eugene has talked about climate action for years. Now we have an opportunity to put real resources behind those commitments and turn them into meaningful action.

The Eugene Clean Energy Fund offers a practical solution: Ask the wealthiest corporations doing business in Eugene to contribute just 2% of their local gross profits to fund clean energy, home energy upgrades, climate resilience and good local jobs. Instead of allowing all those profits to flow out of our community, a small portion would be reinvested in the people that helped generate them.

Large business interests are fighting the measure, warning that it will hurt consumers. But whose interests are they protecting? Families struggling with rising energy bills, or the corporations focused on protecting profits and satisfying shareholders?

More than 100 endorsements demonstrate the breadth of support for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund. These are people and organizations who care deeply about Eugene and are willing to invest in its future. Look around town and see all the signs for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.

This vote asks: Do we continue to prioritize corporate profits, or do we invest in the well-being of our community?

text:
The Shapiro Administration is investing $971,006 through the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection’s (DEP) RISE PA program to help Jubilee Dairy LLC install an anaerobic digester and combined heat and power system that will turn agricultural waste into renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

DEP Secretary Jessica Shirley and Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture Secretary Russell Redding visited Jubilee Dairy, a 10th-generation dairy farm and cheese producer operated by the Nissley family, to highlight the investment and the role innovative technology can play in helping Pennsylvania farms reduce emissions and make productive use of agricultural waste.

The planned system will process manure, food waste, and other organic material to produce biogas. The biogas will fuel a combined heat and power system that generates electricity and heat for the farm. The process will also produce digestate, a byproduct that can be used as fertilizer or animal bedding.

The project is expected to reduce Jubilee Dairy’s greenhouse gas emissions by 38 percent. Over time, the system is expected to generate enough electricity to meet 100 percent of the farm’s electricity needs, with additional heat available for use.

“The RISE PA program is excited to work with award recipients like the Nissley family, who are thinking innovatively about how they can save money on energy costs, reduce air pollution, and continue to grow their dairy farm and cheese business for their children and future generations,” said Secretary Shirley. “Since the launch of this program, I’ve visited printing presses, steel mills, pharmaceutical companies, manufacturers, and more who all are looking at how they can increase energy efficiency, use renewable energy, and help reduce or eliminate pollution, while also continuing to grow their business and position Pennsylvania as an energy and industrial leader.”

RISE PA is a $396 million statewide industrial decarbonization grant program funded through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Climate Pollution Reduction Grants. RISE PA offers grants for small-, medium-, and large-scale projects at agricultural and industrial facilities that reduce emissions through investments in energy efficiency, renewable energy, electrification, and other pollution-reduction technologies, such as anaerobic digesters.

“The Nissley family is a great example of the forward thinking and resourcefulness that have sustained Pennsylvania agriculture for generations,” said Secretary Redding. “They are looking at what they have on their farm – from manure to food waste – and finding innovative ways to turn those resources into energy, reduce costs, and create new opportunities for their family’s 10th generation and beyond. Through investments like these, we are helping farm families build on their legacy while preparing Pennsylvania agriculture for the future.”

In April, the Shapiro Administration announced $267 million in first-round RISE PA Medium- and Large-Award Track grants, which includes Jubilee Dairy, LLC as a MAT recipient. The program is one of the largest federal grants received in Pennsylvania and highlights the Shapiro Administration’s continued commitment to supporting Pennsylvania businesses while also working to ensure clean air, water and land for all in the Commonwealth.

“For a 10th generation farming family, grant programs like RISE PA provide funding for projects that otherwise would not be possible,” said Kendra Nissley of Jubilee Dairy. “We appreciate both DEP and Agriculture for their support of our anaerobic digester project, and our farm. This project will help us continue the growth of our farm in a sustainable manner.”

Pennsylvania Protects Air, Land, and Water Under Governor Shapiro’s Leadership

DEP’s mission is to protect Pennsylvania’s air, land, and water resources and to provide for the health and safety of its residents and visitors. Under Governor Shapiro’s leadership, the agency has:

Plugged over 500 wells, more than the past two administrations combined.

Announced the first round of the RISE PA grants providing $267 million in Medium- and Large-Award Track grants, part of one of the largest federal grants received in Pennsylvania.

Eliminated historic backlog of more than 2,400 permits that were overdue and on-the-clock as of November 1, 2023.

Launched the Streamlining Permits for Economic Expansion and Development (SPEED) program to speed up and streamline permitting process.

Had access to Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) funding to protect the health and safety of Pennsylvanians through plugging wells and reclaiming abandoned mine land through a lawsuit filed by Governor Shapiro against the federal government.

Pennsylvania’s Agriculture Sector is the Backbone of the Commonwealth

With more than 48,800 farms contributing over $153.2 billion a year to the economy and supporting nearly 600,000 jobs in Pennsylvania, agriculture is foundational to the Commonwealth’s heritage and future. Governor Shapiro has prioritized strengthening both agriculture and food security — helping farmers, families, and communities thrive – and last week unveiled Pennsylvania’s first-ever, 10-year Strategic Plan for Agriculture. The ten-year plan outlines the necessary steps to address four critical industry needs including access to capital, efficiency and profitability, modernization and innovation, and public engagement. Through this plan, the Shapiro Administration is working to support farmers and ag producers and build a stronger, more competitive, and more connected agriculture industry.

The 2026-2027 bipartisan budget Governor Shapiro signed earlier this year continues this work by:

Maintaining $10 million for the Agricultural Innovation Grant Program to continue driving innovation in Pennsylvania agriculture.

Continuing $13.8 million to fully fund the Pennsylvania Farm Bill to support business planning, infrastructure, and workforce development.

Increasing the cap for capital development projects, which includes agricultural projects, in the Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority (PIDA) program from $200,000 to potentially up to $2 million.

Directing funding to the Agricultural Business Development Center and the Centers of Plant, Beef, Poultry & Livestock, and Dairy Excellence to support farmers and producers with resources and services that enhance the long-term vitality of Pennsylvania farms.

Sustaining funding for the nation’s leading farmland preservation program, protecting 6,781 farms and 671,082 acres in 58 counties from future development.

The Shapiro Administration highlighted $165 million in investments to strengthen Pennsylvania’s animal diagnostic laboratory network, including expansions at Penn State’s Animal Diagnostic Laboratory ($65 million), a new PennVet laboratory ($94 million), and the Keystone Animal Diagnostic Center at Penn State Beaver ($6 million).

With these investments the Shapiro Administration is planning to maintain this momentum for future farm families and the Pennsylvania ag industry.

Find Pennsylvania’s Strategic Plan for Agriculture here and learn more about Governor Shapiro’s support for Pennsylvania farmers and nation-leading agriculture industry here.

To learn more about RISE PA program, visit dep.pa.gov/rise-pa and the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection’s website, or follow DEP on Facebook, X, Instagram, or LinkedIn.

text:
The University of Minnesota Morris is preparing to test a battery that could offer a cheaper, more reliable alternative to lithium technology, especially in cold weather.

By Kristoffer Tigue

The Minnesota Star Tribune

October 31, 2026 at 7:00AM

Advertisement

The University of Minnesota Morris could soon have a battery big enough to power its campus for almost an entire work day and made from one of the world’s most widely available metals: zinc.

The $5.9 million pilot project, which the university is developing in partnership with utility Otter Tail Power Co., Pittsburgh-based battery manufacturer Eos Energy Enterprises and micro-grid manager OATI, could help the U.S. gain a better foothold in a global battery market currently dominated by China.

About $1.6 million of the battery’s funding was provided by the Minnesota Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund, as recommended by the Legislative-Citizen Commission on Minnesota Resources.

Once completed, the 1 megawatt capacity battery is rated to run at full power for six hours before needing to recharge, university officials said. While this will be Minnesota’s first long-duration battery using zinc, similar projects have already been constructed in California, Texas, Nebraska, Utah and West Virginia.

Advertisement

If successful, the project could lead to cheaper battery costs and a wider adoption of the technology, potentially helping Minnesota achieve its ambitious clean energy goals.

“The wind blows great some days, some days it doesn’t. The sun shines about half the time, and we have to find a way to bridge those gaps if we are going to rely more on renewables,” Minnesota Rep. Paul Anderson, R-Starbuck, said at the pilot project’s groundbreaking ceremony Monday afternoon.

Expanded image view

Anderson called battery storage the “missing piece to this puzzle” as the state works to decarbonize its energy grid.

By law, Minnesota utilities must produce 100% of their electricity from carbon-free sources by 2040. More than half of the state’s electricity was generated by solar, wind, hydro, biomass or nuclear power sources last year, Minnesota officials reported.

title: Editorial: Surging oil costs spur renewables development - Rocky Mount Telegram
description: Despite continuing Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, oil shipments from the Middle East have now surpassed prewar levels. The might of the U.S. military is to thank for
text:
If a muscle atrophies, our bodies weaken. We can’t walk very…

Accusing political leaders of gerrymandering used to be quite the insult. It was…



A flare burns off methane and other hydrocarbons as oil pumpjacks operate in the Permian Basin in Midland, Texas, on Oct. 12, 2021.

Despite continuing Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, oil shipments from the Middle East have now surpassed prewar levels. The might of the U.S. military is to thank for the recovery of oil flows through the strait itself. But the proliferation of alternative routes around the region, new production outside the Middle East and declining fuel consumption are thanks to the might of the free market.

Oil flows throughout the Middle East averaged more than 24 million barrels a day last week, up from 23.3 million before the war, according to the ship tracker Kpler. Heavier reliance on Saudi and Emirati pipelines has allowed more crude to bypass the strait: 40 percent of non-Iranian Gulf crude is going through pipelines, up from 17 percent before the war.

At the same time, the U.S. military has helped restore flows through the strait even as an American embargo has mostly choked off Iranian crude. Oil flows through the strait have rebounded to 82 percent of prewar levels, facilitated by a clever ship-to-ship transfer system in which the military escorts shuttle tankers through Hormuz to cargo ships in the Gulf of Oman.

While the work-around has proved effective, oil flows cannot rely on costly military escorts in perpetuity. Attacks by Iranians and their proxies, combined with an expectation that hostilities will escalate following the midterm elections, keep prices elevated. These were foreseeable consequences of President Donald Trump’s war of choice. Picking this fight in February all but guaranteed trouble in the strait.

Oil production across the Western Hemisphere is projected to surge in the next decade, as high prices justify investments in marginal projects. Chevron, for example, plans to put nearly $14 billion into Argentina over the next decade, tripling production there. Four out of five institutional investors say that disruptions in Middle Eastern markets make them more likely to invest in Canada, according to a recent survey by ATB Cormark Capital Markets.

Thanks to a freer, more diversified energy market, the Iran war has not re-created the crippling shortages Americans endured in the 1970s. While high gas prices are certainly a major political headache for the party in power, the U.S. has been relatively insulated.

Over the past decade, the U.S. has expanded energy production through fracking and horizontal drilling, leading to record-high domestic crude output and growing exports. Before the war, Americans were already importing far more petroleum from Canada than the Middle East. Last year, only 8 percent of U.S. crude imports came from Gulf countries.

President Richard M. Nixon instituted disastrous price controls on oil after a 1973 OPEC embargo. Whenever prices are artificially capped below the market equilibrium, demand outstrips supply, leading to the shortages and gas lines that endured through the decade. Trump floated a ban on diesel exports last month, but advisers convinced him that the idea would backfire by causing supply disruptions.

Finally, high prices cause people to use less oil. Electric vehicles become more attractive. So does public transit. The IEA forecast in August that global oil demand would decline 1.6 million barrels per day this year.

The lesson for long-term energy security is that government should welcome abundance, competition and trade. Let prices rise when oil gets scarce. Let producers profit by finding more of it. Let consumers decide when substitutes make sense. Free markets cannot prevent wars, but they can make their fallout much harder for adversaries to dictate.

text:
Awash in cash after their third-highest quarterly earnings on record, the world’s largest oil companies are uncharacteristically wary about how to spend it.

ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. and Chevron Corp. are stockpiling the cash, BP Plc is paying down debt and other liabilities, and Shell Plc and TotalEnergies SE promise they’ll be cautious about future investments. It all points to an industry that has suffered the ill effects of overspending during previous booms — and a feeling that current high prices may not last much longer.

“We will be disciplined — we will not allow the surplus cash to burn a hole through our pockets,” Shell Chief Executive Officer Wael Sawan said on a call with analysts. “That is the flaw that we have seen historically in our sector and in our company. And this time, we have learned our lesson.”

The five Western oil majors spent heavily on megaprojects during previous periods of high crude prices only to be caught out when oil subsequently fell, and they wrote down about $180 billion in assets from 2010 to 2020. Executives are rarely able to correctly call the top or bottom of the notoriously boom-and-bust oil business, and the current crop is pledging to give up even trying.

“We’re not going to ride the wave of the cycle,” ExxonMobil Chief Financial Officer Neil Hansen said in an interview after the company said it chose not to raise share buybacks despite surging profits. “We’re not going to overextend during a temporary market disruption.”

Disruption from the US war with Iran has pushed oil prices above $100 during much of 2026. That, along with a global squeeze on refining capacity, has boosted oil company earnings and stock prices. BP has rallied 45% this year, ExxonMobil is up 56% and Chevron 55%.

Those three companies’ shares failed to keep pace with the 2.4% gain in oil prices on Friday, and one reason was the lack of additional buybacks. But there are signs investors like that approach. The five supermajors now carry about $276 billion of debt combined, almost 30% less than at the end of 2020, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

“Discipline is what we’re looking for,” said Marcus McGregor, managing director of commodities research at Conning, which manages about $191 billion in assets. “Just stay the course — don’t be too reactionary and really just protect the balance sheet.”

Chevron reduced its buyback in the third quarter to $2.5 billion, the low end of its guided range, despite posting the fourth-highest profits in its history. Even Shell, which increased its buyback 65%, only did so within a strict investment framework that requires the company to distribute a fixed percentage of cash flow to shareholders.

“We manage our business in decades, not quarters,” Chevron CFO Eimear Bonner said in an interview. “We certainly don’t change our capital allocation or financial priorities on the back of a volatile quarter.”

The conservatism is in stark contrast to Big Tech, which is being punished by investors for a debt-fueled artificial intelligence spending frenzy that has yet to yield much in the way of cash returns. But some investors believe energy companies run the risk of not investing enough in the future.

“We would like to see them do something that would be a little bit more additive to long-term growth,” said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which oversees about $33 billion in assets.

The last time ExxonMobil and Chevron made profits this high was in 2022. A year later, both announced acquisitions worth about $60 billion apiece, for Pioneer Natural Resources Co. and Hess Corp. respectively. But Chevron CEO Mike Wirth tossed cold water Friday on the notion his company is on the verge of another megadeal.

“The history books aren’t full of great deals that were done at $100 oil,” he said.

TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné had similar sentiments, emphasizing he prefers to buy during downturns and that the French oil major has a plethora of bolt-on growth opportunities.

“We will not become procyclical because suddenly we have more cash,” he said.

The windfall was probably more important to BP than any of its peers. Still reeling from writing off many of its clean energy investments, and the more than $60 billion in costs it incurred from the catastrophic 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, the company is squarely focused on strengthening its balance sheet, according to Meg O’Neill, who was appointed CEO earlier this year.

“It’s very easy to get caught up in high prices and think that’s an opportunity to distribute cash,” she said on a call with reporters Friday. BP still carries “more debt and more leverage than we really can afford in a low-price scenario.”

text:
A year after federal incentives ended, the EV market isn't dead. Here are 4 key takeaways on who's winning and what's next.

It's been a year and change since the biggest shock America's electric car market has ever seen. The $7,500 EV tax credit met its untimely demise on September 30, 2025, as the Trump administration and Congress also axed fuel economy regulations and other policies pushing EVs along.

So, a year after the great EV reset, what's changed?

The EV Market Is Bouncing Back, Slowly

EV sales cratered at the end of last year—not just just because a big incentive to buy one abruptly vanished, but also because so many Americans had rushed to get one while the getting was good. In September of 2025, the electric share of retail car sales soared to over 14%, according to data from JD Power. In October, that plunged to 7.1%, but the pain wasn't through. By November, just 5% of retail sales were battery-powered, a level not seen since 2022.

"That was something that nobody expected, and it made very important and sudden changes in the market, and for us too, right?" Hyundai CEO José Muñoz told me last month. "All of a sudden, you either add the incentive, or you lose sales, or you do something in between."

It wasn't clear how quickly or to what degree things would bounce back. But the market is showing new signs of life and has started to gradually rebound.

"In general, the EV market has been perhaps more resilient in some ways than we would maybe expect," Tyson Jominy, JD Power's senior vice president of data and analytics, told me. "Sales certainly fell as expected, but we kind of hit the floor quickly."

Share bounced back over 6% in December, and climbed to over 8% in May, the firm says. JD Power puts September's EV share of retail sales at 7.9%. "We only went back about two years," Jominy said, "which doesn't seem so bad."

While high gas prices haven't produced a big spike in sales like they have in other global markets, anecdotally they may be helping on the margins. Muñoz said Hyundai dealers who had been asking the company to dial back shipments of Ioniq 5s suddenly started asking for more of them after the war in Iran started.

There are other signs of a normalizing market. The number of days EVs are spending on dealer lots has dropped every month from April through September, according to data shared by Cars.com. In September, it took 89.4 days for the average EV to sell, down from 115.6 days in March and only slightly higher than the 80.5 days seen during last year's EV-buying frenzy.

"That, I think, is showing that we're getting closer to the moment where the demand and the supply are in good balance," Jenni Newman, the vehicle marketplace's editor-in-chief, told me.

Tesla And Rivian Are Carrying The Team

That's the macro picture. But the recovery is far from evenly distributed. A few automakers, notably Tesla and Rivian, are carrying much of the industry's comeback.

Between the second and third quarters, overall EV sales in the U.S. grew by 6.1% to hit some 262,000 units, their highest level since the tax credit ended, Cox Automotive says. Take Tesla out of the equation, though, and the market would have shrunk slightly instead, according to the firm's sales estimates. (Tesla doesn't break out its regional sales.) On a year-over-year basis, Tesla's sales fell 19.7% in Q3, Cox says, while the market as a whole contracted by close to 40%. It means Tesla's share of the EV market is back up above 50%.

"Tesla has pretty much withstood the decline we've seen among the non-disruptors," said Tom Libby, director of loyalty solutions and industry analysis at Mobility Global.

In part, that's because Tesla has built a great product that people keep coming back to. Around half of Model Y owners get another one as their next vehicle, Libby said, while model-level loyalty across the board lands at 26%. At Rivian, deliveries have surged this year on the back of the new R2, one of the best all-around Model Y rivals in years and its first product with mainstream potential.

There's another big reason for the divide: EV-only manufacturers couldn't simply pivot to gas models when the policies shifted like other manufacturers did. Since last year, legacy automakers have canceled or delayed some two-dozen electric models, like the Ford F-150 Lightning, Volkswagen ID.4, and Honda Prologue. The product vacuum was bound to hurt sales, but cutting back on EVs also makes perfect sense as a reaction to looser regulations and changing incentives.

"A lot of people, myself included, tend to forget that the manufacturers are not really in business to make cars," Libby said. "They're in business to make money."

While many legacy players struggle to regain momentum, Toyota is a notable outlier, having steadily grown EV sales as it's introduced new models this year.

Used EVs Are Having A Moment

The used EV market is another bright spot. It isn't just surviving, it's thriving, suggesting there's strong demand for battery power at the right price.

Sales took a dive after the EV tax credit went away, but they rebounded quickly and have rocketed upward ever since. Last month, Americans snapped up over 47,000 used electric cars, Cox Automotive says, a 21% year-over-year jump that gave EVs their largest-ever share of the used car market.

The fact that your options aren't limited to low-range Chevy Bolts and Nissan Leafs anymore is certainly helping. There's better supply of lightly used EVs than ever, as an increasing number of modern, long-range cars, particularly ones that were leased over the last few years, hit the secondhand market.

And the demand is there too, boosted in part by $4-a-gallon gas, industry-watchers say. Used EVs are selling in 41 days on average, according to Cars.com, about 12 days faster than internal-combustion models. And while prices for lightly used gas cars have stayed roughly flat over the last year, used EV prices are up close to 10%, iSeeCars says.

The EV Revolution Isn't Canceled. Just Delayed.

Despite the rocky road, industry watchers and auto executives broadly think EVs will continue displacing gas vehicles in the U.S.—albeit at a slower rate than before.

"We remain optimistic, quite frankly, on the space," Jominy said.

EVs are taking off globally, he said, and data shows that once someone goes electric they tend to be hooked. Plus, electric cars have fewer parts and are cheaper to manufacture at scale than combustion vehicles, putting slower-moving automakers at a disadvantage as EV sales climb around the world. At some point, the economics of scale in the industry will be far more favorable to electric propulsion, he said. "Once you can produce something 30% cheaper," he said, "you really can't just maintain the old way for very long."

On top of that, U.S. charging infrastructure is improving quickly; last quarter, the U.S. surpassed 80,000 DC fast charging ports, up from 70,000 at the end of last year. Promising new models like the R2, Ford's $30,000 Fathom pickup, the Slate Truck, and a slew of high-tech cars from luxury manufacturers could take sales to the next level. While Hyundai is investing heavily in various types of hybrids to buck the EV slowdown, Muñoz sees a future for electric cars in America too.

"What you see everywhere when you look at the trends in the market, EV is there to stay," he told me.
