DOE to Loan $5B to Constellation for Reator Uprates

Energy Department to Offer $5 Billion Loan to Constellation to Boost Nuclear Power and Help Lower Costs in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania.

The Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization across Constellation Energy’s nuclear fleet in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. It is the largest single investment in uprates in decades. The loan appears to be positioned like a line of credit with Constellation drawing from it as it implements uprates at each reactor.

The money is the latest in a series of investments in boosting the power rating of Constellation’s fleet of nuclear reactors. Uprates have the advantage of boosting the power of a nuclear reactor to generate electricity without having to also install new steam generators, turbines, and other infrastructure.

The loan follows a series of private sector investments in uprates for the same Constellation’s reactors by Meta in 2025 for 30 MW in Clinton, IL, Amazon in September 2026 for 190 MW in Calvert Cliffs, MD, and Google in October 2026 for 890 MW in Limerick, PA, and Salem, NJ.

While DOE’s $5 billion funding will come in the form of a loan, private sector investments in uprates are tied to 20-year power purchase agreements that will provide revenue not only to cover the costs of the uprates, but also to give the utility confidence to proceed with relicensing its reactors for another 20 years.

DOE’s loan to fund modernization efforts in Constellation reactors will add nearly 1.1 GW of electricity overall, strengthening the grid across the PJM Interconnection, LLC (PJM) and Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) regions.

EDF’s conditional loan commitment also includes an option to finance future uprate projects at additional Constellation facilities. While this conditional commitment indicates DOE’s intent to provide a loan, Constellation must satisfy certain technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before the Department enters into definitive financing documents and funds the loan.

Earlier DOE Loan to Constellation to Restart Pennsylvania Reactor

In November 2025 Department of Energy approved a $1.0 billion loan to cover the costs of restarting TMI-1, renamed as the Crane Clean Energy Center, an 835 MW plant located on the Susquehanna River in Londonderry Township, PA, which is about 100 miles due west of Philadelphia. The loan will partially finance the restart of a reactor which ceased operations in 2019 but was never fully decommissioned.

In 2019, Constellation Energy’s then-parent company Exelon shut down the reactor saying it was losing money. The Pennsylvania state legislature turned down a request to subsidize it to keep it running.

Constellation has estimated the total cost of restarting the plant is $1.6 billion. It will have to make up the $600 million difference between the DOE loan and total cost to complete the restart of the reactor. Constellation and Microsoft have signed a 20-year power purchase agreement to draw electricity generated by the reactors to power the computer giant’s data centers. The software giant reportedly signed on to pay a premium for the power to guarantee it will be available 24/7 365 days a year.

The loan funds are being provided by DOE’s Loan Program Office. The loan is being issued under an existing $250 billion energy infrastructure program initially authorized by Congress in 2022. Neither DOE nor Constellation released terms of the loan. DOE’s Loan Program Office told Reuters that Constellation is guaranteeing the loan, and that loan structure would protect taxpayers if the project does not succeed.

& & &

Meta, Amazon, and Google Made Investments in Constellation

June 2025 META 30 MW Clinton, IL

(WNN) A 20-year power purchase agreement between Meta and Constellation will secure the long-term operation of Constellation’s Clinton Clean Energy Center. The power purchase agreement will also allow Meta to purchase output from the single-unit boiling water reactor (BWR) unit at the Clinton, IL, site. The agreement supports the relicensing and continued operations of the Illinois nuclear facility for another two decades after the state of Illinois’s zero emission credit program expires,

The Clinton plant had been slated for premature closure in 2017 for economic reasons despite being one of the best performing nuclear plants in Illinois, until the state enacted legislation establishing the zero emission credit program, which provides financial support to the plant until mid-2027.

Constellation said in a press statement that the power purchase agreement with Meta is a market-based solution that essentially replaces the zero emission credit program and ensures long-term operation of the plant without the need for ratepayer support.

With the guarantee that Clinton will continue to run for another two decades, Constellation said it is also evaluating strategies to extend the plant’s existing early site permit or seek a new construction permit from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to pursue development of an advanced nuclear reactor or small modular reactor (SMR) at the site.

Sept 2026 Amazon 190 MW Calvert Cliffs

(WNN) In November 2025 Constellation outlined plans for the Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center, including the power uprates for the two pressurized water reactors (PWR), and 20-year life extensions for the units which were connected to the grid in 1975 and 1976, respectively, and which would otherwise shut down in 2034 and 2036. The investment and revenue certainty from the PPA will allow it to relicense the nuclear plant for another two decades. The new capacity will come online between 2030 and 2032.

According to a trade press report, Amazon has also entered a separate retail supply agreement with Constellation to support its operations in the 13-state PJM market, according to the release. PJM is the largest power grid operator in the U.S. and centrally dispatches generation and oversees the movement of wholesale electricity in all or parts of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia and the District of Columbia.

Constellation said all the electricity generated by the Maryland nuclear plant will flow to the PJM regional grid as usual, The utility added that the deal demonstrates “how large energy users can support investments in new, reliable generation while strengthening the broader electric system.”

With energy demands forecast to increase sharply in the coming decades, Constellation also said last year it “will explore building 2,000 MW of new, next-generation nuclear at Calvert Cliffs, effectively doubling the site’s output and creating enough clean generation to power future economic growth.”

October 2026 Google 890 MW Limerick, Salem $4.3 B

(Neutron Bytes) Google and Constellation Energy announced a long-term strategic clean energy collaboration to bring 890 MW of new nuclear capacity onto the PJM Interconnection grid to meet growing demand and increase grid reliability. The massive effort will involve uprates in the power levels to 11 of Constellation’s fleet of megawatt class nuclear reactors. The agreement provides $4.3 billion of new investment in Constellation reactors.

The 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) by Google with Constellation will enable investments in new equipment and technology at Constellation-owned nuclear units in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey, increasing thermal and electrical efficiency to unlock additional power to serve the grid. This capacity is entirely new, expanding total electricity generation available across the 13-state PJM footprint..

According to press statements by both Google and Constellation, there is a second significant collaboration effort between the two firms. In addition to the 20-year PPA, the two companies have agreed to a separate 15-year energy supply agreement for 2,700 MW of power within the PJM region.

In a statement reported by the New York Times, Joe Dominguez, the chief executive of Constellation, said that Google’s willingness to pay extra for power was essential. “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.”

A third deal is a five-year technology agreement for Constellation to use Google’s cloud and artificial intelligence services, including Gemini Enterprise agentic workflows. The “AI for Energy” approach would shorten engineering and regulatory work on uprates, improve construction and operation performance, and better protect critical infrastructure, according to the announcement.

Under the expanded five-year technology agreement, Constellation will build Gemini Enterprise agentic workflows directly into its core operations. Each of the initial three focus areas is tied to a clear benefit for the communities Constellation serves.

Speed to power: AI for intelligent site selection, power flow modeling, permitting and interconnection planning. This shortens the engineering and regulatory work on uprates, so new capacity reaches the grid sooner and at lower cost.

Generation optimization: Asset health monitoring, outage and turnaround management, and scenario optimization to speed up construction. This keeps plants running at full output, so supply keeps up with rising demand.

Protecting critical infrastructure: Google Cloud’s defense-grade platforms for highly regulated work, used to secure operational technology (OT) networks. Many of these networks are air-gapped and connect to the bulk electric system. This helps keep the grid that homes and businesses rely on secure and resilient.

& & &

South Korean Firm Partners Join Elemental Power in $750M Deal

Proposed partnership of up to $750 million would help fund development of multiple Elementl nuclear projects

Elementl Power, a nuclear project delivery and capital management platform, has signed a preliminary agreement to form and fund a development partnership of up to $750 million with a consortium led by South Korean investment firm DS Investment Partners (DSIP). DS Investment Partners (DSIP) is an investment firm focused on energy, technology, healthcare and strategic infrastructure, and is part of a Seoul-based financial group.

The company said in its press statement that Samsung C&T Engineering & Construction Group may at a future time participate in the consortium as a strategic investor. It is not an investor in this round.

Beyond the South Korean consortium, Elementl relies on several established institutional and commercial funding sources. Elementl is backed by major energy and infrastructure investors, including Energy Impact Partners and accounts advised by T. Rowe Price Group. In May 2025,

Elementl signed a separate agreement with Google in May 2025. As part of the agreement, Google will commit early-stage development capital to advance the development of three projects. Each project would generate at least 600 MW of power capacity, with the option for commercial off-take once complete.

The South Korean consortium would fund a portion of the proposed partnership’s projected capital and hold a significant minority interest in the partnership. The agreement consists of a letter of intent and term sheet setting out the proposed terms of the partnership and allows for participation from additional strategic and financial investors. It is not yet a final investment decision by all parties.

The proposed nuclear development partnership is intended to provide a portion of the capital necessary for up to three of Elementl’s advanced reactor nuclear projects to achieve final investment decision (FID), supporting pre-construction activities, including permitting, interconnection and long-lead item procurement.

One of the three projects is Elementl’s 1.5 gigawatt project under development in Ohio, which will use GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s BWRX-300 small modular reactors. The location is a 700-acre site along the Ohio River in Letart Township (purchased from American Municipal Power). The site is located in southern Ohio on the banks of the Ohio River.

The press statement did not identify a customer nor a MOU pending a power purchase agreement from a utility. Buckeye Rural Electric Cooperative and AEP are the two electric utilities serving the rural area. The township itself has a population of about 700 people.

Construction target is set for 2030, with completion of the first unit projected for 2034, pending approvals from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the Ohio Power Siting Board.

Elementl Chairman and CEO Chris Colbert said, “Once finalized, this partnership would expand our early-stage project capital, increase our access to South Korea’s nuclear supply chain and engineering expertise and enhance our position as the financial and development partner best equipped to deliver new nuclear.”

The proposed partnership does not constitute a final investment decision on any project. The agreement remains subject to definitive documentation, regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

& & &

NRC Completes X-Energy Safety Analysis to Build Four HTGRs

Final Safety Evaluation Report formally completes NRC safety review

Marks completion of both primary reviews required for Construction Permit approval

Establishes regulatory precedent to support more efficient licensing of future Xe-100 projects

X-Energy announced the completion of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (NRC) safety review for the initial deployment of X-energy’s Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR). The proposed Long Mott Generating Station, Texas, would be the first grid-scale advanced nuclear reactor at an industrial facility in U.S. history. X-Energy’s development of the HTGR was funded under a cost-shared effort with the Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP).

The NRC’s Final Safety Evaluation Report (FSER) follows a comprehensive review of the Xe-100 plant’s principal design criteria, preliminary design, safety analyses, probabilistic risk assessment, and research and development programs. It documents the NRC staff’s conclusion that the proposed plant and site provide the safety basis to begin construction under 10 CFR Part 50. The Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, an independent body that advises the Commission, earlier in October and separately reviewed the NRC staff’s evaluation and supported issuing the construction permit.

The Xe-100’s safety case leverages the passive physics of its TRISO-X coated particle fuel and pebble-bed core design, as well as traditional defense-in-depth systems to enable a new, broader range of applications for nuclear technology.

The design’s safety profile enables applicants to pursue a compact site footprint with a 400-meter emergency planning zone compared to 10 miles for conventional light-water reactors. This allows new generation to be sited closer to the point of need, including inside the perimeter of a large industrial facility, or closer to populated areas.

While future applications will be reviewed individually, the NRC’s review establishes regulatory precedents for every Xe-100 project that follows, creating replicable pathways for increased efficiency in commercial nuclear licensing.

& & &

DOE Approves Final Safety Analysis for Radiant Nuclear

Radiant announced that the Department of Energy (DOE) has granted approval of its Documented Safety Analysis (DSA). The approval marks a key milestone toward full-power testing of Radiant’s Kaleidos microreactor at Idaho National Laboratory (INL) and allows the company to advance to DOE’s Readiness Review, the next step before nuclear operations can begin. The approval follows DOE’s February 2026 approval of Radiant’s earlier Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis (PDSA) submission.

The DOE document is not an NRC license. Radiant must still comply with all the regulatory agency’s rules regarding construction and operation of its microreactor for commercial customers. However, military nuclear reactors used for authorized defense purposes are expressly excluded from Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) licensing under Section 91(b) of the Atomic Energy Act.

Programs like the Army’s Janus Program or the Air Force’s Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations (ANPI) program deploy nuclear microreactors directly on domestic military bases for energy resilience, often operating outside traditional NRC licenses using Other Transaction Agreements.

Closing the circle, if a private company develops or commercializes a reactor installation on or for a base under a power purchase agreement intended for broader commercial use rather than pure defense operations, standard NRC commercial licensing rules (such as 10 CFR Part 50 or Part 53) apply.

Radiant Reactor Testing at INL

Radiant’s scheduled testing at INL will be the industry’s only full-power, extended-duration demonstration of a nuclear microreactor to-date. In addition to achieving criticality, Radiant will test the same Kaleidos unit for 60 effective full power days (EFPD) over several months, demonstrating its performance under real operating conditions. The reactor being tested at INL uses a similar reactor design and custom-designed fuel as the units Radiant plans to deliver to customers, making the test a crucial step toward commercial deployment.

Radiant’s DSA approval addresses operation at power in addition to initial criticality, enabling the company to advance toward a more comprehensive evaluation of Kaleidos. Powered testing will allow Radiant to evaluate the reactor core, instrumentation, and integrated systems together under operating conditions.

“DOE’s approval is a major milestone because it reflects the scope of what we are preparing to demonstrate with Kaleidos,” said Dr. Rita Baranwal, Chief Nuclear Officer at Radiant.

“We are testing the design of our commercial reactor, the same unit – from fueling through 150 hours of continuous operation without operator assistance and beyond. This approval for full power demonstration is a first within the microreactor industry. It moves us forward to test our complete reactor system under sustained operating conditions.”

With the Kaleidos DSA approved, Radiant is cued for DOE’s Readiness Review, which will assess whether Kaleidos and the team responsible for operating it are prepared to begin nuclear operations. Following successful completion of the review, Radiant will fuel Kaleidos and begin its five-phase test campaign at the National Reactor Innovation Center’s Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (DOME) facility at INL.

Radiant built Kaleidos at its El Segundo, California facility and shipped it to INL in August 2026. The DOME campaign is a key step toward Radiant’s plan to manufacture Kaleidos at its R-50 facility in Oak Ridge, TN and deliver its first commercial units to Buckley Space Force Base and Fort Benning in 2028. Earlier this month, Radiant was selected by the U.S. Navy to deploy Kaleidos at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana.

& & &

BWXT Announces Contract with Antares for TRISO Nuclear Fuel

BWX Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: BWXT) announced that its BWXT Advanced Fuels subsidiary has entered into a multi-year commercial agreement with Antares Nuclear, Inc., establishing a framework for production of tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) nuclear fuel.

The agreement includes terms for an initial allocation of 1 MTU (metric ton uranium), with the ability to increase as deployment requirements evolve to support Antares’ advanced reactor program.

Under the agreement, the fuel will be manufactured at BWXT’s Lynchburg, VA, facility, on the same TRISO fabrication line used to produce fuel for Antares’ Mark-0 reactor and for the U.S. Army’s Project Pele reactor. Earlier this year, BWXT-produced fuel supported Antares’ Mark-0 criticality milestone.

BWXT delivered a full core of TRISO fuel for Project Pele, a 1.5 MW transportable microreactor, to INL in December 2025. The project team plans to begin formal testing of the prototype as early as 2027.

The TRISO fuel manufactured under the agreement will be delivered in accordance with a series of future task orders that define specific quantities, delivery schedules and technical requirements as Antares’ reactor program progresses.

& & &

ARPA-E Funds Eight Projects with $50M for New Nuclear Fuels

The Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E) today announced the selection of eight projects to receive up to a combined $50 million to advance next-generation nuclear fuels through the High-performance Optimized Recycled Nuclear Isotopes for Gen IV reactors (HORNIG) program. The projects will develop innovative approaches to fuel fabrication, testing, and qualification to reduce fuel costs and accelerate commercial deployment of advanced reactors.

The announcement advances President Trump’s Executive Order, Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base, by strengthening America’s domestic nuclear industry and building a more secure, self-reliant nuclear fuel supply chain.

The objective of the HORNIG program is to repurpose transuranic (TRU) waste elements—such as plutonium and other materials derived from used nuclear fuel and nuclear weapons production—into commercial reactor fuels for Generation IV (Gen IV) advanced reactors. It seeks to help establish an economic levelized cost of fuel around 1¢/kWh while reducing long-term radiological waste and foreign uranium dependence

The list of eight selected projects and their innovative approaches to developing advanced nuclear fuels can be found on the HORNIG | ARPA-E webpage.

Selection for award negotiations is not a commitment by DOE to issue an award or provide funding. Before funding is issued, DOE and the applicants will undergo a negotiation process.

NRC Accepts General Matter’s License Application for Uranium Fuel Plant at Padukah, KY

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has accepted General Matter’s first license application, marking the beginning of the nuclear-fuel startup’s formal license review.

General Matter submitted the license application in late September, with the application spanning more than 1,000 pages and detailing how the company plans to build and operate the Paducah, KY, facility.

The Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant (PGDP) was constructed in 1952 to produce enriched uranium, initially for the nation’s nuclear weapons program and later for nuclear fuel for commercial power plants.

The plant is owned by the Department of Energy (DOE), which oversees environmental cleanup activities at the site, including environmental remediation, waste management, depleted uranium conversion, and decontamination and decommissioning. Commercial enrichment was conducted under lease from 1993 until 2013 when operations ceased and the gaseous diffusion facilities were returned to the DOE Environmental Management (EM) program.

The plant sits on a site not far from the Kentucky shoreline of the Ohio River and as the crow flies across the river, is not far from the Coverdyn uranium conversion plant that sits on the Illinois side of the river. The Metropolis, IL, plant coverts enriched UF6 into uranium oxide form which can then be used by fuel fabrication plants to manufacture uranium pellets and fuel assemblies for commercial reactors.

General Matter and NRC Comments on the Quality of the License Application

According to a Substack post from General Matter, the NRC noted in its acceptance letter of the licensse application that “the quality and completeness of the application reflect the effectiveness of General Matter’s constructive pre-application engagement with the NRC staff.” The commission further stated that said quality enabled it “to accept the application in approximately half the timeframe typically allotted for an acceptance review.”

The company plans to submit a license amendment to produce High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium in 2027, with General Matter asserting that this two-part approach reflects many months of open communication with the NRC.

“We believe it will lead to faster licensing and authorization, bringing safe, secure, and commercially competitive American enrichment online sooner,” the company wrote. “Beginning at lower assays will allow us to log operating hours and demonstrate safe, reliable performance ahead of production at higher assays.”

Since General Matter filed the license application in September, the NRC has begun publishing portions of it publicly — including the 457-page environmental report. See the table below from the NRC of licensing milestones for the company.

Key Details of the Acceptance

• Project Location: 100-acre parcel on the U.S. Department of Energy’s former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant site in McCracken County, Kentucky.

• Filing Scope: Submitted under 10 CFR Part 70 to produce special nuclear material (low-enriched uranium).

• Review Speed: The NRC accepted the 1,000+ page application in roughly half the standard acceptance-review timeframe due to application quality and pre-application engagement.

• Fee Cap: The NRC established a fixed fee cap of $3,960,000 for the review.

• Next Steps: A full technical review typically targets an 18-month window (with potential for expedited efficiencies). General Matter plans to submit a license amendment next year to produce High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU).

General Matter has acknowledged that it has requested to keep some parts of the NRC application confidential, “a standard industry practice to protect proprietary and security-related information.”

General Matter’s Enrichment Plans

While the company has not revealed the method by which it will enrich uranium, there are a number of open sources that provide other details about the company’s plans.

General Matter was one of three companies selected in October 2024 by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to provide enrichment services to help establish a domestic supply of HALEU. The company did not emerge from stealth mode until April 2025. In August 2025 it signed a lease with the DOE for the reuse of federal land at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in Kentucky for a new commercial uranium enrichment facility.

General Matter intends to re-enrich depleted UF6 tails left over from the gaseous diffusion program of uranium enrichment that ended at the Paducah site in 2013. The firm confirmed to Politico in September that this is part of its business plan.

General Matter has leased portions of the former Paducah site and secured a $900 million DOE contract in 2024 to establish domestic uranium enrichment capabilities, including, eventually, High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) for advanced reactors. The lease at the Paducah site covers a 100-acre parcel of land at the site and provides General Matter with a minimum of 7,600 cylinders of existing depleted uranium hexafluoride to supply fuel for future re-enrichment operations. Each cylinder weighs about 14 tons.

These numbers mean that the inventory of 7,600 cylinders of depleted uranium hexafluoride (DUF6) to be processed by General matter at Paducah, containing 12.7 metric tonnes, on average, of DUF6 each, comes to 96,520 tonnes of DUF6. The amount of remaining U235 in the “tails” varies widely by cylinder from 0.15% to roughly 0.70% U-235.

Any estimate of how much enriched uranium to 5% U235 can be produced from these cylinders will depend on what General Matter discovers as it works through the inventory of 7,600 of them allocated to the firm by DOE. Reuters reported that production is expected to start by 2030. The firm boasted in its public statement this week, “We will enrich uranium at commercial scale by the end of the decade.”

OPG Firm Joins UK BWRX-300 to Build 14 SMRs

(WNN) The UK-based project company of European SMR developer and investor SGE, and Origin Nuclear, a subsidiary of Ontario Power Generation, have signed a letter of intent to establish a joint venture for the future operation of a planned fleet of 14 BWRX-300 small modular reactors.

SGE SMR UK is the UK-based project company of Poland’s SGE (formerly Synthos Green Energy). Earlier this year, SGE outlined plans for the privately financed deployment of 14 GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactors across three sites in the UK, for which it submitted an application under the UK’s Advanced Nuclear Framework.

The proposed joint venture will see SGE SMR UK and Origin Nuclear work together to establish a UK-based nuclear operating company. Origin Nuclear – whose owner, Canadian nuclear operator Ontario Power Generation (OPG), is developing the first BWRX-300 reactor at Darlington in Ontario – will support the licensing process, commissioning and operational readiness of the reactors, and will also be responsible for plant operations, and centralised support services across the proposed UK BWRX-300 fleet.

The first site in the UK is planned to accommodate six BWRX-300 reactors, with the first unit starting commercial operation in 2034. This would be followed by two further multi-unit sites – an approach SGE says is intended to support repeat construction, coordinated procurement and the transfer of experience between projects. The programme is supported by an international delivery team comprising SGE, GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, Samsung C&T, Laing O’Rourke, Aecon Group Inc, Fermi Development and Etara.

The proposed total generating capacity from the 14 units of 4.2 GW would be enough, SGE says, to meet around 11% of UK power demand, equivalent to the needs of almost eight million homes, for at least 60 years.

About the BWRX-300

The BWRX-300 is a 300 MWe water-cooled, natural circulation SMR with passive safety systems that leverages the design and licensing basis of GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s US Nuclear Regulatory Commission-certified ESBWR boiling water reactor design and its existing, licensed GNF2 fuel design. SGE is a co-investor in the standardised BWRX-300 design alongside GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, OPG and the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA).

The unit under construction in Canada is envisaged as the first of four at OPG’s Darlington New Nuclear site. In September, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued a construction permit to TVA for a BWRX-300 reactor at the Clinch River site in Tennessee.

KHNP Suspends Talks with EPC for Dukovany Reactor Project

Company is supplying two new APR1000 nuclear plants for Czech Republic

(NucNet) Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) has broken off construction contract talks with a Daewoo Engineering & Construction-led consortium for a $18.6 billion (€16.5 billion) project to build two new nuclear plants at the Dukovany site in the Czech Republic.

KHNP said the two sides failed to agree on key contract terms despite prolonged negotiations. In a statement, the consortium said the main sticking point was a set of revised contract terms introduced by KHNP on 10/07/26, giving it only about three weeks to review the changes.

The state-run nuclear operator CEZ said on 10/28/26 it would move to terminate its cooperation agreement with the consortium, which includes Doosan Enerbility, and launch a new bidding process to find a replacement contractor. Reports in South Korea said the breakdown followed more than a year of talks over construction costs and who should bear the financial burden of design changes.

The Dukovany project is for two new large-scale APR1000 plants, supplied by KHNP, at the existing Dukovany nuclear power station site in the southern Czech Republic, about 50 km from the border with Austria. A deal was signed between Czech state-controlled nuclear project company EDU II and KHNP in June 2025. Daewoo E&C and Doosan Enerbility were selected as construction partners in 2018 and participated in the bidding process.

According to industry sources, KHNP demanded a cut in costs of more than 10% from the consortium’s original bid, equivalent to over $750 million.

The Korea Herald reported that Choi Il-kyung, KHNP’s vice-president and head of project operations, played down the risk of major disruption to the project. The consortium called for talks to resume.

Israel Publishes Draft National Fusion Strategy

In October 2026, Israel’s Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure published its first national fusion strategy, a draft now open for public comment. The program recommends three scenarios, ranging from $135-to-650 million as a first step towards establishing an OEM fusion manufacturing industry in Israel. The aim is to position Israel as a key supplier to the global fusion industry.

The global fusion industry has shifted from government labs to private companies, especially over the past few years. The shift accelerated after the US National Ignition Facility first produced more energy from fusion than it delivered to the fuel, in December 2022. Private fusion companies have raised about $16 billion since 2021.

Governments in the US, China, the UK, Germany and Japan are funding national programs and building supply chains. The strategy’s message is that this window is open now. The supply chains are forming, and countries that don’t take part early risk being shut out of a market that will be hard to enter later.

The draft strategy sets out three options and recommends the middle one – option 2

Option 2 – National Fusion Research Center (recommended) Proposed spend: $150-350 million Time Frame: 5–7 years

Several public-private technology consortia; upgrades to national neutron and high-power laser facilities; milestone-based funding for companies, following the US model; a new graduate track and programs to bring experts home.

The Ministry calls Option 2 the most balanced choice. It closes the key gaps without committing the state budget to a full national program up front. The strategy finds that Israel’s edge comes from dual-use technology developed in its defense sector, which can be adapted for fusion. Examples include

Power electronics and RF systems for heating plasma in magnetic-confinement reactors

AI, simulation and cyber: digital twins, real-time plasma control and secure plant operation

Precision engineering and vacuum systems for reactor vessels

With further investment, Israel believes it can also compete in tritium-breeding blankets and in superconducting magnet design. It claims it already has world-class research assets, including the SARAF accelerator at Soreq used for testing materials under neutron radiation.

Organizational and Management Objectives

A regulatory framework that treats fusion separately from nuclear fission, plus a regulatory sandbox to attract companies to test in Israel

A national policy on tritium and other export-controlled fusion components, in cooperation with the United States

Closer ties with international programs and partners, including ITER, the US Department of Energy and bi-national funds such as BIRD

Investment in people and research: doctoral and postdoctoral fellowships, a new inter-university graduate program in fusion, and more.

An annual Israeli-international fusion conference and investor pitch event

What Happens Next?

The draft strategy is open for public comment before the government decides which scenario to adopt and fund. Whichever scenario is chosen, this is the first time Israel has drafted a national direction for fusion. It is a clear signal that fusion is moving up the government’s agenda.

Proxima Fusion and Kyoto Fusioneering to Build Components for Fusion Power

A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed in Tokyo during Germany’s Chancellor Merz’s visit to Japan covers critical fusion technologies such as plasma heating and the fusion fuel cycle.

Proxima Fusion, a stellarator fusion company, and Kyoto Fusioneering, a fusion technology provider headquartered in Japan, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to expand their cooperation on critical technologies needed to build and operate commercial fusion power plants, strengthening the industrial supply chain behind Germany’s ambition to become a global leader in fusion energy.

Under the MoU, the two companies will continue and expand joint work on next-generation gyrotrons for plasma heating and on fuel cycle technologies. Kyoto Fusioneering will also contribute its technologies and engineering expertise to the commercialization and industrial deployment of fusion energy in Germany, including within the national Fusion Hubs initiative of the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space’s (BMFTR).

The agreement brings together Japan’s long-standing expertise in fusion engineering with Germany’s world-leading stellarator research and industrial capabilities. It also strengthens industrial ties between the two countries as governments and companies worldwide race to turn fusion science into a new source of firm, dispatchable and clean energy.

The partnership will support Proxima’s roadmap towards Alpha, its demonstration stellarator planned for the early 2030s, and Stellaris, its first commercial fusion power plant expected to be ready before 2040.

title: The 5 future vehicles you need to watch for, according to Edmunds - Decatur Daily
description: Fall is typically when automakers release the majority of their models for the new year. Most will be continuations of prior designs, but there's also a good number that are
text:
NEW YORK — Americans spent more than $160 billion last year …

NEW YORK — The Ford Foundation, one of the world's largest p…









The fourth-generation Nissan Rogue small SUV debuts with a new hybrid powertrain that promises up to 38 mpg in combined city/highway mileage. [COURTESY OF NISSAN NORTH AMERICA VIA AP]

The 2027 Slate Truck is a new bare-bones electric vehicle from a new manufacturer, and it bucks pretty much every automotive trend of the last few decades. [COURTESY OF SLATE AUTO VIA AP]

The Chevrolet Silverado 1500 gets a significant update for 2027, allowing it to better battle key rivals like the Ford F-150 and Ram 1500. [COURTESY OF GENERAL MOTORS VIA AP]

Fall is typically when automakers release the majority of their models for the new year. Most will be continuations of prior designs, but there's also a good number that are all-new or getting major redesigns. If you're thinking about buying a new vehicle in the next six months, it can be useful to know which ones have major changes or offer notable breakthroughs. To give you an inside scoop on what's coming down the pike in the next few months, the automotive experts at Edmunds have picked five vehicles that promise to be well worth the wait.

--

Small SUV: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid

Nissan's best-selling model is getting its first full redesign since 2021, and it's a significant one. The fourth-generation Rogue small SUV debuts with a new hybrid powertrain called E-Power that works more like an electric vehicle than a traditional hybrid. A small gas engine acts as a generator, recharging a battery that powers the electric motors driving the Rogue. The result is reduced noise and quicker acceleration compared to the regular Rogue, Nissan says. Nissan also estimates that the Rogue Hybrid will get 38 mpg in combined city/highway driving. That's a bit less than what the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4 hybrids can do, but it's still very good for a small SUV.

Starting price: $37,065, including destination fees

--

Three-row SUV: 2028 Toyota Highlander

The Highlander undergoes a massive change for 2028, becoming an all-electric three-row SUV with a quoted range of up to 320 miles. Buyers who still want a gas- or hybrid-powered three-row Toyota SUV will need to look at the larger Grand Highlander. But you needn't step up to the bigger version to get a reasonably comfortable third row, even for adults. Edmunds' first drive in the new all-electric Highlander showed the new version's way-back seat to be much more comfortable than the outgoing model's. Besides the Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Kia EV9, there aren't many three-row EVs aimed at bigger families, so we're excited to see Toyota offering an all-new alternative.

Estimated starting price: $60,000

--

Luxury SUV: 2027 Audi Q9

At the same time Audi is sunsetting the longstanding A8 flagship sedan, it's adding a new full-size three-row SUV. The 2027 Q9 is the largest vehicle Audi has ever built, and it's aimed squarely at rival German stalwarts like the BMW X7 and Mercedes-Benz GLS. Power comes from a 429-horsepower turbocharged V6. Inside, there's seating for seven or a more premium six-passenger layout with second-row captain's chairs. The Q9's third-row seating area is considerably roomier than the one in the Q7, which also gets a redesign this year. Audi has also fitted the Q9 with all of its latest technology and driver assist features.

Starting price: $89,095, including destination

--

Compact pickup: 2027 Slate Truck

No 2027 model has generated more buzz among budget-conscious shoppers than the Slate Truck, the debut model from an American startup automotive company. The Truck is a bare-bones two-seat electric pickup that's smaller than a Ford Maverick. By design, it comes without factory paint or even an infotainment touchscreen. Instead, buyers are encouraged to personalize it to their liking, up to and including the option to turn the cargo bed into a seating area and effectively turn the Truck into a five-seat SUV. The Slate Truck is an intriguing option for affordable vehicle, but go in with your eyes wide open: It lacks many features you might take for granted in other vehicles, and its estimated range of just 205 miles is a concern.

Starting price: $26,400, including destination

--

Full-size pickup: 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500

Chevrolet's full-size truck is getting its first redesign since 2019, and that should make it a more capable rival to the Ford F-150, Ram 1500 and Toyota Tacoma. The 2027 Silverado 1500 brings a bolder exterior design, a new interior and a standard 16.3-inch touchscreen. Two new V8 engine options join the carryover turbocharged four-cylinder and diesel six-cylinder. The 5.7-liter V8 produces 402 horsepower, while the larger 6.2-liter V8 cranks out 481 horsepower. Both are more powerful than the Silverado's previous V8s. Expect Super Cruise — GM's hands-free driving technology — to be available on top trims. And like all full-size trucks, there will be many variants — seven to be exact, topping out at more than $80,000 for the off-road-oriented ZR2 or the luxurious High Country.

Estimated starting price: $40,000

Edmunds says: The new model year is jam-packed with big updates for some of the most popular vehicles on the market. These models we listed above will have some significant advantages over a vehicle in the here and now. Buyers shopping for new wheels will have a lot of exciting options to choose from in the next few months.

— Josh Jacquot is a contributor at Edmunds.

title: WATCH: Kitsap County's Prop 1 pits local public utility against PSE | Washington
description: (The Center Square) - Voters in Kitsap County will decide this election cycle whether to let their public utility district get into the power business and move toward studying a
text:
Puget Sound Energy says its annual power supply costs have increased from approximately $750 million to $2 billion over the past seven to eight years, raising questions about Washington electricity rates and the cost of the state's clean energy policies.

(The Center Square) - Voters in Kitsap County will decide this election cycle whether to let their public utility district get into the power business and move toward studying a shift away from Puget Sound Energy.

The vote is considered a test of whether a shift to public power could bring down skyrocketing power bills and potentially inspire other parts of the state to move away from PSE.

PSE has spent millions in opposition to Proposition One .

“It’s important for people to understand that what they're voting on is the ability for the public utility commissioners — three elected folks from Kitsap County — to condemn all of the PSE infrastructure in the county, at any time without a second vote,” said PSE’s Matt Steuerwalt, senior vice president of external affairs for Puget Sound Energy in a Thursday interview with The Center Square.

“They've said they would do a study after the vote comes. They've also said they don't have the money to do the study, and they would have to stop a water project or a fiber project just to do the study. So, if I was an existing customer of the PUD, I'd wonder why am I not getting my water project or my fiber project that I was promised with the money that I paid to do that,” he added.

Proposition 1 would give Kitsap Public Utility District the authority to explore providing electric service, starting with a feasibility study of the costs and logistics, estimated to cost up to $500,000.

Kimberly Funk, Senior Public Relations Manager for Kitsap Public Utility District, responded to questions via email about PSE’s assertions in opposition to Prop 1.

“The ballot measure asks voters whether KPUD should be authorized to construct or acquire electric facilities for the generation, transmission or distribution of electric power, as provided under RCW 54.08.070. It is not a vote to condemn PSE's infrastructure, transfer ownership of its facilities or immediately begin providing electric service,” wrote Funk.

“Approval of this ballot measure would not, by itself, initiate a condemnation proceeding or result in an automatic or blanket taking of PSE infrastructure. Any potential acquisition would require separate action by the Board and would be subject to the applicable statutory and court-supervised legal process.”

The Center Square asked Steuerwalt at PSE about 30% phased-in rate hikes the investor-owned company is requesting .

“It is true that our bills have gone up a bit in the last five years. We're totally aware of that. We hear the customers, we understand the challenge. I would like to make sure that all the Kitsap County customers know about all the programs that we have to help customers who are struggling,” Steuerwalt said.

“We have programs to help with bill payments. We have programs that give you discounts. All of those are on our website, and a lot of people are eligible for things that they're not taking advantage of.”

If voters in Kitsap County approve Proposition One, it could set the stage for KPUD to take over electric service for about 130,000 electric customers , which would amount to more than 10% of PSE's electric customers.

PSE says it needs to raise rates to fund massive multi-billion-dollar infrastructure investments, and to comply with strict Washington state clean energy mandates.

The Clean Energy Transformation Act and the Climate Commitment Act mandate that PSE meet clean energy goals by 2030. The requirement is that PSE transition away from fossil fuels and provide 80% of its electricity from renewable or non-emitting resources by 2030–2033.

It will require billions of dollars in new wind, solar, and battery storage projects.

“It’s gonna be really hard,” said Steuerwalt. “We have to get to that 2030 number. We’ve doubled our renewables since CETA passed and we’re still a good ways away. I think if we’re going to get there, it’s going to be because we get some help.”

“Maybe the Legislature is willing to think about some flexibility. We have to climb a pretty big hill,” he added.

When PSE made their case for the increase in power rates earlier this year, the utility said their spending plan to meet customer demand and comply with all the clean energy mandates amounts to more than $3.6 billion. The recovery of these project costs will be spread over decades, according to PSE.

KPUD told The Center Square at this point, there are no decisions regarding a future electric system, its costs or how it might be financed.

“KPUD's role throughout this process has been to provide the public with factual information about the ballot measure, what it would authorize and what it would not," Funk said.

"We recognize that voters will have differing perspectives, and our responsibility is to help ensure they understand the measure and the potential steps that could follow.”

Proposition 1 is on the Nov. 3 ballot in Kitsap County. As of late Thursday, 35.87% of Kitsap County voters had returned ballots, according to the Secretary of State.

text:
[Newsworks = Reporter Ahn Kwang-seok] As the U.S. midterm elections approach on November 3 (local time), tensions are rising among major domestic companies with a high proportion of business in the United States. This is because the United States is the largest investor in companies, and the outcome of this election will determine the direction of legislative and budget leadership for the second half of the Donald Trump administration.

In particular, major companies in the automotive, battery, steel, and shipbuilding sectors have begun preparing scenario-based countermeasures by analyzing the pros and cons of five key issues: ▲ Alaska's liquefied natural gas (LNG), ▲ the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) tax benefits, ▲ small modular reactors (SMRs), ▲ tariffs, and ▲ maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO).

◆Alaska LNG: White House Pressure and Korea Gas Corporation's Calculations

Among the five major projects, the Alaska LNG project has the biggest impact, as the intensity of South Korea's response and the U.S.'s pressure will vary entirely depending on the midterm election results.

At a recent midterm election rally, President Trump referred to South Korea's $50 billion (about 68 trillion won) investment as a "result of the trade agreement." If the ruling Republican Party controls both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections, pressure on South Korea is expected to reach its peak, linked to trade measures.

The Republican-led legislature could ease the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) requirements for approving LNG exports to Alaska and expedite the passage of a $2 billion federal debt-guarantee bill. It effectively gives a legislative boost to the Trump administration's demand for the signing of a $50 billion early investment agreement with South Korea. The Trump administration is also expected to raise the general tariffs on Korean automobiles, steel, and other goods further if South Korea fails to implement its LNG investment in Alaska or shows a comparable attitude.

On the other hand, if the Democratic Party controls the House, the situation would favor South Korea. The Democratic Party is reportedly planning a rigorous environmental hearing and budget review into the environmental damage caused by the construction of a 1,300 km pipeline in Alaska and the adequacy of the $50 billion federal guarantee. In this case, federal support legislation for Alaska would be blocked, and permitting procedures would be delayed, putting a brake on the Trump administration's unilateral actions.

Participating companies such as Korea Gas Corporation and POSCO International are likely to use the U.S. Congress's budget and environmental review process as a legal safeguard—namely, the commercial feasibility reassessment and National Assembly approval procedures—to extend the negotiation deadline. They may also take the lead in negotiations by proposing terms focused on steel supply and long-term LNG volume purchases rather than merely equity investment.

◆ Subsidy and tariff risks...Survival Strategies by Industry

The IRA tax benefits for the three battery companies (LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, SK On) and the finished vehicle industry will determine the direction of corporate operating profits depending on congressional control. Under the current IRA, the Advanced Manufacturing Credit (AMPC), which refunds $35 per 1kWh for battery cells and $10 for modules, is a key pillar of the combined annual operating profits of the three major battery companies.

If the Republicans control both the House and the Senate, they could push through legislation to reduce the AMPC rebate rate and tighten eligibility requirements for electric vehicle purchase subsidies of up to $7,500 per vehicle, which could hurt the profitability of South Korean battery manufacturers’ North American plants. On the other hand, if the Democrats regain control of the House, the IRA amendment could be blocked by congressional resistance, allowing them to preserve the current tax benefits and the framework of subsidies.

In the field of nuclear power generation, the pace of SMR legislation also varies depending on parliamentary leadership. If the Republicans hold onto Congress, bills to simplify SMR approval procedures and provide tax incentives to address the massive power shortage caused by the surge in AI data centers could be fast-tracked. In this case, Doosan Enerbility's entry into the North American foundry market, which supplies main equipment to U.S. SMR companies like NuScale Power, will also accelerate.

On the other hand, if the Democrats regain control of the House, stringent environmental hearings and scrutiny of tax benefits for new nuclear power plant permits are expected to be strengthened. It means that the legislation on SMRs is being delayed.

Separately, following the settlement of the intellectual property (IP) dispute between Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power and the U.S. Westinghouse, there is a possibility that the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) may demand controls on strategic materials exports and technical verification. This is a permanent check-and-balance tool that the U.S. government can exercise at any time to protect its domestic nuclear industry.

The automaker and steel sectors are unaffected by changes in the congressional landscape resulting from the midterm elections. Raising the tariff rate through an executive order, which is the president's exclusive authority, is a variable. This is because Section 232 of the U.S. Trade Expansion Act and the General Tariff Guidelines can be invoked at the President's discretion without congressional approval.

In response to concerns over a 10–20% general tariff under U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) guidelines and pressure from steel quotas, Hyundai Motor Group is adopting a local production strategy, including raising the operating rate of its Metaplast plant (HMGMA) in Georgia ahead of schedule. POSCO and Hyundai Steel are offsetting the impact of volume restrictions by focusing on exports of high value-added steel.

The U.S. Navy’s ship MRO and next-generation shipbuilding projects being pursued by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean are also matters that will not be affected by the election results. With the U.S. Navy's ship maintenance backlog, insufficient shipbuilding capabilities, and the reshaping of Indo-Pacific security intertwined, it is expected that the Department of Defense will continue to receive calls for ship outsourcing.

An official in charge of trade with the U.S. said, “The midterm elections are less about changing the broad framework of protectionism and more about the specific pressure tactics and negotiation variables for each company,” adding, “We are operating tailored scenario measures for each project, from adjusting conditions for LNG investment in Alaska to defending IRA subsidies.”

title: EV Sales Fall 23.8% Without Tax Credits [2026] - Tech Insider
description:
EV Sales Without Tax Credits: The Core Numbers Cox Automotive supplied the main volume data for the first half of 2026.
FAQ: EV Sales After the Tax Credit Ended When did the federal EV tax credit end?
Did EV sales improve from Q1 to Q2 2026?
What was the EV share of U.S. new-car sales in Q3 2026?
Have EV sales collapsed?
text:
The federal EV tax credit ended after September 30, 2025, and the first full year without it is now nearly over. The numbers sting but they do not read like a collapse. According to Cox Automotive, U.S. buyers took home 462,892 all-electric vehicles in the first half of 2026, a 23.8% drop from the same stretch of 2025. InsideEVs framed the picture in its headline, After A Year Without Tax Credits, EVs Are Down But Not Out, and the data backs that wording.

This analysis walks through what Cox Automotive, Kelley Blue Book, Edmunds and Inside Climate News have reported about EV sales without tax credits, why year-over-year math looks worse than the underlying demand, and what the shift means for hardware: battery packs, chargers and the trucks and crossovers that carry them. Automakers have already adjusted their plans, as our coverage of Rivian lifting its delivery guidance showed earlier this month.

One caution before the numbers. This piece uses only figures that named outlets have published. Where I calculate a number myself from their percentages, the text says so. Anything the sources have not confirmed, including specific models, prices and company targets, stays out of the story or appears in general terms.

·

Add Now

What Ended on September 30, 2025

The federal credit gave buyers up to $7,500 off a new electric car or light truck and up to $4,000 off a used vehicle. Both ended after September 30, 2025. That single date split the U.S. EV market into two periods: a buying surge as shoppers raced to claim the money, and a long stretch where every sticker price had to stand on its own.

Inside Climate News reported the pre-expiration surge at an 11% share of U.S. new-vehicle sales at its peak. The most recent quarter it cited showed 6%. That gap of five percentage points is the cleanest summary of what the credit was doing. A big chunk of the demand at the peak was buyers pulling purchases forward, and pulled-forward demand does not come back the next quarter.

The distinction matters for anyone reading the headline decline. A 23.8% drop sounds like a market in free fall. A drop measured against an artificially strong comparison period is a different story, and the next sections show how much of the decline sits in that comparison.

EV Sales Without Tax Credits: The Core Numbers

Cox Automotive supplied the main volume data for the first half of 2026. Kelley Blue Book added the most recent share figure. The table below collects every figure the sources confirmed.

Read the table as a trajectory, not a snapshot. Year-over-year declines narrowed from 27.3% in the first quarter to 20.5% in the second. Quarter-over-quarter volume rose. Share climbed from 5.8% to 6.5% between Q2 and Q3 according to Kelley Blue Book. None of these point to a boom, but all of them point upward from a low base.

The Quarterly Shape: A Weak Q1, A Partial Rebound

Cox Automotive’s Q2 figure of 247,226 vehicles, combined with its first-half total, lets us back into the first quarter. Subtract 247,226 from 462,892 and Q1 2026 lands at roughly 215,666 vehicles. That is my arithmetic from Cox’s published totals, not a number Cox printed, so treat it as an estimate.

Check it against the reported growth rate. Moving from about 215,666 to 247,226 is a gain of roughly 14.6%, which fits Cox’s statement that Q2 sales rose more than 14% from Q1. The pieces agree, which gives the derived Q1 figure some credibility.

The pattern tells a story about adjustment. Q1 2026 was a full quarter with no federal credit to lean on, and it posted the steepest year-over-year decline at 27.3%. By Q2 the decline eased to 20.5% while volume climbed. Dealers, automakers and shoppers had a quarter to reset price expectations, and sales responded.

August 2026: A 46.9% Drop With a Small Monthly Gain

August produced the most dramatic number in the dataset. Cox Automotive estimated 78,895 electric cars sold, which is 2.5% above July but 46.9% below August 2025. The monthly gain is small. The annual drop is huge. Both statements are true at once, and the reason is the comparison month.

August 2025 sat inside the rush to beat the September 30 deadline. Working backward from Cox’s percentage, that month came in around 148,600 vehicles by my calculation. July 2026 works out to about 77,000. So the market that sold nearly 150,000 EVs in a deadline-driven month now sells in the high 70,000s in a normal one. The gap, about 69,700 vehicles, is mostly the credit effect plus whatever demand it borrowed from later months.

The honest reading is that August 2026 shows the market’s resting pace without federal support. Whether that pace is a floor or a stepping stone is the question that matters for the rest of the year.

Market Share: From an 11% Peak to 6.5%

Share data shows the shift more cleanly than raw volume, because it adjusts for the size of the overall car market. Inside Climate News reported 11% at the pre-expiration peak and 6% in the most recent quarter it cited. Kelley Blue Book then reported a Q3 2026 share of 6.5% of U.S. new-car sales, up from 5.8% in Q2.

Be careful mixing those series. Different outlets count differently, and I cannot confirm that the 6% and the 5.8% describe the same quarter or method. What the sources do confirm is the direction: share fell hard after the credits ended, bottomed out in the mid-single digits, and has started to recover. A 0.7 point rise from Q2 to Q3 sounds modest, but it is a rise, and it arrived without any new federal incentive.

For hardware planners, that matters more than the monthly noise. A market that holds a share near 6% to 7% still moves hundreds of thousands of vehicles a year, which keeps battery plants, charger lines and software teams running, just at a lower throttle than the surge implied.

Why Edmunds Says EVs Have Not Fallen Off a Cliff

Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds, said EV sales had “not fallen off of a cliff.” His point lines up with the data above. A cliff would show volume dropping and staying down, with share sliding quarter after quarter. Instead, volume rose from Q1 to Q2, and Kelley Blue Book recorded share improving into Q3.

Drury’s phrase also fits the way the decline concentrates around one comparison period. Year-over-year percentages swing wildly when the earlier period includes a deadline rush. Analysts at Cox, Edmunds and Kelley Blue Book all have the same raw ingredients, and they read them in a similar way: weaker than 2025, steadier than the headlines suggest.

I would add one caveat of my own. Edmunds’ view is an expert’s read of a few quarters of data. A year without credits is a short window, and a move in interest rates, fuel prices or a major model launch could change the picture quickly in either direction.

How the Pre-Expiration Surge Distorts the Math

Deadline surges create two distortions. The first is a spike in the months before the deadline. The second is a hole afterward, because shoppers who would have bought in the following months bought early instead. Year-over-year comparisons then punish the post-deadline months twice, once against the spike period and once for the borrowed demand.

The table below uses Cox Automotive’s reported percentages to back into the implied 2025 comparison volumes. These are my rounded calculations, not Cox’s published figures, and they show how large the comparison base was.

The implied numbers show why August stands out. First-half 2025 averaged roughly 101,000 vehicles a month on my math, and August 2025 ran about 47% above that pace. Deadline buying pulled sales well above the normal run rate, so the 46.9% decline in August 2026 compares a regular month with an abnormal one.

What Buyers Lost: $7,500 on New, $4,000 on Used

New vehicles

The new-vehicle credit topped out at $7,500 for an electric car or light truck. For a shopper weighing a mid-priced electric crossover against a gas equivalent, that sum could erase most of the sticker gap. Without it, buyers lean harder on lease deals, manufacturer incentives and running-cost savings. Our report on the Blazer EV lease-end decision shows how that pressure plays out for drivers who have to decide what comes next when a lease expires.

Used vehicles

The used credit was up to $4,000, and it served a different buyer: someone priced out of new EVs who wanted a first electric car. Losing it hit the lower end of the market. The sources I reviewed do not break out used-EV sales volumes, so I will not guess at the size of that effect. The mechanism is clear though. Every dollar of credit removed raises the effective price for the shopper with the tightest budget.

The Hardware Angle: Batteries, Packs and Home Charging

With the credit gone, hardware cost becomes the main lever. Battery packs rank among the costliest parts of an EV, so every design change that cuts packaging, parts count or assembly steps feeds straight into price. Our piece on the four-module Cybercab battery pack and the earlier look at structural battery repair in the Model Y both show how packaging choices shape cost and repairability.

Home charging hardware sits on the other side of the ledger. A buyer who loses a $7,500 credit looks harder at every extra cost, and a wall charger counts. Our comparison of the EVDANCE charger against a Tesla wall unit covers a price gap of several hundred dollars between two ways of getting the same job done. For new owners on a tight budget, that kind of saving now matters.

Browse the rest of our hardware coverage for the chip, storage and device stories that sit next to this one. EV hardware increasingly shares supply chains, memory and power electronics with the rest of tech, and the cost pressure runs in both directions.

How Automakers Are Responding

The sources I have do not name specific automaker strategies for 2026, so I will keep this section to patterns visible in our own recent reporting and to general logic. When a subsidy disappears, manufacturers have three ways to respond: cut prices, move buyers into leases where incentives still work, or add value in the package. Each shows up somewhere in the current market.

Ford’s Fathom truck program is a useful example of the value-add route. Our report on the Fathom’s home backup feature covers a truck pitched partly on what it can do for a household beyond driving. The related look at how Ford’s unicastings cut parts addresses the cost side: fewer parts means a cheaper build, which is the same lever buyers lost when the credit left.

Rivian’s quarter offers another read. Our coverage of Rivian’s Q3 earnings shows how one EV maker is reporting results in a market where overall volume is lower than a year ago. One company’s results do not prove a market-wide recovery, so read it as a single data point.

Comparing the Five Sources Behind the Story

Five outlets supply the facts in this story, and each measures something slightly different. Knowing who measured what keeps readers from stacking incompatible numbers on top of each other.

Cox supplies volume, Kelley Blue Book supplies share, and Edmunds supplies interpretation. They converge on the same conclusion from different angles, which strengthens the case that the market has stabilized below its peak. When three independent measures point the same way, the odds of a data artifact fall.

Historical Context: A Policy Cliff, Not a Demand Cliff

The federal credit worked as the main national purchase incentive for EVs. When a policy like that disappears on a fixed date, markets respond in a predictable pattern. Demand surges into the deadline, falls off right after, and then settles at a level determined by price and product quality alone.

The U.S. now sits in the third phase of that pattern. The peak share of 11% reflected the surge. The trough near 6% reflected the hangover. The 6.5% Q3 reading from Kelley Blue Book suggests the market has begun building from a floor. I can only describe that arc with the data these outlets published, and I would avoid forecasting a precise recovery path from three quarters of observations.

The more useful frame for readers is that the market no longer receives a government-assisted boost. Everything that sells now sells on price, range, charging convenience and product appeal.

Market Impact on Suppliers, Charging and Used Inventory

Lower unit volume ripples through the supply chain. Battery makers, power-electronics suppliers and charger manufacturers all plan capacity against expected EV demand. A 23.8% first-half decline against 2025 means those plans have to flex, and companies with the lowest costs gain an edge when volume is tight.

Charging providers face a similar squeeze. Fewer new EVs on the road means slower growth in charging sessions, though the existing fleet keeps charging. Home hardware sellers feel it too, since a home charger often rides on the back of a new EV purchase.

The used market is harder to read. Without the $4,000 used credit, resale economics shift. I have no confirmed used-EV volume data in the sources for this story, so I flag the topic as an open question rather than a finding. Readers tracking residual values should watch Cox Automotive and Kelley Blue Book releases for that data.

Four Predictions for the Rest of 2026 and Early 2027

These are my analytical forecasts, not statements from any named source. They rest on the figures above and carry real uncertainty.

Year-over-year declines will narrow. Q4 2025 was already the first quarter without credits, so Q4 2026 faces a much easier comparison than Q3 did. Expect the percentage drop to shrink even if volume stays flat.

Share will stay in a 6% to 7% band through year-end. Kelley Blue Book’s 6.5% Q3 reading, up from 5.8%, supports slow improvement. A return toward 11% without a new incentive looks unlikely.

Hardware cost cuts will drive new launches. Parts-count reductions, simpler pack designs and bundled home-energy features will matter more than headline range, because buyers now pay full price.

Lease and incentive tactics will grow. Automakers will push price relief through channels they control rather than waiting for federal help.

The biggest swing factor is something none of these outlets can forecast: a policy change. A new federal incentive, or new state-level programs, would shift every number in this article. Until then, the market’s resting state is the one visible in the Q2 and Q3 data.

What to Watch Next

Three data releases will settle most of the open questions. First, Cox Automotive’s Q3 sales report should show whether volume followed share upward. Second, the Q4 figures will reveal how the market behaves once it laps the first post-credit quarter. Third, any used-EV data from Cox or Kelley Blue Book will show how the loss of the $4,000 credit changed the entry point for budget buyers.

For now, the supported conclusion is narrow but clear. EV sales without tax credits are lower than they were during the 2025 surge, they have stopped falling quarter by quarter, and the share is inching back up. Down but not out remains an accurate summary.

FAQ: EV Sales After the Tax Credit Ended

When did the federal EV tax credit end? The credits ended after September 30, 2025. They offered up to $7,500 for a new electric car or light truck and up to $4,000 for a used vehicle.

How many EVs did Americans buy in the first half of 2026? Cox Automotive counted 462,892 all-electric vehicles, down 23.8% from the first half of 2025.

Did EV sales improve from Q1 to Q2 2026? Yes. Cox Automotive reported that Q2 sales of 247,226 rose more than 14% from Q1. Year-over-year, the decline eased from 27.3% in Q1 to 20.5% in Q2.

What was the EV share of U.S. new-car sales in Q3 2026? Kelley Blue Book reported 6.5%, up from 5.8% in Q2. Inside Climate News cited a peak of 11% during the pre-expiration surge and 6% in a later quarter.

Why did August 2026 show a 46.9% decline? Cox Automotive estimated 78,895 sales in August 2026, which was 2.5% above July. The 46.9% annual drop reflects a comparison against August 2025, when buyers rushed to beat the credit deadline.

Have EV sales collapsed? Not by the available evidence. Edmunds’ Ivan Drury said EV sales had “not fallen off of a cliff,” and volume and share data from Cox Automotive and Kelley Blue Book show stabilization and a modest rise since Q1.

text:
Rare earth companies are attracting the attention of investors as the U.S. looks to reduce its reliance on overseas suppliers of these critical minerals.

From defense technology to electric vehicles to the most innovative technological innovations shaping the world today, at their core are the 17 elements that are grouped into the category of "rare earths".

So, it is clear why a reliable supply is important.

However, developing new mines can take years, while processing rare earths into usable materials presents its own technical and financial challenges. It is a timely, expensive process and one that doesn't help the U.S. gain momentum in the short-to-medium term.

Some companies have found a different solution, and Tactical Resources (Nasdaq:TREO) is one of them.

Rather than starting a new mining operation, it is targeting rare earth-enriched material that has already been mined and stockpiled.

A different way to source rare earths

Traditionally, for a rare earth company to begin mining, they need to identify a deposit, develop the mine, and construct the necessary infrastructure required before the company can even begin production. This is a costly and time-consuming activity.

Tactical Resources, however, is taking a different approach.

Its Peak Project in West Texas is focused on rare earth-enriched material that is already stockpiled at the existing Sierra Blanca Quarry, which is currently also used to produce ballast for the Union Pacific Railway.

Instead of excavating a new deposit, Tactical Resources aims to recover valuable rare earth elements from 1.5 million tonnes of material that is lying there, already mined and stockpiled.

The advantage is that this means that Tactical can skip the exploration, excavation, and infrastructure development associated with a conventional mining project and a lot of the costs that come with it.

Why Tactical's processing approach matters

It isn't just the use of tailings that sets Tactical Resources apart from many other rare earth miners; it is also how they intend to process the minerals.

Rare earths aren't just sitting around waiting to be found.

In fact, the name rare earths gives a picture of the difficulty of mining the material. Believe it or not, rare earths are not rare; in fact, they are very abundant. The issue is that they are rarely found in high concentrations in a large, convenient, and mineable.

Rare earth processing usually involves crushing and grinding the ore, concentrating the rare earth-bearing minerals, chemically extracting them, and then separating and purifying the individual elements.

Tactical Resources hopes to simplify that sequence. It is using a process known as direct leaching.

Rather than mining a new deposit, Tactical aims to extract rare earth elements directly from material that has already been mined, crushed, and stockpiled at the Sierra Blanca Quarry. Its proposed direct-leaching process uses a chemical solution to recover the elements, potentially avoiding some of the processing stages required by conventional rare earth projects.

Tactical Resources calls its Peak Project one of the few direct-leach-extractable rare earths projects in the world.

Can Tactical turn its different approach into a viable business?

There is no question that Tactical's strategy aligns with the US effort to develop domestic sources of critical minerals and reduce reliance on overseas supply chains.

In fact, given Tactical's Peak Project, both through the use of an existing stockpile of material or tailings and its use of direct leaching as a way to process, there is an argument that it offers a way for rare earth supply to come online faster than some alternatives if successful.

However, the company remains at an early stage of development.

Tactical has several milestones ahead before the question of whether it can turn potential into profitable business can be answered.

Its next phase of work is expected to focus on refining the processing method, assessing permitting requirements, advancing engineering plans and developing relationships with potential downstream partners. These steps should help establish what it would take to move the Peak Project towards commercial production.

If it can overcome these challenges, Tactical could offer a different route towards domestic rare earth production, using material that is already above ground. But until the economics and processing performance are established, the potential advantages remain unproven.

About Tactical Resources

Tactical Resources is a natural resources company focused on rare earth elements critical to advanced technologies, including semiconductors, electric vehicles, robotics, aerospace systems, and national defense applications. The Company is advancing the Peak Project in Hudspeth County, Texas, as part of its strategy to help build a secure domestic supply chain, reduce reliance on foreign-controlled sources and strengthen North American critical mineral security.

Tactical Resources is also pursuing innovative metallurgical processing and separation technologies designed to improve the economics, scalability, and sustainability of rare earth production. Through this integrated approach, the Company aims to become a key participant in the rapidly growing U.S. critical minerals ecosystem.
