If the agency terminates consultation, "the head of the agency or an Assistant Secretary or other officer with major department-wide or agency-wide responsibilities" must submit its findings for termination to the ACHP for comment, at which point the ACHP has 45 days to respond to the decision and provide comments.91 The head of the federal agency is then required to "take into account the Council's comments in reaching a final decision on the undertaking" but is not required to revise its initial decision based on ACHP comments.92 The head of the agency must prepare a summary that contains the rationale for the decision and evidence of consideration of the ACHP's comments. This summary is then provided to the ACHP and all consulting parties and made available to the public.93 Section 110(l) of the NHPA prohibits the head of the agency from delegating the responsibility to document a decision in the event an agreement between parties is not reached.94

As discussed above, if an agency determines that a proposed undertaking will result in adverse effects, BAAJA would require the agency to complete and submit a "report" that documents various such findings to the applicable entities (e.g., SHPO, THPO) for review. Within 90 days of submission of the report discussed above, BAAJA would require agencies, in consultation with relevant entities, to (1) make a determination that the adverse effects of the undertaking would not diminish the integrity of the historic property so as to make it ineligible for listing on the National Register; (2) make a determination that other considerations outweigh the historic preservation concerns raised by potential adverse effects;95 or (3) enter into an agreement with the applicable entity or entities that describes how the adverse effects would be avoided, minimized, or mitigated. If an agreement is not reached within 90 days, agencies must engage applicable entities in a 60-day consultation period. If no agreement is reached at the end of this period, BAAJA would require the agency to request comments from the ACHP. The ACHP would have 45 days to submit comments to the relevant agency. The head of the federal agency then would have 30 days to make a final determination on the undertaking that "demonstrates how the formal advisory comments were considered." The bill also would authorize the head of the agency to delegate an agency official to make such a determination. BAAJA would not require additional documentation nor notification of the ACHP, consulting parties, or the public.

Multiple Determinations

At present, NHPA regulations do not explicitly limit what is known as project "segmentation."96 Segmentation occurs when a single project or multiple closely related projects are broken up into small pieces and permitted and evaluated separately, potentially obscuring the project's or projects' full impact on historic properties. Nonetheless, the ACHP has issued comments that indicate that it believes that segmentation violates the NHPA.97 For instance, in comments submitted to the USACE in 2020, the ACHP stated that the USACE was engaged in segmenting a single project that required multiple USACE permits by evaluating the impact on historic properties separately for each permit, not for the project as a whole.98 The comments stated: "The ACHP acknowledges that at times, a federal agency may have limited jurisdiction over a small portion of a larger undertaking. However, in such cases, the federal agency remains responsible for considering the effects of the larger undertaking on historic properties beyond areas of its specific jurisdiction."99

Section 306108(c)(2) as amended by BAAJA would appear to affirmatively authorize project segmentation under certain circumstances. Where an undertaking "involves multiple corridors or large land areas," the federal agency would be able to issue multiple determinations for a single undertaking "in a phased process."

"54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(4) – Lead Federal Agency"

Current ACHP regulations authorize, but do not require, the designation of a lead federal agency to oversee compliance with Section 106 in instances where more than one agency may be involved in an undertaking.100 If no lead agency is designated, each agency remains individually responsible for compliance with Section 106.

BAAJA would require the designation of a lead federal agency within 15 days of an agency receiving "notice of a proposed undertaking." BAAJA does not specify how such notification would be conveyed to the agency or what constitutes "notice" for the purposes of this provision. If no lead agency were designated within 15 days, BAAJA would require the Secretary of the Interior to designate a lead agency.101 In instances wherein a lead federal agency has been designated for the purposes of complying with NEPA, that agency would be required to serve as the lead agency for the purposes of Section 106 as well, unless the agencies involved determine collectively that another agency is better suited to carry out the NHPA duties.

"54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(5) – Timelines for Consultation"

Current ACHP regulations do not establish when Section 106 consultation must begin (see "54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(2) – Initiation and Report"). Once Section 106 consultation is initiated, federal agencies are required to make certain determinations or findings at various stages of the review process and provide SHPOs and THPOs the opportunity to concur or object based on the documentation provided.102 The regulations generally require SHPOs and THPOs to respond within 30 days of receipt of such determinations or findings.103 If a SHPO or THPO fails to respond during this window, the agency is authorized to proceed to the next step in the process based on the finding or determination, or consult with the ACHP in lieu of the SHPO/THPO104. If a SHPO/THPO re-enters the Section 106 process at a later date, the agency official is not required to reconsider previous findings or determinations; however, consultation with the relevant SHPO/THPO at subsequent stages of the review process is still required.105 Although current regulations specify certain timelines at certain points in the review process, as discussed above, neither the NHPA nor the current regulations impose timelines around consultation and the review process more broadly.

BAAJA would establish certain initiation triggers and completion deadlines for any consultation resulting from Section 106 reviews provided for under the bill.106 Specifically, BAAJA would tie "any consultation with respect to the project, activity, or program" to the review process conducted pursuant to NEPA, if such an undertaking requires the preparation of an environmental document under that law.107 BAAJA would require agencies to initiate Section 106 review no later than the date on which environmental review is initiated and to complete any review process no later than the date on which an environmental document under that law is required to be completed.108

If the consultation process is not completed by the deadline for the completion of the relevant environmental document under NEPA, BAAJA would require that the head of the relevant SHPO or THPO devote 50% of each work week to completing the NHPA process.109 The requirement would also apply to any federal official in the Senior Executive Service with supervisory authority over employees at a federal agency with consultation responsibilities. It is not clear from BAAJA whether missing the NEPA deadline, but ultimately completing the NHPA process through the devotion of extra staff time, would be considered inconsistent with the statute under the program audit provisions discussed above (see "Subsection (b) – Program Evaluation"). The audit provisions could be interpreted to allow completion of the NHPA process pursuant to the NHPA because completing via this section would still be complying with the statute even if a deadline were missed.

BAAJA would create a new cause of action for a project proponent to sue an agency in federal district court to enforce the completion of the NHPA process concurrently with the NEPA process. Under the bill, where a court finds that the agency failed to comply with this deadline, the court could issue an injunction—a court order directing the agency to take action—to "give effect" to the deadline provision. This provision of BAAJA also would direct a court to retain jurisdiction over the case after it issued its order to the agency to ensure that the agency complied with the order.

BAAJA also would limit an agency's obligations to consult with or consider objections from SHPOs, THPOs, or other consulting parties if they failed to respond within 30 days of receiving a "request for review of any report or finding." As discussed above, BAAJA would require an agency to "seek, discuss, as appropriate, and incorporate, as applicable" information from applicable SHPOs, THPOs, and other entities prior to determining the APE and identifying historic properties. The bill also would require an agency, in instances where it is determined there will be adverse effects associated with an undertaking, to submit a "report" to applicable SHPOs, THPOs, and other entities for review. Although BAAJA would establish a 90-day window for consultation following the submission of this report, this provision appears to authorize agencies to move forward with issuing determinations related to undertakings if the applicable SHPOs, THPOs, or other entities did not provide an initial response within a more limited 30-day window. The bill would require an agency to provide a response to the applicable entities if, within the 30-day window, they offered "substantive objections" to certain findings or information contained in the report. If such objections were not "substantive" in nature, the agency could move forward with issuing a determination. The bill does not provide additional context for how an objection may be deemed "substantive" in nature. Whether an objection is "substantive" will likely be left to agencies and the courts to define. In addition, it is unclear how this 30-day window interacts with other consultation and response timelines established elsewhere in the bill.

"54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(6) – Coordination with NEPA"

Current regulations and ACHP implementing guidance encourage federal agencies to use their broad environmental review process, carried out under NEPA, as an "umbrella" compliance process.110 However, compliance with reviews required under NEPA does not substitute for an agency's compliance with the requirements under Section 106.

BAAJA would allow agencies to use draft documents prepared as part of an environmental review conducted under NEPA to comply with the Section 106 requirements as proposed in BAAJA.111 Specifically, BAAJA would allow agencies to submit such documents to comply with the reporting requirements outlined above. Agencies would be required to provide notice of their "intent to use the environmental document for such purposes" to the applicable SHPO, THPO, or other consulting entities.

"54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(7) – Programmatic Agreements"

Current regulations authorize—but do not require—federal agencies to work with the ACHP to establish alternative methods for meeting their obligations under Section 106, known as "program alternatives."112 Program alternatives allow federal agencies to work with the ACHP and SHPOs and THPOs to tailor the Section 106 process to meet their needs. The most commonly used program alternative is a programmatic agreement (PA). PAs allow agencies to negotiate agreements with the ACHP to govern Section 106 compliance for an individual agency program, complex project, or group of related undertakings.113 PAs are typically developed in consultation with the relevant SHPOs, THPOs, and other entities depending on the type of activities, programs, or geographic region(s) covered by the PA.114

BAAJA would require federal agencies to consult with the ACHP to develop and implement PAs that covered certain specified categories of undertakings. The bill would separately authorize—but not require—SHPOs and THPOs to develop and implement PAs "within their applicable jurisdiction" to govern similar categories of undertakings. In instances where an agency and a SHPO or THPO each have a PA governing the same category of undertaking, BAAJA would require the SHPO or THPO PA to apply. Given that PAs typically operate as formal agreements negotiated between a federal agency and SHPOs, THPOs, and other applicable entities to govern an alternative compliance procedure for Section 106, it is unclear how this provision would be implemented. BAAJA appears to provide for PAs to be established independently by both an agency and a SHPO or THPO but does not expand on whether or how an agreement would be implemented for the purposes of meeting consultation requirements established elsewhere in the bill.

"54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(8) – Qualified Historic Preservation Officers"

As discussed above (see "Subsection (b) – Program Evaluation"), the NHPA establishes certain requirements for state programs to be approved for the purposes of carrying out certain responsibilities under the law, including consultation pursuant to Section 106. Specifically, the law requires state programs to employ or appoint "such professionally qualified staff as may be necessary."115 Implementing regulations require that state program staff include a professionally qualified architectural historian, historian, and archeologist.116 To be "qualified" for these purposes, the regulations specify that staff must meet the Secretary of the Interior Professional Qualifications Standards, which establish minimum educational and professional experience standards for certain historic preservation disciplines.117 In 2002, NPS proposed regulations to establish similar qualification standards for tribal programs, with certain modifications and additional flexibilities to take into account their "unique cultural settings, smaller workloads, more limited program scopes, and limited funding" as compared to state programs.118 These regulations were not finalized.

BAAJA would require the Secretary of the Interior to collaborate with THPOs, tribal leaders, and relevant nonprofit organizations to develop "standard requirements" for THPOs. Such requirements would be required to reflect the "traditional knowledge, expertise, and access to traditional cultural leaders required for a successful tribal historic preservation program."

"54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(9) – Judicial Review"

Under current law, Sections 701-706 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) govern legal challenges to agency compliance with the NHPA.119 NHPA suits brought pursuant to the APA are subject to a six-year statute of limitations.120 These suits are brought in the federal district courts (trial courts).121 Where a court finds legal deficiencies in the agency's compliance with the NHPA, the court may vacate (i.e., nullify), remand (with or without vacatur), or preliminarily or permanently enjoin (i.e., stop) an agency action or in circumstances stop or limit the activities of a project proponent.122 Courts have the discretion to choose one or multiple of these remedies that best address the specific case before it.123

To bring a claim under the APA, a plaintiff need only be "adversely affected or aggrieved" by a final agency action.124 Separately, Article III of the Constitution limits the federal courts' jurisdiction to plaintiffs who have suffered a concrete and particularized injury that is fairly traceable to the conduct of the defendant and likely to be redressed by a favorable court decision.125 Neither the APA nor the NHPA currently limits suits challenging compliance with the NHPA to those who participated in the comment process.126 For claims challenging compliance with the NHPA, the APA provides for original jurisdiction in the federal district courts.127 Venue is determined by Section 1391 of Title 28 of the U.S. Code, but as a practical matter a case brought pursuant to the APA can be brought in the district courts of Washington, D.C., or the district or districts in which an agency action causes a legal harm.

The judicial review provisions of the NHPA portion of BAAJA would work a significant change to judicial review of NHPA claims. BAAJA would limit the remedies available after a court has determined the agency violated the NHPA to remand without vacatur only. Allowing only remand without vacatur would remove the ability of a court to vacate (i.e., nullify) an agency action or stop an agency action with an injunction. A plaintiff's only available remedy under BAAJA for violations of the NHPA would be an order from a court instructing the agency to address whatever legal deficiencies the court identified in its decision. In the meantime, the agency action and any construction premised on the agency action could continue. Even a total refusal to engage in the NHPA process likely would not be a basis for enjoining or vacating the federal undertaking. Conversely, while this section of BAAJA would limit remedies for violations of the NHPA, it would not limit them for violations of other statutes. It is possible that were a plaintiff to allege violations of the NHPA in addition to some other statute (e.g., the Endangered Species Act), a court may still be able to vacate or enjoin the undertaking if the court found that the agency violated that other statute.

Whether violations of the APA's "contrary to law" or "arbitrary and capricious" standards would qualify for the exception to the limitation on remedies remains unclear. Section 706 of the APA specifies several bases on which a reviewing court shall "hold unlawful and set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions"; many of these bases refer back to the statute that underlies the action an agency took and that specifies the procedures the agency is required to observe to take that action.128 For example, the APA permits courts to vacate agency action that is "contrary to law,"129 but the law in question is often some other statute. In the NHPA context, a claim that an agency failed to comply with the procedures of the NHPA could satisfy the APA's "contrary to law" standard and accordingly permit a court to vacate the agency action. The limits on judicial review in BAAJA, however, would appear to bar vacatur in this circumstance.

The APA's Section 706's direction to courts to vacate agency action that is "arbitrary and capricious" could potentially permit a court to vacate or enjoin agency action that fits this description.130 Agencies can violate this standard by either taking unreasonable action or failing to explain their action reasonably.131 As a practical matter, agencies often attempt to conform their actions to avoid being found to have acted in an "arbitrary and capricious" manner. In this way, the APA's standard could be seen to impose a reasonableness standard on agency action despite the fact that by its own terms the APA's arbitrary and capricious standard is a direction to courts on how to review agency action rather than a direction to agencies to act reasonably. It is possible, although unlikely, that in a case where a court finds that an agency action taken as a part of the NHPA process was arbitrary and capricious, a court might find that the APA violation falls within the scope of the exception to the limits on remedies for violations of the NHPA and could vacate or enjoin that undertaking.

BAAJA would also bar the availability of preliminary injunctions for potential violations of the NHPA, but not for potential violations of other federal laws.132 The bill would otherwise codify the judicially created standard for issuing a preliminary injunction, which requires a plaintiff to show that it is likely to succeed on the merits of its claims, faces irreparable harm, the balance of equities favors the injunction, and the injunction is in the public interest.133

Under BAAJA, the duration of a preliminary injunction also would be limited to the time the court finds is reasonably necessary to take the agency to cure any legal deficiencies identified in the court's determination of the likelihood the plaintiff will succeed on its non-NHPA-related legal claims and only long enough to prevent any irreparable harm to the plaintiff. Under current law, preliminary injunctions last until the final resolution of the case on the merits unless an intervening court order stays or dissolves the injunction.134 It is unclear how this duration requirement could be implemented given that at the preliminary injunction stage of litigation, a court has not conclusively determined that the agency in fact did violate the law. Moreover, there is no mechanism for a court to preliminarily remand the agency action to the agency. Both the ultimate legality of the agency action and the ability to remand to the agency to cure any legal deficiencies are only determined at the end of the litigation, not while the litigation is proceeding.

BAAJA would also limit who could bring suit claiming violations of the NHPA. In order to bring a claim, under the bill, plaintiffs would be required to file their suit within 150 days after the approval of the federal undertaking being made public or the notification of the relevant SHPO or THPO, whichever is later (see "54 U.S.C. §306108(a)(3) – Made Public"). Plaintiffs would have to have first submitted a comment during a public comment period to the extent there was one, and their comment would have to have been substantive, unique, and sufficiently detailed to put the federal agency on notice as to the issue for which the plaintiffs seek review, and any future legal challenge would be required to be based on the same subject matter as the comment. The consultation procedures in BAAJA, however, would not provide for public comment during the NHPA process. With no public comment required, this provision may not apply to plaintiffs challenging an agency's compliance with the NHPA process.135

In addition, under the bill, a plaintiff would have to have suffered or be in danger of imminently suffering a direct harm from the federal undertaking. Exactly what kind of harm would qualify as a "direct harm" is not further defined in the bill. BAAJA does not indicate whether the "direct harm" language would add a new limit to a plaintiff's ability to bring a claim under the NHPA or restates the current constitutional standing requirement.

The "direct harm" limitation and the commenting requirement would not apply to SHPOs, THPOs, local governments, NHOs, or Indian Tribes so long as they provided a detailed comment during the consultation process and their subsequent legal claim was related to the comment.

BAAJA would direct all NHPA claims to the federal courts of appeals, as well as claims based on other statutes related to the same federal undertaking. The bill does not include a venue provision identifying which court or courts of appeals among the 13 federal courts of appeals would be the proper court in which to bring claims. Also, it is likely that sweeping related claims under different statutes into the federal courts of appeals would also subject those claims to the duration limits in the preliminary injunction provisions of BAAJA. If it is the case that the preliminary injunction limitations in BAAJA do apply, preliminary injunctions issued for likely violations of statutes other than the NHPA may be limited in their duration as discussed above.

BAAJA also would direct the reviewing court to give "substantial deference" to the agency in its review of whether an undertaking complies with the NHPA and would prohibit the court from substituting its judgement for that of the agency. This language largely codifies current Supreme Court precedent on the meaning of the arbitrary and capricious review standard generally, and judicial review of compliance with NEPA in particular.136 The arbitrary and capricious standard of review applies to a court's review of an agency's exercise of any policymaking discretion delegated to it by statute.137 In practice, this standard often applies to an agency's application of law to the facts it gathered in its administrative process. The arbitrary and capricious standard does not apply to agency interpretations of law, which after the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo must be reviewed without deference to the agency's interpretation.138

"54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(10) – Challenges to Programmatic Agreements"

This provision would limit legal challenges to PAs to parties to those agreements. It also would strip the federal courts of jurisdiction over any legal challenge related to the implementation of a PA brought by a plaintiff not a party to the PA. It is not clear how this provision would be implemented given BAAJA's amendments to 54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(7) – Programmatic Agreements. In those amendments, both federal agencies and SHPOs and THPOs appear to gain the ability to issue PAs unilaterally, without the agreement of another party. With the possibility that a PA may have no parties to the agreement, it appears that legal challenges to those PAs would be entirely unavailable for any person.

"54 U.S.C. §306108(d) No Post-Deadline Requirement for Reinitiation"

For the purposes of the NHPA and Section 106, a "historic property" includes properties that are both already listed on, or eligible for listing on, the National Register.139 Current regulations specify that after identifying the APE for a particular undertaking, agencies are required to identify any historic properties located in the APE, in consultation with the SHPO or THPO. For properties not already listed on the National Register, this identification process often includes conducting cultural resource surveys within the APE, evaluating primary research and past studies, and consulting with SHPOs and THPOs. When disagreements occur regarding whether a potential property should be considered "historic" for the purposes of Section 106, current regulations specify that the agency "shall obtain a determination of eligibility" from the Secretary pursuant to regulations outlining National Register criteria.140 In addition, ACHP regulations provide for certain agency requirements in the event that historic properties are discovered or unanticipated effects on historic properties are found after Section 106 review is completed.141

The BAAJA provision would specify that any "identification of a property for, nomination of a property to, or listing of a property on the National Register," which occurs after an agency's initiation of Section 106, would not require the agency to "delay, reopen, supplement, or otherwise modify the review or consultation process under this section." As discussed above, the proposed bill would require agencies to identify any historic properties within an APE following a determination that a proposed project, activity, or program is an undertaking. Agencies are required to "seek, discuss, as appropriate, and incorporate, as applicable" information from SHPOs, THPOs, and other entities, if such information is provided within 30 days of the request from the agency; consultation at this stage of the review would not be required.142 Although this provision does not preclude the subsequent identification of historic properties after this window, it appears to limit the agency's responsibility to consider potential effects to such properties. In addition, subsequent discoveries or identification of historic properties would not trigger additional consultation with relevant parties.

Subsection (d) – Conforming Amendment

As discussed above, Section 110(l) prohibits the head of the agency from delegating the responsibility to document a decision for the purposes of Section 106 review (see "54 U.S.C. §306108(c)(3) – Determination"). BAAJA would authorize such delegation to occur. This provision conforms with that new authority provided in BAAJA by striking the prohibition on delegation found in Section 110(l), codified at 54 U.S.C. §306114.

Section 2302 – Funding for the Historic Preservation Fund; Use and Availability; Grants for Tribal Historic Preservation Officers; Additional Funding

The HPF—administered by NPS—is the primary source of funding for federal preservation awards to states, tribes, local governments, and nonprofit organizations. Although federal funding for historic preservation was available under the 1966 NHPA and subsequent amendments in 1970 and 1973, Congress did not officially establish the HPF to carry out the activities specified in NHPA until 1976.143

The HPF typically funds historic preservation activities in two ways: (1) formula-based apportionment grants and (2) competitive grant programs.144 Historically, most HPF appropriated funds have been used to provide formula-based matching grants-in-aid to SHPOs and THPOs and sub-grants to certified local governments (CLGs). Congress also has provided appropriations for additional competitive grant programs that fund specific historic preservation activities.145

Subsection (a) – Funding for Historic Preservation Fund

Pursuant to the NHPA, the HPF is authorized to receive deposits of $150 million annually.146 Deposits to the fund are generally sourced from revenue generated by outer continental shelf (OCS) oil and gas receipts.147 In 2016, Congress reauthorized deposits of $150 million annually into the HPF for FY2017 through FY2023.148 Since FY2023, extensions of HPF's authorization of deposits have generally occurred on an annual basis. Most recently, the HPF was reauthorized at $150 million per year through FY2026.149

Section 2302(a) of BAAJA would amend 54 U.S.C. §303102 by authorizing to be appropriated deposits of $200 million annually for FY2027 through FY2036 to the HPF. It appears that deposits into the HPF would no longer be mandatory appropriations, as the bill does not identify a dedicated funding source for deposits to the HPF. As a result, unless otherwise specified in subsequent laws, it appears that appropriations made to the HPF would derive from the General Fund of the U.S. Treasury starting in FY2027.

Subsection (b) – Use and Availability

Although deposits into the HPF are mandatory, the funding is available for expenditure only to the extent appropriated by Congress.150 Since the HPF's establishment, annual appropriations from the account have typically been less than the deposited amount. Until FY2022, Congress had never appropriated the full annual deposit of $150 million for the fund in a single fiscal year (not counting emergency supplemental appropriations); however, appropriations have generally increased over the past decade and in certain years have exceeded the annual deposit.151 Recent estimates place the unobligated balance for the HPF at $3.4 billion.152

BAAJA would amend 54 U.S.C. §303103 by making any deposits for FY2027 and subsequent years available "without further appropriation or fiscal year limitation," starting in FY2028. It is not specified whether BAAJA would affect the availability for appropriation of the accrued unobligated balance in the HPF.153

Subsection (c) – Grants for Tribal Historic Preservation Officers

Since FY1996, NPS has awarded annual formula-based grants to THPOs. Eligibility for grants under the THPO grant program is limited to federally recognized Tribes that have signed agreements with NPS designating them as having an approved THPO.154 For reference, in 1996, the first year of the program, 12 tribes had approved THPOs. Since then, the number of approved THPOs has increased, and as of January 2026, there were 235 approved THPOs.155 Over the last decade, grants-in-aid for THPOs have risen by 71% after adjusting for inflation;156 however, whether this increase is adequate to keep pace with the increase in authorized THPOs has been debated.157

text:
The 81st Geneva Motor Show will be the stage for a series of major new vehicle and customer focused technology announcements by Ford.

Ford of Europe Chairman and CEO Stephen T. Odell will unveil a groundbreaking new vehicle during a Ford news conference on March 1 at the Ford stand. The Ford show stand in Geneva will be packed with four new additions to its upcoming product range and highlighting exclusive Ford technologies designed to significantly enhance the driving experience for customers.

Ford also plans the European debut of the C-MAX Energi, a pre-production version of the plug-in hybrid first shown at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit, that will launch in Europe in 2013. It will be joined by a C-MAX HEV when they both go on sale in Europe in 2013. They offer low fuel consumption and emissions as well as a distinctive body design and a flexible interior.The vehicle will be built at Ford’s Valencia plant in Spain.

The all-new Ford Ranger Wildtrak is making its global debut at the 2011 Geneva Motor Show, a sporty compact pickup that delivers impressive power and safety, excellent fuel efficiency and significant capability. Due to go on sale in the UK towards the end of this year, the new Ford Ranger will feature a range of class-leading safety and "smart" technologies to make it easier, safer and more fun to drive than ever before.

Ford’s vision for a sleeker, sportier and more stylish compact SUV makes its European debut at the 2011 Geneva Motor Show. First shown at the North American International Auto Show in January, the Ford Vertrek concept signals the direction of the next-generation Kuga, with leading design and fuel efficiency.

The Vertrek concept is based on Ford’s global C-segment platform, which includes the all-new Ford Focus range and the latest C-MAX and Grand C-MAX multi-activity vehicles.

The all-new Focus Electric, Ford’s first-ever all-electric passenger car, was unveiled at the North American International Auto Show in January and comes to Europe in 2012. The zero emission, fuel-free, version of Ford’s popular compact car will be a flagship for the company’s growing fleet of hybrid, plug-in hybrid and all-electric vehicles to go on sale in Europe in 2012 and North America by 2013.

Focus Electric is designed to offer sufficient range to cover the majority of daily driving habits and will introduce new features developed especially for electric vehicles which encourage efficient driving style whilst maximising driver enjoyment.

Ford’s commitment to a global vehicle electrification strategy is further demonstrated by a show car development of its zero-emission Transit Connect Electric in Geneva.

Based on the Transit Connect Kombi it is one of several electric Ford vehicles currently on test in the UK and features the same battery electric power train as the Transit Connect Electric Van, which goes on sale in the UK later this year.

Developed in conjunction with Ford’s US-based electric vehicles partner Azure Dynamics, it has a proprietary Force Drive™ battery electric drive train powered by an advanced battery pack designed by Johnson Controls-Saft.

Ford is boosting its flagship large car family with a new 114g/km CO2 Mondeo ECOnetic and introducing a range of additional powertrain enhancements for its Mondeo, S-MAX and Galaxy models.

A new and efficient 1.6-litre Ford Duratorq TDCi, with peak power of 115 PS, has been added to the comprehensive range of engines offered in Ford’s large cars. At the same time the Ford Auto-Start-Stop system is being made available for this small displacement diesel engine, as well as for the recently introduced 1.6-litre Ford EcoBoost engine (160 PS).

The combination of the 1.6-litre Duratorq TDCi and Ford Auto-Start-Stop system also builds a solid foundation for the new Ford Mondeo ECOnetic, which boasts homologated CO2 emissions as low as 114 g/km.

Ford's small car has a new eye-catching styling scheme. The new Metal Ka is part of Ford’s Individual programme. Sitting alongside the established Ka models, the Metal Ka will come to the UK in April.

Ford's all-new Fiesta RS World Rally Car in full team livery will be displayed at the Geneva Motor Show, straight from its debut appearance at Rally Sweden, first round of the 2011 World Rally Championship. Ford’s four-wheel drive WRC challenger is derived from the best-selling Fiesta road car and developed from the 2010 Monte Carlo Rally-winning Fiesta S2000 rally car by the Blue Oval's long-term British-based partner M-Sport, with support from Ford of Europe.

text:
Borgwarner Inc ((BWA)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

BorgWarner Inc’s latest earnings call struck an upbeat tone despite clear macro and segment-specific headwinds. Executives highlighted expanding margins, stronger EPS, accelerating eProduct growth and robust cash generation that is being aggressively returned to shareholders. These positives were framed as outweighing weaker auto production, battery-business softness and limited near-term visibility in some new industrial lines.

Profitability Holds Up As Production Slows

Third-quarter sales came in just under $3.5 billion, but profitability improved even as global vehicle production declined. Adjusted operating margin rose to 10.9% from 10.7% a year ago, and adjusted EPS climbed 12%, or $0.15 per share. Management credited ongoing cost-reduction actions and disciplined execution across its core operations.

EV-Linked eProduct Sales Deliver Double-Digit Growth

Light vehicle eProduct sales reached $630 million in the quarter, jumping 33% year on year, with Europe a key driver. PowerDrive Systems sales increased about 20% on a reported basis, while overall light vehicle eProduct growth was roughly 32%, underscoring BorgWarner’s traction in electrified powertrain solutions despite broader market softness.

New Awards Extend Visibility Across Combustion And EV

The company secured nine new business awards that span both foundational and eProduct portfolios. Wins include engine control modules for a high-volume internal-combustion pickup platform running through 2034, turbocharger programs in South America and Europe, three e-motor awards in China and a next-generation high-voltage inverter for future battery-electric vehicles.

Aluminum Wire E-Motor Targets Cost And Weight

BorgWarner announced its first commercial award for aluminum wire e-motor technology with a major Chinese automaker. The design maintains peak torque and power versus traditional copper wire motors while cutting wire weight by more than 60% and wire cost by over 80%, positioning the product as a compelling option for cost-sensitive EV platforms.

Turbine Generator Moves Toward Production

The turbine generator program made notable progress, with external demonstrations set to expand in the fourth quarter amid strong customer interest. Subsystem UL certification is largely complete, system-level work is underway, construction of the North Carolina final assembly plant is finished and production trials are scheduled to begin by year-end.

Data Center Demand Underpins Turbine Backlog

Management reported a strong backlog and demand for the turbine generator from data center customers, including multiple hyperscalers. Ongoing discussions focus on technical requirements such as tolerances, reliability, uptime, efficiency and emissions, as well as speed to market, signaling potential for a meaningful new revenue stream.

Battery Storage Platform Tracks Toward 2027 Launch

Development of BorgWarner’s battery energy storage system continues to advance, with customer validation and UL compliance progressing well. The company sees solid engagement across both NMC and LFP cells and still views the product as on track to be ready for production in 2027, positioning it for future data center and industrial energy applications.

Microgrid Inverter Draws Interest On Efficiency Edge

Microgrid inverter samples have been shipped to seven customers, with further outreach underway. Early feedback suggests system efficiency is ahead of peers, while customers also favor the product’s value proposition, U.S. manufacturing footprint and high-voltage, power-dense liquid-cooled electronics expertise, and initial quoting has started with a first major customer.

Industrial Power Electronics Portfolio Expands Inside The Rack

To broaden its industrial offering, BorgWarner developed an 800-volt power supply unit aimed at data center applications. Management noted the PSU opens new opportunities because it is installed inside the data center near servers, complementing the microgrid inverter, which is deployed outside in grid-related infrastructure.

Auto-Derived Technology Shortens Industrial Ramp

The company is leveraging its light vehicle silicon and silicon carbide inverter technology and 800-volt architectures for industrial solutions. Management believes its automotive supplier base and manufacturing capabilities could support industrial production ramp-up in 18 to 24 months, roughly half the timeline of some purely industrial rivals.

EPS Guidance Raised As Buybacks Boost Per Share Metrics

Full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance was lifted to a range of $5.20 to $5.35 per diluted share, up from $5.05 to $5.30. The increase reflects solid third-quarter results, planned fourth-quarter share repurchases and a lower full-year effective tax rate, with the midpoint implying about 7% growth over 2025 adjusted EPS.

Margins Hold Firm Despite Sales Pressure And R&D Spend

BorgWarner maintained its full-year adjusted operating margin outlook at 10.7% to 10.9%, compared with 10.7% in 2025. The midpoint indicates margin expansion even with lower production, battery-business headwinds and $10 million to $15 million of additional industrial R&D investment, highlighting continued operational discipline.

Robust Free Cash Flow Fuels Shareholder Returns

Third-quarter free cash flow reached $195 million as the business converted earnings into cash effectively. BorgWarner returned about $210 million to shareholders via $175 million of buybacks and $35 million of dividends, exceeding quarterly free cash flow, and expects more than $700 million of returns in 2026, or roughly 70% of anticipated free cash flow.

Leverage Sits Below Target After Debt Tender

Management reported that a third-quarter debt tender was EPS accretive and positive on a net present value basis. Gross net leverage stands at 1.5 times versus a target of 2.0 times, giving the company flexibility to fund investment, pursue M&A and sustain shareholder distributions without stressing the balance sheet.

Diversified Auto Portfolio Supports Resilience

Executives emphasized BorgWarner’s status as a market leader in foundational powertrain components paired with a fast-growing eProduct franchise. With one of the sector’s most diverse customer bases and regional exposure that captures electrification growth in Europe and Chinese OEM exports, the company sees its portfolio as resilient through cycles.

PowerDrive Systems Growth Strong But Still Loss-Making

PowerDrive Systems converted incremental growth at about $0.24 per dollar during the quarter and is expected to grow roughly 20% this year after 30% growth last year. Despite an EBIT loss of $5 million tied to ongoing investment, management remains confident in achieving mid-teens conversion as scale and efficiency improve.

Commercial Vehicle Sales Track Above The Market

The global commercial vehicle market is growing around 3%, led by about 11% growth in North America. Excluding the battery-business drag, BorgWarner expects mid-single-digit sales growth in commercial vehicles, reflecting its solid exposure to truck and bus customers even as overall auto demand moderates.

M&A Lens Stays Disciplined Across Auto And Industrial

Management reiterated that mergers and acquisitions remain an active lever to expand earnings power in both automotive and non-automotive areas. Potential deals must fit BorgWarner’s core capabilities, be accretive in the near term and be appropriately valued, supporting a disciplined capital allocation framework.

China Exposure Skews To Export Champions

While China’s vehicle market is expected to decline 6% to 8% in 2026, BorgWarner’s exposure is concentrated with six or seven leading equipment manufacturers. Many of these OEMs are strong exporters, and BorgWarner is working with them on localization in Europe and South America, providing some offset to domestic market pressure.

Organic Sales Slip In Line With Auto Production

Overall organic sales fell by $58 million, or 1.6% year on year, roughly matching the decline in light vehicle production. Excluding currency effects, adjusted operating income dipped just $6 million on $112 million of lower sales, illustrating that cost controls and mix shifts helped cushion the impact of weaker volumes.

Battery Business Remains A Significant Headwind

The battery segment cut year-over-year sales by $54 million and is expected to remain a drag into 2026. Management cited the absence of key incentives in North America and softer demand in Europe, estimating the battery-business decline will represent roughly a 170 basis point headwind to overall year-over-year sales growth.

Full-Year Sales Outlook Trimmed As Markets Weaken

The company narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to a range of $14.0 billion to $14.2 billion, trimming the high end slightly. Weighted end markets are now expected to fall 1% to 2%, and organic sales are projected to decline 4% to 2.5% year on year, reflecting an increasingly cautious stance on auto demand.

Fourth-Quarter Revenue Expected To Step Down

Average quarterly revenue for the first three quarters was about $3.55 billion, but fourth-quarter revenue is expected closer to $3.43 billion. That roughly $120 million decline is tied to lower industry production, and management anticipates a mid-teens decremental margin on the reduced revenue base.

Macro Headwinds Pressure Auto Volumes

BorgWarner expects market volumes to decline and is closely monitoring macro risks including higher interest rates and vehicle affordability challenges. The company anticipates its light vehicle business will broadly track its weighted light vehicle market, suggesting resilience but limited room for outperformance in the near term.

China Market And Foundational Products Under Strain

China’s auto market decline of 6% to 8% in 2026 is expected to weigh on foundational product demand. Management noted that higher export volumes from leading Chinese OEMs and BorgWarner’s customer mix should provide offsets, but the region remains a clear source of downside risk.

Electronics Cost Inflation Adds Another Challenge

The company is seeing rising input costs, particularly in electronics-related components, in 2026. Management believes current teams can manage the pressure within this year’s incremental conversion metrics but plans to monitor the trend closely as it could have greater impact heading into 2027.

Political Backdrop Clouds Timing Of Data Center Deals

Executives cautioned that the current political environment may slow the finalization of some data center program awards. However, they characterized the issue as short term and said quoting activity and work on contractual details remain strong, suggesting underlying demand is intact despite timing uncertainty.

Limited Near-Term Visibility On Industrial Revenue Ramp

Management declined to provide detailed projections for turbine generator revenue until early 2027, citing too many moving pieces at this stage. Additional clarity on the microgrid inverter’s total addressable market is also expected only after the first few business awards, leaving the shape of the industrial growth curve still emerging.

Industrial R&D Spend Rises To Support Long-Term Growth

The company plans $10 million to $15 million of incremental industrial R&D in the second half of 2026 to back increased quoting and product development. That includes $5 million in the third quarter and $10 million in the fourth, representing a deliberate investment to secure future positions in data center and grid markets.

Energy Storage Pricing And U.S. Grid Rules Still Evolving

Management said it is not yet ready to assess whether energy storage pricing in data centers has become more favorable than initially expected. The company is also awaiting clarification on U.S. rules restricting foreign-sourced grid equipment, though it believes domestically produced electronics could ultimately benefit from these orders.

Guidance Highlights Resilient Margins And Strong Cash

For 2026, BorgWarner expects total sales of $14.0 billion to $14.2 billion, with weighted end markets down 1% to 2% and organic sales down 4% to 2.5%, including a battery headwind of about 170 basis points. Adjusted operating margin is projected at 10.7% to 10.9%, adjusted EPS at $5.20 to $5.35 and free cash flow at $900 million to $1.1 billion, with Q4 revenue near $3.43 billion.

Looking to 2027, the company anticipates modest automotive growth ahead of its markets, around $300 million of turbine generator revenue and mid-teens conversion on incremental growth. While macro risks remain, BorgWarner’s guidance underscores confidence that new industrial platforms and its eProduct portfolio can support earnings and cash generation.

BorgWarner’s earnings call painted a picture of a company using cost control, technology leadership and a disciplined capital strategy to navigate a softer auto backdrop. Investors heard a story of solid margins, rising EPS, strong cash returns and promising industrial growth options, tempered by battery-business weakness and macro uncertainty that will bear watching over the next two years.

text:
Dive Brief:

General Motors Co. is preparing its Lansing Delta Township plant in Michigan to produce hybrid-electric vehicles, and repurposing an old grant to support the move, per an Oct. 27 press release.

The Department of Energy is restructuring a $500 million grant that was previously awarded to GM for EV conversion work. That funding will now be used to prepare GM’s factory for future hybrid production, per the release.

GM’s Lansing Delta Township plant currently builds the three-row SUVs, including the Chevrolet Traverse, Buick Enclave and GMC Acadia. Details about specific hybrid models that will be built there, as well as expected launch timelines, will be shared in the future, per the release.

Dive Insight:

GM’s investment in Lansing is part of a broader commitment by the automaker aimed at boosting domestic manufacturing in the U.S., as well as for engineering and innovation. In July, the company said it will invest approximately $9 billion across its U.S. manufacturing footprint and more than $7 billion on U.S. research and development.

Specifically, the investment in Lansing is part of a larger commitment of over $2 billion in the region over the next several years, which includes a previously announced $1.25 billion in investment by GM to prepare the plant for future vehicle production.

GM was previously selected to receive the $500 million grant from the Department of Energy in 2024. It was part of former President Joe Biden’s Investing in America Agenda funded by the Inflation Reduction Act, which allocated a total of $1.7 billion for at risk auto manufacturing facilities.

Along with GM, Stellantis also received a $335 million commitment from the DOE through the Domestic Manufacturing Conversion Grants program to convert its shuttered Belvidere assembly plant in Illinois for electrification, as well as an additional $250 million to convert its transmission plant in Kokomo, Indiana to produce electric drive modules for EVs.

The investments were intended to ensure that the U.S. automotive industry remained competitive. However, the Trump Administration paused some funding designated for EVs in 2025, then eliminated the $7,500 federal tax credit effective Sept. 30, 2025.

In October 2025, the DOE also announced the cancellation of more than 300 other financial awards for various energy initiatives, which were projected to save $7.6 billion. At the time, the DOE confirmed in an email to WardsAuto that it had not yet made any determinations regarding the $500 million awarded to GM, and the plans were essentially put on hold until the restructuring agreement was announced this week.

The Lansing Delta Township plant, which the grant will now support, had record productivity in 2025, when it built more than 291,000 vehicles, the highest-ever annual production in the factory’s history, per the release.

“Lansing’s strength starts with its people. Their skill and experience are why we continue to invest here,” said Mike Trevorrow, senior vice president of global manufacturing at GM, in a statement. “We’re building on what this team does well today while preparing for what customers will need in the years ahead. That means investing in our people, our facilities, and the ability to build a broad range of vehicles.”

title: EVs, CNG and CBG: Why India's clean mobility transition also needs an agricultural lens
description:

An electric vehicle is also only as clean as the power that charges it.

text:
India’s clean-mobility debate is usually staged as a contest between machines: batteries against cylinders, electric against CNG. It is the wrong contest. The better question is what vehicle runs on, and where that energy comes from and the answer could lead to the paddy fields of Punjab and Haryana.

Numbers are encouraging but incomplete. Electric vehicles make up about 11 per cent of all vehicle sales in 2026, and nearly 43 per cent of passenger three-wheelers sold in the first seven months of this year were electric. For short, stop-start city trips, the battery is winning. But electric buses were under 5 per cent of sales and heavy trucks just 0.4 per cent.

An electric vehicle is also only as clean as the power that charges it. Coal and lignite supplied about two-thirds of India’s electricity in the July to September quarter of FY 2026, and officials expect coal to provide about half of generation as late as 2035-36.

The life-cycle reality

This is why a recent TERI study on vehicular emission becomes important. It compared petrol, diesel, CNG, electricity and LNG across six vehicle categories over their full life cycles. Electric mobility offered favourable economics for two- and three-wheelers and certain urban uses, while CNG gave a competitive mix of affordability, life-cycle performance and practicality for cars, taxis, buses and several light commercial applications. The life-cycle record of EVs remains sensitive to electricity generation and battery manufacturing. The lesson is not one fuel, but the right fuel for each vehicle.

That is where compressed biogas (CBG) fits in. It is produced by digesting crop residue, dung and organic waste in sealed tanks, making CBG interchangeable with CNG, which can run through the same pipelines and engines. TERI’s earlier assessment found it can be carbon-negative: up to 1.141 kg of CO₂ equivalent avoided per kilometre for a four-wheeler, the result of avoided methane leakage from unmanaged dung and of digestate replacing synthetic fertiliser. The study estimates that blending 20 % CBG into CNG could make the fuel carbon-neutral over its life cycle. Same fact was also highlighted by Niti Aayog in its Net Zero Report for the Transport Sector released in February 2026.

In fact, an earlier NRI report states that a single CBG plant can eliminate 11,000-12,000 kilograms of PM emissions annually, which is equivalent to emission savings from 1.5-1.75 lac EVs or that achieved by removing 25000 older vehicles from the roads.

The agricultural lens matters because of the feedstock issue. Punjab and Haryana together produce about 29 million tonnes of paddy straw, which are sometimes burnt because the window for sowing wheat after the paddy harvest is extremely short. While the official picture on emissions from stubble has improved, tens of millions of tonnes of residue need a permanent, paying destination, that fines and machines cannot supply.

A prize not a penalty

A CBG plant offers farmers a price for straw instead of a penalty for burning it, villages get a local employer and soil a nutrient-rich digestate. While policy has helped in building demand—blending obligations is set at 1 per cent in 2025-26, 3 per cent in 2026-27, 4 per cent in 2027-28 and 5 per cent from 2028-29 yet existing plants are reported to run at only 20 to 60 per cent of capacity, The reason: feedstock is seasonal and collection is fragmented and year-round aggregation of biomass, long-term offtake contracts and simpler clearances would change that.

None of this competes with the electric future. Electrons for two- and three-wheelers and urban fleets, increasingly green gas for heavier, high-mileage vehicles, and the farm as supplier of one and beneficiary of the other. The test is not which technology wins but whether every vehicle runs on the cleanest energy available to it.

India’s mobility transition will not only be decided in showrooms and power stations, but in the fields, by what we do with the straw left behind after harvest.

text:
The costs of keeping Louisiana homes and businesses comfortable can add up quickly. Air conditioners often run for most of the year, while older buildings, insufficient insulation and inefficient equipment can drive electricity consumption even higher.

Entergy is helping residential and business customers address those challenges through programs that identify sources of wasted electricity, recommend practical improvements and provide financial incentives to make upgrades more affordable.

Energy Smart is a longstanding program for Entergy New Orleans customers, while Entergy Solutions is available for Entergy Louisiana customers. Both programs offer customers a free energy assessment, recommendations for efficiencies and connections with certified contractors who can make improvements.

“People often know their energy usage is increasing, but don’t know what to address first. They might know their air conditioner needs cleaning, or an appliance is getting older. They may not necessarily think about insulation and ductwork. Those are all things we can help with,” said Heather LeBlanc, a manager of energy efficiency with Entergy Louisiana. “Our certified energy assessors identify the areas that can benefit most from upgrades and guide the customer toward improvements that will yield the most savings.”

Since launching in New Orleans in 2010, Energy Smart has helped more than 176,600 residential and business customers, awarded more than $86.7 million in incentives and helped the community save more than 569 million kilowatt-hours of electricity. Those are tangible impacts, especially in a city that faces unique energy challenges.

Nate Wolf, Entergy New Orleans energy efficiency project manager, said the city’s infrastructure frequently creates a heat island effect. That means certain areas – particularly ones with dense buildings, little greenspace and minimal tree cover – can be 8 to 10 degrees hotter at times. Meanwhile, building codes have evolved significantly, leaving many older homes without the modern standards required to drive energy savings.

Energy Smart addresses these challenges with solutions tailored to the local climate and housing stock.

“Once the assessment is complete, we send recommendations to area contractors who meet our program criteria. They have gone through our vetting process and are our on-the-ground experts,” Wolf said. “Beyond making efficiency improvements, they are trained to look for potential health and safety issues. For example, they won’t do anything that exacerbates other problems, such as moisture or mold.”

Energy Smart, created by the New Orleans City Council and administered by Entergy New Orleans, is inclusive by design, and all Entergy New Orleans residential, commercial and industrial electric customers are eligible to participate, regardless of income. All customers can receive cash incentives and rebates to cover significant portions of upgrade costs. Customers with household incomes at or below 80 percent of the Area Median Income can access additional benefits.

Common Energy Smart upgrades include smart thermostats, power strips, energy-efficient air conditioners, ENERGY STAR-certified appliances, attic insulation and air sealing.

“I think there’s still sometimes a misperception that not everyone can participate in Energy Smart, but it is open to everybody,” Wolf said. “Energy affordability is at the heart of what we do. We know rising costs are a real burden. That’s why we want to help all customers reduce their energy consumption and thus lower their monthly energy bills.”

On the commercial side, Wolf said Energy Smart has helped entities from small businesses to large industrial facilities. Businesses receive a free comprehensive assessment, and can receive cash incentives for upgrading HVAC systems, lighting, refrigeration and other equipment.

“We can do prescriptive improvements, or custom improvements based on the specifications of each building or system,” Wolf said. “There can be huge savings to business owners, depending on the size and scope of their facility.”

Entergy Solutions offers energy-saving opportunities for Entergy Louisiana customers, including homeowners, renters and businesses. Following a detailed assessment, customers can receive financial discounts and incentives for upgrades such as air conditioner tuneups, air sealing, duct sealing, improved insulation and smart thermostats.

“A lot of residential customers get the most savings from AC tuneups and duct sealings,” LeBlanc said. “In a lot of homes, we find little to no attic insulation, or holes or leaks in the ductwork. We also do a lot of high efficiency AC tune-ups that cleans the outside and inside units. South Louisiana temperatures mean that ACs can run daily for more than half of the year. That makes it important to keep those units clean and in top condition.”

LeBlanc said Entergy Solutions contractors are fully vetted and trained to prioritize improvements that will make the most impact. They also offer recommendations on everyday habits that can improve efficiency, such as setting the thermostat higher when a building or home is empty, closing blinds, turning off lights and fans when possible, unplugging items that aren’t in use and cleaning appliance vents and filters regularly.

“Once the Entergy Solutions upgrades are made, the savings are almost immediate if a customer is paying a monthly bill. If they are on Level Billing, it may take a little more time because a customer’s bill is based on their rolling twelve-month billing average,” LeBlanc said.

Over the last 11 years, Entergy Louisiana has given back over $65.5 million in customer incentives for energy efficiency upgrades in customers’ homes and businesses. These upgrades have an estimated 1,338,742 GWh of lifetime savings. The Entergy Solutions program has an additional $100 million in customer incentives available for customers to apply for over the next four years.

Through myEntergy and the Entergy mobile app, customers can access billing information, review energy usage and explore payment options. LeBlanc said monitoring that data can help customers see the impact of energy efficiency measures. Customers with advanced meters can access usage information through their online accounts or the Entergy mobile app.

“It’s important to watch that kilowatt-hour usage each month to see how it fluctuates, especially in conjunction with your billing,” she said.

In New Orleans, Wolf said a new program helps customers compare their energy usage to homes that are similar in size, age and location.

“That gives people some context and insights,” he said. “We’re always looking for opportunities to help customers gain more information and take more steps toward efficiency.”

Entergy New Orleans customers can learn more about Energy Smart at energysmartnola.info or call 504-229-6868.

Entergy Louisiana customers can contact Entergy Solutions at 844-829-1300 or email entergysolutionsla@entergy.com for information about available assessments, incentives and energy-saving services.

text:
Any bipartisan bill to update the nation’s permitting laws was always going to be a compromise, with advantages for the oil and gas industry as well as clean energy. Proponents of the Senate’s latest attempt at permitting reform have painted it as a delicate balance, a hard-won opportunity, and an all-or-nothing deal.

What, then, to make of drafting errors, or unintended consequences?

In the weeks since senators released the text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, lawyers have been doing what lawyers often do, which is scour the bill for loopholes and ambiguous language. Many have raised concerns about the risks of one section in particular titled “Project Certainty” that’s designed to prevent presidents from discriminating against projects they dislike, such as by throttling projects that are already under construction, or outright refusing to permit certain types of energy — both of which Trump has tried to do to wind farms.

The red flags range from what were clearly accidental oversights, like that the bill would exempt projects that have obtained all their permits from complying with future regulations, to much more nitpicky, hypothetical issues, like that it might enable a company to orchestrate a permitting delay in order to win a big payout in court.

The question now in front of Senate negotiators before they put the whole package to a vote on November 9 is which of these issues are possible, or even desirable, to address in an amendment without destabilizing the whole package.

“I think there are legitimate legal readings of the bill that are not what was intended, and I think those are where you can make technical fixes,” Nat Keohane, the president of the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, which supports the bill, told me. “I think there’s some of it that was worked out as part of the broader package that was negotiated over months. And so, which things fall into which bin? That’s up to the authors.”

It’s no secret that getting politics out of permitting was table stakes for the bill’s Democratic authors, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico. Neither responded to questions about whether they were aware of critics’ concerns about these provisions or open to revising the language, although many sources I spoke to for this story told me they were aware of efforts underway on the Hill to make corrections to this section.

Heinrich’s office instead forwarded my inquiry to the American Council on Renewable Energy. In an interview, ACORE’s CEO Ray Long argued that some of the concerns lawyers have raised are valid, and tweaks and technical corrections are “fine” — but only if they don’t hold back the bill from a vote this year. He stressed that between the bipartisan permitting bill debated by the previous Congress and BAAJA, the Hill has been working on this issue for four years. “I think we should stop trying to make this bill perfect,” he said. “Consider it for what it is, which is a well-intentioned bill on both sides to get to a compromise that addresses a whole range of things and move forward with that.”

Certainty for existing permits

The “Project Certainty” section of the bill has two key components that critics are concerned about. The first is a set of provisions meant to prevent an administration from yanking permits or otherwise messing with projects that have all of their approvals, such as when the Trump administration revoked the Lava Ridge wind farm’s right-of-way, or when it issued stop-work orders on five offshore wind farms that were under construction.

The main issue here is that the text is written very broadly. It doesn’t just say that agencies can’t revoke permits; it says they can’t take any action “to interfere with or prevent the construction or operation at full capacity of a project” that has secured all of its federal approvals.

“That ‘operation at full capacity’ language seems to prevent any future action that could require existing facilities to modernize their technology or take steps to reduce their pollution,” Liz Zeleda, the federal regulatory director at the Southern Environmental Law Center, told me.

Of all the issues critics of the bill have raised, this one seems to have pretty unanimous support for a correction. “Nobody, I think, wanted to negotiate some kind of regulatory freeze here, and it’s a pretty clear technical fix,” Jane Flegal, a senior fellow at the Searchlight Institute, told me. “I have confidence that the negotiators will fix it.”

Then there are concerns that the bill would render any permits or authorizations issued by the Trump administration irrevocable, even if they were issued illegally. John Podesta, Biden’s former senior climate advisor, recently raised that possibility during a fireside chat at the University of Colorado Boulder. “They’re going to have a permit gorge like you’ve never seen, not really caring about whether they’re going through the legal steps to do it, and under this bill that’s not going to be reversed,” he said. His comments quickly ignited a fierce debate on social media over whether this was an accurate reading of the text.

The bill does list several exceptions that would allow agencies to revoke permits or authorizations, such as under a court order, or when the developer has violated the terms of the permit or another applicable law, or if the developer obtained the permit under false pretenses, or if revoking the permit is necessary to prevent imminent harms that were not identified in the original review process. Notably, “when the government’s authorization violates the law” is not on the list.

Nonetheless, a harmed party would still be able to make the case that Trump violated the Administrative Procedure Act in issuing a permit and get a court to vacate it, Ben Schifman, a senior technology fellow at the Institute for Progress and former Department of Justice lawyer, told me. The only edge case where that would not be true, as far as he can tell, is if the sole legal infraction in the permitting process was a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act, and no other applicable law. In that situation, the bill would, in fact, restrict the court from vacating the permit. However, a case like that is unusual, he said. “I will tell you, in all of my 10 years of practicing this kind of law at DOJ, it was very rare, and I’m struggling to think if there was even a single case that literally only brought one claim that was a NEPA claim.”

On the other hand, Sambhav Sankar, the senior vice president of programs at Earthjustice, argues that this interpretation assumes groups like his have the means to challenge all of the potentially illegal permitting decisions Trump makes. “We don’t have anywhere near the resources required,” he wrote in a blog post about Podesta’s comments, “and this legislation is explicitly aimed at making our challenges much harder to bring.” It’s not like the next administration will be able to sue itself to get a court order to vacate permits, he noted.

When I asked Schifman about this, he suggested the agency might be able to sue the permit holder, but admitted this was an ambiguity in the bill and “a good candidate for a few-word technical amendment.”

Certainty for permit applicants

The second component of the “Project Certainty” title that’s raising alarm is a series of provisions meant to prevent unfair delays or denials for projects trying to obtain permits. The Trump administration, for example, has subjected wind and solar projects applying for permits to heightened reviews at the Interior Department, and simply stopped providing Department of Defense clearances to wind farms altogether.

The bill sets up a new legal pathway for project developers to sue the government for delaying or denying permits if they can demonstrate they are being targeted as part of a larger “pattern of disparate treatment.” To bring such a case, the developer would have to show its specific project type — a wind farm, for example — has seen a “substantial increase” in delays or denials compared to the previous five years. It may, but doesn’t have to, also produce supporting evidence, such as statements made by federal officials demonstrating a bias.

The choice of five years is the first thing that caught lawyers’ attention. Shortly after the bill came out, Matthew Littleton, a former deputy assistant attorney general at the U.S. Department of Justice’s Environment and Natural Resources Division, argued on LinkedIn that this baseline would be unlikely to help clean energy projects in the near term, since once the law goes into effect, the preceding five years will be dominated by Trump administration obstruction.

If you’re optimistic that the next administration will be less hostile to renewable energy, that’s only a short-term problem. But by that same token, imagine a Democrat takes the White House in 2029, and for entirely legal reasons, their administration rejects more natural gas plant permits than Trump did. Perhaps the previous Environmental Protection Agency didn’t account for some newly significant risk. Under BAAJA, developers would have grounds to sue the government for exhibiting a “pattern of disparate treatment.”

While the choice of five years has been debated, a lot of the risks with this provision actually stem from the bill’s limits on what the government can do to defend its actions. While the text gestures at “improper” denials, “unreasonable” delays, and a show of government intent, it doesn’t actually require the plaintiff to prove any of those things to win a case. It specifically limits the court’s review to three things: the evidence produced by the project sponsor; the administrative record for the particular project in question (i.e. the permit application and agency response); and raw, statistical data from the government showing the number of projects of the same type that received approvals over the past year compared to the previous five, as well as the number that received denials or got delayed.

Per Littleton’s interpretation, the developer need not prove the agency acted in bad faith, and the court can’t even take into account a potentially well-reasoned explanation by the government for why the data display a certain pattern. Schifman mostly agreed with this, but noted that it’s possible the administrative record would contain evidence about why the disparity occurred.

It’s possible that technical fixes to this section requiring “credible evidence of intentional targeting” for claims and that courts review the entire evidentiary record, as the Natural Resources Defense Council has suggested, could go a long way toward addressing this issue. Scholars at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy have recommended limiting these claims to delays, which are tied to clear timing benchmarks, and removing the provision for denials. “Courts can already overturn unlawful denials, so the denial provision adds little protection while creating most of the risk,” they wrote.

But there are other complications.

The bill specifies that if a developer wins a “disparate treatment” case, the government has to fork over 50% to 100% of the project’s total costs, in addition to any attorney fees and monetary damages resulting from the permitting delay or denial.

Justin Pidot, a law professor at the University of Arizona who served as General Counsel to Biden’s Council on Environmental Quality, told me that this could have the effect of “putting handcuffs on the government,” in that agencies will be under pressure to make decisions that avoid a legal challenge. That is, of course, the point of the provision, but to Pidot, it impinges too much on agency discretion. The Columbia scholars raised this concern as well, writing, “Facing that risk, agencies may approve projects they would otherwise reject, potentially including projects they consider unsafe.”

At the same time, the prospect of such a big payout may tempt developers to test agencies’ limits. “It just creates all sorts of perverse incentives,” Pidot said. “In that world, a project sponsor would be wise to try to figure out how to get the government to delay approving their projects so that they could bring this lawsuit.”

What’s more, the project sponsor is only allowed to keep its winnings if it actually completes the project, but nothing in BAAJA requires the government to approve a permit in these cases. A court might order an agency to make a decision on a delayed permit or reconsider an application it rejected, but the administration could just go on delaying or denying the project until the developer runs out of financing and can’t hold on any longer.

“As far as I can tell, if you have to abandon the project before you can build it, you don't get anything,” Littleton said. “I'm just sort of flummoxed by the way this is set up.”

Are technical fixes enough?

While everyone I spoke to seemed to agree that the project certainty title in the bill could use some redlining, there was a split between those who believed small “technical fixes” would do the trick and those who were skeptical the provisions would be successful without an overhaul.

The Environmental Protection Network, a group of former EPA staffers, recently published a number of suggested technical changes to improve the section on revoking existing permits. They called for adding several more exceptions for when an agency can revoke or amend a permit, such as when the action is “authorized by Federal law and brought by the Federal department or agency alleging a violation of Federal law.” The challenge with adding more exceptions is that it will give the government more wiggle room to justify revoking permits — a slippery slope.

EPN also suggested adding a clause specifying that “nothing in this title affects the applicability of any requirement under” the Clean Water Act, the Clean Air Act, and the like, and protecting taxpayers “from potentially hundreds of billions of dollars” in fines paid out to litigants by limiting the financial remedies to “actual damages and court costs.”

The NRDC suggested changing the five-year baseline in the disparate treatment section, and eliminating the “disproportionate” stipulated financial awards, although it did not specify how. The Columbia scholars urged Congress to consider tying the financial awards “more closely to a developer’s actual losses while keeping enough of a penalty to deter deliberate abuse.”

While these kinds of changes may “curb some of the worst excesses” of the project certainty provisions, Littleton told me, that’s not his preferred outcome. “Ultimately, I think they need to be rethought in order to accomplish their purpose.”

Long, of ACORE, held that concerns about project certainty “aren’t a reason to hold up all the work that’s been done so far,” and suggested that Congress could pass a corrections bill down the line should they turn out to be real problems.

One funny thing about this “project certainty” part of the permitting bill is that critics and proponents both seem to accept that there is no foolproof way to stop a president who is truly hell-bent on messing with an industry from doing so. The question is, is it worth trying?
