TINY HOME LIVING — DUKE’s off-grid tiny home, recently featured on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., will be giving tours at the Energy Fair.

Check out the latest advances in electric vehicles, solar power for home and business and home efficiency applications at an Energy Fair from 11 a.m.-3 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 7, at the Waynesville Rec Park.

Retailers, dealers, service providers and nonprofits will be onsite — providing a one-stop-shop for those gathering information. The Energy Fair will be hosted by the town of Waynesville and local nonprofit Environmental Action Community of WNC. It will be set up near the greenway pavilion below the Rec Center off Vance Street.

• Try out EVs: Explore and ride in more than 20 EV trucks and cars for free including Rivian R2, R1, Ford, Hyundai, Chevy, Kia, Tesla, Lucid, BMW and more. Learn how drastically EV prices have fallen this year.

• Free solar power estimates: No commitments or pressure. Find out how many tens of thousands you could save on your energy bills going forward. Solar leases with no money down. Lock in low energy rates for years to come.

• Lower your utility bills: Explore many programs. Free for income-qualified and discounts for all.

• See mobile microgrids in action. Learn how a battery and a few solar panels can make you truly storm resilient.

Entry is free. Parking can be found at the pavilion lot or the Rec Center lot. Event held rain-or-shine (will move to gym if raining). There will also be games, prizes, freebies, music by The Rich Manz Trio and Doug Jernigan Trio and food trucks.

The Environmental Action Community is a 501c3 nonprofit based in Haywood County whose mission is creating opportunities to enjoy the outdoors, respond to climate challenges, and promote a resilient mountain environment in WNC.

text:
Posted 30 October 2026 at 12:48 pm

Edwards Vacuum builds $319 million facility which will have 600 employees at full capacity

Press Release, Genesee County Economic Development Center

BASOM – Edwards Vacuum, a global leader in vacuum and abatement solutions and part of Atlas Copco Group, has celebrated the official opening of its new manufacturing facility in Genesee County.

The facility represents Atlas Copco Group’s continued investment in US manufacturing and semiconductor supply chain infrastructure, helping strengthen America’s ability to produce critical technologies domestically while supporting the continued growth of the semiconductor industry.

Purpose-built to produce the advanced dry vacuum pumps used in semiconductor manufacturing, the Genesee facility expands Edwards’ North American production capabilities and will cater for the demand driven by investments in semiconductor manufacturing across the US.

Powered by renewable hydroelectric energy generated from nearby Niagara Falls, the facility combines advanced manufacturing capabilities with Edwards’ commitment to sustainability, innovation and long-term regional investment.

The Genesee site will support customers across North America and around the world while creating high-quality manufacturing, engineering, and technical career opportunities in Western New York. The investment further strengthens the region’s growing position within the semiconductor and advanced manufacturing ecosystem.

“This facility reflects our confidence in both the future of the semiconductor industry and the strength of the Western New York community,” said Dan Papsidero, General Manager of Edwards’ Product Company Genesee. “As someone who grew up in this region, it is especially rewarding to help lead an investment that creates opportunities for local talent, supports advanced manufacturing, and contributes to the continued growth of our community. We are proud to be building world-class products here, while creating long-term partnerships that will help strengthen the region for generations to come.”

The project is the result of strong collaboration between industry, government, economic development organizations, educational institutions, and community stakeholders. Edwards also recognizes the contributions of regional partners whose support helped advance the project and reinforce Western New York’s growing role in the semiconductor industry.

“The opening of Genesee marks an important milestone in Edwards’ commitment to serving the global semiconductor industry,” said Martin Tollner, President of Atlas Copco Group’s Semiconductor division. “As chip manufacturers continue to invest in next-generation technologies and expanded production in the United States, Edwards is proud to invest alongside them. This facility strengthens domestic manufacturing capabilities, supports a more resilient semiconductor supply chain, and demonstrates our commitment to providing world-class vacuum technology built in the United States.”

“Edwards Vacuum, America’s first semiconductor dry pump manufacturing facility, is open for business right here in Genesee County!” said U.S. Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer. “Today, major semiconductor companies look to Genesee County as home to the advanced vacuum technology they need for their chip fabs that only Edwards Vacuum will make in the USA.”

“When I wrote and passed into law the CHIPS & Science Act, it was with bringing to the U.S. and New York cutting-edge facilities like this in mind,” Schumer said. “Four years ago, I personally called on Edwards to locate their new factory along Upstate New York’s emerging semiconductor superhighway. Thankfully, Edwards agreed Genesee County was the best place for their business, bringing up to 600 new, good-paying jobs to Western New York and boosting the region’s growing semiconductor Tech Hub. I’m proud to have delivered $18 million in federal CHIPS funding to Edwards Vacuum to bring this state-of-the-art facility to life. America’s next era of chip manufacturing is underway here in Upstate, and I can confidently say New York’s best days are ahead.”

Empire State Development President, CEO and Commissioner Hope Knight said, “Edwards Vacuum’s newly completed state-of-the-art facility represents hundreds of good-paying jobs and millions of dollars invested in Upstate New York. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, New York is building a strong semiconductor ecosystem statewide, furthering its global reputation as the preeminent hub for advanced manufacturing.”

The grand opening celebration brings together employees, customers, community leaders, educational partners, economic development organizations, and elected officials to recognize the collective effort that helped bring the facility from vision to reality.

The Genesee opening reflects Atlas Copco Group’s continued investment in North American manufacturing and innovation. Together with other recently announced investments across the US, the project underscores the Group’s long-term commitment to advancing technology leadership, supporting strategic industries, strengthening American manufacturing capabilities, and creating sustainable growth opportunities for the future. Atlas Copco Group’s US footprint includes 26 production, remanufacturing, and distribution centers, more than 160 locations, and approximately 7,500 employees, demonstrating the Group’s longstanding commitment to American industry and innovation.

About Edwards

For over 100 years, we’ve been a leading developer and manufacturer of sophisticated vacuum and exhaust management systems and innovative service solutions. Our technology is essential in industries ranging from semiconductors and renewable energy to pharmaceuticals and scientific research.

Part of Atlas Copco Group, we operate as part of a global family of brands. Over 8,000 Edwards employees work together to create, engineer and enable environments where innovation thrives.

Editor’s Note Gov. Kathy Hochul issued this statement about Edwards Vacuum’s new facility in Genesee County: “The completion of the state-of-the-art Edwards Vacuum manufacturing facility is proof positive that there is no place else for advanced manufacturing than New York State. Edwards’ decision to choose New York means hundreds of good-paying jobs and millions of dollars in investment in the Upstate economy while helping to strengthen our domestic semiconductor supply chain and ensuring that New York remains a global hub of innovation and the epicenter of semiconductor manufacturing nationwide.”

State Assemblyman Steve Hawley issued this statement: “This is an exciting milestone for Genesee County and all of Western New York. The opening of Edwards Vacuum represents a tremendous investment in our community, bringing hundreds of good-paying jobs, strengthening our local economy and positioning our region as a leader in advanced manufacturing. Projects like this demonstrate what is possible when we invest in American manufacturing and create opportunities for hardworking New Yorkers to build successful careers right here at home.”

“Western New York has a proud history of manufacturing, and investments like this are helping build its future. I am proud to celebrate this achievement alongside Edwards Vacuum and our local partners. This facility will not only create new opportunities for our workforce but also help ensure Genesee County remains a competitive destination for businesses looking to grow and innovate. I look forward to seeing the positive impact this investment will have on our community for generations to come.”

text:
The energy upgrades reduce reliance on foreign oil, save farmers money & ease the strain on electric & natural gas supplies

SAINT PAUL, MN – U.S. Senators Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith (both D-MN) are pushing the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) to reverse major changes made to a grant program helping farmers and producers install energy upgrades at their operations. The Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) was the target of a new Trump Administration rule on Oct. 1, making it harder for farmers and producers to pay for expensive energy upgrades without going into major debt.

Farmers and producers utilize REAP to pay for energy upgrades like an energy-efficient grain dryer or solar panels to power all the buildings on a farmstead. Previously, the program granted money to farmers and producers upfront, helping them put a down payment on the expensive equipment. Now, farmers won’t be able to apply for the program until their projects have been fully built and are operational, all without any guarantee they would actually receive a grant.

Sens. Klobuchar and Smith, along with 19 of their colleagues, urged USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins to change the REAP payment method in a letter on Oct. 23. The Senators write, “This rule would foreclose many of its intended beneficiaries from utilizing this popular and important program at a time when energy costs are soaring. This goes against the intent of the REAP program—to incentivize and support renewable energy projects that farmers might not otherwise have the capital to undertake and instead provides a windfall to individuals that have the resources to make the investment without federal assistance.”

The Senators are demanding a staff briefing on this issue by Oct. 31 and a written response from the USDA by Nov. 5.

The full letter can be found here and below:

Dear Secretary Rollins and Administrator Jansonius:

We are writing to express our disappointment and respectfully request the reconsideration of your decision on the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) final rule revising the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) issued on October 1, 2026, which would require farmers to make a substantial upfront investment to secure grant funding, a major change to the program’s structure. This rule would foreclose many of its intended beneficiaries from utilizing this popular and important program at a time when energy costs are soaring. This goes against the intent of the REAP program—to incentivize and support renewable energy projects that farmers might not otherwise have the capital to undertake and instead provides a windfall to individuals that have the resources to make the investment without federal assistance.

REAP is an incredibly successful and popular program. In the last ten years, USDA has invested more than $1.6 billion dollars in REAP grants across all fifty states,2 helping over 10,000 agricultural producers and rural businesses reduce their energy costs, improve energy efficiency, and promote energy independence. The program supports a wide range of projects, including installing solar panels, purchasing energy efficient equipment, and making upgrades to meet energy efficiency codes.

The final rule issued on October 1, 2026, represents a significant departure from the program’s longstanding structure. Under the new rule, USDA requires projects to “be fully built and operational” before an applicant can apply for assistance and the applicant must provide “actual energy production or savings data for the prior 12 months, alongside 12 months of pre-installation data.” This change goes against the intent of the REAP program—to incentivize and support projects that farmers might not otherwise have the capital to undertake.3 Many farmers and small rural businesses cannot afford to finance the upfront costs without any guarantee that they will be reimbursed for their investment. Rather than incentivizing projects that might not otherwise occur, the rule risks limiting financial support to applicants able to finance projects independently. The new rule also narrows the size and scope of eligible projects, increases administrative burdens for applicants, and imposes strict supply chain restrictions.

USDA issued the final rule prior to a public comment period. While we understand USDA’s authority to do this under the Administrative Procedure Act, stakeholder input is critical to ensuring that federal programs are implemented effectively. We urge USDA to demonstrate its commitment to meaningful engagement by considering stakeholder feedback and making appropriate revisions to ensure producers and small business owners are able to upgrade their energy systems to make them more efficient and affordable.

Given the significance of these changes, we request a Congressional staff briefing on the major changes to the program no later than October 31, 2026. In addition, we ask that you provide a written response to the following questions by November 5, 2026:

Congress intended for REAP to, in part, help producers and small businesses purchase a renewable energy system (RES). What language under 7 U.S.C. § 8107 permits USDA to shift REAP from a financial assistance program for the purchase of a RES to a reimbursement program for a completed RES that has been operational for 12 months?

Has USDA estimated how many applicants will meet the new eligibility criteria announced in the final rule? Does USDA expect the final rule to increase or decrease the number of farmers and rural businesses served by REAP?

Has USDA estimated how the rule change will affect the size of farms and enterprises that will apply? How will USDA ensure that the rule change does not disadvantage small and family-owned farms and rural businesses?

The final rule states “This revision streamlines, simplifies, and reduces burden for the application process.” Please provide additional details on how this rule achieves these goals, and how it compares to the administrative requirements under the previous program structure.

Please provide documentation of the feedback USDA received about REAP before issuing the final rule, including the number of emails, calls, and in-person conversations considered (as mentioned on page 62600 of the final rule), the names of the stakeholders and others that provided feedback to USDA, and whether USDA considered the feedback they received to reflect a diverse range of perspectives.

Why did USDA decide to change the structure of the program to a reimbursement model? What evidence or data did the agency use to back up the need for this change?

How many farmers and businesses were eligible under the previous rule and procedures that no longer are able to meet the new requirement to pay 100% of the costs upfront? What portion of these potential applicants cannot obtain a private loan? Does the agency have a plan to provide an opportunity to apply prior to completion of the project for these individuals?

The new rule eliminates state level competition for awards, which potentially may limit the role of state energy coordinators, who have historically contributed local expertise to the award process. What role will state energy coordinators have under the new rule, and how will USDA ensure that local needs are considered in funding decisions?

USDA Rural Development has lost over 2,000 employees since 2024. Does USDA have sufficient staffing capacity to implement these changes effectively?

REAP has not distributed any grant awards in over six months, how much funding is available in the REAP program? Provide the breakdown between funding from the Farm Bill and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

title: Why Everyone Loves BAAJA's Transmission Section - Heatmap News
description:
First of all, it codifies — and therefore protects from legal challenge — existing orders by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission around transmission planning and requires regular transmission planning within and among regions.
For even higher voltage lines, transmission developers can apply for federal permits in parallel with the state permit, shortening the permitting timeline.
But when it issued an order to begin a competitive process for building new lines, it added exceptions for immediate reliability needs or building lines in your local territory.
While experts have been criticizing the existing transmission planning system for as long as it’s been cobbled together, it took increased demand on the entire grid to spur at least the potential of bipartisan agreement on transmission planning reform.
“If you make it significantly easier to build long-range, high-voltage transmission lines, that is going to make it easier to put renewables on the grid,” Fisher told me.
text:
As the intra-Democratic fight over permitting reform gets ever more intense, with objections piling up from tribes, elected officials, and environmental groups, one thing everyone seems to agree on is that the transmission provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 are a good idea.

One major environmental group, the Natural Resources Defense Council, “still sees great benefit in the transmission language that was negotiated,” its executive director Christy Goldfuss posted on X on Wednesday, hours after warning about other provisions in the bill. Former Biden climate advisor John Podesta lauded the bill’s “needed reforms on transmission” as “pretty good” and “pretty strong” before criticizing other elements, while Holly Bender of the Sierra Club listed the section as an example of “policies we’ve championed before.”

And while clean energy industry groups support the bill wholeheartedly, they overlap with the critical environmentalists in their enthusiasm for transmission.

“The transmission provisions in BAAJA are essential to deploying more clean energy,” a coalition of five clean energy trade groups said in a letter to congressional leaders. Climate philanthropist and investor Tom Steyer wrote that the bill’s expanded transmission siting authority “means more power lines carrying more affordable energy to more people across America … which means lower bills for all of us.”

When New Mexico Senator Martin Heinrich, one of the two Democratic co-authors of the bill, first presented it to the public about a month ago, he opened with a discussion of the SunZia transmission project, a 550-mile transmission line designed to bring a staggering amount of wind power — 3.6 gigawatts, more electricity than the Hoover Dam generates and the largest renewable project in the country — from New Mexico to Arizona and California. “That transmission line,” Heinrich said, “took 17 years to permit and build. That’s why I’m here today, because I was part of that process, which should have taken probably five years … We need to be able to build big things in this country again.”

“Right now, clean, affordable energy is stuck waiting for transmission lines that take a decade or more to build, leaving Americans to pay sky-high utility bills,” Heinrich added in an emailed statement.

For years, climate and energy experts have pointed to transmission as the sine qua non of a renewable buildout, because clean energy generation is sited where the rocks are hot (like Utah), or the sun shines (like Nevada), or the wind blows (like New Mexico), and that’s not necessarily where the people consuming the electricity are (California).

“There’s effectively no way to have a high penetration renewable grid without a lot more regional and interregional transmission,” David Pomerantz, executive director of the Energy and Policy Institute, told me. (He also spoke at length to my colleague Robinson Meyer about the transmission section of the bill on this week’s episode of Shift Key.)

And beyond the specifics of the bill, a bipartisan Congressional vote and presidential signature “would be an expression of the national sentiment that, for a whole variety of reasons, we need a better grid in the U.S.,” Michael Skelly, the co-founder and chief executive of the transmission developer Grid United, told me.

For wind energy especially, which is quite sensitive to siting, transmission investments allow it to be “more competitive compared to some of the other technologies,” said Aaron Bergman of the energy research group RFF, which released modeling showing BAAJA reducing emissions compared to the status quo through 2041. “I confess before we did this, I actually did not expect to see the effect we saw,” Bergman said, referring to the emissions reductions.

That modeling also found overall transmission capacity in the U.S. growing by over 30% by 2041 and that “interregional capacity specifically is projected to grow by 10 to15 gigawatts per year between 2032 and 2041, leading to a rough doubling of capacity over the period modeled.”

But actually building that transmission requires the type of overhaul of transmission planning that’s been attempted for over 25 years with little success.

So what does BAAJA actually do?

First of all, it codifies — and therefore protects from legal challenge — existing orders by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission around transmission planning and requires regular transmission planning within and among regions.

“If you want a better grid in America, this is a hell of a bill to make that happen because it requires interregional planning,” Skelly said. “Those provisions are very, very helpful, and I think they’ll encourage a lot of activity in the transmission sector,” he added, referring to how the bill puts in place mechanisms for regions to coordinate development of power lines and come up with a consistent way to allocate their costs.

It also gives more power to transmission developers to drive the process for siting and approving lines. FERC would be required to issue permits to interstate high-voltage lines (or lines using advanced conductoring) that meet certain public interest criteria after states get a year to act on a permit application. If BAAJA passed, FERC would also have to issue permits to lines that meet a national interest, reliability, and voltage criteria. For even higher voltage lines, transmission developers can apply for federal permits in parallel with the state permit, shortening the permitting timeline.

The law also puts some muscle behind the perennial critique that utilities are overinvesting in transmission that’s less useful to the whole system. BAAJA would allow states to refer utilities to FERC to be investigated for not picking cost-effective projects.

If FERC determines that a utility’s planning is making it harder for regional transmission to get built, FERC could subsequently dock a utility’s return on equity and remove discretion from the utility for planning or even issue fines.

FERC had tried to coax utilities into building more transmission back in 2011. But when it issued an order to begin a competitive process for building new lines, it added exceptions for immediate reliability needs or building lines in your local territory. This loophole “resulted in what was just mass gaming to the point where around 90% of the transmission built by utilities in the country over the last decade plus has fallen into those two categories,” Daniel Palken, director of infrastructure at Arnold Ventures, told me. “So you’ve avoided building large-scale, efficient, economically driven transmission, and you’ve instead built incremental band-aids.”

The bill both writes down these planning provisions into statute and provides real backstops for FERC to approve lines and exercise oversight over utilities.

“You’re talking about lines that can stretch across electricity markets, across utility jurisdictions. The sense among pretty much all electric system advocates is our current legal structure, for one reason or another, is totally insufficient to the task,” Chirag Lala, vice president of research and chief economist at the Center for Public Enterprise, told me.

There is also the actual permitting reform part of the permitting reform bill, which may have some of the most outsize effects on transmission lines, which are notoriously hard to permit due to the number of territories they run through. In the West, where transmission is often the most needed to connect far-flung resources like wind, solar, and geothermal to large urban areas, transmission lines almost inevitably trip up the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act as they traverse public lands.

Transmission projects would see the largest time savings from the bill, according to an analysis by Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh for Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy. Some of the biggest time savers come from FERC’s expanded ability to approve lines and in running National Historic Preservation Act reviews concurrently with the Environmental Impact Statement required by the National Environmental Policy Act.

SunZia especially had an extremely drawn-out NHPA process that continued past the completion of construction of the line.

So where would these highly planned and permitted lines actually go?

“Interregional planning has worked nowhere in the country in the last 15 years,” said Palken, and while there has been some regional planning, the Intermountain West could be a prime candidate going forward.

Two of the bill’s authors, Republican Senator Mike Lee and Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich, represent the energy-rich adjacent states of Utah and New Mexico, respectively. The governors of Nevada and Utah, both Republicans, have endorsed the bill, while the governor of New Mexico, a Democrat, has not.

“The Intermountain West is both a growth region and a growth region that has seen virtually no transmission come out of FERC's existing processes,” Palken said.

One potential beneficiary of transmission investments in the West would be geothermal developers like Fervo. A recent short seller report identified transmission access as one of the reasons to doubt the company’s prospects, as it will require it to connect to customers in California. Jefferies analysts described transmission as an “execution item” for the company and noted that Fervo is “still working to secure roughly 100 MW” to serve Google as part of an offtake deal.

More generally, for there to be any hope that new load (i.e. data centers) could be served by a clean grid, more transmission investment will be needed. “A lot of what we’re building now is wind and solar and, inherently, whatever you’re building more of needs the new transmission,” Pomerantz said.

While experts have been criticizing the existing transmission planning system for as long as it’s been cobbled together, it took increased demand on the entire grid to spur at least the potential of bipartisan agreement on transmission planning reform.

Transmission has long been tagged in energy policy circles as a Democratic priority because more long-range transmission could threaten utilities’ existing business models (and utilities were seen as quite influential among Republicans) and because transmission investments are needed to fully unlock wind and solar potential across the country, which Democrats tend to want to favor (and subsidize).

Two things changed: load growth and rising electricity rates. “People are growing frustrated with utilities,” Travis Fisher, director of energy and environmental policy studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, citing both rising costs and data-center-related investments leaking onto residential ratepayers’ bills.

“There’s a lot of scrutiny on returns on investment. There’s this local transmission issue where there has really been a bipartisan sense among state and federal regulators that utilities have maybe gotten away with a lot of spending with almost no oversight from the state or federal government, and that, at a minimum, deserves looking into,” Palken said.

And with higher electricity demand, new transmission isn’t just about reallocating demand towards new resources, but letting everyone connect to the grid. “It’s very clear that load growth is here to stay. So there’s a pro-industry argument for expanded transmission now that we didn’t necessarily have before,” Fisher told me.

Fisher also cited the sunsetting of Inflation Reduction Act subsidies for wind and solar as another reason why Republicans could sign on to the transmission title — there was less fear that the new transmission projects would supercharge the IRA’s subsidies.

“If you make it significantly easier to build long-range, high-voltage transmission lines, that is going to make it easier to put renewables on the grid,” Fisher told me. “I don't think that's inherently bad, and you shouldn't oppose that if you’re a technology-neutral advocate like I am. But it does change the calculus when there’s significant subsidies on the table.”

And even if, say, wind power isn’t getting subsidies, new transmission investments could make them more economically viable.

“Even absent further policies, transmission is very valuable for wind and it could lead to greater deployment and reductions in emissions,” Bergman said.

text:
This week, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed to roll back federal rules regulating methane emissions. Methane is a super pollutant that causes a large amount of damage to our environment by trapping heat in the atmosphere. It has a shorter shelf life in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, but it is 87 times more potent as a contributor to climate change.

For years, I’ve called attention to this and pushed legislation that would strengthen federal regulations to prevent harmful leaks. Regulations protect public health, curb the climate crisis, create jobs, and bolster our national energy security.

The new rules loosen requirements to curb methane emissions from hundreds of thousands of “marginal” (meaning low producing) oil and gas wells that contribute about half of the industry’s methane emissions, while only producing about 7 percent of our natural gas. Weakening our ability to restrict these emissions is not only bad for the environment — it’s bad for business. Most U.S. producers have already invested in methane-reduction technology, giving them a real edge in global markets where our customers - in Europe, Korea, and Japan, for instance - have been demanding "clean" natural gas, produced with minimal leaking. Rolling back the rules rewards the least efficient, least responsible polluters and puts that edge at risk. We can and should back American industry and protect its competitive advantage without gutting environmental protections. And with the President’s ongoing war in Iran, we shouldn’t be going backwards on saving energy and reducing costs while minimizing pollution.

name: Detroit Environment
title: Michigan AG challenges electricity contracts for Google's massive data center outside Detroit
description:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed a petition for rehearing, citing a "litany of errors," after the Michigan Public Service Commission approved a 20-year electric service contract between DTE Energy and Google to power a hyperscale data center in Van Buren Township.
The commission approved the contract earlier this month, saying it "ensures no costs are passed on to DTE Electric’s other customers.” Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel doesn't believe it.
Nessel said the data center's electric costs will be aggregated over the entire 20-year period of the contract, so there will be years when customers do, in fact, have to subsidize Google's data center.
"That simply swings the doors wide open for customer cost-shifting, and that’s how the data center crash-lands onto your electric bill,” Nessel said in a statement.
Nessel said the costs and benefits from the contract should be accounted for and reconciled annually to protect ratepayers.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel doesn't believe it.

Nessel said the data center's electric costs will be aggregated over the entire 20-year period of the contract, so there will be years when customers do, in fact, have to subsidize Google's data center.

"That simply swings the doors wide open for customer cost-shifting, and that’s how the data center crash-lands onto your electric bill,” Nessel said in a statement.

Nessel said the costs and benefits from the contract should be accounted for and reconciled annually to protect ratepayers.

The MPSC declined comment on Nessel's petition filing. Google did not respond to a request for comment.

EVWorld Exclusive

The Second Life of EV Batteries: A Billion-Dollar Opportunity Meets a Reality Check

| Millions of EV batteries will eventually retire from automotive service, creating an opportunity for a second life in solar storage, grid support and commercial backup power. But reusing old batteries isn't as simple as connecting them to a new application. Testing, refurbishment, safety certification and falling prices for new batteries are challenging the economics. The emerging industry must prove that reuse can compete with recycling and newly manufactured storage systems.

Read Full Story

Electric School Buses Didn't Fail. Washington's Rollout Did

| The $5 billion federal Clean School Bus Program has encountered delivery delays, manufacturer bankruptcies, reliability concerns and serious EPA oversight failures. But these shortcomings do not establish that electric school buses are a failed technology. They expose Washington's inability to manage a complex transportation transition. The real lessons involve procurement, infrastructure, manufacturer accountability and the need to measure actual results rather than simply announce ambitious spending targets.

Read Full Story

Beyond the Driverless Car: Who Controls the Future of Canada's Cities?

| As Waymo enters Canada, cities face a crucial choice between passive tech adoption and proactive urban stewardship. Navigating northern blizzards, black ice, and hidden road markings requires rigorous local safety standards over corporate assertions. To avoid gridlock and public transit decay, municipalities must deploy congestion pricing and curb management, integrating robotaxis as last-mile complements. Safer driverless tech enables cities to reclaim asphalt for pedestrian plazas and bike networks, setting a sovereign playbook where civic priorities govern the algorithm.

Read Full Story

Auckland's Hybrid Ferry Forced to Burn Diesel Until Delayed Megachargers Arrive

| Auckland's flagship hybrid-electric ferry, Waitemata 1, was designed to operate primarily on battery power but remains dependent on diesel generators because its shore-based megawatt charging system is years behind schedule. Delays involving permitting, grid integration, and waterfront infrastructure have pushed completion of the Queens Wharf charging project to mid-2027, forcing the vessel to conduct nighttime diesel-powered charging runs to maintain daily service.

Read Full Story

From Burial Pits to Bridges: Giving Wind Turbine Blades a Second Life

| As thousands of first-generation wind turbines reach retirement, the industry is confronting a long-overlooked challenge: what to do with massive fiberglass blades. While many were once buried in landfills, a growing U.S. recycling sector is transforming them into cement feedstocks, infrastructure materials, and industrial composites. Combined with next-generation recyclable blade designs, these innovations point toward a more circular future for wind energy.

title: THIS WEEK IN CLIMATE ACTION - OCTOBER 30, 2026 - League of Conservation Voters
description:
This was the final stop of a two-week series of marches across the state organized by Chesapeake Climate Action Network Action Fund, Virginia LCV, and partners.
OUR TAKE: LCV said, “Dolores Huerta — who received California Environmental Voters’ Environmental Leadership Award in 2016 — was a labor and environmental justice hero.

NOVEMBER 4: Climate and environmental groups’ post-election press conference on how energy issues shaped the midterms.
text:
Your weekly resource to learn what the environmental movement is saying about the news of the day and the political fight of our generation. This week, with just days left before the election, we’re tracking key races and ad campaigns alongside growing calls for action on energy affordability and data center development. We’re also covering the fight to defend public lands, clean air, and clean water from polluters as Trump continues to roll back climate protections.

Be sure to follow LCV on Facebook, Instagram, BlueSky, and TikTok.

QUOTES OF THE WEEK:

“The Earth is not ours to abuse and poison – not the land itself, and not the people living and working on it.”

– Dolores Huerta, a labor and environmental justice hero, who passed away earlier this week.

“Native people need to understand that their votes do count.”

– Molly Miller, Mohican elder, reminding Indigenous voters in Wisconsin to participate in the upcoming elections.

“We believe that everybody, regardless of where they live or what their income is, deserves clean air, clean water, access to the outdoors, to be protected from the extreme heat, and to have their voices heard.”

– Vianey Olivarría, Chispa Arizona Executive Director, on ensuring all communities are protected from the worst impacts of climate change and have the resources they need to participate in elections.

“Democrats have really hammered home that they are going to work to deliver affordability for families and to stand up to the Big Polluters who are making record profits while we all suffer, and I think that that is a strong and unifying theme across these various races.”

– Matthew Davis, LCV Action Fund Vice President of Federal Policy, on the role of energy policy and costs in competitive Senate races.

TOP NEWS IN ENERGY AFFORDABILITY

STATE NEWS

VIRGINIANS MARCH TO DEMAND A PAUSE ON DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT: More than 300 people marched to Virginia’s state Capitol on October 24th to call for a moratorium on new data center development until environmental and ratepayer protections are in place. This was the final stop of a two-week series of marches across the state organized by Chesapeake Climate Action Network Action Fund, Virginia LCV, and partners. Protesters raised concerns about rising electricity bills, data center water use and pollution, and the targeted siting of data centers in Black and brown communities. They demanded clean energy standards, protections for communities, and guardrails to ensure ratepayers don’t foot the bill for data centers.

VALCV TAKE: Virginia LCV Deputy Director of Advocacy and Campaigns Sarah Ahmed said, “While our electricity bills creep higher and higher, while our wells run dry, and while families and pets live with a constant industrial hum in their ears, the richest corporations in history are cashing in and we are bearing the cost. This is not some arbitrary talking point being said by some environmentalists. This is what the people of Virginia who elected you [state leaders] are demanding.”

MARYLAND LAUNCHES $200 MILLION PROGRAM FOR CLEAN ENERGY: Maryland’s Utility RELIEF Act created the “Megawatts for Maryland” program, which will award $200 million to large-scale solar, wind, and battery storage projects over the next two years. The program aims to expand in-state electricity generation and help lower energy bills as demand rises.

MDLCV TAKE: Maryland LCV Director of Climate Policy and Justice Rebecca Rehr said, “An investment today in this type of program means people save over time.”

CLIMATE ATTACKS FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

TRUMP WEAKENS FEDERAL RULES ON METHANE POLLUTION: The Trump administration announced a proposal to roll back federal requirements for oil and gas companies to detect and reduce methane leaks, including from hundreds of thousands of low-producing wells that are responsible for roughly half the industry’s methane emissions. The changes would also allow companies to flare more gas and end EPA’s Methane Super Emitter Program, which used satellites and other technology to identify major methane leaks and help deliver an increasingly costly product to consumers rather than wasting it.

OUR TAKE: Ahead of the proposal, Healthy Communities Program Director Madeleine Foote said, “By announcing EPA’s intent to roll back the 2024 Methane Rule, Administrator Zeldin and President Trump are making it crystal clear that they are willing to sell out the health and safety of our families and environment in order to reward their buddies in the oil and gas industry. Weakening these common-sense safeguards will expose our communities to even more unnecessary, dangerous air pollution, harming public health and exacerbating the climate crisis, all so that Big Polluters can rake in even more profits. This action puts on full display the corruption of Trump, his administration, and the oil and gas industry, as outlined in Senate Democrats’ corruption report. We urge EPA to not release this proposal and maintain strong methane pollution standards to protect public health and our environment for generations to come.”

ICYMI: STATE NEWS

ARIZONA ADVOCATES GATHER TO DISCUSS MULTIRACIAL VOTERS’ PRIORITIES AHEAD OF MIDTERMS: Black, Latino, and Indigenous Arizonans gathered in Phoenix for the Arizona People’s Convention to learn about community members’ priorities and goals after the midterms. Multiple speakers addressed issues including workers’ rights, voting access disparities, and housing affordability.

CHISPA AZ TAKE: Chispa Arizona Executive Director Vianey Olivarría said, “Our vote speaks volumes, and when we march later to the polls, we’re going to make sure we’re heard. We’ll keep showing up, organizing and demanding that our elected officials listen to the people of Arizona because our power does not end on Election Day.”

NEVADA ADVOCATES WARN DATA CENTER EXPANSION WILL STRAIN WATER AND ENERGY SUPPLIES: Environmental and community advocates held a press conference to push back against data center expansion in Nevada. Speakers cited concerns about data center water use, rising energy demand and costs, and fossil fuel development, including plans for new methane gas plants to fuel data centers.

NCL TAKE: Nevada Conservation League Communications Organizer Bri Schmidt said, “We’re spending millions on new methane gas plants in the proposed plan… When we have solar, we get over 300 days of sunshine in Nevada. These are solar panels that are already installed in our homes that people already have that could be helping to meet demand.”

WISCONSIN APPROVES NEW GROUNDWATER STANDARDS FOR PFAS: Wisconsin’s Department of Natural Resources unanimously approved groundwater limits for six PFAS chemicals, a step toward protecting drinking water from these pollutants. PFAS were found in 71% of private wells in Wisconsin sampled in 2022, and these standards will help address this contamination, which is linked to serious health risks..

WCV TAKE: Wisconsin Conservation Voters Government Affairs Manager Peter Burress said, “There are real costs of inaction. There are real costs associated with facing cancer treatments, miscarriages, heart surgeries and developmental challenges.”

ICYMI: NATIONAL NEWS

DOLORES HUERTA, LABOR AND CIVIL RIGHTS LEADER, DIES AT 96: Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers and helped secure the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers, has died at 96. A lifelong organizer, Huerta also fought against toxic pesticides, advocated for healthy environments for workers, and championed environmental justice education through the Dolores Huerta Foundation.

OUR TAKE: LCV said, “Dolores Huerta — who received California Environmental Voters’ Environmental Leadership Award in 2016 — was a labor and environmental justice hero. Thank you, Dolores, for always fighting for people and the planet.”

CHISPA AZ TAKE: Chispa Arizona said, “We honor the life and legacy of Dolores Huerta, a fearless organizer whose fight for dignity, justice, and the rights of farmworkers helped shape generations of social movements. Dolores showed us what it means to stand with our communities, stand up against injustice, and organize for a better future. Her work opened doors for countless Latine organizers, women, and young people who continue to carry that fight forward. As we mourn her passing, we also celebrate the movement she helped build and the generations she inspired. Her legacy lives on in our communities, in our organizing, and in every person who believes a better world is possible. Rest in power, Dolores. ¡Sí se puede!”

ENVIROVOTERS TAKE: California Environmental Voters CEO Mary Creasman said, “Dolores Huerta is a matriarch of the climate movement. She was a tremendous partner in our fight for climate justice, pushing our state to address the intersectional issues of health, environmental, racial, gender, and economic justice.”

LCV, LCV ACTION FUND REACH OVER 500,00 VOTERS AHEAD OF ELECTION DAY: LCV Action Fund and its state affiliates have endorsed 186 federal candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. LCV also invested $3.5 million in its organizing programs, including its GreenRoots voter mobilization program and newly launched Clean Energy Corps field program. Combined, these efforts have reached over 500,000 voters, with LCV members and organizers completing nearly 30,000 volunteer shifts. Organizing programs focused on mobilizing LCV members to volunteer on behalf of LCV Action Fund-endorsed candidates and turning out voters who have been historically excluded from outreach efforts.

LCVAF TAKE: LCV Action Fund Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “In the days leading up to the election, voters are turning out for the pro-environment, pro-democracy candidates up and down the ballot who are committed to putting families and communities first, and who support real energy solutions that put us on the path to a more affordable, clean energy future.”

LCV VICTORY FUND TARGETS ENERGY BILL VOTERS IN MIDTERM ELECTIONS: LCV Victory Fund and its state affiliates have invested over $110 million in federal, state, and local races to elect pro-environment candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. The effort has targeted millions of voters through knocking on over 4 million doors, sending over 6 million pieces of mail, and serving streaming, linear TV and digital ads to tens of millions of voters. LCV Victory Fund focused on the “Energy Bill Voter,” a new bloc of swing voters concerned about rising energy costs, and highlighted how Trump and Republicans in Congress have repeatedly broken their promise to lower costs in favor of giving handouts to Big Oil, Big Polluters and monopoly utility companies.

LCVVF TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “We identified Republicans’ self-inflicted vulnerability on energy affordability early on and were consequently able to deploy our biggest midterm investment ever, over $110 million, aimed squarely at voters’ concerns. We focused our efforts on targeting a new voting bloc, the “Energy Bill Voter” – this bloc of swing voters are more likely to be Women, Black and/or Latino, non-college-educated, less engaged with politics, independent, moderate, or soft partisan voters – critical voters to win in a midterm. To reach these voters, we went on offense and invested more and earlier than ever before in districts Trump won in 2024 to communicate with voters early about who is responsible for their rising energy costs and cutting clean energy.”

LCV VICTORY FUND RELEASES NEW MEMO HIGHLIGHTING KEY STATE AND LOCAL RACES: LCV Victory Fund outlined the most important state and local races that will shape energy costs, the fight against Big Polluters, and environmental protections. LCV state affiliates have invested $20 million in 2026 races, including gubernatorial races in Michigan, Ohio, and Wisconsin; utility commission seats in Arizona and Georgia; and state legislative races in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. The memo also highlighted Colorado’s Amendment 82, a ballot measure that could overturn bedrock health and safety protections for residents and workers.

LCVVF TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “State leaders have been our best bulwark against Trump’s worst attacks. They have also been the major source of progress over the last two years; Governors who have expanded clean energy infrastructure, attorneys general who beat the Trump Administration in court, utility boards that froze rates increases, and legislatures that have passed laws to lower energy costs and hold big polluters accountable… These are the races to watch that will be a harbinger for the shift in the country and could lay the groundwork for major policy opportunities in 2027 and beyond.”

LCV VICTORY FUND LAUNCHES $225K AD CAMPAIGN IN IOWA HOUSE RACE: LCV Victory Fund launched a new $225,000 digital ad program targeting former Representative Joe Mitchell in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District. The ad calls out Mitchell’s support of hiking up healthcare costs for Iowans, and his record of receiving more than $300,000 from corporate interests.

LCVVF TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “Joe Mitchell has made it clear who he is siding with and it is not Iowan. Iowans deserve a leader like Lindsay James who has a plan to lower costs, including healthcare and energy costs.”

NEW ON THE POWER SOURCE BLOG AND SOCIALS:

ON THE BLOG: Stay tuned for more new content coming soon to The Power Source! In the meantime, check out last week’s midterm voting mythbusters blog to get the facts on voter ID, mail-in-voting, and early voting before Election Day.

ON OUR SOCIALS: Trump’s oil and gas stocks are doing just fine, even as families face high costs at the pump. We’re calling out some dangerous rhetoric from the Georgia GOP Senate nominee, busting myths about renewable energy, and chatting about things that just feel MAGA. Don’t forget to check out some Good Climate News you might have missed. And with Election Day right around the corner, we’re reminding you that showing up for the outdoors means showing up at the polls, too.

COMING UP:

title: Republicans want you to forget that Big Oil paid for this government - NJTODAY.NEWS
description:
Days before another election, Americans are watching prices climb at the gas pump while the world’s largest oil companies count their winnings.
In April 2024, Donald Trump met with oil executives at Mar-a-Lago and reportedly asked them to raise $1 billion for his campaign.
After Trump’s victory, fossil fuel companies contributed $11.8 million to his inaugural committee.
The fossil fuel companies helped finance the campaign.
Big Oil would like to collect the windfall while treating the resulting anger as somebody else’s problem.
text:
Days before another election, Americans are watching prices climb at the gas pump while the world’s largest oil companies count their winnings.

For working families, the energy crisis means another demand on a paycheck already stretched thin. For Big Oil, it means a spectacular quarter.

ExxonMobil reported $17.5 billion in adjusted quarterly earnings. Chevron reported $10.4 billion. Shell’s adjusted earnings reached $10.8 billion, nearly double the previous year’s figure. BP’s profit soared to $8.6 billion, nearly quadrupling from the same quarter of 2025, and TotalEnergies booked $9.1 billion in third-quarter adjusted net income, doubling earnings from a year earlier.

War and disrupted supplies have been punishing consumers and enriching producers.

The same crisis appears on opposite sides of their ledgers.

The companies are eager to explain the refining margins, but they are considerably shy when it comes to explaining the politics.

Their earnings announcements offer the familiar vocabulary of corporate success: production, efficiency, capital discipline, shareholder returns. What disappears behind that language is the relationship between the industry collecting the windfall and the government it spent lavishly to influence.

To investors, the message is: Look at this magnificent cash machine.

They are telling voters, “We just drill the holes.”

But an industry that bankrolls politicians and demands specific government favors cannot claim political innocence when the public gets the bill.

In April 2024, Donald Trump met with oil executives at Mar-a-Lago and reportedly asked them to raise $1 billion for his campaign.

In return, he offered policies the industry wanted: expanded drilling opportunities, an end to the pause on new liquefied natural gas export approvals, and the reversal of vehicle emissions rules. Congressional investigators subsequently pressed the companies for answers about the proposed exchange.

This was a presidential candidate putting a price on access to the machinery of government.

After Trump’s victory, fossil fuel companies contributed $11.8 million to his inaugural committee. Apparently, helping a president take office also requires helping pay for the celebration.

The industry’s investment was followed by hefty payoffs from an accommodating administration, detailed in a report from the Brennan Center for Justice.

Trump’s signature legislative package delivered roughly $18 billion in new and expanded oil and gas tax benefits, according to the Joint Committee on Taxation.

The Republican administration also moved aggressively to dismantle environmental protections and accelerate fossil fuel development.

Executive Actions and Structural Changes

National Energy Emergency: Declared an energy emergency on Day 1 to bypass regulatory barriers and rapidly increase domestic oil, natural gas, and coal production.

National Energy Dominance Council: Established a new federal council specifically dedicated to ramping up traditional energy extraction.

Regulatory Freeze: Directed all federal agencies to pause new rulemakings and systematically review existing guidelines that burden domestic energy production.

Accelerating Fossil Fuel Development

Alaskan Drilling: Lifted federal restrictions on energy production in Alaska, opening millions of acres of public land for expanded oil and gas exploration.

LNG Export Approvals: Resumed the processing of export permits for new liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects, reversing previous restrictions.

Drilling Permits: Significantly accelerated federal approvals, resulting in a 55% increase in drilling permits issued by the Bureau of Land Management.

Dismantling Environmental Safeguards

Methane Rule Rollbacks: Proposed sweeping rollbacks under the Clean Air Act to weaken 2024 standards that required oil and gas operators to limit methane leaks and routine flaring.

Power Plant Emissions: Repealed federal emissions standards for new and existing fossil fuel-fired power plants while targeting the legal basis of carbon regulations.

Vehicle Efficiency Standards: Gutted Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards and vehicle tailpipe emissions rules.

Halting Clean Energy Initiatives

Tax Credit Repeals: Signed legislation to dismantle clean electricity, fuel, and electric vehicle tax credits previously established under the Inflation Reduction Act.

Renewable Energy Moratoriums: Implemented an offshore wind moratorium and placed temporary holds on processing new wind and solar permits on federal lands.

EV Infrastructure Cuts: Froze approximately $3 billion in federal funding earmarked for national electric vehicle charging networks.

International Climate Shifts

Climate Finance Defunding: Revoked the U.S. International Climate Finance Plan, halting monetary commitments to international bodies assisting developing nations with climate transitions.

Paris Accord Withdrawal: Formally withdrew the United States from the Paris Climate Agreement for a second time.

The fossil fuel companies helped finance the campaign. They got the policy as a payoff, but now the polluters and the Republicans would prefer that voters forget about those criminal transactions.

That is the disappearing act.

When favorable rules are being written, the industry knows exactly where Washington is. When angry motorists start asking questions, corporate responsibility dissolves into a lecture about global markets.

Of course oil prices reflect global forces. War disrupts supplies. Refining constraints matter. No honest accounting should pretend otherwise.

But those explanations do not erase the industry’s political spending, its demands for public subsidies or its obligation to answer for the government policies it sought.

A company that understands the market perfectly may still owe the public an explanation for its participation in crimes like bribery.

Trump, meanwhile, has supplied his own explanation with the delicacy of a man announcing a jackpot in a room full of people holding overdue bills.

At his Corpus Christi rally, he declared that the country was making a fortune from events in the Middle East.

He also acknowledged anticipating higher oil prices: “I knew that oil would go up.” He said he had expected an even larger increase and was willing to proceed.

Whose fortune, exactly?

The parent calculating whether a full tank can wait until payday is entitled to ask. So is the worker whose commute has become another financial emergency. A corporation’s earnings are not a household’s prosperity merely because both happen within the same national borders.

The president’s own finances make that distinction especially ugly. Democrats on the Joint Economic Committee estimate that the value of his oil and gas stock holdings, including net transactions and appreciation, increased substantially this year. That calculation does not establish realized profits or personal control of individual trades. It does expose the grotesque collision between a president celebrating expensive energy and a public forced to pay for it.

For millions of Americans, higher prices consume income. For wealthy shareholders, they can increase wealth. Calling both outcomes a national fortune requires either extraordinary ignorance or extraordinary contempt.

Big Oil would like to collect the windfall while treating the resulting anger as somebody else’s problem. The companies want credit for their business decisions and distance from their political decisions. They expect shareholders to remember the returns and voters to forget the checks.

Democrats should make that impossible, but too many of them are silent because they rely on those same corporate aristocrats to fund their campaign operations.

Put the campaign contributions beside the tax benefits. Put the quarterly earnings beside the household fuel bill.

Voters should ask candidates and company executives, in public and under oath where warranted, what they requested, what they received, and what they expect next.

Corporate silence is not proof of a crime. Neither is it an answer.

An industry that spends freely to shape public policy should expect relentless public scrutiny.

It cannot purchase influence by the barrel and then plead helplessness by the gallon.

At the pump, Americans have to watch every dollar.

At the ballot box, they should remember who collected them.

The Second Life of EV Batteries: A Billion-Dollar Opportunity Meets a Reality Check

| Millions of EV batteries will eventually retire from automotive service, creating an opportunity for a second life in solar storage, grid support and commercial backup power. But reusing old batteries isn't as simple as connecting them to a new application. Testing, refurbishment, safety certification and falling prices for new batteries are challenging the economics. The emerging industry must prove that reuse can compete with recycling and newly manufactured storage systems.

Read Full Story

Electric School Buses Didn't Fail. Washington's Rollout Did

| The $5 billion federal Clean School Bus Program has encountered delivery delays, manufacturer bankruptcies, reliability concerns and serious EPA oversight failures. But these shortcomings do not establish that electric school buses are a failed technology. They expose Washington's inability to manage a complex transportation transition. The real lessons involve procurement, infrastructure, manufacturer accountability and the need to measure actual results rather than simply announce ambitious spending targets.

Read Full Story

Beyond the Driverless Car: Who Controls the Future of Canada's Cities?

| As Waymo enters Canada, cities face a crucial choice between passive tech adoption and proactive urban stewardship. Navigating northern blizzards, black ice, and hidden road markings requires rigorous local safety standards over corporate assertions. To avoid gridlock and public transit decay, municipalities must deploy congestion pricing and curb management, integrating robotaxis as last-mile complements. Safer driverless tech enables cities to reclaim asphalt for pedestrian plazas and bike networks, setting a sovereign playbook where civic priorities govern the algorithm.

Delays involving permitting, grid integration, and waterfront infrastructure have pushed completion of the Queens Wharf charging project to mid-2027, forcing the vessel to conduct nighttime diesel-powered charging runs to maintain daily service.

description:

At the end of the day, the U.S. market needs reliable power at unprecedented scale and speed, and we believe Ansaldo Energia is well positioned to contribute.
Power Engineering: Looking beyond this first project in America, how is Ansaldo Energia evaluating the potential for a larger and longer-term presence in the U.S. market?
text:
Editor’s Note: This interview has been excerpted and edited for length and clarity. Watch the full conversation with Stefano Gianatti in the video above.

Power Engineering: What prompted Ansaldo Energia to re-enter the U.S. power generation market now, and how does the Pacifico Energy Project fit into that broader strategy?

Gianatti: First of all, the market opportunity is real, and it’s growing very fast. What we are seeing today is one of the strongest power demand growth cycles in decades, driven by AI factories, data centers, electrification and industrial reshoring. At the same time, customers are not simply looking for generation capacity; they need reliable and dispatchable power available when they need it. That’s why we believe this is the right moment for Ansaldo Energia to return to the U.S. market. The Pacifico Energy Project is a very important milestone because it marks our return to the U.S. new-build power generation market after more than 30 years. We will supply eight 64.3A gas turbines for a major AI factory initiative in Texas, with deliveries starting in 2027. This is a proven technology with more than 70 units installed worldwide and over 4 million equivalent operating hours. But honestly, we do not see Pacifico as a standalone opportunity. We see it as the first step in rebuilding a long-term presence in one of the most important power markets in the world. At the end of the day, the U.S. market needs reliable power at unprecedented scale and speed, and we believe Ansaldo Energia is well positioned to contribute.

Power Engineering: After decades away, I’m curious: what kind of interest have you seen from the U.S. market since announcing the Pacifico Energy project, particularly from data center developers, maybe utilities, IPPs, or other power producers?

Gianatti: What we are seeing is strong interest across the whole market. Of course, data centers are getting a lot of attention, but they are only part of the story. We are also having discussions with utilities, independent power producers, and developers that are facing growing demand and increasing pressure on grid reliability. What’s interesting is that the message to hear from all these customers is remarkably consistent. They are looking for reliable technology, operational flexibility and long-term fuel optionality. But if I had to highlight one priority, I would say speed, with no doubt, speed. Today, rapid deployment has become a key decision factor. Customers want certainty. They want projects that can be delivered on realistic schedules and that will perform reliably from day one. The discussion is increasingly shifting from adding megawatts to guaranteeing energy availability when and where it’s needed. What customers are telling us is very simple: they need fast and reliable power delivered on time.

Power Engineering: Gas turbine demand is extremely strong right now, but the industry is also dealing with supply chain constraints and long delivery timelines. How is Ansaldo thinking about that opportunity while making sure it can meet its commitments?

Gianatti: You are fully right. It’s a great opportunity, but it requires discipline. Demand for gas turbines is strong worldwide, and customers are paying as much attention to delivery dates as they are to technical performance. For us, growth has to remain balanced with execution capability. Our approach is very straightforward. Make realistic commitments and then deliver on them. We are continuing to expand our supplier base, strengthen strategic partnerships, and invest in additional manufacturing capacity. For certain critical components, we are also evaluating selective vertical integration to increase resilience, because the reality is that reliability today is not only about equipment; it is also about execution. Customers want predictable schedules, reliable delivery, and long-term support. The market rewards companies that consistently deliver, and that’s exactly where we are focused.

Power Engineering: As renewable penetration increases and grid conditions become more dynamic, how important is operational flexibility becoming for gas-fired generation?

Gianatti: I believe operational flexibility is becoming one of the most valuable characteristics of modern power systems. As renewable penetration increases, grid conditions naturally become more dynamic. As a result, operators need generation assets that can react quickly, operate efficiently under different conditions, and provide reliable, dispatchable power whenever required. In many cases, flexibility is becoming just as important as efficiency and power output. As an example, our GT36 H-class gas turbine, rated at 550 MW (more than 800 MW in combined cycle), is a good example. It combines around 63% combined-cycle efficiency with outstanding operational flexibility. It can ramp at up to 100 MW per minute, which is best in class, allowing operators to respond very quickly to changes in grid demand. Another good example is our F-class AE94.3A, rated at 340 MW (500 MW in combined cycle). This unit also offers excellent operational flexibility, with ramp rates above 50 MW per minute and a long track record of reliable operation. And there is another important aspect: modern grids need more than energy production. They need inertia, voltage support and stability services that rotating equipment naturally provides. In tomorrow’s power systems, flexibility will be every bit as important as traditional metrics such as efficiency and power output.

Power Engineering: Looking beyond this first project in America, how is Ansaldo Energia evaluating the potential for a larger and longer-term presence in the U.S. market?

Gianatti: The United States is clearly a strategic market for Ansaldo Energia, and the Pacifico project is a very important milestone, but we see it as the beginning of a broader journey rather than the final destination. We are actively evaluating opportunities across data centers and industrial applications, both grid-connected and behind the meter. Of course, any future expansion must be based on sustainable growth and strong customer relationships. But we also understand something very clearly: long-term success in North America requires localization. That means being closer to customers, strengthening local capabilities, building partnerships, and developing an increasingly local support structure. I do not want to go into specific initiatives today. But localization is certainly an important part of how we think about the future on this market. Our ambition is simple: we want to become a long-term technology and service partner in the United States, not simply an equipment supplier.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman August Pfluger (TX-11), Chairman of the United States Air Force Academy (USAFA) Board of Visitors, led the Board's fall meeting at the Academy in Colorado Springs this month. The meeting focused on the Academy's leadership priorities, infrastructure improvements, and cadet well-being.

Chairman Pfluger opened the meeting by reviewing the recommendations in the Board’s Semiannual Report. Members then heard from the Academy’s new Superintendent, Lieutenant General Paul Moga; Commandant, Brigadier General Brandon Tellez, and Provost, Brigadier General James Valpiani, about their priorities and discussed ways the Board can support their efforts. Under Secretary of the Air Force Matthew Lohmeier met with the Board during the Board’s Administrative Session. Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Manpower and Reserve Affairs Richard Anderson and Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Energy, Installations, and Environment Michael Borders also participated in the meeting.

A portion of the meeting was dedicated to discussing USAFA’s infrastructure. The Board heard from Assistant Secretary Borders on the urgency of funding infrastructure projects at the Academy. Department of the Air Force personnel also highlighted the importance of the USAFA Board of Visitors-led provisions in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

During their visit, the Board engaged with the Air Force Academy Association of Graduates Board of Directors, the Air Force Academy Foundation Board of Directors, and the Air Force Academy Athletic Corporation Board of Directors. The Board also identified a new focus area regarding cadet nutrition. Members plan to review cadet nutrition and Mitchell Hall funding more thoroughly.

Members of the Board experienced life at the Academy firsthand. They participated in an orientation experience at the airfield, attended classes, toured the dormitories, and had lunch with cadets in Mitchell Hall. They also visited the Academy’s new Visitor Center. These activities gave Members numerous opportunities to interact with cadets and USAFA staff.

"As Chairman of the Air Force Academy Board of Visitors, I was proud to lead a productive meeting in Colorado Springs. We focused on modernizing the Academy’s infrastructure so cadets have the facilities they deserve, and we’re committed to working with the Department of the Air Force leadership to make that happen. I also appreciated the chance to meet with cadets and staff, whose dedication and professionalism give me great confidence in the future of our Air Force. The Board is also taking a close look at cadet nutrition, because the men and women who will defend our nation should be properly fueled to perform at their best. The Academy shapes the leaders our nation will rely on, and it’s our duty to make sure it remains the best in the world," said USAFA Board of Visitors Chairman August Pfluger (TX-11).

text:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Costumed environmental activists joined Hawaiʻi lawmakers on Halloween Eve to warn of severe environmental consequences and push back against proposed federal legislation that would grant legal immunity to oil companies.

Protesters rallied against companion measures introduced in Congress: House Resolution 8330 and Senate Bill 4340, known as the “Stop Climate Shakedowns Act.” Sponsored by U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman, R-Wyo., the legislation is intended to “protect American energy from leftist legal crusades punishing lawful activity.”

If passed, the measures would shield fossil fuel producers by barring retroactive climate liability lawsuits, dismissing active court cases, and preempting state energy penalty laws.

“Legal immunity for big oil companies would provide an insurmountable challenge for those fighting to combat climate change,” said Ella Diaz of the Environmental Law Society.

Lawsuits target fossil fuel giants

Hawaiʻi and 10 other states have filed lawsuits against BP, Chevron, ExxonMobil, and other major energy producers. The complaints allege that fossil fuel companies understood for decades that their emissions contributed to global warming, yet misled the public while continuing aggressive promotion.

“It’s documented that they knew what they were doing,” said state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole, D-Kāne‘ohe, Kailua. “They took deliberate steps to mislead the public, caused confusion, and get people hooked on gasoline.”

Community leaders point to recent hurricane activity, storm surges, and localized flooding as evidence that climate impacts are arriving faster than communities can absorb them.

“So many coastal districts across the islands are facing huge costs for the coastal tidal rise that’s caused directly by global warming,” said state Rep. Kim Coco Iwamoto, D-Ala Moana, Kaka‘ako, Downtown.

Concerns over fast-tracking

With the general election approaching, U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda expressed concern that congressional leadership could try to fast-track the legislation quickly before new lawmakers take office.

“It’s just an insult to everyone who is fighting back against both the rising cost of gas, the obscene profits that oil companies are making,” Tokuda said.
