title: From China to Pittsburgh, Eos bets on American manufacturing - Washington Examiner
description:
Eos has drawn about $178 million so far, including an $87 million advance to build the second production line here in Warrendale.
Pennsylvania committed $22 million through a $10 million Pennsylvania First grant and $12 million from the Redevelopment Assistance Capital Program, including $3 million awarded in 2022.
Under a Department of War contract, Eos is developing long-duration energy storage for the proposed Golden Dome for America missile-defense shield.
Eos has done something rare in Pennsylvania politics: it has drawn enthusiastic support from both sides of the aisle.
And Trump singled out Eos and its Golden Dome contract during a manufacturing announcement in Pennsylvania with McCormick.
text:
Every worker on the production floor is a member of the United Steelworkers, a choice management says was deliberate. It is a traditional union shop that reflects the manufacturing legacy of the place it calls home.

On Thursday, Alex Fitzsimmons, associate deputy secretary of energy and senior adviser to Energy Secretary Chris Wright, toured the 432,000-square-foot facility alongside Mastrangelo and Chief Administrative Officer Michelle Buczkowski to see what an American-made alternative to the lithium-ion battery looks like at scale.

“With Eos, you have a company that left the United States for China in 2016 under the Obama administration, and then returned to America in 2018 in President Donald Trump’s first term,” Fitzsimmons said. “Now, in President Trump’s second term, Eos is rapidly expanding manufacturing capacity for advanced battery technologies, spurring economic growth and employment opportunities in the Pittsburgh region.”

What Eos does here is almost impossible in the lithium-ion world: It turns raw materials into complete battery systems under one roof, with a predominantly domestic supply chain.

At the heart of the product is a gray battery module about half the size of a carry-on suitcase. Each module contains 20 cells, with a design that borrows from the familiar lead-acid battery: Plastic plates called bipolars sit in a row, with a zinc-and-bromine electrolyte flowing between them. As the battery charges, zinc coats the plates and bromine settles into carbon felt. As it discharges, the two recombine, releasing a whisper of heat and a great deal of electricity.

“It’s more of a chemical reaction than it is what you would see in lithium,” Buczkowski explained.

That chemistry is the point. The batteries are nonflammable. Mastrangelo said engineers in Alabama overcharged them by roughly 300% to try to provoke a thermal event, then put a live flame to them. They would not ignite. The plastic smoked, then melted, and the electrolyte that spilled out extinguished anything that might have caught fire.

“So it’s like self-extinguishing,” Fitzsimmons said.

Because the modules will not burn, they can be safely stacked in ways competitors’ batteries cannot. Stacked three high, they match lithium-ion’s energy storage per acre. Six high doubles that capacity; 12 high quadruples it. Eos is also working with the Department of War to develop a new design: A stackable cube about six feet on each side that stores 133 kilowatt-hours and can be moved by forklift. Each cube is about one-sixth the size of a shipping container.

The batteries also do not wear out the way lithium-ion batteries do. After a small amount of degradation as the battery “settles into itself,” Buczkowski said, the performance curve stays flat for 20 years. They can discharge over milliseconds or for as long as 16 hours, with a sweet spot of four to 16 hours, and they actually perform better the more they are cycled.

That flexibility matters in the age of artificial intelligence. Data centers need power systems that can handle both millisecond spikes from AI inference and hours of steady demand. Eos’s own software, DawnOS, controls each module individually. If one charges faster than the others, the system pauses its charging to let the rest catch up, bringing all modules to full charge together.

Mastrangelo calls one of the biggest emerging uses an “electron parking lot” — batteries near a grid connection that store incoming power, whether generated by gas, nuclear, or solar, and help utilities avoid costly new transmission lines.

The company focused on research and development from 2008 to about 2016, then tried building dry batteries in China to be filled and shipped to customers. When Mastrangelo arrived in 2018, he reversed course.

“We came back from China in the first Trump administration because we couldn’t afford to do it, and I was worried about the IP getting stolen,” he said. He brought the equipment back to the Turtle Creek building where it all started.

When the company brought its supply chain home, it gave engineers a strict rule: No custom materials. Everything had to be an off-the-shelf commodity. The electrolyte is similar to the fluid used in horizontal drilling for oil and gas, while the felt is the same kind used to insulate nuclear warheads. Working with those common materials, the company has developed technology it owns from the ground up, backed by more than 200 patents.

Eos applied for its Department of Energy loan during Trump’s first term. The $303.5 million loan guarantee from the department’s Loan Programs Office closed in the final days of the Biden administration, and the money has flowed since Trump returned to office. Eos has drawn about $178 million so far, including an $87 million advance to build the second production line here in Warrendale.

“We’re moving much faster,” Fitzsimmons said.

State and local governments have bet on the company, too. Pennsylvania committed $22 million through a $10 million Pennsylvania First grant and $12 million from the Redevelopment Assistance Capital Program, including $3 million awarded in 2022. Allegheny County added $2 million, which County Executive Sara Innamorato called the county’s largest contribution of its kind. Eos is investing $352.9 million of its own in the expansion.

The only major component not yet sourced domestically is that carbon felt, which Eos buys from South Korea. It accounts for about 12% of the system’s cost and carries a 12.5% tariff. Mastrangelo said the tariff puts the company’s goal of becoming gross-margin positive by the end of the year at risk.

Eos is working with Sen. Dave McCormick (R-PA) and members of Congress from Pennsylvania, Ohio, and New Jersey to press the U.S. trade representative for relief. It is also pursuing a project at a long-shuttered Ohio facility to make the felt from recycled carbon fiber taken from retired wind turbine blades.

Fitzsimmons said the department still has money available for those kinds of supply-chain efforts and intends to put all of it to work.

Defense is a growing part of the story. Under a Department of War contract, Eos is developing long-duration energy storage for the proposed Golden Dome for America missile-defense shield. The prototype sits on the factory floor here. The company is also involved in an Army project to strengthen energy resilience at Tobyhanna Army Depot in northeastern Pennsylvania.

Fitzsimmons, who previously ran the department’s grid-security office, said the administration is balancing speed and security as it writes new rules for equipment on the power grid. “If we don’t build this stuff here, China will build it,” he said.

Eos has done something rare in Pennsylvania politics: it has drawn enthusiastic support from both sides of the aisle.

Gov. Josh Shapiro came to Turtle Creek last October to announce the expansion, the headquarters move, and this plant, which is expected to help create 735 new jobs. McCormick has championed the company and is helping it fight the felt tariff. And Trump singled out Eos and its Golden Dome contract during a manufacturing announcement in Pennsylvania with McCormick.

All three men recognize what is taking shape here: part of the region’s future is being built by Steelworkers on a factory floor, making a product invented and engineered at home.

THE CONSERVATIVE WHO SAID YES TO BUCKS COUNTY, USA

Fitzsimmons put it in national terms. “Eos moved into a shuttered Westinghouse plant, revitalized it, and is now producing some of the most advanced batteries in the world to meet rising energy demand,” he said. “With common-sense energy policies and a focus on reindustrializing America, President Trump is bringing historic levels of investment and jobs to parts of the country, including Pennsylvania, that haven’t seen these levels of investment in decades.”

Back on the mezzanine, Mastrangelo looked down at the line once more. Seven years ago, he had a handful of workers and equipment shipped back from China. Now he has two plants and a union workforce doing what many said America could no longer do.

Voters across the country have made it clear: they cannot afford the economic disaster of Trump and MAGA Republican’s dirty energy agenda. Trump and Congressional Republicans are raising costs, banning clean energy, and gutting protections for our air, water, public lands and climate so Big Polluters, corrupt utilities, and Big Tech can line their pockets. People are fed up with Trump’s failed energy policies which are making us poorer, sicker and less safe.

In the days leading up to the election, voters are turning out for the pro-environment, pro-democracy candidates up and down the ballot who are committed to putting families and communities first, and who support real energy solutions that put us on the path to a more affordable, clean energy future.

Together with our state affiliates, LCV Action Fund has endorsed nearly 190 candidates in the 2026 midterm election cycle.

This year, LCV invested $1.5 million into a brand-new field program, Clean Energy Corps. It’s among the first canvass efforts in the nation to work in collaboration with campaigns in battleground states with the goal of knocking 150,000 doors by Election Day. LCV also mobilized its national membership to volunteer through an approximately $2 million dollar investment in GreenRoots. Combined, these efforts have reached over 500,000 voters. LCV members and organizers have completed nearly 30,000 shifts to ensure voters have a plan to make their voice heard this election, and as we near Election Day, are continuing to canvass, phonebank, and meet voters where they are across the country.

LCV Action Fund Endorsements

This election cycle, LCV Action Fund endorsed 186 pro-environment, pro-democracy federal candidates, including 23 for the U.S. Senate and 163 for the U.S. House of Representatives. Candidates LCV Action Fund endorsed include 40% who are people of color, 47% who are women, and 5% who identify as LGBTQ+. Find all of LCV Action Fund’s publicly endorsed candidates here.

LCV Action Fund-endorsed candidates who will make history if elected include:

Amish Shah (AZ-01), would be the first Indian American to represent Arizona in Congress.

Jonathan Nez (AZ-02), would be the first Navajo member and the first Indigenous member to represent Arizona in Congress.

Dan Koh (MA-06), would be the first Asian American to represent Massachusetts in Congress.

Abdul El-Sayed (MI-Sen), would be the first Muslim and the first Egyptian American to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Peggy Flanagan (MN-Sen), would be the first Native American woman to serve in the U.S. Senate and the first Native American to represent Minnesota in Congress

Chris Pappas (NH-Sen), would be the first openly LGBTQ+ man to be elected to the U.S. Senate.

Cait Conley (NY-17), would be the first openly LGBTQ+ woman to represent New York in Congress.

Dr. Annie Andrews (SC-Sen), would be the first woman to be elected to the U.S. Senate from South Carolina.

Elevating Energy and Climate

It is clear that rising costs of energy and health are the top issues for voters across the country, especially as people experienced record heat and their highest energy bills ever this summer. People blame the Trump administration and their rubber-stamping allies in Congress for handing out corrupt deals to their Big Polluter and billionaire CEO donors. The same Big Polluters who backed Trump’s campaign and are making our air and water dirtier and our communities sicker while fueling the climate crisis. And this election, we saw how concerns about the impacts of data centers on energy bills, air and water pollution, and communities increasingly became top of mind for people across the country.

Our endorsed candidates up and down the ballot ran on the need for clean energy solutions to the climate crisis, protecting clean air and water, safeguarding public lands, and standing up for free and fair elections. Just a few examples include:

Energy affordability and advancing clean energy were clear priorities in races across the country. Senate candidates including Josh Turek (IA-Sen), Abdul El-Sayed (MI-Sen), Roy Cooper (NC-Sen), and James Talarico (TX-Sen) spoke extensively about the impact of rising energy costs on families and opportunities to lower costs with clean energy solutions.

Data centers and their impacts on the environment and energy affordability were also front and center in elections across the country, including New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. Up and down the ballot, candidates like Sherrod Brown (OH-Sen) and Rebecca Bennett (NJ-07) highlighted the impact of rapid data center development on electricity bills. Ads from other candidates including Representative Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), Will Lawrence (MI-07), and Paige Cognetti (PA-08) called for an end to data center giveaways that are raising electric bills and ensure data centers pay their fair share instead of passing costs on to families.

Extreme weather also played a role in this cycle, especially in Florida where Kathy Castor (FL-14), Leela Gray (FL-13), and Pia Dandiya (FL-22) highlighted the challenges paying for skyrocketing home insurance costs — if you can even find insurance — as fossil-fueled climate impacts swamp their districts.

Reaching Voters Where They Are

We met voters where they were — as people experienced skyrocketing energy prices across the country, affordability remained top of mind for voters. And poll after poll reaffirmed what our volunteers and organizers saw in states across the country: voters, especially Black and Latino voters, are deeply concerned about rising costs, including rising energy costs.

LCV invested $3.5 million in our organizing programs this midterm cycle, spending more than ever to reach young voters and leveraging every tool in our toolbox to reach voters. This year’s investments included $1.5 million for our newly launched Clean Energy Corps field program and approximately $2 million for GreenRoots, our voter mobilization program.

See more details on this year’s organizing programs below.

Clean Energy Corps: New Program Mobilizing Voters Alongside Campaigns

LCV launched its new field program, Clean Energy Corps, to work alongside campaigns in three battleground districts. This program mobilized voters in support of Representative Kathy Castor (FL-14) and candidates Rebecca Bennett (NJ-07), and Paige Cognetti (PA-08). Clean Energy Corps organizers helped add capacity to campaigns to reach and turn out voters who are historically excluded from outreach efforts, and they have knocked on over 137,000 doors so far.

Concerns in FL-14 centered around costs; many are worried about the future of Medicare and Medicaid while others pointed to the cost of fuel and groceries. Tampa Bay area residents expressed frustration with Republicans’ response to these compounding expenses and committed their support to Rep. Kathy Castor because she’ll fight to protect their healthcare and community. Just this week, we spoke with a lifelong Republican who said the Republican majority hasn’t handled the cost of living crisis so they decided to vote for Rep. Kathy Castor for real change.

Voters across NJ-07 shared stories about the tough decisions they faced to pay for basic necessities like energy bills, healthcare, and housing. Rebecca Bennett’s plan to lower costs and make New Jersey more affordable has been a selling point on the doors. Many also experienced flooding in their communities and are excited about Bennett’s plans to Invest in climate-resilient infrastructure projects that create good-paying jobs and protect New Jersey from damage from intensifying storms and flooding.

In PA-08, we regularly heard from voters that they’re fed up with rising costs and are concerned about data centers driving up their energy bills even higher. Her service as mayor is often referenced by voters as a reason they trust she’s right for the job.

GreenRoots: Mobilizing LCV Members and Engaging Young Voters

This midterm cycle, GreenRoots mobilized LCV’s national membership in support of 30 LCV Action Fund-endorsed candidates in 13 battleground states. GreenRoots has mobilized LCV members to volunteer on behalf of LCV Action Fund-endorsed candidates in every election since 2012.

This includes a new tactic: writing 11,500 postcards to other LCV members aged 18-35 to drive their support for LCV Action Fund-endorsed candidates and turn out young voters.

LCV has invested more than ever in turning out young voters this cycle, hosting virtual volunteer webinars so members can learn more about LCV’s midterm electoral priorities and key races, and take action by sharing personalized vote guides, making plans to vote, and promoting LCV’s endorsement guide. We also partnered with creators to reach over 800,000 people across social media platforms to encourage them to get involved in the fight for climate champions this election cycle.

text:
This election season, transportation policy issues have arisen in a variety of forms in races across the country, most frequently tied to national affordability issues. The question of how to pay for transportation investments is never an easy one to answer and is made much more difficult when the focus is on reducing household costs. In general, candidates –particularly non-incumbents– in elections across the country appear largely aligned across parties in not wanting to expand user fees or taxes for transportation investments, and even wanting to suspend or repeal those already in place.

The cost of gas and diesel and related affordability challenges and the President’s disapproval ratings have both been central stories in election coverage this year. Graphing them together makes clear that the two issues are highly related.

Gas Taxes

Gas prices and gas taxes have been an issue in several U.S. Senate elections, with non-incumbent candidates often proposing to repeal or suspend federal gas taxes regardless of party. For instance in the Texas Senate race, both Republican candidate Ken Paxton and Democratic candidate James Talarico have called for gas tax relief (Paxton proposed permanent repeal while Talarico suggested a temporary suspension). Similarly in the Michigan Senate race, both Republican candidate Mike Rogers and Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed have supported suspending both state and federal gas taxes to provide households with price relief, as have Republican candidate Ashley Hinson and Democratic candidate Josh Turek in the Iowa Senate race.

In the North Carolina legislature, where Republicans control both chambers, Republican leadership proposed and passed a bill to suspend the state’s 41 cent gas tax in early October through the end of November. Many Democrats supported the bill while also deriding it as a campaign ploy by Republicans concerned about the possibility they will lose their veto-proof Senate majority.

Tolling, Pricing and other Road Funding

The question of tolling has come up in several gubernatorial races around the country. In the Illinois Governor’s race, in which incumbent Governor J.B. Pritzker is facing Republican challenger Darren Bailey. Bailey has made a campaign promise to eliminate tolls. The Illinois tollway board—all of whom are Pritzker appointees— has approved a 45-cent increase for motorists on Illinois toll roads along with a 30% increase for commercial vehicle tolls as part of a $1.3 billion statewide funding measure that will fund tollway construction projects along with public transit systems across Illinois.

A somewhat similar dynamic is playing out in the New York Governor’s race, where incumbent Governor Kathy Hochul has defended the success of the NYC congestion pricing and the funding it provides for MTA a signature accomplishment despite her initial misgivings and implementation delays. Her opponent, Republican gubernatorial candidate and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, has pledged he would end congestion pricing, potentially by simply ending enforcement, and has called congestion pricing a tax on the middle class.

Without an incumbent in the Rhode Island Governor’s race, the tolling debate has played out somewhat differently and could result in changes to the state’s planned resumption of tolling next year. In a televised debate between leading candidates including Republican Aaron Guckian and Democrat Helena Foulkes, all the gubernatorial candidates agreed they would choose not to reinstate the truck tolls out of concern about costs to businesses. The RI truck-only tolls were put into place in 2018 by then-Governor Gina Raimondo but collection was paused in 2022 after a court ruled that the truck-only taxes were unconstitutional. However, a new ruling issued in late 2024 cleared the path for reinstating the tolls if the per-day cap on tolls were removed, since that cap gave an advantage to local trucks. RIDOT has been pursuing reinstatement of the tolls through ongoing work to upgrade the gantry infrastructure and the billing system at a cost of $20 million set aside in the state’s FY27 budget, to be paid for by the revenues to be produced once the tolls resume. Unless a new governor changes the plans, tolls will be reinstated in Spring 2027 and are expected to generate roughly $40 million in annual revenue.

In the Wisconsin Governor’s race, Democrat David Crowley is running against Republican Tom Tiffany. On the debate stage on October 21, moderators asked the candidates about funding for transportation, including whether they’d support indexing the gas tax—to which both answered in the negative. Slightly more daylight emerged on the question of tolling, with Tiffany offering the same “No” to the question of tolling while Crowley indicated “we should be open” to the idea.

Republican Senator and gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn declined to attend the Tennessee Governor’s race debate with Democratic nominee Jerri Green and other third-party candidates, but did respond to questions from the Tennessean that asked about the state’s $58 billion backlog in road maintenance and investment needs. Jerri Green pledged to raise revenues from taxing the growth and sale of cannabis to fund the backlog, and Blackburn promised to “complete a DOGE to remove waste, find savings and reduce what we spend” noting further that from there innovative solutions such as “choice lanes are one consideration”. The Tennessean also raised the question of support for debt financing or new taxes for transportation, to which Green responded “No” with regard to taxes but “leave all options on the table” with regard to debt. Blackburn declined to answer either question.

Transit

Public transportation issues have come up in only a few races. In the NY gubernatorial race, in which Republican candidate Blakeman has focused on the issue of crime on public transit.

In the Georgia Governor’s race, Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms has pledged “there should be dedicated state funding to transit statewide” including for MARTA as well as for other transit systems statewide, calling state funding “the missing piece” that would help transit systems expand in Atlanta and in the midsize cities that don’t currently have adequate transit.

EVs, Fuel Economy, and Restoration of Tax Credits

One issue that hasn’t gotten as much attention as you might expect—in an era of affordability concerns about high gas prices—is the topic of electric vehicles and fuel economy standards. Democratic Congressional leadership has been relatively silent on whether restoration of the EV tax credits that were repealed in the One Big Beautiful Bill would be back on the table in a Democratic-controlled Congress. Sales of EVs fell off sharply after repeal of the EV tax credits but this year, even without tax support, sales of EVs have grown steadily, presumably in response to high gas prices.

In the Michigan Senate Race, Mike Rogers’s campaign ads have accused Abdul El-Sayed of wanting to ban gas-powered vehicles—an accusation that various fact checkers and the El-Sayed campaign have rejected as untrue.

In the Nebraska Senate race, Senator Pete Ricketts is running for re-election after leading the effort to repeal California’s waiver for their clean cars rule and pledging support for eliminating cafe standards. His statements on the issue describe his support rooted in the desire to increase consumer choice and lower vehicle prices.

text:
Jacobs will support AEP's seven-state eastern transmission portfolio, with WSP USA handling the four-state western portfolio. Neither firm disclosed its contract value; AEP's $37 billion represents planned systemwide transmission investment, not the value of the two awards.

Of that investment, approximately $17 billion is earmarked for projects driven by regional transmission organizations, $11 billion for system reliability and $9 billion for transmission serving individual customers. AEP expects its transmission rate base to rise from approximately $37 billion this year to $69 billion in 2031 and plans to nearly triple the mileage of its 765-kV network, of which it already owns about 90% of the nation's existing lines.

Driving much of that expansion is a sharp increase in contracted electricity demand. AEP signed 15 GW of new load commitments during the third quarter and expects incremental contracted load to reach 84 GW by 2031. Of that total, 92% is tied to data centers, including cryptocurrency customers, according to the company's investor presentation.

AEP Sets Regional Delivery Structure

Jacobs said work under its eastern assignment is already underway and will ramp up as AEP's portfolio grows. Its scope includes project management and controls, engineering and design, siting, public outreach, right-of-way acquisition and environmental services. Jacobs will lead a team that includes ORC, GFT and RC Commonwealth.

“Our integrated delivery model will help AEP standardize and scale project delivery across its growing portfolio,” Jacobs Chair and CEO Bob Pragada said in a statement.

WSP disclosed fewer specifics about its western assignment but said its work could span planning, environmental review, permitting, engineering, program management and project delivery.

ENR reported Oct. 20 that the U.S. Energy Dept. finalized a $1.6-billion loan guarantee supporting AEP's planned reconductoring and rebuilding of 5,000 miles of high-voltage transmission lines across five states, part of a $3.56-billion program. Contractors will be selected “on a project-by-project basis,” an AEP spokesman told ENR.

$5B Ohio Project Shows Scale of Buildout

One of the largest projects now included in AEP's transmission plan is an approximately $5-billion, 765-kV build serving SB Energy's planned 10.4-GW data center campus at the former Portsmouth gaseous diffusion plant site in Piketon, Ohio.

AEP finalized commercial agreements for the project during the third quarter. Construction is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, and AEP has secured substantially all required rights-of-way, Fehrman said during the utility's Oct. 28 earnings call.

Three planned 765-kV transmission lines would each provide approximately 3.2 GW of incremental capacity, with targeted in-service dates at the end of 2028, 2029 and 2030, according to AEP's Oct. 28 quarterly filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The campus's initial 800 MW of load is expected to be served using existing transmission capacity.

The customer will cover project costs through payments extending 20 years after each line enters service. Before the remaining transmission work moves ahead, AEP still needs approvals from PJM, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

text:
Democracy Defenders Fund finds Musk’s companies received at least $10 billion in new federal contracts since he left DOGE, while federal agencies reduced fines, dropped enforcement actions, and eased restrictions on his businesses.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Seventeen months after Elon Musk left the Trump administration, his companies have received at least $10 billion in new federal contracts, while 25 federal departments and agencies have taken actions benefiting or potentially benefiting his businesses, according to a new report released today by Democracy Defenders Fund. That amount is in addition to the estimated $6.3 billion in contracts his firms were awarded during his stint as a special government employee.

The report, “Trump and Musk, 17 Months Later,” finds that Musk’s net worth has more than doubled since he left DOGE in May 2025, growing from approximately $419 billion to between $900 billion and $1 trillion. Musk has also spent more than $445 million supporting Republicans during the 2026 election cycle, making him the largest known political donor in U.S. history. His unprecedented political spending, combined with the billions in government contracts awarded to his companies and favorable decisions by federal regulators, raises serious questions about whether the Trump administration is putting the interests of one of its biggest donors ahead of the American people.

The report states, “The central finding is that the current government ethics framework allows the world’s richest person—a major political donor and former government official—to earn billions from federal contracts while his companies receive favorable treatment across government. The same framework may leave room for other wealthy individuals to exercise comparable influence.”

Among the largest contracts identified in the report are two Pentagon awards to SpaceX worth $4.2 billion and $2.3 billion for the Golden Dome missile defense program. Both contracts were awarded through an accelerated process that bypassed many standard contracting procedures. The Pentagon imposed requirements so specifically tailored to SpaceX that some competing companies decided not to bid, raising concerns about whether other defense contractors were given a fair opportunity to compete for billions in taxpayer-funded contracts.

The report also details how federal agencies have repeatedly acted in ways that benefit Musk’s businesses. The Securities and Exchange Commission settled a case against Musk for $1.5 million after initially seeking $150 million over alleged securities violations related to his purchase of Twitter. The federal judge who approved the settlement questioned whether Musk was receiving preferential treatment. “The court is left to wonder whether the SEC will afford other alleged securities-law violators such solicitude,” wrote U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan.

Other federal agencies have also eased enforcement or intervened on behalf of Musk’s companies. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration reduced a $49,650 fine against Tesla to $9,900 following a worker’s death. The Justice Department attempted to block an NAACP lawsuit alleging that Musk’s xAI data centers violated federal clean air requirements. Meanwhile, the Federal Communications Commission granted a waiver allowing SpaceX to expand into the mobile phone market.

Not all Trump administration policies have benefited Musk’s businesses, however. The report also notes that the elimination of federal tax credits for electric vehicles and changes to vehicle emissions standards have hurt Tesla, while Trump’s tariffs have increased costs for the company, particularly its energy business.

Read the full report, “Trump and Musk, 17 Months Later,” here.

text:
Module maker First Solar, Inc. celebrated the opening of the first 1.7 GW phase of its new South Carolina facility, part of a $330 million investment to onshore final production processes for its photovoltaic product manufacturing from its international fleet.

The South Carolina facility in Gaffney, Cherokee County, is expected to bring First Solar’s total annual nameplate capacity to 3.4 GW once fully completed by mid-2027, according to a company release. The solar PV tech and manufacturing company is focusing on final domestic production of its Series 6 Plus modules, thin-film PV solar panels made from cadmium telluride and engineered for utility-scale installation.

According to a First Solar and National Renewable Energy Laboratory study, Group V (or Group 5) elements like CdTe solar cells have historically relied on copper to generate the electric field required to harvest solar energy. However, some instabilities copper introduces include rapidly diffusing through PV layer materials, degrading the solar cell over time.

First Solar notes that each Series 6 Plus module provides up to 480 watts of power, leveraging the company’s CuRe (copper replacement) technology. CuRe tech aims to improve the panel's cadmium telluride semiconductor structure by replacing copper with what First Solar considers more stable Group V elements to reduce long-term power degradation.

“Less than a year after we selected Gaffney, this facility is ready to produce American solar technology, built by South Carolinian workers,” said First Solar CEO Mark Widmar during a ribbon-cutting ceremony. “That pace reflects what is possible when sound policy, strong state and local partners and a committed workforce align.”

Widmar noted that every module produced at the Gaffney facility is made without foreign dependence on countries like China for crystalline silicon supply chains as American electricity demand grows.

Over the next two to four years, research firm Wood Mackenzie outlined that sourcing components free from Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC) status could emerge as a critical market bottleneck amid a massive imbalance in the U.S. clean energy transition.

First Solar leaders add that because of this, investment in the South Carolina facility aligns with the current U.S. administration’s trade policies and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which supports President Donald Trump’s American energy dominance and affordability agenda goals. While the South Carolina facility aims to strengthen First Solar’s ability to deliver to its U.S.-based customers, the company is on track to support nearly 700 jobs in the process. Approximately 500 of those domestic jobs have reportedly already been filled.

The new plant expands First Solar’s footprint in South Carolina, which includes a distribution center in Duncan, Spartanburg County, and a longstanding supply chain partnership with the intermodal rail facility Inland Port Greer, operated by the South Carolina Ports Authority. By the end of this year, First Solar noted that it forecasts approximately 17 GW of U.S. module manufacturing capacity, none of which will have any dependence on Chinese crystalline silicon supply chains.

text:
The Second Life of EV Batteries: A Billion-Dollar Opportunity Meets a Reality Check

Fair Use [17 U.S.C. § 107] Rebaba Brings Second-Life EV Batteries into Homes with New 40 kWh System

By EVWorld.com AI Editorial Team

The electric vehicle revolution is creating an unexpected industrial challenge: What happens to millions of lithium-ion batteries when they are no longer good enough to power an automobile?

The obvious answer seems to be recycling. But there may be a more valuable alternative. A battery that has lost a portion of its original capacity could still have years of useful service remaining. Instead of dismantling it for raw materials, companies could give it a second life storing electricity from solar panels, wind farms and utility grids.

It is an appealing proposition, combining the economics of energy storage with the principles of a circular economy. Unfortunately, turning that promise into a profitable industry is proving more complicated than simply finding another use for an old battery.

Michael Barnard, writing in The Future Is Electric, makes a compelling argument that the second-life battery market must pass a fundamental test: It must deliver a safe, dependable and economically competitive product. The environmental appeal of reusing batteries is not enough.

An Automotive Reject Isn't Necessarily Scrap

Consider an electric vehicle originally equipped with a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. After years of driving, its capacity may have declined to 75 or 80 kWh. For an automobile owner, that means diminished driving range and potentially reduced resale value.

But stationary energy storage has different requirements. A battery doesn't need to propel a vehicle, withstand road vibration or deliver rapid acceleration. It simply needs to store electricity and release it when needed.

That makes retired EV batteries attractive candidates for stationary applications, including solar energy storage, commercial backup power, industrial peak-demand management and microgrids.

Yet remaining capacity alone tells only part of the story. Individual battery cells deteriorate differently depending on temperature, charging patterns, operating conditions and age. Two battery packs removed from identical vehicles may have substantially different performance and safety characteristics.

Before reuse, batteries must be tested, graded and evaluated. Their remaining capacity, internal resistance, cell balance and thermal behavior all matter. A poorly matched or damaged battery can create serious safety hazards, including thermal runaway and fire.

In other words, a second-life battery must become a properly engineered commercial product, not simply a collection of used cells.

The Economics Are Getting Harder

The second-life concept initially benefited from an obvious advantage: New lithium-ion batteries were expensive, while used batteries were potentially available at a substantial discount.

That equation is changing.

Battery manufacturing costs have fallen, particularly with the growing adoption of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry. Meanwhile, recovering a used battery involves transportation, disassembly, inspection, testing, reassembly, safety systems and warranties.

Those costs can quickly erode the apparent savings.

A 2024 Stanford study found that the economic case for reusing retired batteries varies considerably by chemistry. LFP batteries showed stronger potential for reuse than some nickel-based alternatives under the conditions examined.

This distinction matters. There is no universal second-life battery. Different chemistries, degradation patterns and applications produce different economic outcomes.

If a new stationary battery offers better performance, a longer warranty and competitive pricing, a refurbished automotive battery may have little commercial appeal.

China Offers a Cautionary Lesson

China, the world's largest electric vehicle and battery manufacturing market, has been an early advocate of battery reuse. Its enormous EV fleet creates an approaching wave of retired batteries, making recovery and reuse strategically important.

However, China has also recognized the dangers of an inadequately regulated second-life market. Its evolving rules emphasize product quality, traceability and safety rather than simply encouraging companies to repackage used battery modules.

This should not be interpreted as abandoning battery reuse. It is an acknowledgment that the circular economy requires standards, accountability and commercially viable products.

Three Possible Destinations

The emerging battery industry is likely to divide retired batteries into three distinct pathways.

Batteries with substantial remaining capacity and acceptable safety characteristics can be refurbished for stationary storage. Those that cannot economically meet reuse requirements should be recycled to recover lithium, nickel, cobalt, copper and other valuable materials.

A third opportunity lies in diagnostics and certification. Companies capable of accurately evaluating battery health could become essential intermediaries, determining whether individual packs are better suited for reuse or materials recovery.

This sorting process could ultimately determine where the greatest economic and environmental value resides.

The Real Test Is Economics

There is a larger implication for the renewable energy industry. As solar and wind generation expand, demand for energy storage will grow. Retired EV batteries could become an important supplemental resource, potentially reducing the need for newly manufactured stationary batteries and additional raw-material extraction.

But the industry must demonstrate that reused batteries can compete on cost, safety, reliability and useful service life.

The environmental argument is compelling, but environmental virtue alone does not sustain a business.

The electric vehicle revolution will eventually produce millions of retired battery packs. Some will have valuable years of service remaining. Others will be better candidates for immediate recycling.

The companies that succeed will be those that understand the difference.

The future of EV batteries may not end when they leave the automobile. But their second life must make economic and engineering sense - or it won't happen at meaningful scale.

text:
Texas Border Business

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced a $237 million funding opportunity to boost American manufacturing and strengthen supply chains for critical electric grid components. The investment is expected to deliver an estimated $125 million in annual utility savings and keep an estimated $50 million per year in the U.S. economy that would otherwise go to foreign suppliers.

The investments will help facilitate the reliable flow of electricity for American families and businesses and position the U.S. as a global leader in foundational technologies, by incentivizing the refurbishment and reuse of critical equipment and encouraging the adoption of alternative materials and subcomponents that are sourced and made in America. These efforts will lower costs, strengthen grid reliability, and meet growing electricity demand.

“President Trump is bringing American industry and manufacturing back home, including the critical equipment and components needed to power our nation,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “The Energy Department is investing in American-made technologies and modernizing our grid to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and deliver affordable, reliable, electricity.”

This funding opportunity will support projects in two key areas:

Up to $50 million will be provided to projects that promote greater refurbishment and reuse of existing grid equipment and materials;

Up to $187 million will be provided to projects that will increase the use of alternative materials and subcomponents sourced and made in the U.S, reducing dependence on imports.

“America should never have to rely on foreign suppliers to keep the lights on,” said Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza. “We’re putting American ingenuity to work, developing next-generation grid technologies that strengthen our domestic supply chain, help lower costs, and make our grid more reliable. The power to secure our energy future should be in our own hands.”

The Grid Supply Chain Alternatives to Lead Energy Dominance (Grid SCALED) funding opportunity is the first of DOE’s Grid Supply Chain Program, which is authorized to provide up to $375 million to strengthen domestic supply chains for the manufacturing of distribution and power transformers, grid components, and materials. Additional funding announcements are anticipated in 2027 to strengthen domestic supply chains for next-generation technologies, including solid-state transformers, and promote common configurations to streamline manufacturing.

Applicants must submit a concept paper by November 20, 2026, to qualify to submit a full application. Full applications are due by February 8, 2027.

description:

text:
Detroit taxpayers will likely bear the burden of millions of dollars in fixes related to testing and replacement of contaminated backfill at hundreds of demolition sites across the city.

Detroit’s top attorney said Friday that the contractor responsible for the “dirty dirt” is unlikely to have the resources to cover the costs and, absent state or federal grants, the bill for remediation will most likely fall on Detroiters.

“Unfortunately, what we have is a cost burden to the citizens that they should not have to bear, directly related to what we believe to be at least significant contractual violations if not criminal behavior that has resulted in all of these costs,” Corporation Counsel Conrad Mallett told BridgeDetroit following a special session of the Detroit City Council.

The city has grappled with a $20 million-plus price tag to address 655 questionable sites stemming from the work of the now-defunct contracting firm Gayanga Co., which is now the subject of city, state and federal investigations, as well as a site in Milford that provided the contaminated backfill dirt.

Mallett’s Friday statements come after the Law Department previously signaled that Detroit would pursue a cost recovery action against Gayanga for total damages, which Tim Palazzolo, director of the city’s Demolition & Construction Department, told BridgeDetroit Friday is “pushing the $20 million mark.”

Detroit-based Gayanga Co. and its owner, Brian McKinney, have been accused by the city of using contaminated dirt to backfill demolition sites. The company and McKinney have been the focus of federal, state and city investigations.

Mallett said Friday that investigations being conducted by the state’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) and the Detroit FBI office are ongoing. The city’s Office of the Inspector General suspended Gayanga and McKinney last fall from doing work in Detroit based on the contaminated dirt findings. Gayanga had been awarded tens of millions in city demolition contracts since 2018.

McKinney announced in May that Gayanga was shutting down and filing a defamation lawsuit against the city, noting the court action, “arises from false and materially misleading public statements.” On Friday, Mallett said that McKinney had not yet been served with legal action from the city.

Detroit City Council President James Tate, who convened the Friday meeting, asked Mallett whether Detroit could recover testing and remediation costs from Gayanga.

“I don’t have good news,” Mallett told council members. “I think that the Gayanga organization, if not bankrupt, soon will be. Therefore, our ability to collect for what we think is, in fact, bad acts will be difficult.”

Additionally, the city’s environmental insurance company “is resisting, forcefully, responsibility for this particular program.”

Steps can be taken by the city for future contract language, Mallett said. At this time, Detroit will continue to focus on the insurance company for recovery. Iron Horse, the Milford site that supplied much of the contaminated fill dirt, Mallett noted, did not have a contract with Detroit when the material was provided. Rather, it was an approved site for dirt based on a consultant.

Mallet said Friday that he wanted to assure the council that, thus far, the contamination concerns appear to be isolated.

“There has been no evidence that we have discovered ourselves that would suggest that this was a systemic problem that extended beyond Gayanga,” he said.

Detroit officials said Friday that the city expects costs of around $12 million to remediate the remaining demolition sites with contaminated dirt.

Palazzolo said that the majority of the sites identified – 533 overall – are owned by the Detroit Land Bank Authority. Of the publicly-owned sites tested, 500 have not met safety standards.

As of Friday, 380 haven’t yet been excavated – and 195 sites present an “elevated risk,” Palazzolo said.

“The nature of contamination (for the 195 parcels) is such that it could evaporate and rise up through the soil and potentially get into adjacent structures and cause unsafe air over time to those areas,” Palazzolo said Friday. “Those are properties with the biggest concern. Those are the properties we need to remediate first.”

Palazzolo pegged that fix at around $6.7 million. The estimated replacement cost per property is $34,554, he said. The city has divided the remaining work into three priority tiers. The first two are slated for completion by 2029 based upon the time it will take for contracting, approvals and seasonal limitations, Palazzolo told BridgeDetroit.

A dedicated cost center was established within the Construction & Demolition Department’s budget for the remediation work via blight funding. Palazzolo said Friday that $8.4 million remains from the original $15 million set aside in late 2025 to address the site testing and remediation.

“One of the things I want to make clear is that this fund of money is not used for any other purpose,” said Palazzolo, adding within the department’s current fiscal budget there’s separate dollars for emergency demolition and stabilization work.

Council Member Angela Whitfield-Calloway argued Friday to Detroit’s Chief Public Health Officer Ali Abazeed that the city should declare a public health emergency over the contamination.

“This is, to the public health director, a public health emergency. It may not be in your opinion, but it really is and should be declared as so,” said Whitfield-Calloway, noting that the temporary orange fencing around the sites “is not containing the dirt.”

“It’s still seeping out into the air. There are air particles that, if there’s a wind, the dirt is flying everywhere. It’s traveling everywhere. I don’t know how far it’s getting on people’s properties, cars. Kids are walking through it, adults are walking through. It’s landing on the sidewalk. It’s not contained.”

Abazeed, who joined the department this spring, said he can’t speak to how things were handled before he arrived. But under Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield, health officials are closely scrutinizing the potential health impacts, he said.

The department, he said, is taking the issue “seriously and urgently,” but stressed to council members that “contamination does not always equal exposure.”

Council Member Denzel McCampbell said he wants assurances that the city won’t encounter similar issues in the future with soil supply sites and contractors.

Mallett acknowledged Friday that there were past “hiccups” in the city’s contracting process, and some contractors did not have adequate documentation in place before contracts were authorized. But those “have been corrected” and they “won’t happen again,” he said. The city, he said, is also exploring whether it can secure its own fill dirt in the future.

Although the great majority of sites being reviewed for contamination are publicly owned, the city is also contending with 120 privately owned parcels.

The city reached out to those property owners earlier this year, seeking permission to test those sites. Fifty of those owners have approved the request, seven others have denied the city’s request, and Detroit did not get responses from 63 others. If the city doesn’t hear from those remaining property owners by spring, the city will pursue an administrative warrant.

“What I want to assure the public is, if there are public health implications in which we are consulting with the health department about, we will move more quickly than the springtime that I talked about,” Mallett added after the meeting.

As another measure toward process improvements, Palazzolo reiterated Friday, is that the demolition department now sources its backfill materials from just seven public pits with native gravel and soil from longstanding operations – down from 14 source sites previously. Two of the sites are located in Milford, and the others are in Pinckney, Washington Township, Petersburg, Milan and Maybee. The sites are inspected monthly by the demolition department and its environmental consultants. The soil is also sampled and analyzed before it leaves the source sites.

Earlier this year, the council approved a $3.5 million contract increase with Mannik and Smith Group, environmental consultants conducting due diligence related to the dirt issues. Originally, a $1 million contract was approved with Mannik and Smith for general environmental consulting services. The $3.5 million amendment was to cover costs associated with backfill testing.

For more information about locations and progress on testing and excavation, visit this webpage on the testing, removal and replacement process and an FAQ. Questions can be directed to demo-info@detroitmi.gov or (313) 224-4737.

BridgeDetroit reporter Jasmine Snow contributed to this report.

text:
Renewable energy will account for nearly three-fourths of new generation built under Xcel Energy’s five-year, $70 billion capital plan that the company unveiled Thursday during its third-quarter earnings call.

The new plan — up 17% from its previous $60 billion spending plan — calls for building 9.2 GW of renewable generation, 2.3 GW of energy storage and 3.3 GW of natural gas generation. Xcel expects the renewable portion of the buildout would cost about $21.7 billion. The plan also includes 2,400 miles of new transmission and $4 billion for wildfire mitigation.

“These investments are critical to serve growing electric demand, to keep customer bills low, to deliver clean energy, and to ensure system safety and reliability,” Chairman, President and CEO Bob Frenzel said, later adding that Xcel “continue[s] to lead a clean energy transition” and believes its commitment to clean energy will attract additional data centers to its service territory.

About $7 billion of the capital plan will go to data center projects already under contract at Xcel. Xcel could spend an additional $10 billion for projects not included in its spending plan, according to Frenzel. That spending would cover the more than 15 GW that is included in pending utility requests for proposals, high-voltage transmission projects and infrastructure needed to serve the 4 GW of new data centers the company expects to contract before the end of next year, he said.

“As we think about future data center growth, our contracting principles are based on our longstanding commitment to ensure that the needs of our customers and our communities are met,” Frenzel said. “We believe in responsible development. We believe that existing customers should not subsidize new large loads.”

To finance the updated capital plan, Xcel will take on $26 billion in debt and issue $8 billion in equity, about 40% of which is already contracted, CFO Brian Van Abel said. The company also agreed earlier this month to sell gas and electric assets in Michigan — including 9,000 electric customers and 6,000 gas customers — valued at $150 million to Upper Peninsula Power Co. and SEMCO ENERGY Gas Co. Van Abel said the sale should close by the end of 2027 and that the price was confidential.

Xcel’s net income jumped 83% to $960 million in the third quarter, up from $524 million a year ago, the company said. Favorable weather, increasing electric sales and this year’s “heavy rate case calendar” all helped Xcel increase its third-quarter earnings, Van Abel said.

A July order by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission approved a 2.9% annual rate increase expected to generate $211 million over two years. Xcel filed a rate stability plan in Minnesota on Oct. 9 that would freeze rates at this level in 2027 and 2028, as an alternative to the rate case it is due to file in 2027. In Colorado, a September decision by the CPUC approved a 1.7% annual rate that will bring in $184 million. The company expects a final decision on a rate case in New Mexico by the end of this year.

name: EPA
title: EPA Proposes Broader Rollback of Methane Waste Safeguards
description:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing another round of changes to its 2024 rule establishing requirements to reduce methane emissions from oil and gas operations.
When operators waste gas produced from publicly owned resources, federal, state and tribal governments can lose potential royalty revenue.
Eliminating the Super Emitter Program EPA proposes eliminating the Super Emitter Program, which addresses methane releases of at least 100 kilograms, or about 220 pounds, per hour.
Other emissions requirements could still apply to a release, but this specific mechanism for requiring an investigation would disappear.
Allowing more reliance on flaring EPA proposes changing the regulatory approach to associated gas, the natural gas produced alongside oil—sometimes unintentionally.
text:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing another round of changes to its 2024 rule establishing requirements to reduce methane emissions from oil and gas operations. After delaying implementation and loosening some requirements, the agency now proposes eliminating its Super Emitter Program for investigating large methane releases, reducing safeguards at certain wells, and allowing more gas to be burned rather than captured.

EPA presents these changes as a way to lower costs for operators. But they would weaken safeguards intended to prevent natural gas from being wasted through leaks, deliberate releases, and flaring. EPA’s own analysis projects more pollution under either of its two proposed approaches. Compared with a baseline that incorporates the 2024 rule, the agency estimates an additional 60 million short tons of methane emissions between 2027 and 2050 under its approach for low-producing wells. Its alternative approach for conventional wells would add an estimated 88 million short tons over the same period.

For taxpayers, the concern extends beyond emissions. Natural gas is a valuable resource. When operators waste gas produced from publicly owned resources, federal, state and tribal governments can lose potential royalty revenue. Weaker monitoring and response requirements also raise questions about how much waste will be detected and addressed.

Moving beyond delays to weaker requirements

EPA’s 2024 rule required oil and gas operators to find and repair leaks, restricted routine flaring, and established a process for investigating unusually large methane releases. It set standards for new and modified facilities and directed states to develop plans for existing facilities.

The agency has already delayed implementation of several requirements. In April 2026, it also extended the time operators could temporarily flare gas during certain interruptions and loosened monitoring requirements for flares and other combustion devices.

This proposal would make broader changes to the safeguards themselves. It would eliminate the Super Emitter Program, reduce monitoring and equipment requirements for certain well sites, and allow greater reliance on burning gas instead of capturing it for sale.

Eliminating the Super Emitter Program

EPA proposes eliminating the Super Emitter Program, which addresses methane releases of at least 100 kilograms, or about 220 pounds, per hour. The program created a process for approved outside organizations to report large releases detected through technologies such as satellites and aircraft. EPA reviews those reports before notifying the relevant operator. That notification triggers requirements for the operator to investigate and report its findings.

The proposal would remove that process, including the approval of outside monitoring organizations and technologies and the requirement for operators to respond to program notifications. Other emissions requirements could still apply to a release, but this specific mechanism for requiring an investigation would disappear.

In its latest proposal, EPA questions whether the evidence supporting the program adequately establishes how often these events occur, how long they last and what causes them. It also argues that other emissions requirements make the program less useful. The agency cites difficulties identifying responsible operators, limited participation by outside organizations and concerns about its legal authority. TCS is skeptical but will more thoroughly assess these claims as we prepare comments on the proposed rule.

Reducing requirements for low-producing or conventional wells

EPA is proposing a loophole that would allow operators of certain wells to operate under reduced requirements – the only question is who will qualify. EPA is considering two alternatives:

Marginal Wells: The first is based on production. “Marginal” wells produce no more than 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day, averaged over the previous year. Oil equivalent is a way to express oil and natural gas production in a common unit. To qualify as a marginal well site, all wells at the location would have to be marginal, and their combined production could not exceed that same daily threshold.

Conventional Wells: Broadly, this means a site where all wells draw from deposits that do not require intensive techniques, such as multistage fracking, to produce oil or gas. The conventional-well alternative could apply to sites producing more than the marginal-well threshold.

Under either approach, operators at qualifying sites would still have to inspect every three months using sound, sight, and smell to identify leaks or malfunctioning equipment. For leaks found through those inspections, operators generally would have to attempt a repair within 15 days and complete it within another 15 days, although exceptions could allow delays. The proposal would also allow certain equipment that uses and releases natural gas to remain in service.

Allowing more reliance on flaring

EPA proposes changing the regulatory approach to associated gas, the natural gas produced alongside oil—sometimes unintentionally. Under current rules, EPA rules favor capturing associated gas and delivering it to a sales pipeline, bringing more domestic energy to our homes and businesses. Now, EPA is proposing to favor burning it in a flare or another device that reduces emissions by at least 95 percent. This would make flaring a broader option for meeting the standards.

EPA argues that operators cannot always control access to pipelines and other infrastructure needed to bring gas to market. It says the 2024 rule assumed that infrastructure would become available in time, and that those assumptions have not been borne out. Connecting wells to pipelines can require agreements with other companies, permits and substantial investment.

What EPA counts as savings

EPA estimates that the proposed changes would save operators approximately $2.5 billion a year in compliance costs under the marginal-well approach and approximately $2.3 billion under the conventional-well alternative. These annualized estimates cover 2027 through 2050, are expressed in 2024 dollars, and account for changes in the value of gas recovered. EPA also projects changes in energy production and prices.

EPA projects more methane and other air pollution under either approach. Those estimates do not cover all the proposed changes, including elimination of the Super Emitter Program.

EPA is counting the savings for operators, but taxpayers deserve a full accounting of what more wasted gas and less oversight would cost them.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy announced that Alliant Energy could get a $5.1 billion loan to invest in new natural gas plants, gas pipelines or battery storage systems across Iowa and Wisconsin.

“The investments will add more than 2.6 gigawatts of new or upgraded power generation capacity and deliver up to $1.2 billion in electricity cost savings for American families and businesses across both states,” Alliant spokesperson Taylor Adams wrote in an email.

Alliant estimates most of those savings — roughly $800 million — would be for Iowans.

Adams said the loan could help projects like the Bobcat Energy Center, a new 720-megawatt natural gas plant in Marshalltown, and the Lansing Battery Energy Storage System, a lithium-ion battery storage system at the decommissioned Lansing Generating Station site. Additional projects could be included, too.

“Examples include new natural gas generation, Advanced Gas Path projects, gas pipelines and battery energy storage systems,” Adams wrote.

Meanwhile, Linn County is trying to stop plans for an Alliant natural gas plant near Cedar Rapids.

The federal loan announcement came the same day Linn County supervisors sent a request to the Iowa Utilities Commission to deny a generating certificate for Alliant’s proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center.

Linn County supervisors had previously unanimously denied the rezoning request that would have allowed for the 720-megawatt natural gas plant. Supervisors said they're concerned for ratepayers, worried about air quality and convinced the plant doesn’t fit the county’s comprehensive plan.

“With prevailing winds carrying emissions towards Cedar Rapids, we must consider the potential consequences for public health,” said Supervisors Chair Kirsten Running-Marquardt. “This is not a fair balance between economic development and the well-being of our community, especially when Alliant already has some of the highest utility rates in the area, and our county faces some serious concerns about asthma and cancer rates.”

Supervisor Sami Scheetz voted against the rezoning, but said he had trouble making a decision.

“This could become a state project controlled by the Iowa Utilities Commission, and not Linn County,” he said. “The county could lose the ability to enforce its own natural gas ordinance, the strictest ordinance in Iowa.”

Alliant Energy said the plant is critical to meet growing energy demand. Linn County said Alliant didn’t meet the threshold to prove that. But if the state utilities commission agrees with Alliant, it could override the county’s decision.

The Iowa Utilities Commission is set to hear the proposal on Dec. 7.

In the joint agreement, Amazon.com, Inc. is expected to provide certain project development funding for the effort, marking the second commercial deployment under X-energy and Amazon’s partnership that is aimed at bringing more than 5 GW of new nuclear capacity to the U.S. grid by 2039.

X-energy and AEP are expected to evaluate the development of a 12-unit Xe-100 plant near the former site of the retired Breed Generating Station in Sullivan County, Indiana. The proposed project would redevelop the AEP-owned brownfield site for advanced nuclear power, adding clean baseload capacity to help meet growing demand for safe, reliable energy across Indiana and the region.

What does the project signify for X-energy as it seeks to finish the year strongly?

Building on Amazon’s investment in, and ongoing collaboration with X-energy, the project is intended to be a second grid-scale partnership to support grid reliability with new clean generating capacity, joining Energy Northwest’s Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington State.

While a huge focus for the U.S. has been on diversifying the energy portfolio of every state, there are still places that are seen as the hub for the generation of certain energy sources. For instance, Indiana has made advanced nuclear energy a central part of its energy strategy as part of the state’s all-of-the-above approach to affordable, reliable power.

The anticipated transformation of the nuclear sector expected in 2027

X-energy’s Xe-100 is an 80 MWe high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, using helium as a coolant, and powered by Tri-structural, Isotropic (TRISO) fuel, described by the U.S. Department of Energy as the most robust nuclear energy fuel on earth because of its ability to handle extreme temperatures without melting.

Collaborations on their own are not enough to guarantee the completion of a project because companies must still be able to complement each other effectively instead of just relying on the past success that they have enjoyed.

title: Matt Huckleby: Don't ignore the politics behind data center protests - Indianapolis Business Journal
authors: Matt Huckleby, Susan Orr, Mickey Shuey, Dave Lindquist
description:
The campaign now forming around data centers looks very familiar.
Computing power requires data centers and enormous amounts of reliable electricity.
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have introduced legislation calling for a federal moratorium on AI data-center development.
Its activists have connected data centers to border enforcement, war and capitalism.
One campaign put it plainly: “Fighting back against data centers means fighting for socialism!” Believe them.
text:
I’ve seen this playbook before.

I’ve spent most of my career in Republican politics. I served as the executive director of the Indiana Republican Party for nearly seven years, and I’ve advised Republican governors, members of Congress, state legislators and local candidates all across Indiana. After watching campaigns of every stripe for more than two decades in politics, I’ve learned to recognize the radical left’s playbook when I see it.

The campaign now forming around data centers looks very familiar.

To be clear, there are legitimate questions surrounding these projects. Communities should ask questions about electricity rates, water, noise, setbacks and infrastructure, and developers should work with communities to solve them.

But legitimate concerns are increasingly being drowned out by misinformation, exaggerated claims and talking points being pushed by some very familiar political actors.

Let’s start with communist China.

Artificial intelligence may be the most consequential economic and national security competition of our lifetime. AI requires computing power. Computing power requires data centers and enormous amounts of reliable electricity. President Trump has made his position unmistakable: America needs to build this infrastructure or risk falling behind China.

Apparently, China understands that, too.

X recently discovered a suspected Chinese bot farm containing roughly 200,000 accounts, some 200 of which were specifically seeking to manipulate the American debate over AI, energy and data centers. They pushed claims about rising electricity bills and grid strain and used AI-generated cartoons portraying data-center companies getting rich at the public’s expense.

OpenAI separately uncovered a likely China-based influence operation doing something remarkably similar. Operators posed as Americans and created anti-data-center content designed to exploit existing concerns over energy costs.

China didn’t create American opposition to data centers. But Chinese-linked actors are clearly trying to fuel and amplify it.

And they aren’t alone.

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have introduced legislation calling for a federal moratorium on AI data-center development. Democratic Socialists of America chapters are organizing against projects across the country. In DSA’s own publication, organizers discussed the value of framing data-center opposition as a “nonpartisan issue” capable of bringing people from across the political spectrum into their movement.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is even less subtle. Its activists have connected data centers to border enforcement, war and capitalism. One campaign put it plainly: “Fighting back against data centers means fighting for socialism!”

Believe them.

Behind this community organizing sits an advocacy infrastructure built over decades. Michael Bloomberg poured tens of millions into the Sierra Club’s campaign against coal-fired power generation. Other progressive organizations involved in today’s data-center debate have received support from massive liberal funding networks including George Soros’ Open Society Foundations and the Sixteen Thirty Fund. Neville Singham, a wealthy socialist donor whose relationships with China have drawn congressional scrutiny, has funded organizations active in the same broader protest ecosystem.

This isn’t new. From the Green New Deal and open-border advocacy to protests against the Keystone XL pipeline and major industrial projects, the target may change, but the playbook stays the same.

At some point, the pattern raises a bigger question. Maybe the objections and propaganda from the radical left are not to the merits of each issue or project. Maybe they object to the basic tenets of free enterprise and the American way of life.

There are real issues surrounding data center development that should be addressed through thoughtful negotiations and reasonable state and local policies. But Hoosiers, and specifically Hoosier Republicans, need to recognize that legitimate concerns are being weaponized to deceive us and turn us against each other.

When self-described socialists, anti-capitalist organizations, longtime opponents of American energy development and foreign influence operations all see strategic value in convincing us not to build the infrastructure of the AI economy, that ought to tell us something.

I’ve seen this playbook before. We don’t have to take the bait. •

text:
By KIERA KEMPPAINEN

Capital News Service

LANSING – Detroit’s defunct municipal utility may run again.

In a recent meeting, the city council voted unanimously to explore alternatives to DTE Energy after a tornado left thousands of residents without power.

The city had a public electric utility until 2013 when the city was facing bankruptcy.

Galen Hardy, the Michigan Environmental Council program director in Detroit, said he would like to see the city taking action on bringing back an independent utility.

“I do not trust what we’re doing because we pay so much and we’re getting quite little. Quite frankly, I feel like we’re being robbed,” council member Gabrielle Santiago-Romero said during the meeting.

Santiago-Romero said that the city’s Legislative Policy Division should look into what other cities are doing with public power.

The Michigan Municipal Electric Association represents the state’s 41 municipally owned electric utilities. The association provides services and education for member municipalities and those looking to make the shift.

The association’s executive director, Katie Abraham, said the state’s public electric utilities saved residents and businesses over $400 million in rates and reliability in 2023.

Abraham said that the affordability of public power is a big draw for people wanting their cities to municipalize electricity.

Abraham said reliability is also a leading factor.

“When it comes to reliability, our service territories are much smaller than the investor-owned utilities, so we can respond very quickly,” Abraham said.

“Our workers live in the community, they know when the lights go out and they’re there and they’re ready to respond.”

Abraham said that while she has not heard from the Detroit city government on municipalizing, she expects officials are waiting to see what happens with Ann Arbor which has a proposal on the Nov. 3 ballot to create a municipal utility.

The association’s members include utilities in Traverse City, Marquette, Zeeland, Harbor Springs, Lansing, Newberry, L’Anse, Baraga and Escanaba.
