text:
Union Minister for Heavy Industries H D Kumaraswamy on Friday urged the automobile industry to invest more in electric powertrains, batteries, power electronics, lightweight materials, vehicle software and hydrogen technologies.

Speaking at the inauguration ceremony of six manufacturing facilities of electric mobility firm EKA Mobility in collaboration with Pinnacle Industries here, the Minister also said that India is making rapid strides towards becoming a global manufacturing powerhouse. The vision of Aatmnirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat in 2047 has provided a strong bridge to indigenous manufacturing, technological innovation and sustainable mobility.

Advt

The expansion of indigenous manufacturing capabilities in electric commercial vehicles, automotive components and engineering solutions emancipates the growing confidence of India's manufacturing ecosystem, he said.

The automotive and auto-component industry is central to India's manufacturing strategy, the minister said, adding that it supports millions of livelihoods, anchors a vast electricity ecosystem and is a powerful multiplier effect across steel, electronics, engineering, large-scale and services.

"The Ministry of Heavy Industries has focused on translating policy intent into measurable outcomes. Our schemes are supporting investment, domestic value addition, advanced technology, manufacturing and transition to cleaner mobility," he said.

"However, our success cannot be measured only by the number of electric vehicles sold. It must also be measured by how much technology is designed in India, how much value is added domestically, how many MSMEs participate in new supply chains and how effectively Indian products compete in the global market," he added.

The six facilities were inaugurated virtually by Nitin Gadkari, Union Minister of Road Transport & Highways, in the presence of HD Kumaraswamy, Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, Sunetra Pawar, Deputy Chief Minister of Maharashtra; BJP National General Secretary (Organisation) BL Santhosh and Murlidhar Mohol, Union Minister of State for Civil Aviation and Cooperation, among others.

Advt

Terming the automobile industry as the backbone of Indian industry, Union Minister Gadkari said, "To become a self-reliant India, we need 100 per cent indigenous electric vehicles, and this is our dream."

Earlier, all the dignitaries joined EKA Mobility and its group companies to unveil an over ₹3,500-crore manufacturing ecosystem for India's electric commercial mobility.

"The inauguration of six manufacturing facilities across our group reflects our unwavering commitment to innovation, indigenous engineering, sustainable mobility, and manufacturing excellence. These facilities are more than infrastructure; they represent our vision of creating world-class capabilities, generating meaningful employment, nurturing talent, and contributing to India's emergence as a global manufacturing powerhouse," said Sudhir Mehta, Founder and Chairman, EKA Mobility and Group Companies.

As we take this significant step forward, we remain focused on delivering transformative mobility solutions that create lasting value for our customers, our nation, and future generations, he added.

EKA Mobility and the group operate 11 manufacturing facilities spread across 120 acres, 6 of which were inaugurated at EKA Avirbhava, with the capacity to build more than 40,000 electric vehicles a year.

The group has invested over ₹3,500 crore in building this ecosystem, making it one of the largest investments in commercial electric vehicles in the country. It has also invested more than ₹600 crore in R&D.

With these 11 facilities, EKA expects to create more than 2.5 lakh jobs over the next five years across its operations and wider ecosystem, the company said.

Robinson Meyer:

Hello, it's Thursday, October 29. And as you know, the biggest story in U.S. Energy policy right now, at least other than the upcoming midterm elections, is that Congress will take up bipartisan permitting reform next month. This was a legislative proposal advanced in September by four senators called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. And if you read Heatmap or you look at social media, or even sometimes if you look at Instagram Reels, you will see that this package is very controversial. American environmentalists, climate activists, clean energy folks, they have been arguing about this bill essentially constantly since it came out. That's partially because it would just do a lot of different things: It would encourage the expansion of the power grid. It would change environmental review laws. It would make it easier to build clean energy and also pipelines. And it would make it harder for presidents to revoke permits from some energy projects. There's a lot of different views about those provisions and how they would all work together.

But just about everyone involved agrees the bill's power grid policies are really, really good. The Natural Resources Defense Council described this section as one of the bill's, quote, “green flags,” as opposed to what it saw as its red flags. And even John Podesta, the former Biden climate advisor who's been more critical of the proposal, said the grid section was, quote, “pretty strong,” unquote, and told our reporter that this section was actually worth passing the bill over if negotiators could fix some of his other criticisms.

All of this has had an interesting effect on what we cover, both at Heatmap and I think more broadly. And that's because the media — we love to cover conflict. That's not just because conflict or disagreement is more interesting, although I think often it is, but also because it lets us as journalists be useful. It can actually be helpful for reporters or an informed person to poke around a disputed question, try to learn new information, and then try to figure out what's true. That's really one of our jobs as journalists. What all of that means, though, is that when there's less conflict over something, we don't cover it as much, even when it's really, really important.

And that's happening, I think, with this power grid section, which will be one of the most important parts of the law if it passes — but which nobody has really talked about because nobody disagrees about it very much. So today I want to talk to someone who knows a lot about this package, knows a lot about this particular area of the law, and is really jazzed about the changes that this bill would make.

David Pomerantz is executive director of the Energy and Policy Institute, a watchdog and research group that investigates fossil fuel and monopoly utility lobbying. He's been at the Institute for more than 10 years, but his background is in climate activism. He was previously at Greenpeace for eight years, where he rose to be a senior climate campaigner. Dave and I discuss what this bill would do and how it would take on the power of monopoly utilities. We talk about why a bill like this could only really pass now in recent U.S. political history. And we also discuss why utilities are, at least in Dave's view, one of the biggest enemies of the energy transition, even though utilities are in charge of the electricity system and at least in theory generating more electricity is what we want to do if we want to decarbonize the economy. It was a really interesting conversation. I learned a lot.

I'm Robinson Meyer, the founding executive editor of Heatmap News, and it's all coming up on ShiftKey. David Pomerantz, welcome to Shift Key.

David Pomerantz:

Thanks so much for having me.

Robinson Meyer:

It's funny. I mean, we were talking about this right before we started, but we have known each other for a long time. I feel like I read Energy and Policy Institute work all the time, but we've never had you on the show. So it's very exciting to have you finally here on Shift Key.

David Pomerantz:

Well, I'm very grateful for the invitation. I am an avid listener and so honored to be here with you. Thanks, Robinson.

Robinson Meyer:

I think for those of us who do anything around electricity, the Energy and Policy Institute is a very familiar name. But it might not be a name that everyone in Climate World, so to speak, or climate and energy world is familiar with. Could you just give us a brief intro to your work and what the Institute's work does?

David Pomerantz:

Yes, happily. So the Energy and Policy Institute, or EPI, is a utility watchdog organization. So we do a mixture of investigative work and analysis and communications. What we're investigating and trying to document is the harms posed by monopoly utility companies to ratepayers and to the transition from fossil fuels to clean energy. So most of the people, my colleagues who I work with, are kind of climate people. We are motivated by trying to hasten the transition away from fossil fuels. With that said, as we've been doing this work, or at least I've been doing it for the last decade, and getting more and more exposure to how utilities are set up and organized and what incentives they have and how they behave, I think our purview has gotten a bit broader than that. And nowadays, we're sort of — as much as we are interested in utility reform in so much as it affects the transition to clean energy, we're also just generally interested in how utilities act toward their customers and what can be done about that.

Robinson Meyer:

I feel like this is not an atypical pattern, where people get into a policy area because they care about decarbonization and climate change. And then once they get into it, they're like, oh, my gosh, this thing is really screwed up. I feel like this has happened to me to some degree with manufacturing and industrial policy in the U.S. I'm like, oh, my gosh, we've got to get a handle on this kind of for decarbonization reasons. But also just generally, often when you look closer at something that you care about for some other reason, you discover that actually there's a ton of work to be done there, regardless of the importance of decarbonization.

David Pomerantz:

That's definitely been my experience and journey about utilities. I mean, I got into this stuff a little over a decade ago. And even then, I think in the climate community, this sort of two-part equation that people are so familiar with now, which is moving the electric sector to clean sources of energy that don't emit carbon, and then electrifying everything else that we can. That was well in place when I started working on utilities and so, if that's the equation you're thinking about, electric utilities kind of are right at the center of all that. So it made a lot of sense for me from a climate perspective as I've gone — and coming from a place of humility, like really not being a technical expert in electricity and learning a lot as I've gone along the way, you realize from all these other perspectives sort of a general good government and campaign finance and concentration of power in the economy and just generally —I mean, the cost of electricity is kind of the base input for so many parts of the economy. If it's even a little bit higher than it needs to be, the spillover effects of that on everything are really big. So, yeah, that's certainly been my experience as I've gone along, is like, utilities are so important for climate and also so important for just about everything else.

Robinson Meyer:

You described this two-step plan to decarbonize the economy. The first is you clean up the electricity system. You shift as much demand as possible to zero carbon and clean fuels. And then you expand the electricity system. You try to electrify everything you can. And the way that the technologies that we want to electrify work is that you can do this a little bit out of order. If you're also gradually decarbonizing the electricity system, it's better to have more EVs, even if you power them with natural gas in the short term, because then you lock in the EV infrastructure and then you can gradually clean up the grid. It's like a two-part race and you can kind of run both at the same time.

David Pomerantz:

Totally in parallel.

Robinson Meyer:

OK. But when people hear this game plan, I think there's a sense that the utilities will be on board with it or certainly that the utilities will not oppose it. What has your experience been of how utilities feel about this plan? I mean, are they a fan of expansion and not as much a fan of decarbonization? Or are their incentives so misaligned, let's say, that they don't even necessarily care about the kind of expansion in terms of kilowatt hours that we all care about? And what they're really focused on is just building a lot of infrastructure of any kind that then they can make their customers pay for.

David Pomerantz:

I'd say a few things. So one thing — this is such a boring disclaimer that everybody gives when they talk about utilities, but it's true and worth making the caveat up front: they're not all the same. Putting aside the big differences within the sector, right? So you have about two-thirds of America served by investor-owned electric utilities. So these are corporations owned by investors on Wall Street. And then the other third is split between, you know, different versions of public power entities, either cooperative utilities, mostly in rural parts of America, or municipal utilities. Those are all very different.

But even if you just look within the investor-owned utilities, which I think is mostly what we're going to talk about, they're not all the same. So for instance, one important distinction for this question about their posture toward decarbonization and electrification, there are some utilities that all they do is electricity, right? Like they sell electricity, they distribute electricity. There are others who also own gas utilities. This has become more common as the industry has concentrated and as a function of mergers and acquisitions over the last couple of decades, really conglomerated a lot. And so if you're a utility holding company that owns multiple utilities.

Robinson Meyer:

Like Berkshire Hathaway Energy.

David Pomerantz:

Sure, that's a good example, right? So taking Berkshire Hathaway Energy, they own electric utilities. Berkshire Hathaway, their pipeline group, runs about 20,000 miles of pipe and moves about 15% of the gas consumed in the U.S. in 2024. So they have a different set of incentives. The people who run their electric utilities might be relatively positively inclined toward electrification, but the people who run their gas pipeline certainly aren't. They own a majority stake of a LNG terminal, Cove Point. So even within a single corporate utility, you might have pretty mixed incentives towards something like electrification. I think one very broad way to answer this is I think most electric utilities, just looking at the electric part of the sector, they're going to be relatively positively inclined toward electrification, mixed on decarbonization.

But actually, I think this is one of those cases where everybody who is really interested in climate change, and I certainly put myself in that category, even people who are really opposed to climate action, say from the political right, are way overindexed on how and whether that is a defining principle of how utilities make decisions. The way utilities make decisions, the most important thing to them, the most valuable commodity to them by far has nothing to do with, like, is it solar or gas or wind or coal? It's their monopolies. That is the crown jewel of how a utility makes money. And that leads to some situations where, like, you've had utilities in blue states who will accept government policy to speed up transition to renewable energy, but they'll try to get their pound of flesh as part of that acceptance. And usually that pound of flesh is a retrenchment or reification of their monopoly. And it was coming from the White House.

And so, like, traditionally, utilities have probably at the federal level been closer with Republicans than Democrats. They give more money to Republicans by about a two to one margin in most election cycles. But I think that has changed in the last couple of years. I mean, if you just look at Trump one versus Trump two, Trump's first Department of Energy was rife with staffers who came from electric industry, came from industry. That is not the case now. Like, there is a strong sort of anti-monopoly sentiment in parts of the Republican Party, whether it's always expressed is a different question. But I think you're seeing a lot of that bubbling up. And then with everything happening on energy prices and data centers, it sort of became a perfect storm for utilities to very quickly lose a lot of institutional power that they had previously held with Congress.

Robinson Meyer:

Do you think that this will continue just from what you're getting a sense of? Will this decline in utility political clout continue or is this limited to this moment? And if this bill doesn't pass, then utilities are going to close ranks. And there won't be another chance to take on utility power again.

David Pomerantz:

That's kind of the million-dollar political question from where I sit. On the one hand, unfortunately for ratepayers and customers, I don't see investors and utilities having like a sudden change of heart, and doing the things that they could and should do to arrest inflation and lower people's bills. I do want to make it clear, like, they could do that. There are a lot of things that utilities could do if they weren't looking at their next quarterly returns and just sort of maxing cap-ex, that they could do to bring people's bills down. Like, you could see that on the public side of the sector. I don't think they will. I think their incentives are too perverse. And because of that, I think they're going to keep getting themselves into trouble politically by going for rate increases and bill increases. And so I see that at least for the next couple of years as being somewhat secular. Some of it, by the way, is actually not wrong, right? Like the grid is aging and they do need to spend money. That's why it's unfortunate that they're not saving money where they can because they are kind of in a pickle there. So like, that part I see as sticking around at the same time on the other side of that argument.

I think one thing doing this work has taught me is that these companies have been around for over 100 years. If you read some of the history on some of the big political fights that investors and utilities were in the 1930s, they do the exact same things now. They did that. They spent on propaganda. They route their money through trade associations. They recruit other parts of the political economy, like labor, to back them with politicians for whom that constituency is important. Like, they have and this is something EPI has has really tried to investigate and highlight and ultimately address they have at the end of the day like a publicly subsidized pool of money of ratepayer money to spend on politics that almost no other industry has and so I think like they will regroup. Counting them out is probably a mistake. a utility CEO a couple weeks ago, I think for Eversource, got caught sort of saying the quiet part out loud, which is, I think he was trying to appease investors, but he said, “Look, I know you're hearing a lot of pretty nasty things about us from governors around the country, but those people, you know, they text me privately, we talk, and they'll tell me privately we're still friends and this will all blow over after the election.” So I think that is the hope of the sector, that, all this stuff, all this anger about prices, their political misfortunes right now, that only lasts through November and people will find something else to be angry about given enough time. I don't think that's true when so many Americans are being forced to choose between their medicine and groceries and rent and their utility bills. And you can see it in the polling. It's pretty dramatic, but that is what they'll be working toward, and they'll have a lot of political money to try to make people forget.

Robinson Meyer:

You observe basically that municipal utilities, publicly owned utilities, government owned utilities have not risen rates as fast as inflation. Well, investor owned utilities have risen rates much faster than inflation. So this was because of corporate greed. I think what's interesting is like whenever I hear this account, like this was not happening in the 2010s. It is happening now. And I assume greed being one of the seven deadly sins has a somewhat monotonic relationship in the economy. So what changed in the past few years that allowed these companies to exert their greed or their authority much more aggressively than they could, say, in the decades before? Like what has helped trigger this broader inflationary hike?

David Pomerantz:

Yeah, it's a little bit hard to pin down to a particular year because the way so much of utility finance works is like, a lot of their profitability is driven by the return that they're able to secure from regulators. And that return then compounds over years and years. So like, if a utility secures a really high return on equity in one year, like you're still seeing that drive its profit margins up, like 15, 20 years later, which makes it really hard to sort of draw lines between cause and effect, like what period at which they started making a lot more money versus what period the regulatory changes happened. One thing I'll say though is we have been in a period in recent years where, for a couple of reasons, the grid genuinely has needed investment, sort of alluded to this before, but one of those reasons is just like the cycling out of infrastructure. So a lot of the grid is pretty old. The other reason is because of increasing effects of extreme weather. So that's storms in the south and wildfires in the west and utility infrastructure, electric infrastructure is very exposed to all that stuff.

So we are in a period in the last decade of utilities genuinely needing to turn over a lot of that investment. They should be allowed to do that. The problem is they shouldn't be allowed to sort of rake people and laugh all the way to the bank along the way. I think probably if you ask most Americans and even just most politicians, like, should utilities be able to profit at really high levels from the stuff that they need to build or rebuild as a result of a hurricane or wildfire or some other tragedy, I think most people actually, if you ask them, would assume they were doing that at cost. Like, they wouldn't even understand that that can be such a big utility profit center in the first place. So I think it's a combination of really poor regulation at the state level by public utility commissions who are in charge of this stuff, and FERC for that matter, and being in a period of needed cap-ex investment for the grid.

Robinson Meyer:

Do you think the bill is good for data centers? And what's been your observation of how utilities have behaved during the data center boom?

David Pomerantz:

I think the bill is good for keeping data centers on the grid and making them pay more for it. So let me unpack that a little bit. Right now, data centers have this choice they have to make where they can either try to get a grid connection, which is hard because the grid is so broken. I mean, the sort of fundamental reason it's hard is because it's so hard to build transmission. And the bill seeks to address that. Because it's been really hard for data centers to get a grid connection, some of them are instead building these off-grid gas parks. We need a more malevolent sounding word than park, but like these behemoth facilities.

Robinson Meyer:

Totally islanded, basically massive, extremely dirty natural gas power plant fields.

David Pomerantz:

Yes, that's much better. These are cropping up in West Texas or cropping up in Ohio and other places. From my perspective, this is the worst possible outcome. Like, these are climate super emitters. To the extent you believe, and I do, that data center development that was done really well could lower people's rates. It takes away that possible upside, right? And I don't even know that it totally insulates people from rate impacts of data centers, like putting aside the pollution, like nothing is totally disconnected from supply chains, right? So even the off-grid data centers, that's part of the implicit promise there is that they're going to hold rate payers harmless. Well, they're still buying up all the turbines and all the transformers and like everything that the grid needs.

Robinson Meyer:

I think this is a particularly salient concern in Pennsylvania and Ohio because the Trump administration is trying to expedite 9 gigs of gas in Ohio. And like, I know there's a ton of gas in the Marcellus, it's completely conceivable to me that, like, production increases and we just get an extra 9 gigawatts of gas every day out of the Marcellus. But like, it just does seem to me that there's going to be a bottleneck somewhere and that is going to increase natural gas prices for everyone else in the Marcellus and everyone else in that basin. And it's not good for the climate, but that's how energy prices work in equilibrium. But it means we need to be realistic about what adding 9 gigawatts of quite dirty gas consumption would do to the entire region and that you can never prevent new energy demand of that scale from not doing something to everyone else's rates when you're talking about a system that can only grow so fast.

David Pomerantz:

Yes, I totally agree with that. I see that off-grid gas as basically like a failure mode for everybody. It's not really what the data center operators want. It's not really what the utilities want. They'd rather have the load. It's terrible for the climate and I don't think it does anything for ratepayers, so to me, the goal should be: data centers, if they're going to be built, that are on the grid paying their fair share and even like going beyond their fair share, right. There's some interesting fights actually happening between the data centers and the utilities, where in places like Virginia, some people are saying — and some of the hyperscalers, at least in selected cases, are volunteering for this, since utility capital is so expensive and that's where they make their profit, and what the data centers really want is speed, but they're somewhat price insensitive, or at least more price insensitive than they are speed sensitive: Like, why don't you displace all that utility financing with data center financing? Make them pay for the stuff we need on the grid.

That to me is the best case scenario, is that the data centers that are built are built on the grid, and they not only pay for their stuff, but they pay for the grid that we all want and need. What BAAJA does on data centers moves toward that goal. So it makes a policy change that allows utilities to charge data center customers for not only the cost of using specific transmission infrastructure that their data centers cause to be built, but also the cost of the existing power grid. And I think that's a significant change. Now, like, if your whole orientation toward this issue is to stop all data centers at any cost, independent of whether they're on-grid or off-grid, then, like, I guess a reform that makes the on-grid solution a little bit easier for data centers and everybody else — factories, hospitals, everybody, but also sort of makes them pay more — then maybe you don't like that. If your goal, from a climate perspective, is to have data centers that are going to be built on the grid be less polluting and contribute more toward funding the grid, then I think the bill is progress on that goal.

I also don't think those things are totally mutually independent. People can do whatever they want, of course, but people could support data center moratoria and support legislation that makes it more likely that data centers that are built are on the grid and paying their fair share. So anyway, that's what the bill does with regard to data centers.

Robinson Meyer:

One of the many problems that Americans seem to have with data centers is this disproportionate effect they have on electricity rates. And sometimes that's an effect of how the local electricity market works. And increasingly, it will become more and more just a result of the enormous electricity demand from data centers. And Americans have other problems with data centers, too. And people who fight data centers have lots of problems with them and would prefer to see a world with no data centers. And so this bill is not a data center bill, but it's trying to fix some problems around data centers in the energy system because it is an energy bill. And I think to some people, they look at that and they go, well, this is just going to make it easier to build data centers. And data centers are bad for X, Y, and Z reasons, not this reason. And that drives why, to their perspective, this can be a bad thing.

Notably, the politicians who have had the most success talking about data centers are not running on a — Abdul El-Sayed, Gina Hinojosa in Texas, right? They are actually not running on a “no data centers anywhere, anytime ever” platform. They're running on a “data centers if they solve this set of problems” platform. And the bill does in fact solve the energy set of problems around data centers.

David Pomerantz:

I think it at least moves the ball forward. One area where I'm somewhat sympathetic to people who say — I've seen this point made — that there's an asymmetrical time horizon issue in the bill where parts of the bill that will make it easier to build fossil fuel infrastructure could take effect pretty quickly, whereas the parts of the bill designed to encourage transmission development, I think, like we said, the tradeoffs may be a little more complicated than that, but that's the oversimplified version is that the transmission development parts of the bill will take some time. And I actually think that's pretty fair. People can make their own judgments about how they should treat the bill in light of that. The reason the transmission development portions of the bill will take some time to implement is because, like, mechanically the way a lot of this works is it kicks things to FERC to make rulemakings. And in those rulemakings — utilities will spend millions of dollars on lawyers to block the intentions of the bill. So I don't think that means the bill's transmission reforms aren't going to be effective. I do think what it means is if people want to see transmission reform happening, this bill passing would not be the finish line. If it overcomes the utility lobbying, which will be furious in the next two weeks or so or three weeks to either kill it or define it, even in that event, even if it basically passed as written, that will open a whole series of new fights.

And so to the extent this is a moment where Congress is interested and recognizing the detrimental effect that utilities are having on repairs, there's no reason they need to stop. I mean, there are a whole load of other things Congress could do, and certainly that dozens of new state legislatures and governors could do, to crack down on concentrated utility monopoly power that the utilities will use to subvert the transmission reforms in this bill if they pass.

Robinson Meyer:

As someone who's written basically saying we should create a continent-wide macro-grid of some kind, however we do it, it doesn't need to be the government who does it. I think that would make sense. It seems like that would be faster in a lot of ways, but it doesn't need to be. Like, this is the opening gun on that. This bill to me seems like the door opening to that possibility, like you cannot execute that plan without a piece of legislation like this passing but you cannot actually but it will not result it will produce a much better grid than the one we have. And if this, I think, bill were to pass alone, it would be an improvement, at least from the transmission perspective, on what exists right now. But this is like the door opening and then basically legislators, lawmakers, policymakers, potentially Democrats will have to walk through that door in the future. The John the Baptist of saving America's electricity grid — this is not the final salvation.

David Pomerantz:

I agree with that characterization 100%. And if there's an optimistic note to end on for that in terms of like what could happen next, what might happen next, I do think the fact that from all the reporting I've read, the transmission reforms and the bill have been relatively bipartisan, could mean that policymakers, both in Congress and hopefully at the state level, are ready to take the next steps in that, journey and not say, well, we sort of poked the big bad utilities in the eye this one time, but now let's all be friends again, but that they're actually ready to move consistently, which I agree with you, is critical. I think from a transmission and a grid perspective, the reforms in here are very necessary progress and wholly insufficient. So if they pass, there will be a lot of work to build on.

Robinson Meyer:

No matter what happens to this bill, I want to keep talking about it. I think it's such an important conversation. So I'm looking forward to continuing the conversation in the future. And in the meantime, David Pomerantz, thank you for joining us on Shift Key.

text:
This story was originally published on WardsAuto. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily WardsAuto newsletter.

Dive Brief:

General Motors Co. is preparing its Lansing Delta Township plant in Michigan to produce hybrid-electric vehicles, and repurposing an old grant to support the move, per an Oct. 27 press release.

The Department of Energy is restructuring a $500 million grant that was previously awarded to GM for EV conversion work. That funding will now be used to prepare GM's factory for future hybrid production, per the release.

GM's Lansing Delta Township plant currently builds the three-row SUVs, including the Chevrolet Traverse, Buick Enclave and GMC Acadia. Details about specific hybrid models that will be built there, as well as expected launch timelines, will be shared in the future, per the release.

Dive Insight:

GM's investment in Lansing is part of a broader commitment by the automaker aimed at boosting domestic manufacturing in the U.S., as well as for engineering and innovation. In July, the company said it will invest approximately $9 billion across its U.S. manufacturing footprint and more than $7 billion on U.S. research and development.

Specifically, the investment in Lansing is part of a larger commitment of over $2 billion in the region over the next several years, which includes a previously announced $1.25 billion in investment by GM to prepare the plant for future vehicle production.

GM was previously selected to receive the $500 million grant from the Department of Energy in 2024. It was part of former President Joe Biden's Investing in America Agenda funded by the Inflation Reduction Act, which allocated a total of $1.7 billion for at risk auto manufacturing facilities.

Along with GM, Stellantis also received a $335 million commitment from the DOE through the Domestic Manufacturing Conversion Grants program to convert its shuttered Belvidere assembly plant in Illinois for electrification, as well as an additional $250 million to convert its transmission plant in Kokomo, Indiana to produce electric drive modules for EVs.

The investments were intended to ensure that the U.S. automotive industry remained competitive. However, the Trump Administration paused some funding designated for EVs in 2025, then eliminated the $7,500 federal tax credit effective Sept. 30, 2025.

In October 2025, the DOE also announced the cancellation of more than 300 other financial awards for various energy initiatives, which were projected to save $7.6 billion. At the time, the DOE confirmed in an email to WardsAuto that it had not yet made any determinations regarding the $500 million awarded to GM, and the plans were essentially put on hold until the restructuring agreement was announced this week.

The Lansing Delta Township plant, which the grant will now support, had record productivity in 2025, when it built more than 291,000 vehicles, the highest-ever annual production in the factory's history, per the release.

"Lansing's strength starts with its people. Their skill and experience are why we continue to invest here," said Mike Trevorrow, senior vice president of global manufacturing at GM, in a statement. "We're building on what this team does well today while preparing for what customers will need in the years ahead. That means investing in our people, our facilities, and the ability to build a broad range of vehicles."

text:
There’s buzz going around the power industry, and it has nothing to do with electricity.

Word that Nosy Tarsee sniffed up is that the scion of a power magnate, who’s now running the family’s energy empire, was recently on the receiving end of a very shiny gift from a Chinese tech giant: a brand new car. And not just any car. It reportedly came with what is billed as the fastest battery charger around, installed in the young executive’s home.

Generous? Certainly. Coincidental? That’s what industry watchers are asking.

Our little bird points out that the scion’s company happens to be a major supplier of a key raw material in battery manufacturing, which is precisely whom a company in the electric vehicle and battery race would want a good relationship with. In business, as in love, nobody sends flowers without expecting something in return.

The Chinese firm in question, sources say, is Huawei.

Power insiders insist they’re not accusing anyone of anything. They’re simply asking, popcorn in hand, what is the quid pro quo? Or is it just a very expensive gesture of goodwill with no strings attached, the kind of thing that happens every day in boardrooms?

One industry observer put it this way: “When someone installs a gift charger at home, the next thing to watch for is who’s being plugged in at the office.”

text:
The proposal—according to Trump—is a win for oil and gas producers, especially small operators. Whether it moves the price at the pump, before next week’s midterms or for years after, is another question. The $45 billion savings estimate is spread over 2027 to 2050—and the rules cover leaks and venting at the wellhead, and gasoline prices track crude oil, which is trading around $103.99 as of October 30 as the Iran war continues.

Regular gasoline averaged $3.472 a gallon during Trump’s second presidency, narrowly exceeding the $3.471 average during Biden’s four years in office, according to Reuters. The national average climbed to $4.20 per gallon as of October 30.

On Tuesday in Lubbock, Texas, President Trump and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced a proposal to revise Biden-era oil and natural gas regulations—with an estimated $45 billion in savings for consumers and businesses from 2027 to 2050. The proposal also projects an additional 210 million barrels of domestic oil production and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas over the same period.

“The Biden administration’s short-sighted plan to kill domestic energy production hurt hard-working families, crushed our businesses, and threatened the communities that power our nation,” Doug Burgum, the U.S. secretary of the interior, said in the EPA press release. “Since day one, President Trump has been putting real money back into the hands of American people by putting American energy back in the hands of the American workers, businesses, and communities.”

The proposal is part of Trump’s effort to expand fossil fuel production. “We will frack, frack, frack and drill, baby, drill,” Trump said during a campaign event in October 2024.

But Trump’s EPA proposals throughout his tenure haven’t been accepted by every expert. Jody Freeman, a professor of law and director of the environmental and energy program at Harvard Law School, wrote concerns regarding the president’s earlier 2025 EPA proposal to rescind the 2009 “endangerment finding”—the scientific basis that greenhouse gases contribute to global warming and harm human health.

“The irony is that no industry asked for this extreme step,” Freeman wrote in a guest piece for The Los Angeles Times in August 2025. “Car makers need stable federal rules to compete globally. Power companies have invested billions in renewable energy, which regulatory uncertainty puts at risk. Even most oil and gas companies support a national approach to limiting methane.”

What the Biden rules required

Trump’s EPA proposal targets regulations finalized by the Biden administration in 2024 under the Clean Air Act. The rules established methane-emissions standards for new and existing oil and natural gas operations, including requirements for detecting and repairing leaks and limiting the release of natural gas from oil wells.

The Biden administration’s rules were intended to reduce emissions from methane, a greenhouse gas that escapes during the production of fossil fuels. But the Trump administration argues the requirements imposed excessive compliance costs, especially on smaller operators and owners of marginal wells.

“The proposal also emphasizes reforms for marginal wells, which account for roughly four out of every five producing wells in the nation,” an EPA press release read. “Many are family-owned wells that play a critical role in family economics by powering homes and fueling farm equipment; ultimately offsetting other daily expenses. Families also often use the money from these wells for their retirement savings. Reducing regulatory burdens will provide financial security for thousands of American families.”

The EPA is also considering separate regulatory standards for marginal and higher-producing wells, as well as rescinding the Biden-era Super Emitter Program—which allowed certified third-party organizations to identify and report major methane leaks to regulators. The EPA’s own regulatory impact analysis estimates about 60 million additional short tons of methane from 2027 through 2050.

text:
Approximately 5,500 megawatts of modern natural gas capacity in key markets enhance company's ability to meet customer needs

IRVING, Texas, Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vistra Corp. (NYSE: VST) today announced it has completed the acquisition of Cogentrix Energy, consisting of 10 modern natural gas generation facilities totaling approximately 5,500 MW of capacity, from funds managed by Quantum Capital Group. The transaction closing follows receipt of all required regulatory approvals. Combined with Vistra's existing fleet, the additional assets bring Vistra's generation portfolio to nearly 50,000 MW of capacity across the U.S.

With this acquisition, Vistra further expands its diverse generation portfolio, adding efficient combined-cycle combustion turbine and cogeneration assets in some of the most attractive and fastest-growing power regions in the country: PJM, ISO New England, and ERCOT. The closing builds on Vistra's track record of completing and integrating large acquisitions, including Energy Harbor in March 2024, which added approximately 4,000 MW of nuclear generation, and seven natural gas plants from Lotus Infrastructure Partners in October 2025, which added more than 2,300 MW of capacity to Vistra's current fleet.

"Natural gas plays a critical role in meeting our nation's growing energy needs, and the Cogentrix assets are a strong strategic fit for Vistra as we continue to grow our generation portfolio," said Jim Burke, president and chief executive officer of Vistra. "We're excited to bring these experienced teams together around a shared commitment to safety, operational excellence, and reliability. Our Vistra team knows how to successfully integrate generation assets into our fleet, and we look forward to building on Cogentrix's strengths and delivering long-term value for our stakeholders."

description:

text:
U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly announced on Thursday, Oct. 29, that the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station (TEES) has been awarded a $5.4 million U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) grant to develop innovative reactor fuel technology that could help transform long-lived nuclear waste into a valuable energy resource while advancing the future of nuclear power.

The project, Turning Nuclear Waste into Fuel with a Thorium Molten Salt Reactor, is led by Dr. Lin Shao, professor in the Department of Nuclear Engineering at Texas A&M University. It brings together researchers from TEES, Savannah River National Laboratory and industry partner, Natura Resources, to address one of the most significant challenges facing the nuclear energy sector — the management of used nuclear fuel and its long-lived radioactive components.

Danly announced the award during a visit to the Texas A&M campus, where he met with university leaders, toured energy research facilities and learned more about the institution’s contributions to advancing the nation’s energy security and nuclear innovation.

“America’s energy future depends on bold innovation and strong partnerships between the federal government, national laboratories, universities and industry,” Danly said. “This project demonstrates how we can address long-term nuclear waste challenges while advancing technologies that strengthen our nation’s energy security. The Department of Energy is proud to support research that has the potential to unlock new value from existing nuclear materials and accelerate the deployment of advanced reactor systems.”

The grant represents a significant milestone for Texas A&M’s research enterprise and highlights the university’s growing role in furthering technologies crucial to the nation’s energy future. The project exemplifies the collaborative approach needed to solve challenges at the intersection of energy security, innovation and reliability.

“The Department of Energy’s investment in this project reflects the critical role universities play in advancing technologies that serve our state and nation,” said Texas A&M University President Dr. Susan Ballabina. “Texas A&M is proud to contribute research that addresses complex energy challenges while creating opportunities for innovation, workforce development and economic growth.”

The project further expands Texas A&M Engineering’s leadership in advanced nuclear energy research and reinforces the university’s longstanding partnership with the DOE.

“Texas A&M Engineering is honored to receive this support from the Department of Energy to advance groundbreaking nuclear energy technologies,” said Dr. Robert H. Bishop, vice chancellor and dean of Texas A&M Engineering and director of TEES. “This research aligns directly with our mission to solve the nation’s most pressing engineering challenges through innovation and collaboration. We have an opportunity to develop solutions that reduce nuclear waste, improve energy reliability and help maintain American leadership in advanced nuclear technologies.”

According to Shao, the project aims to address two critical national priorities, including reducing the long-term burden of nuclear waste and developing advanced reactor technologies capable of delivering reliable energy for future generations. Researchers will integrate fuel preparation, experimental testing, computational modeling and reactor design throughout the project.

As energy demand continues to grow nationwide, advanced reactor concepts such as molten salt reactors are drawing increasing interest for their potential to provide reliable, carbon-free power while improving fuel utilization and addressing long-term waste management concerns.

The grant-supported research builds on Texas A&M Engineering’s extensive nuclear energy research portfolio and its commitment to developing technologies that strengthen U.S. energy security and economic competitiveness.

title: Republicans' Failed Energy Record Is Losing Them the Midterms - Evergreen Action
description:
Once in power, Trump and Republicans put boosting fossil fuel profits at the top of their agenda, no matter the cost to working people.
Click here to read our full, running analysis of Trump’s Energy Price Hikes.
Faced with skyrocketing energy costs they promised to cut, Republicans pretend the problem isn’t real, blame anyone but themselves, or flip-flop when the pressure is on.
Ads hammering rising energy bills blanket the airwaves, and Republicans won’t even say the name of the law that helped drive those bills up.
In Wisconsin, ads brand incumbent Rep. Derrick Van Orden “Data Center Derrick.” – Energy costs have emerged as one of the defining issues of this election, and Republicans’ failed record is likely to cost them the midterms.
text:
To: Interested Parties

From: Seth Nelson, Evergreen Action Communications Director

Date: October 30, 2026

Re: Republicans’ Failed Energy Record Is Losing Them the Midterms

“‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ That’ll be the headline. But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn. I’m gonna say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.’”

— President Donald Trump, Oct. 24, 2026

Talk about saying the quiet part out loud. Two years after Trump promised to cut energy bills in half, families are paying more at the pump and on every electric bill—and voters blame Republicans. His most vulnerable allies in Congress are running from a record that lands in their constituents’ mailboxes every month—a record that’s losing them the midterms.

Trump Promised To Cut Energy Costs In Half. Instead, Families Got Hit With Bigger Bills.

Nearly two years into his final term, everything Trump swore he’d make cheaper costs families more: electricity bills, heating bills, and a full tank of gas.

Trump’s promise: “Within one year, you’re going to have electric bills and energy bills, and your gasoline for your car, it’s going to 5-0, 50% cheaper than it is right now.” He repeated that pledge nearly 50 times on the 2024 campaign trail.

The reality: Residential electricity prices are up 9.4% nationally over the past two years, and by double digits in states with some of the most competitive races for Congress.

State Change in Residential Electricity Prices From Aug. 2024 to Aug. 2026 Republicans in competitive races Wisconsin +10% Rep. Derrick Van Orden (WI-3) Michigan +16% Mike Rogers (U.S. Senate), Reps. Tom Barrett (MI-7), Bill Huizenga (MI-4) Pennsylvania +24% Reps. Rob Bresnahan (PA-8), Ryan Mackenzie (PA-7), Scott Perry (PA-10) New York +14% Rep. Mike Lawler (NY-17) New Jersey +19% Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (NJ-7)

Percent change in average residential electricity price, August 2024 to August 2026. Source: EIA, Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.A (2026; 2024)

And it’s getting worse: EIA forecasts wholesale power prices in PJM—the nation’s largest grid, serving 67 million people across 13 states and D.C., including Pennsylvania and New Jersey—will jump 41% this year, the largest increase in the country.

At the pump: As of October 26, gas averages $4.27 a gallon, up $1.33 (45%) since the week before Trump launched his war in Iran on February 28 and 41% from a year ago. Gas averaged $4 or more for 26 weeks this year—more than any year since EIA’s weekly records began in 1990.

Republicans Chose Their Oil And Gas Donors Over Lower Bills.

This wasn’t bad luck or a failure to deliver. It was a choice. Republicans doubled down on expensive, polluting oil and gas, blocked renewable energy projects that communities were counting on to deliver affordable power, and gutted federal clean energy investments to choke off the competition.

Their oil and gas donors sure got their money’s worth. In 2024, Trump struck a clear quid pro quo with Big Oil, asking industry leaders to steer $1 billion to his campaign in exchange for delivering on its policy wish list, and the industry gave more than $24 million in direct contributions to Republican House and Senate candidates. Once in power, Trump and Republicans put boosting fossil fuel profits at the top of their agenda, no matter the cost to working people. Dozens of Republicans in the House and Senate even warned publicly that killing clean energy tax credits could bring “severe economic consequences.” Then they voted for Trump’s multi-trillion-dollar tax law that gutted those credits anyway.

Reps. Mike Lawler (NY-17), Tom Kean Jr. (NJ-7) and Rob Bresnahan (PA-8) voted for the megabill in the House, then signed a letter begging the Senate to scale back the clean energy cuts they just voted for. Weeks later, all three folded and voted for the final law that kept the cuts.

Donors over drivers: By protecting Big Oil at every turn, Republicans have left American families more exposed to oil shocks than anyone else around the world, and Trump’s war in Iran proves it. Americans have absorbed a third of the world’s added fuel costs since the war began—$160 billion, more than any other country. That’s $471 per person, nearly eight times the global average.

Republicans’ tax law made it worse: Killing the $7,500 tax credit for new electric vehicles (EVs) also eliminated the best protection families have against oil shocks. U.S. EV drivers have paid just $17 more to charge since the war began. Yet with the credit gone, EV demand has stalled, American automakers like Ford have rolled back EV production, and only 7.3% of new cars sold in the U.S. through August this year were plug-ins, compared to 57% in China.

Trump Is Sabotaging Cheap, Clean Power, And Propping Up Fossil Fuels. Republicans Are Cheering Him On.

Republicans’ behemoth tax law was just one piece of the plan to dismantle cheap, clean power. Trump has made sabotaging wind and solar—the cheapest and fastest-to-build ways to meet skyrocketing demand and keep bills down—a central plank of his presidency. He has pulled every lever he can get his hands on to do it, and Republicans in Congress have egged him on.

Paying off companies to quit: Trump has paid off developers nearly $4 billion in taxpayer money to walk away from their offshore wind leases—and pour the vast majority of that cash into fossil fuels.

Punishing states that didn’t vote for him: Trump canceled $7.6 billion in clean energy grants for more than 200 projects, including in New York, New Jersey, and Maryland. His own administration admitted in court documents that it killed them “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state.”

The big coal bailout: Trump invoked the Defense Production Act to hand the coal industry $700 million in taxpayer money to build two new coal plants and extend the lives of 13 others—including restarting a shuttered Maryland plant. It’s a lifeline to an industry the market has already rejected: 99% of coal plants in the U.S. cost more to run than replacing them with new local solar, wind, or storage.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden (WI-3) stood in the Oval Office alongside Trump for the announcement, then bragged that the handout would “lower costs for families.” It won’t. Propping up coal plants that cost more to run than cleaner alternatives doesn’t cut a single bill. But it does lock families into paying for some of the most expensive power on the grid.

Forcing old, costly coal plants to keep running: That bailout comes on top of more than two dozen “emergency” orders from Trump’s Department of Energy, blocking scheduled coal plant retirements. Take Michigan’s J.H. Campbell plant, for example. Retiring it was projected to save customers nearly $600 million. Instead, Trump’s orders have racked up $295 million in extra costs that the utility operating the plant is seeking to pass on to customers. Keeping every plant slated to retire through the end of Trump’s term open this way could cost customers more than $3 billion a year.

Rep. Bill Huizenga (MI-4) cheered Trump’s abuse of emergency powers to keep Campbell, which sits in his district, running past its retirement date, leaving his constituents to foot the bill.

The consequences: Between Trump’s attacks and Republicans’ tax law, at least 216 major clean energy projects have been canceled, closed, or scaled back since he took office—including at least a dozen in Michigan and 20 in New York—wiping out $68 billion in private investment and 468,000 jobs those projects would have supported.

These are only a fraction of the actions Trump has taken to drive up energy costs. He has used the full power of the federal government to kill cheap, clean energy while rigging America’s energy system for Big Oil, coal barons, and his wealthy donors. Every one of these actions shows up on a family’s utility bill or at the pump, and Trump’s Republican allies have cheered him at every turn. Evergreen is keeping the receipts. Click here to read our full, running analysis of Trump’s Energy Price Hikes.

Voters Are Paying the Price, And They Know Who Sent The Bill.

Each of these choices lands on a family’s monthly bill, and the damage is staggering. One in six U.S. households is now behind on its utility bills, and Americans’ utility debt is on track to hit $23 billion by the end of this year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. The average household was expected to spend nearly $800 on electricity over the summer alone, up more than 10% from 2025. And voters are tracing every dollar straight back to Republicans:

Trump’s energy price hikes are on the ballot, and voters are ready to pull the plug: In a survey of competitive U.S. House districts, the price at the pump (46%) and utility costs (37%) rank as voters’ top issues after groceries, and both have climbed in importance since May.

They know who to blame: In the same poll, 60% of voters said Trump is making energy prices worse, and 54% said the same of Republicans in Congress.

Voters once gave Republicans the benefit of the doubt on energy costs. Not anymore: In December 2024, just before Trump took office and a new Congress was sworn in, 42% of voters expected congressional Republicans to make energy prices better, while 35% expected they would make them worse. By May 2026, that had flipped. 58% now say they’re making prices worse and just 20% say better.

Their playbook is a loser with swing voters: The moves Republicans backed are deeply unpopular in competitive House districts. 77% of voters oppose paying off companies to abandon offshore wind projects, 63% oppose Trump’s abuse of emergency powers to force coal plants to stay open, and 59% oppose cutting clean energy tax incentives. Among voters still undecided, opposition climbs to 88%, 75%, and 69%, respectively.

Grand Old Panic: Republicans Deny, Deflect, Peddle, and Flip-Flop.

Faced with skyrocketing energy costs they promised to cut, Republicans pretend the problem isn’t real, blame anyone but themselves, or flip-flop when the pressure is on.

Deny: Trump has spent nearly a full year insisting the cost of living crisis isn’t real. Days after the November 2025 elections, he called affordability “a con job by the Democrats,” and within a month he was calling it a “hoax.”

With prices still climbing, he’s only doubled down. Less than three weeks before the election, he told a Georgia rally that affordability is “a word [Democrats] made up” and complained that “they’ve been hitting me with that word for the last year.” (For the record, Merriam-Webster traces “affordable” back to 1647. What’s new isn’t the word; it’s a president who refuses to take accountability for it.)

Deflect: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (PA-7), who won his seat by just 4,000 votes in 2024, blames rising electricity costs on the previous administration—nearly two years into Trump’s term—and has faced tough town hall questions on gas prices.

Rep. Scott Perry (PA-10) insists that rising diesel costs have “nothing to do with Iran” (even though diesel exports from the Middle East have dropped sharply since Trump started the war), and is pitching a gas tax holiday instead.

Flip-flop: Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat, reversed course and backed a statewide moratorium on data centers—days after new reporting revealed he holds millions in stock that could benefit from data centers’ rapid growth.

Running From Trump—and Their Own Record.

In the final stretch, Republicans are running from Trump on the trail and voting with him in Washington. But they cannot outrun their energy record. Ads hammering rising energy bills blanket the airwaves, and Republicans won’t even say the name of the law that helped drive those bills up.

Trump, erased: In May, nearly half (47%) of Republican ads mentioned Trump. So far in October, only 1% do, according to the advertising analytics firm AdImpact.

Their votes tell the truth: Republicans in the most competitive House races have voted with Trump a whopping 96% of the time this year, nearly the same rate as Republicans overall (97%).

Many of the most vulnerable Republicans actually voted with Trump more often this year than they did last year—including Reps. Rob Bresnahan (PA-8), Ryan Mackenzie (PA-7), and Derrick Van Orden (WI-3)—despite the president’s historic unpopularity with voters. And Mackenzie and Van Orden have backed him on every single vote they’ve taken this year.

Energy bills are flooding the airwaves: More than $191 million in ads about utility and energy bills have aired this year, surging from $25.5 million in the first quarter to $138.5 million in the third, according to a Climate Power analysis of AdImpact data.

“Data Center Derrick” (and friends): New York’s 17th Congressional District, Wisconsin’s 3rd, and Pennsylvania’s 8th have each seen more than $1 million in ads about data centers driving up costs. In Wisconsin, ads brand incumbent Rep. Derrick Van Orden “Data Center Derrick.”

–

Energy costs have emerged as one of the defining issues of this election, and Republicans’ failed record is likely to cost them the midterms.

Trump promised to cut energy bills in half. He and Republicans in Congress jacked them up instead. “I don’t give a damn,” says Trump. Well, voters do. No last-minute ad buy or musing about the legitimacy of the word “affordability” can hide the prices at the pump or what shows up in the mailbox every month: a bigger bill, and a reminder of who promised to cut it in half.

For more information or to speak with a policy expert, please contact Evergreen Action Communications Director Seth Nelson at seth@evergreenaction.com.

text:
This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

The midterm elections are upon us. While most of the country has its eyes on who will control Congress, there’s plenty at stake for clean energy at the bottom of some voters’ ballots, too. Here are five ballot measures to keep an eye on come Tuesday night.

California’s environmental overhaul

Proposition 45 looks to revise the California Environmental Quality Act, which for more than 50 years has governed how housing, energy, and other developers account for their environmental impacts. Specifically, this ballot measure would set a 365-business-day time limit on most state environmental reviews, excluding fossil fuel construction. Supporters say that will allow for speedier development of clean energy and other important infrastructure. But some groups have lined up against the measure, contending that it would curb tribes’ input on projects and put California’s lands, waters, and air at risk.

Eugene, Oregon’s clean energy fund

Canary Media’s Alison F. Takemura has the lowdown on Eugene, Oregon’s attempt to tax major corporations to fund clean energy projects — a measure that’s similar to one already in place in Portland. Eugene residents will vote on whether to approve a fee on Amazon, Walmart, and other companies that make $1 billion or more in gross profits nationally and at least $500,000 in gross profits within Eugene. Money raised could go toward electrifying restaurants, clean energy job training, and other climate-friendly initiatives that prioritize low-income and historically marginalized residents.

Colorado’s right to natural gas

A proposed amendment to Colorado’s constitution wants to make sure households can use natural gas for cooking and heating forevermore. Amendment 82 is the brainchild of conservative advocacy group Advance Colorado, which contends that ​“natural gas in Colorado is under attack” as the state moves toward a zero-emissions target and as some cities look to limit gas use in new construction. Environmental and public health groups say continued reliance on the fossil fuel would saddle residents with safety risks and higher utility bills.

Michigan’s political spending ban

Voters in Michigan will consider Proposition 2, which would go further than any other state has to keep utility money out of elections. While Michigan already bars corporations, including investor-owned utilities, from donating directly to political campaigns, companies can easily sidestep those rules by funding political action committees. Proposition 2 would not only prohibit utility-funded PACs from giving to campaigns; it would also stop utility executives and their family members from donating. Utilities clearly aren’t fans of the measure: They’ve spent at least $215,000 opposing it, according to the Energy and Policy Institute.

Ann Arbor’s utility takeover

Michigan has utilities on the mind this election as residents in the city of Ann Arbor consider whether to establish a municipal utility board. If established, the board would discuss a potential takeover of investor-owned utility DTE Energy’s grid resources in the city. People opposing Proposition E say that would be an overly expensive endeavor, costing as much as $1 billion. Supporters think the price tag will be far smaller, and argue that a municipal utility can provide cleaner, more reliable, and more affordable power than DTE. Environmentalists and city leaders warn the proposition will derail work already underway to create a Sustainable Energy Utility in Ann Arbor; the city even sued this week to keep the proposal off the ballot.

More big energy stories

Data centers will erase emissions cuts — or will they?

A new report and an AI giant’s impending IPO are raising questions about the climate impact of the data center rush.

Tech companies’ buildout of fossil gas plants to run data centers is on track to erase 15 years of emissions reductions achieved in U.S. power generation, according to an internal Sierra Club analysis covered by Bloomberg. The sector will emit 618 million more metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030 than it did in 2025, the environmental group estimates — an increase driven largely by off-grid fossil-fuel power.

But that number would come to fruition only if many, many more data centers actually get built, and even top AI company Anthropic the industry faces some serious hurdles. In its initial IPO paperwork filed this week, Anthropic raised concerns about data centers’ increased reliance on gas power, which could become harder and more expensive to build and run due to supply chain shortages and rising fuel prices. Couple that with growing public opposition to data centers, and the AI sector has a tough journey ahead.

The latest on the permitting bill: Wind concessions, new allies, and more

The U.S. Senate is marching toward a vote on its bipartisan permitting bill, and more stakeholders are taking sides. As I wrote last week, many in the clean energy industry are backing the legislation because it could dramatically speed the development of transmission and energy projects. A coalition of geothermal, nuclear, and other energy developers and funders joined their ranks this week, signing onto a letter that argues the bill’s passage is essential for America to stay competitive.

At the same time, John Podesta, former senior climate adviser to the Biden administration, warned the legislation would hand President Donald Trump a ​“loaded Howitzer” to make irreversible decisions about public lands. The NAACP also came out with concerns about the bill’s environmental justice implications. And Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) says energy developers are ​“overwhelmingly” telling him that they’d build gas in response to the legislation.

Meanwhile, Democrats and the Trump administration are trading demands and concessions that could determine the bill’s fate. After Democrats took umbrage with the Interior Department’s renewed attacks on offshore wind, the administration started letting some long-delayed onshore wind projects get moving again. But four Democratic senators are also calling for the DOE to reinstate blue-state climate funding it clawed back last year, saying it will build their trust that the White House would actually execute the permitting bill as written.

Clean energy news to know this week

Atomic advantage: The DOE announces a conditional loan of up to $5 billion for Constellation Energy to upgrade its nuclear fleet in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania — a move that will get power online more quickly than building new plants. (Canary Media)

Loans, loans everywhere: The DOE closes a $5.1 billion loan for Alliant Energy to expand gas power generation and battery storage, improve its existing generation facilities, and strengthen grid reliability across Iowa and Wisconsin. (news release)

The cost of coal: The Trump administration has propped up nearly half of the nation’s 184 U.S. coal plants with taxpayer-funded handouts, air pollution exemptions, and emergency stay-open orders, according to the Environmental Defense Fund. (Canary Media)

Batteries roll forward: BloombergNEF revises its predictions for U.S. energy storage deployment, suggesting the country will install 30% more battery storage over the next decade than the firm predicted just six months ago. (Utility Dive)

And methane rules roll back: The EPA formally proposes rescinding Biden-era regulations that aimed to curb planet-warming methane leaks and emissions from the oil and gas industry. (Associated Press)

We decarbonized a zoo: The Detroit Zoo is exploring ways to heat and cool its animal habitats with less, and cleaner, energy as part of a state grant program helping five organizations decarbonize their operations. (Canary Media)

title: In its Final Days, this Congress Can Take Bold Steps for Peace and Dignity
description:
Following the mid-term elections, the 119th Congress is set to return for a final session.
Members of Congress should take bold steps to end the war in Iran, stop funding foreign wars, and begin to restore a budget process that centers the needs of working families.
The Trump administration has willfully ignored or distorted Congress’ spending directives with little consequence.
This Congress is on track to have passed fewer bills into law than any other session in a half century.
As the Congress takes up three pending bills, FCNL urges members of Congress to take bold steps to promote peace and dignity.
text:
Following the mid-term elections, the 119th Congress is set to return for a final session. Members of Congress should take bold steps to end the war in Iran, stop funding foreign wars, and begin to restore a budget process that centers the needs of working families.

The past two years have seen a further weakening of Congress’ influence, especially regarding federal spending and the use of force at home and abroad. The Trump administration has willfully ignored or distorted Congress’ spending directives with little consequence. This Congress is on track to have passed fewer bills into law than any other session in a half century.

Americans want more from their legislators. According to recent polling, a strong majority of Americans support stronger congressional oversight and checks on executive power. This is especially the case with consequential, costly decisions to launch foreign wars.

As the Congress takes up three pending bills, FCNL urges members of Congress to take bold steps to promote peace and dignity.

Defense Authorization: It should not be business as usual as the United States continues to spend over a $1 billion a day on an unauthorized war in Iran. We urge Congress to use the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) to press for end to the war or at least an explicit prohibition on funds being used to sustain the war without authorization. At the same time, Congress should oppose dangerous provisions in the NDAA that would establish or expand new nuclear and autonomous weapons systems, or that would deepen U.S. military integration with Israel or other foreign countries engaged in human rights abuses. Congress should prevent the diversion of military resources into domestic enforcement, such as immigration and local civilian policing. FCNL has provided Congressional negotiators with recommendations for ensuring defense policies that promote peace and dignity.

Appropriations: As Congress debates and finalizes its FY27 appropriations package, we urge that it rebalance federal spending away from a skyrocketing military budget to programs that foster peace, well-being, and safety at home and abroad. We join faith groups across the country in rejecting the proposed increase in military spending to $1.15 trillion, while urging increased, dedicated funding for peacebuilding and humanitarian assistance in the Middle East, Africa, and beyond. At home, we call for: increased funding for programs to prevent community violence; increased resources for detention oversight measures; report language on strengthening guidance, training, and reporting related to immigration enforcement at sensitive locations; and investments to fulfill the U.S. federal government’s public safety obligations to tribal nations. Finally, we urge Congress to enhance legislative safeguards to ensure that funds are spent as intended. FCNL has outlined specific recommendations for Congressional negotiators working on appropriations bills.

Farm Bill: Congress should advance a bipartisan Farm Bill that strengthens environmental conservation, supports sustainable agriculture, and protects the natural resources upon which rural communities depend. Legislation should maintain robust funding for voluntary conservation programs, including the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP), Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP), and Regional Conservation Partnership Program (RCPP), which help farmers improve soil health, conserve water, and protect wildlife habitats. Congress should also preserve and expand the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) to help farmers and rural small businesses invest in renewable energy and energy efficiency, reducing operating costs and strengthening energy security.

In whatever legislative vehicle possible, it is critical that Congress acts before the end of the year to delay a major shift in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits that could cause millions of more Americans to lose access to food assistance. Since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) passed in July 2025, more than 5 million people have lost these benefits, including 2 million children. Under the current provisions, for the first time in the program’s history, states will soon have to pay a portion of SNAP benefits, based on the state’s error rate. This could cost states hundreds of millions of dollars they do not have and lead to more people losing benefits. A few select states, those with the highest error rates, get an additional two years before they must pay part of SNAP benefit costs.

Along with a coalition of faith-based partners and others, FCNL is urging Congress to act before the end of the year to delay the SNAP benefit cost shift onto all states and give states additional time to responsibly get their error rates down without dropping eligible people from the program. The timing is urgent because state legislatures will soon be deciding their budgets. Amid an affordability crisis, now is not the time to cut people’s food assistance.
