title: Autumn Budget 2026: a Sustainability Stocktake | Travers Smith
description:
When it comes to climate and sustainability, the Autumn Budget 2026 is cautious.
Indeed, sustainability got barely a mention in last year's Budget, outside of the context of reducing bills.
A headline energy-related piece of the Budget is the £2.6 billion Household Energy Payment.
The overall package therefore provides substantial short-term help with energy bills, but reduces some of the support intended to lower household energy demand and fossil-fuel exposure permanently.
High electricity costs can otherwise make retaining or expanding UK manufacturing difficult, particularly where international competitors face lower prices.
text:
When it comes to climate and sustainability, the Autumn Budget 2026 is cautious. That's not in itself a surprise. But read between the fiscal lines, and there are plenty of telling decisions and hints at more impactful medium-term plans.

This is the first major test of the Burnham administration's commitment to Net Zero, and the Starmer-led election manifesto, including Clean Power by 2030. And as far as rhetoric is concerned, it seems this administration is at least as committed to that path as its predecessor. Indeed, sustainability got barely a mention in last year's Budget, outside of the context of reducing bills. But this year, the new Chancellor was keen to stress that the government remains "unshakably committed" to the UK's Net Zero by 2050 targets, and to putting clean power and electrification at the centre of those plans. There is a recognition that a passive approach will not facilitate the radical change required – with references to "deep reform" to energy markets, grid build-out, restructuring hydrogen and CCS support, renewable contracts and energy security woven throughout the Budget. There does appear to be more recognition of the need to join-up all of these complicated regulatory enablers, as well as announcing new funds (there was some of that too). That said, all of this is framed very much within language and policy (again, consistent with the previous administration) positioning the transition not primarily as a question of carbon targets, but as a route to lower bills, energy security, industrial competitiveness and local growth. This is a constructive approach - climate policy is more likely to endure if people can see a connection between decarbonisation and lower costs, secure employment and economic resilience. That said, measures that reduce the visible cost of energy may not actually reduce emissions or fossil-fuel dependence. Equally, a focus on short-term affordability can also weaken long-term investment. The feeling is that balance is being sought but not achieved.

The dashboard below pulls out some of the Budget's key sustainability-related measures, highlighting where the measure falls on the scale between sustainability-focus vs cost-focus. Note it is intended as a strategic overview rather than a simple environmental scorecard.

A headline energy-related piece of the Budget is the £2.6 billion Household Energy Payment. From January 2027, eligible households in council tax bands A to D in England will receive a £100 rebate, with funding for comparable support available for other parts of the UK. Zero VAT on domestic electricity—introduced in October—is also extended until 1 July 2027, which the government estimates will take around £50 off the annual Ofgem price cap in April.

The measures will be funded by temporarily increasing the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months, ending on 31 March 2028. It is notable that the principal household energy intervention is being funded through a targeted business-tax increase rather than by adding further charges to consumer bills.

The abolition of gas standing charges is more structural. Around 23 million homes are expected to be affected. The government estimates that approximately 60% of account-holding households will save an average of £45 a year, although the underlying fixed costs will not disappear: they will instead be incorporated into the unit price of gas.

Moving costs from a fixed daily charge to the unit rate increases the financial reward for using less gas. But it may also increase costs for some higher-use households, including those living in larger, colder or poorly insulated homes. The promised protection for vulnerable households will therefore be an important balancing factor.

The VAT decision also contains an understated but potentially helpful sustainability signal. Electricity is taxed at zero while gas continues to attract VAT. Although temporary and relatively small, it does improve the relative economics of electric heating and transport compared with fossil-fuel alternatives. That said, the electric vehicle industry will be disappointed that the government is maintaining VAT on electricity drawn from public (rather than domestic) chargers.

That said, the overwhelming purpose of these measures is affordability rather than decarbonisation. A £100 payment protects households from high energy prices; it does not reduce the amount of energy their homes require or their exposure to fossil-fuel volatility in future winters, and is unlikely to be enough to meaningfully incentivise improvements to less energy-efficient homes. That tension is sharpened by the Budget’s treatment of the Warm Homes Plan. The government is reducing capital grant funding under the Plan by £1 billion as part of its wider spending reprioritisation. The Boiler Upgrade Scheme will continue, preserving the £7,500 grant offer, but its budget will be held at £400 million in 2027-28 rather than rising to the £600 million previously planned for that year. Funding thereafter is expected to increase broadly in line with inflation, rather than following the earlier trajectory of £683 million in 2028-29 and £709 million in 2029-30.

The new Warm Homes Loan Scheme provides a partial counterweight. It offers government-supported low-interest and no-interest finance for technologies including heat pumps, solar panels and batteries, allowing households to spread installation costs over a longer period. That may improve accessibility for owner-occupiers and landlords with sufficient borrowing capacity. It is, however, a materially different intervention from grant funding: it transfers more of the cost and financial risk to the householder and may be less accessible to households in fuel poverty or with constrained credit.

The tax treatment also moves in two directions. While the temporary zero rate on domestic electricity is extended, the existing zero rate for the installation of qualifying energy-saving materials, including insulation, solar panels and heat pumps, is not extended beyond 31 March 2027. Those installations will revert to the reduced VAT rate of 5% from 1 April 2027. The overall package therefore provides substantial short-term help with energy bills, but reduces some of the support intended to lower household energy demand and fossil-fuel exposure permanently.

That makes the interaction with home efficiency and electricity-market reform crucial.

The Budget’s most consequential sustainability measures may ultimately be those that attracted fewer immediate headlines. The first of those is the promise by the government of a comprehensive Cost Control Framework at the 2027 Spending Review, which is intended to set budgets for the different policy components of energy bills over the following decade. Until that framework is in place, no further policy costs will be added to bills unless they reduce bills or are essential to maintaining security of supply. This could be helpful if it brings greater transparency, stops inefficient interventions and makes clear which costs should sit on bills and which should be funded through progressive taxation.

It could be less helpful if it becomes a hard political ceiling that prevents the government from making the investments needed for the transition. A reference has been made to buying only clean power that is both cheap and ready to connect in the Contract for Difference Allocation Round 8, which appears sensible at face value, but could operate to disadvantage commercially viable schemes that are strategically valuable but trapped behind network constraints, or higher-risk schemes which could unlock more promising and scalable new opportunities.

The government is therefore still pushing for investment in infrastructure, but increasingly does not want its costs appearing directly on consumer bills – evidenced as well by the scrapping of a planned levy on gas bills that was intended to fund hydrogen projects which will instead be publicly funded. That can make funding more progressive, depending on the taxes used, but it also subjects long-term energy projects to competition within departmental budgets and future spending reviews.

The additional £20.4 billion for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank is potentially the strongest long-term growth measure in the package.

The National Wealth Fund (a public finance institution created in October 2024 to mobilise private capital for clean energy and industrial transformation) is expected to receive £15.4 billion and the British Business Bank £5 billion over approximately five years. The government estimates that the additional capital could support around 100,000 jobs by 2035 across green energy, defence and artificial intelligence.

The British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme is also relevant. From April 2027, around 10,000 eligible manufacturers will receive electricity discounts of approximately 20–25%, principally through exemptions from the Renewables Obligation, Feed-in Tariffs and Capacity Market costs. A payment in 2027 will also reflect support that participating businesses would have received during 2026-27.

This may help reduce carbon leakage and make industrial electrification more commercially attractive. High electricity costs can otherwise make retaining or expanding UK manufacturing difficult, particularly where international competitors face lower prices.

But affordability is not itself decarbonisation. There is no obvious direct requirement in the Budget announcement for businesses receiving support to invest in efficiency, switch from fossil fuels or adopt transition plans. A stronger model from a sustainability perspective would combine competitive electricity prices with clear incentives for emissions reduction, electrification and low-carbon capital investment; potentially building on the Climate Change Agreement framework.

Within the additional £15.4 billion National Wealth Fund capitalisation, £2 billion has been earmarked for a new Energy Wealth Fund. The Fund is intended to invest North Sea revenues in clean-energy projects and infrastructure. The idea of recycling North Sea tax revenues into renewable and low-carbon infrastructure has a clear (if contentious) economic logic. The fund is intended to finance the transition away from the same revenue base on which its future contributions depend. Clear governance, an investment mandate and an approach to maintaining capital as North Sea receipts decline will therefore be important.

The Budget creates opportunities, but also a more complex policy environment for businesses to navigate.

1) Energy procurement strategies may need to change

Businesses should monitor the proposed fixed-price arrangements for existing renewables, the Cost Control Framework and wider electricity-market reforms. These measures could affect wholesale-price exposure, the availability and pricing of power purchase agreements, and the economics of onsite generation.

2) Grid position is becoming a strategic asset

Faster connections will benefit some projects, but prioritisation is likely to become more rigorous. Businesses developing clean-energy, storage, data-centre or industrial projects should assess not only whether they have a connection agreement, but whether they can demonstrate readiness, strategic value and deliverability. This is becoming an increasingly volatile and investment-critical issue, particularly in the context of ongoing Ofgem consultations on reforms to the demand queue.

3) Public capital may create new routes to investment

The expanded National Wealth Fund, British Business Bank and Energy Wealth Fund could provide debt, equity, guarantees or cornerstone capital for projects that struggle to secure purely commercial finance.

Businesses should assess eligibility early and be prepared to demonstrate additionality, regional benefits, credible delivery plans and measurable transition outcomes.

4) Transition plans should be tested against policy inconsistency

Businesses should not assume that every part of the policy framework will move in the same direction at the same time. Electricity taxation may favour electrification while fuel-duty policy protects fossil-fuel use. Public capital may encourage clean investment while planning and grid constraints delay delivery.

Robust transition plans will need to account for those tensions rather than relying on a single policy trajectory.

EPA itself has told this same court that PFAS are dangerous to humans, including children and fetuses, and persist for decades or even millennia. Among EVs on display, a right-hand drive MODEL B gave attendees a chance to check out the result of CDMS collaboration, while onstage, Honda R&D and Mitsubishi Electric Mobility discussed, in separate remarks, their electromobility developments with Foxconn.

MODEL A+

An expressive luxury style yet authentic SUV for affluent drivers, the MODEL A+ is a deliberate move to expand B2B product portfolios in the fastest-growing B-segment SUV. MODEL K+

This is an expressive yet affordable SUV designed for active youth. Playful styling with nostalgic touches recall Japan's city pop music era of the '70s and '80s, but with a neo city pop take for the modern day. The highly distinctive lifestyle SUV for a niche market targets B2B looking to develop their own brand's lifestyle SUV EV, as well as OEMs looking to offer affordable yet distinctive vehicles for younger customers. With In-Wheel Motor technology, the MODEL K+ offers personalization of exterior, interior, driving range, and EEA for purpose-built capability at a competitive price.

MODEL K

This is a functional yet futuristic truck for forward-thinking business owners. Aimed at the specialized commercial kei truck class, the MODEL K finds use as last-mile and mobility service applications. Its alignment to support compliance to environmental regulations makes it attractive for decarbonization-focused entrepreneurs, municipalities, and government agencies while offering lower total cost of ownership (TCO) through reduced energy and maintenance costs. A functional beauty, inspired by the design language of Foxconn's award-winning MODEL T electric bus, the canopy-ready MODEL K conceptualizes a lower bed height and longer bed length.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Friday, October 30, 2026

Read the full sign-on letter here.

CONTACT

Dana Kuhnline, 513 601 9854, Dana@reimagineappalachia.org

APPALACHIA — This week, a coalition of 20 Appalachian organizations signed a letter denouncing the Trump-Vance administration’s newly proposed rule that severely limits farmers’ access to benefits from the U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Energy for America Program.

“The rule changes imply that farmers can’t make sensible business decisions about how much solar they want and where on their own land to place it,” said Dana Kuhnline, Program Director at ReImagine Appalachia. “Historically, the USDA has been a reliable partner to farmers and rural communities. However, USDA issued this rule as final before a public comment period opened, and implemented changes that make the REAP program much more burdensome and risky. Stakeholder input is key to the effectiveness of federal programs; the USDA should make revisions to this rule that reflect the knowledge and wisdom of the farmers and small businesses that make use of the program.”

​REAP is a USDA program that awards grants and loans to help farmers and rural small businesses install renewable energy and energy efficiency improvements. REAP funds can help pay for projects like HVAC systems, insulation, and renewable energy installations. The Appalachian coalition’s letter notes that when REAP passed as part of the 2008 Farm Bill, it had strong bipartisan backing, but the new changes would severely limit the cost-saving supports for rural communities.

The organizations that signed onto the letter aren’t alone in raising alarm about the program changes; earlier this week, 19 senators joined a letter expressing concern that the new rules go against the intent of REAP’s mission.

Titled “Unleashing American Energy and Economic Prosperity,” the USDA’s newly proposed rule would drastically reduce financial awards, limiting the full grant amount farmers can receive to 25% of project costs, reduced from 50%. Other items echo the Trump-Vance administration’s combative stance on solar energy. For example, it bars small rural businesses from installing ground-mounted solar outright. It also requires applicants to pay costs for any upgrade upfront and keep the project running for at least a year before they are eligible to compete for a grant that may never be awarded. This puts farmers and small business owners at high financial risk. Historically, 70% of REAP funding has supported solar projects, which many farmers install on their land (often in areas unsuitable for growing) to save on energy costs, protect grid stability and sustain their businesses.

The coalition also opposes the proposal to ban applicants from using equipment components manufactured by foreign adversary nations. This provision could disqualify whole systems over a single part, even if that equipment is assembled in an American factory. Instead, the letter invites a REAP rule structure that incentivizes purchasing American-made clean energy products through tax credits.

The letter cautions against stripping farmers and rural businesses of autonomy to choose how to source, install and scale energy and operations systems, emphasizing that farmers know best what their businesses need to thrive.

Signatories on the letter included: Appalachian Voices, Center for Progressive Reform, Community Climate Collaborative, Community Project Hub, Kentucky Environmental Foundation, MaGrann Associates, Mayor Patricia M. DeMarco, Ph.D., Borough of Forest Hills, PA, Pasa Sustainable Agriculture, PennFuture, Protect Penn-Trafford, ReImagine Appalachia, Solar United Neighbors, West Virginia Citizen Action Group, West Virginia Environmental Council, Energy Efficiency Alliance, Warren Energy, Renew Rocktown, Rural Action, Rural Power Coalition, Energy Efficiency Empowerment

text:
As the Vineyard heads into the midterm elections in less than a week, voters will determine whether to keep incumbent Democratic Congressman Bill Keating for another two-year term or elect a new candidate in the Republican challenger R. Tyler Macallister.

Early voting is already underway, and the state election is on Nov. 3. The two candidates have been busy on the campaign trail to meet voters and debate on various issues from affordability to Roe v. Wade, most recently at a political forum hosted by WATD radio.

Keating and Macallister clash on varying issues, and they come from different backgrounds: a longtime politician and former district attorney running against a businessman and select board member.

And despite Massachusetts not being a battleground state, there’s been an uptick in voter interest compared to last year. According to Vote.org, a nonprofit that promotes voter education and resources, 9,740 people registered through its site this year, an 18 percent increase from the previous year.

“Massachusetts voters are sending a clear message: They are paying attention, and they intend to make their voices heard,” Andrea Hailey, CEO of the organization, said in a press release.

The Times reached out to both candidates to ask questions of interest to Islanders, from stances on certain ballot questions to offshore wind. Their answers have been edited for style and clarity.

MVT: Please introduce yourself (age, occupation, town/city, background).

Keating: I’m Bill Keating, 74 years old, a resident of Bourne, and the Congressman representing Massachusetts’ Ninth Congressional District. I’m married to my wife, Tevis, and we have two adult children, Kristen and Patrick.

I was the first generation in my family to attend college, earning my bachelor’s degree and MBA from Boston College while working as a postal worker and in other jobs to pay my way through school. I later earned my law degree from Suffolk University Law School. I was elected to the Massachusetts House of Representatives at 23 and sworn in at 24. I also started a small business and went on to serve in the State Senate as Norfolk County District Attorney and now in Congress.

My grandparents came to America as immigrants with little more than a small wooden chest containing their belongings. But I know one thing they carried in that chest: hope. Hope for a better life and the opportunity to pursue the American Dream. That belief has guided my career in public service and my commitment to ensuring future generations have those same opportunities.

Macallister:

R. Tyler Macallister, 59.

Commercial and charter fishing captain and business owner. Energy broker and analyst, and partner in Walden Liberty Solar, LLC. Co-founder of the 501(c)(3) Bluefin Collaborative.

Mattapoisett. I grew up on Cape Cod, graduated from Barnstable High School in 1986 and have been a resident of the district my entire life.

B.S. in Marine Biology, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth; Master of Business Administration, Isenberg School of Management.

Mattapoisett Conservation Commission, 2005–2011; Mattapoisett Select Board, 2011–2025.

MVT: Why are you the best candidate for the role? What are your priorities in office for the Cape and islands, specifically for Martha’s Vineyard?

Keating: I’ve represented Martha’s Vineyard in Congress for over a decade and have been lucky enough to own a home on the Island for over a decade. As the grandson of immigrants who came to America seeking a better life and someone who worked his way through college, started a small business, and began serving in elected office at age 24, I understand the importance of opportunity and economic security. I also understand firsthand the unique challenges facing Martha’s Vineyard, particularly the high cost of living, housing affordability, healthcare, and reliable transportation.

Trump’s self-manufactured crises, including illegal tariffs and an illegal war, have driven up the costs of gasoline, groceries, electricity, and goods transported to the Island. Trump and his Republican Congress also enacted the largest healthcare cuts in American history, threatening insurance coverage for millions of Americans and disproportionately harming communities like Martha’s Vineyard. Many of the most damaging Medicaid cuts were delayed until after the election. I hope to return to Congress as part of a Democratic majority that will reassert Congress’s constitutional authority over tariffs and war powers, reverse these devastating healthcare cuts, and hold this administration accountable.

On issues unique to Martha’s Vineyard, I will continue working to improve transportation and accessibility, including the Cape Cod bridge replacements, airport infrastructure, and Steamship Authority ferry service. During the COVID-19 pandemic, I intervened to expedite more than $12 million in federal assistance to keep the Steamship Authority operating. I also helped secure a $2.5 million federal grant for the Woods Hole terminal and have continued pursuing investments in fleet modernization, safety improvements, and infrastructure. Reliable ferry service is essential to Island residents, workers, and businesses.

I will also continue supporting affordable housing, protecting our fisheries and coastal environment, strengthening healthcare access, and helping small businesses sustain our year-round economy. Defending our constitutional rights, restoring checks and balances, and holding this administration accountable are fundamental responsibilities. My experience in local, state, and federal government, along with my longstanding personal connection to Martha’s Vineyard, will continue to guide my work for the Island and the entire Ninth Congressional District.

Macallister: I have lived and worked in this district my entire life, and my career has been spent on the water, in local government, and in business. As a fishing captain, I know firsthand what the working waterfront needs and what is at stake for it. As a member of the [Mattapoisset] Conservation Commission and then the [Mattapoisset] Select Board for nearly two decades, I have dealt with the zoning, water, and wetlands decisions that shape our towns. As an energy analyst and solar partner, I have studied what energy projects actually cost and deliver, with an MBA to back up the numbers. My priorities for the Cape and islands, including Martha’s Vineyard, are:

Protecting our fisheries and working waterfront. Commercial and recreational fishing is part of the economy and the identity of the Cape and islands, and I will fight to end offshore wind development that is damaging these waters.

Affordable, reliable energy. I support advanced nuclear, including Thorium Salt Reactor technology, as a path to dependable power and real local jobs.

Local control. Towns and islands understand their own natural resources and carrying capacity better than Washington or Boston, and zoning decisions should stay with them.

Protecting water and the environment. Cape Cod has a finite aquifer, and the islands have fragile ecosystems. Development has to respect those limits.

Defending constitutional rights. I am a strong supporter of the Second Amendment and will defend it in Washington.

MVT: Earlier this year, whether the Martha’s Vineyard Commission (MVC) has the authority to review Chapter 40B housing proposals came under threat by a ruling by the Massachusetts Housing Appeals Committee. While litigation and appeals mean we still have to wait for results, where do you stand on the MVC’s jurisdiction over these types of projects?

Keating: While I will not comment on pending litigation, I will continue to support federal funding for affordable housing, with those resources best administered and implemented by local and regional agencies that understand their communities’ unique needs.

Macallister: While this is a state matter, as a member of the Mattapoisett Select Board, I am in full support of local zoning control because the localities are much more adept in understanding natural resources and carrying capacities of their respective municipalities. There is no “one size fits all” zoning.

MVT: Offshore wind is an industry that’s been touted by many Massachusetts officials and

conservationists as a vital part of the state’s renewable energy sector. However, it has been targeted by the Trump administration and some Martha’s Vineyard residents have expressed concern about changes to the viewshed and possible impact to sea life. How do you see the future of this industry in the state?

Keating: I strongly support offshore wind as an important part of Massachusetts’ energy future. It is critical to diversifying our energy supply, reducing our dependence on fossil fuels, and creating thousands of good-paying jobs, including union jobs.

I also recognize the importance of protecting our fisheries, marine ecosystems, and coastal communities. That is precisely why projects like Vineyard Wind underwent years of extensive environmental review by both federal and state agencies. These reviews examined impacts on commercial fishing, marine mammals, underwater construction noise, seafloor habitats, and coastal resources, resulting in environmental protections, construction restrictions, and ongoing monitoring requirements.

My office was actively involved throughout this process, participating in meetings and helping bring together fishermen, industry representatives, regulators, and other stakeholders to ensure concerns were heard and addressed. I have always believed that protecting our marine environment and supporting responsible offshore wind development must go hand in hand.

These projects were not approved without scrutiny. They underwent years of scientific review, public input, and regulatory oversight. We must continue enforcing those protections and working with our fishing communities as these projects move forward. I strongly oppose the Trump administration’s efforts to undermine an industry that is vital to our region’s economic and energy future.

Macallister: I will end offshore wind. I have done six years of research in the area of offshore wind and fished these waters since very young. The data, observations, and testimony from commercial fishermen clearly show that offshore wind has dramatically impacted the offshore environment and has done generational damage to the commercial and recreational fisheries. I have studied the ROI on wind as a partner in a renewable energy company, and at no time was I able to make the project profitable or efficient despite large subsidies. Additionally, the money that went into the projects went to the countries of the developers, Denmark and Spain. No significant job creation was recognized by these installations. I am a strong proponent of Thorium Salt Reactor technology and their development in the district at locations in Plymouth, Sandwich, [and] New Bedford.

MVT: ICE has been a concern for immigrant communities. On the Vineyard, there was a large operation in 2025 in which 20 individuals were arrested, and a father and son were arrested earlier this year while fishing, leading to local outcries. What is your stance on the agency’s activities in Massachusetts?

Keating: The actions of ICE agents continue to operate in violation of standard police protocols, illegally and in violation of constitutional due process protections.

As a former District Attorney, I understand lawful criminal enforcement efforts. What ICE does, as it did on the Vineyard, is aimed at stoking community fear and chaos. Along with the immoral tearing apart of families, it is a coercive effort to force self-deportation.

With a new House majority, I will work for congressional oversight and a complete overhaul of ICE’s leadership and operations.

Macallister: Immigration is a federal responsibility, and I support enforcing our immigration laws, with the first priority being people who pose a danger to our communities. At the same time, I understand why these arrests have caused real concern on the Vineyard. Many of these neighbors work in our fishing, farming, hospitality, and construction industries, and they are woven into the fabric of our Island and Cape communities.

I believe enforcement should be targeted, carried out with due process, and conducted in a way that respects the rights of everyone involved. Congress has failed for decades to fix a broken immigration system, and the answer is for Washington to do its job: secure the border, create workable and lawful pathways for the workers our coastal economy depends on, and give local communities clear information about what federal agencies are doing in their towns.

MVT: Please briefly provide your stances on Ballot Questions 6, 7, 8, and 9.

Keating:

Question 6: No

Question 7: Yes

Question 8: Vote NO

Question 9: YES

text:
Tennessee-headquartered Eastman will receive a major federal grant the Trump administration canceled last year, originally meant to help fund the company’s second chemical recycling plant in Texas.

The reinstated US Department of Energy (DOE) grant will cover capacity expansions at the Kingsport methanolysis facility and development of the potential second plant, but in an Oct. 30 earnings call CEO Mark Costa hinted at potential acquisitions of recently closed RPET processing capacity.

“There are recycling plants that have shut down in this country that we can get up for a very – we can purchase for a very low price,” he said. “There are polymer lines that have been shut down, and there’s infrastructure around both of them that are sitting there in those sites.”

About 25% of US post-consumer PET processing capacity has closed in the past 18 months, according to the Association of Plastic Recyclers (APR), amid a prolonged influx of cheap imported resin, both virgin and recycled. APR owns Resource Recycling, Inc., publisher of Plastics Recycling Update.

Producer Alpek announced closure of its Pennsylvania RPET plant in January, after also closing an operation in North Carolina. Evergreen closed operations in Ohio and New York as well this year. Last year, Phoenix Technologies closed one of its Ohio RPET plants, and rPlanet Earth in California also closed, but water bottler Niagara later bought and restarted the California facility.

In September, several members of Congress including Diana Harshbarger, who represents Tennessee’s 1st District that contains Kingsport, appealed to the US Trade Representative to consider the struggling sector in its Section 301 investigations of excess capacity in foreign manufacturing.

Although the grant originally was meant to help fund construction of Eastman’s second methanolysis plant, located in Longview, Texas, the company has revised the project scope.

The money will go toward a previously announced capacity increase of about 30% at Eastman’s flagship methanolysis plant in Kingsport, through debottlenecking and technology advancements.

In addition, the money will support “restart and repurposing of underutilized US recycling assets,” according to a company statement, including expanded feedstock processing capabilities as well as polymer capacity. The grant also will support “milestone-based planning for a potential second US methanolysis facility.”

Under the reinstated grant – amounting to $340 million, after Eastman previously received $35 million – the company must provide about half the costs for capacity expansion and development of the planned Texas plant. Costa said the grant “is structured where up to 50% of the capital, if we can get the number at the right target, can be paid for by the DOE.”

The second plant was postponed after the DOE canceled the grant in 2025. During the call, Costa said the project would have “substantially less capex” than in previous plans. “You have to remember that the Longview project was not just a methanolysis plant; it was also a polymer line. It was feedstock processing, the front end, it was infrastructure to support all that together. And about 40% to 50% of the capital is actually not the methanolysis plants; it’s all the other things: the processing, the polymer lines, the infrastructure, etc.”

Costa added, “We are very excited to get the grant back. I would say that the Department of Energy has been a phenomenal partner in coming back to us and talking about how we could collaborate on a reinstatement.”

Reiterating Eastman’s positioning of the plant as part of shoring up domestic manufacturing capabilities, he said, “I think we’re fully aligned in their vision, which is priority on reindustrializing US supply chains to America, building resiliency.”

In recent years, China has built up vast capacity for the entire PET value chain, in a push toward self-sufficiency for the massive polyester sector. During the call Costa said, “When China is getting to be 75% of the industry, you know, you have a serious issue about how you can put food and water on the shelves, and so [supply] security is incredibly important.”

“The Department of Energy is proud to support this strategic investment in American ingenuity, industrial competitiveness, and the future of U.S. manufacturing,” said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “By expanding its proven, American-made recycling technology and putting underutilized assets back to work, Eastman is demonstrating how innovation can strengthen domestic manufacturing, revitalize existing industrial infrastructure, and build more resilient supply chains. DOE will continue to collaborate with private industry to make U.S. manufacturing the strongest in the world and grow jobs and economic prosperity.”

name: North Carolina and Evs
title: States must take a critical eye to gas plants proposed over clean energy | Utility Dive
authors: Hudson Kingston, Robert Walton, Diana DiGangi, Will Scott
description:
While customers are forced to pay increasingly higher energy bills, utility shareholders are guaranteed profits on centralized fossil energy projects.
Once new energy infrastructure is approved by state regulators, utilities can start recovering the costs through customer rates even before the project is built and in use.
Wind and solar have been cheaper than gas plants for nearly a decade in the U.S. Clean energy keeps getting more affordable while the cost of constructing new gas plants has increased by 66%, and the time required to bring them online grew by 23% between 2023 and 2025.
Utilities justify this build out of gas plants on the basis of projected data-center demand, rather than the current needs of households and local businesses.
Duke Energy was found to have artificially capped energy storage and solar energy in its modeling to justify the need for new, lucrative gas plants.
text:
Will Scott is the North Carolina policy director of the Environmental Defense Fund. Hudson Kingston is the legal director at CURE, a nonprofit rural environmental and energy democracy organization in Minnesota.

The data center boom has become a cash cow for investor-owned utilities across the country. Many utility companies are seeking approval for costly new gas plants and other fossil fuel infrastructure based on uncertain projections of future demand for data centers and other large customers. If those projections fall short, ratepayers are left with 30 years of payments for projects that are increasingly expensive to build and slow to develop. We can’t let phantom projections for new data centers leave regular ratepayers with the bill.

Historically, state regulators have given utilities significant latitude to pursue new generation. Yet, as heating and cooling bills become painfully unaffordable for families and local businesses, utility regulators are increasingly skeptical of proposals that could leave them paying for decades of dirty and expensive fossil fuel infrastructure, when clean, renewable energy and batteries provide a reliable, homegrown and affordable alternative. Indeed, a recent study found that batteries are now cheaper than gas peaker plants, globally.

While customers are forced to pay increasingly higher energy bills, utility shareholders are guaranteed profits on centralized fossil energy projects. The bigger and more costly the construction, the more money energy corporations make. Once new energy infrastructure is approved by state regulators, utilities can start recovering the costs through customer rates even before the project is built and in use. Because utilities make profits off the infrastructure they build, and not the energy they sell, executives have a financial incentive to keep building to benefit shareholders.

To be clear, getting ahead of potential demand is not inherently problematic. Investing in clean and affordable energy generation to meet everyday customers’ future needs for things like home heating and cooling and electric vehicle charging would lower prices and improve reliability. The issue is that utilities are using that incentive and uncertain future demand to justify spending customers’ money on new fossil fuel infrastructure that will raise prices and pollution.

Amid this surge in data center proposals, regulators must be proactive and diligent in protecting customers from imprudent utility spending on fossil fuels, particularly when clean energy offers an affordable alternative.

In the Midwest, Minnesota Power proposed large amounts of new gas generation as part of its plan to meet future electricity demand. Instead of granting the utility carte blanche to build more gas infrastructure, as is common in these proceedings, Minnesota’s regulators have directed the utility to explore less costly alternatives, including a scenario that adds wind, solar and storage instead of expensive and polluting gas power plants that would run afoul of the state’s carbon-free standard.

Wind and solar have been cheaper than gas plants for nearly a decade in the U.S. Clean energy keeps getting more affordable while the cost of constructing new gas plants has increased by 66%, and the time required to bring them online grew by 23% between 2023 and 2025. Despite that, in 2025 utilities reported plans to build 24 GW of gas plant capacity, representing a 570% increase over 2023. Utilities justify this build out of gas plants on the basis of projected data-center demand, rather than the current needs of households and local businesses. Not all regulators are buying it.

In North Carolina, regulators rejected a Duke Energy $584 million gas turbine that the company argued is needed to meet the energy needs of anticipated large customers, particularly data centers. Regulators found that Duke’s anticipated load projections were not justification enough to saddle customers with another expensive gas project, that the project put too much risk on residential ratepayers and that the utility had not adequately examined potentially cheaper alternatives, like batteries.

With profits driving spending decisions rather than what’s in the best interest of customers, utilities wielding monopoly power often deliberately squeeze out more affordable energy sources, such as wind and solar — which are also faster to bring online — when forced to split ownership of those facilities with project developers.

In fact, some utilities are actively working against cheaper energy options. Duke Energy was found to have artificially capped energy storage and solar energy in its modeling to justify the need for new, lucrative gas plants.

In Minnesota and North Carolina, we’ve seen what happens when state regulators use their authority to stand up to utilities and protect residents from unnecessarily high energy costs. Both states offer examples of how regulators can push back against costly gas projects and put the interests of ratepayers first. Speculative demand should not be the burden of customers, and customers shouldn’t have to pay for gas when solar and wind are cheaper.

Read More in Generation

The question for regulators is no longer simply whether utilities can find a reason to build another gas plant. It is whether utilities can prove that customers actually need it, whether clean energy and batteries could do a better, more cost-efficient job, and whether families and businesses should unnecessarily shoulder decades of debt risk to cover short term demand projections driven by data center developers.

text:
There are so many negative consequences of our country’s reliance on fossil fuels: exposure to pollution (e.g., for children exposed to diesel fumes on school buses). Price increases in energy and transportation, caused by faraway conflicts. Climate change caused by spiking CO2 concentrations in the atmosphere. Loss of American leadership.

At this point, a major stumbling block is simple red tape. There are a great many clean energy projects that are funded and ready to go, but are awaiting a permitting approval system that Rube Goldberg would be proud of. Over 90% of the projects in the “interconnection queue” are clean-energy projects, and it’s an unfortunate fact that, for these kinds of projects, delay often means cancellation, as investors find quicker returns elsewhere.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is a solution to this problem. It will greatly streamline our current permitting system. It is technology neutral, but, because such a large fraction of queued projects are clean, it will, on balance, move us away from fossil fuels. It was introduced by a Republican (Sen. Capito of West Virginia) and is cosponsored by two Democrats and another Republican. So it has solid support from both parties — imagine that!

Please encourage Sens. Klobuchar and Smith to join in that support.

Scot Adams, Eden Prairie

Scot Adams is a member of Citizens’ Climate Lobby.

name: American Energy
title: How Much More Financial Aid Will Nuclear Industry Get During Trump 2.0?
description:
Will U.S. nuclear projects receive additional financial aid from the federal government?
So far, this office has made over US$34 billion in loan commitments to the domestic nuclear power industry.
Despite its strong operating safety record, the U.S. nuclear power industry has a history of cost overruns and missed milestones.
But the U.S. nuclear industry has been warmly embraced by the second Trump administration.
Hefty financial commitments to proposed, existing and closed nuclear power plants, and to rebuild a domestic nuclear supply chain, raise several questions.
text:
Written by John Egan for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

The U.S. nuclear power industry has received at least US$34 billion in loan commitments so far during the second Trump administration. IIR is tracking about US$247 billion in proposed nuclear power projects scheduled to begin construction in 2027 and beyond. The U.S. Department of Energy is said to have as much as an additional $250 billion to lend to energy projects favored by the president. Will U.S. nuclear projects receive additional financial aid from the federal government? If so, which ones?

Proposed Nuclear Power Projects, DOE Loan Commitments

Tuesday's announcement that the U. S. Department of Energy (DOE) will issue a conditional loan of up to US$5 billion to Constellation Energy Corporation to expand its nuclear generating capacity increased the Trump administration's financial support for nuclear power industry to at least US$34 billion. For more on the Constellation loan, see October 28. 2026, IIR Breaking Energy News article - Constellation Secures $5 Billion Conditional DOE Loan for Nuclear Expansion.

Industrial Info Resources is tracking approximately 218 U.S. nuclear power capital and maintenance projects valued at about US$249 billion that are scheduled to begin construction in 2027 and beyond. That list includes plans to build dozens of small modular reactors (SMRs); construct a number of traditional large new plants, some using the Westinghouse AP1000 nuclear design; reopen closed plants; finish construction of partially built plants; restart closed plants; and perform a variety of in-plant capital projects such as power uprates, plant modernizations and steam turbine replacements. That list also includes several planned decommissioning and demolition of closed nuclear plants. Readers can access that list of proposed projects here.

The DOE has a division, the Office of Energy Dominance Funding (DOE EDF), that makes loan commitments to energy projects favored by the president and his administration. So far, this office has made over US$34 billion in loan commitments to the domestic nuclear power industry. An official from the DOE EDF told an energy conference this summer that it had about US$250 billion in remaining lending authority, and it was seeking more authority from Congress. For more on that, see August 25, 2026, article - DOE Seeking Loan Applicants for U.S. Energy Projects Favored by Trump.

Expanding and Upgrading Existing Plants

The loan commitment to Constellation will be for expanding nuclear generating capacity at eight existing facilities across Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania.

On October 5, the DOE EDF made a conditional loan commitment of up to US$4.2 billion to a unit of Vistra Corporation to support expanding and modernizing operations at three operating nuclear power plants in the PJM Interconnection: Perry and Davis-Besse in Ohio and Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania. For more on that, see October 7, 2026, article - U.S. Plans to Loan $4.2 Billion for Vistra's PJM Nuclear Plants.

The DOE EDF said the loan commitment would "preserve nearly 4,000 MW of reliable baseload power -- enough to power more than 3 million homes -- and add 433 megawatts of new nuclear capacity" by uprating the plants.

PJM is the wholesale grid manager overseeing power delivery to an estimated 67 million people in 13 states and the District of Columbia. Its reserve margins have dwindled in recent months in the face of the explosive growth of planned data centers in its geographic footprint.

The loan commitment to Vistra also includes an option to finance potential future uprates at its Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant in Texas, DOE said October 5.

IIR was unable to reach a DOE official to learn whether, and how many, nuclear asset owners have requested loan guarantees from the agency's EDF.

IIR is tracking over a dozen proposed in-plant capital and maintenance projects at U.S. nuclear power plants, including:

Several in-plant capital projects at the Surry and North Anna plants, operated by a unit of Dominion Energy

Power uprates at the Columbia station, operated by Energy Northwest

Power uprates at the McGuire, Brunswick and Catawba stations, operated by Duke Energy

Power uprates at the Comanche Peak station, operated by a unit of Luminant, a unit of Vistra, and

Power uprates at the Hatch and Vogtle nuclear stations, operated by Georgia Power Company.

Funding in-plant capital and maintenance projects at operating nuclear plants is a quicker way to bring new nuclear capacity online compared to building new units or taking closed units out of mothballs. IIR believes one or more of these projects will be funded by the DOE EDF.

DOE Loan Seeks to Rebuild Nuclear Supply Chain

In June 2026, the DOE EDF finalized a US$17.5 billion conditional loan commitment to rebuild the domestic nuclear supply chain in order to accelerate the deployment of 10 new AP1000 nuclear reactors manufactured by the Westinghouse Electric Company. For more on that, see June 24, 2026, article -- U.S. Plans to Loan $17.5 Billion to Boost Nuclear Reactor Construction.

The first two AP1000 reactors to be deployed were installed at the Alvin W. Vogtle Nuclear Power Station in Georgia, which was completed in 2024 years late and billions of dollars over budget.

The DOE EDF award announcement said the AP1000 reactors are planned to be built at five locations, which have not yet been disclosed. However, the names of several utilities have been mentioned as potential hosts.

William J. Smith, a spokesperson for one of those utilities, New Jersey-based Public Service Enterprise Group Incorporated (PSEG), said this in an emailed statement to IIR: "We are proud of the people and performance of PSEG's existing nuclear generating sites, and we are excited about the future opportunities available associated with our early site permit in Salem County. Nuclear provides reliable power that is a carbon-free, 24/7, baseload power source. As previously stated publicly, PSEG is interested in enabling new nuclear development for the State at the PSEG nuclear generating site."

Stephen Tait, nuclear communications manager for another utility, DTE Energy Company, told IIR, "At this time, DTE has no immediate plans to build a new nuclear power plant."

Mark Sullivan, communications director for Entergy Corporation, said this in an emailed statement to IIR: "As a company, we continue evaluating all forms of new nuclear generation, large and small. We've not made any firm decisions on our next steps. Ultimately, we will ensure any decision we make is in the best interest of our customers and other stakeholders."

Energy Agency Also Funds Efforts to Reopen Closed Plants

In separate decisions, the DOE EDF has guaranteed loans totaling up to US$4.4 billion to restart three closed nuclear power plants, according to an Associated Press article. The shuttered plants include the Palisades Nuclear Generating Station in Michigan, owned by Holtec International; the Crane Clean Energy Center in Pennsylvania, formerly known as Three Mile Island, owned by Constellation; and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa, owned by NextEra Energy Incorporated. For more on the loan to the Arnild Center, see September 8. 2026, IIR Energy Breaking Energy News article - DOE Closes $1.9 Billion Loan for 606 MW Duane Arnold Nuclear Restart.

The three plants have combined generating capacity of about 2,250 MW. The three plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive, AP reported.

There are about 20 other nuclear plants in the U.S. that have closed for one reason or another. Some have been mothballed while others are in varying stages of decontamination and demolition. A list of those non-operating nuclear plants can be viewed here. It would be easier, but by no means easy, to reopen a plant that has been recently mothballed compared to one undergoing decommissioning and demolition.

By the Numbers

249: Dollar value, in US billions, of proposed U.S. nuclear power projects scheduled to kick off construction in 2027 and beyond.

250: The amount of remaining lending authority, in US billions, that the DOE Office of Energy Dominance Funding had as of August 2026 to support energy projects favored by the Trump administration.

34: The publicly released value of loan guarantees, in U.S. billions, made so far in the second Trump administration to nuclear power operators.

Next-Generation Projects Also Receive DOE Funding

This year, two next-generation nuclear power projects in Wyoming and Tennessee were awarded construction licenses by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). For more on that, see October 15, 2026, article - U.S. Nuclear Body Gives Second SMR Permit in Six Months.

Both of those planned nuclear projects received DOE funding.

The DOE has awarded about US$2 billion to the Natrium sodium-cooled project now under construction in Kemmerer, Wyoming. This project is being developed by TerraPower Incorporated.

Last December, the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) was awarded US$400 million to accelerate the deployment of SMRs. A DOE statement from December 2 said the grant to TVA will support deployment of a GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 at the Clinch River Nuclear site in Tennessee. For more on that award, and a separate award made the same day to Holtec International, see December 4, 2025, article - DOE Awards $800 Million for U.S. SMR Development. The award to Holtec is intended to support deployment of two SMR-300 reactors at the Palisades Nuclear Generating Station site in Covert, Michigan.

Roughly three dozen other next-generation nuclear projects are under development. Many of these are for SMRs.

Why Nuclear? Why Now?

Despite its strong operating safety record, the U.S. nuclear power industry has a history of cost overruns and missed milestones. But the U.S. nuclear industry has been warmly embraced by the second Trump administration. The president, and DOE leaders, have justified its financial support for nuclear because electricity generated by those plants is dispatchable, unlike intermittent resources like wind and solar, and thus can be used to support the 24/7/365 power needs of actual and planned data centers, which continue to grow very rapidly, as well as advanced manufacturing and other large energy loads. For more on the unprecedented growth of data centers, see October 20, 2026, article - Data Center Construction Starts Still Soaring Despite Some Bumps in the Road.

Hefty financial commitments to proposed, existing and closed nuclear power plants, and to rebuild a domestic nuclear supply chain, raise several questions. Multiple efforts to reach DOE were unsuccessful.

Key Takeaways

text:
Written by Paul Wiseman for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

The expansion of electric vehicles (EVs) and battery energy storage systems (BESS) is expected to triple the demand for lithium. Today's worldwide mining supply chain will need significant help to handle that. Industrial Info Resources is tracking 171 lithium mining projects worldwide with completion dates by 2050, with a total investment value (TIV) of $53.72 billion.

More, More, More Lithium

The expansion of electric vehicles (EVs) and battery energy storage systems (BESS), the latter largely to supplement intermittent generation sources like wind and solar, is expected to triple the demand for batteries' foundational mineral, lithium. Today's worldwide mining supply chain will need significant help to handle that.

Because of that, supply chain research firm Benchmark Minerals sees a need for 134 new lithium mines to be producing by 2050. EVs are expected to account for 76% of demand despite rapid growth of the BESS market. Benchmark also sees China surpassing Australia as the world's largest producer, while North America's share of production expands from 1.7% to 13% in that time frame.

Industrial Info Resources is tracking 171 lithium mining projects worldwide with completion dates by 2050, with a total investment value (TIV) of $53.72 billion.

To Benchmark's prediction that North America's share of lithium mining activity will increase greatly by 2050, Industrial Info Resources' data does show the region greatly leads the world in new projects. North America is home to 36 of the world's 168 lithium mining projects being tracked, with TIV of $19.4 billion, 37.4% of the world's TIV.

South America is second with 39 projects totaling just under $13.7 billion, while Asia is third with 34 projects and TIV of $12.3 billion.

By nation, the U.S. is number one, at $13.8 billion, followed by China with $12.32 billion.

While the Industrial Info project count is higher than Benchmark's listed number, the company's Vice President of Research, Metals and Minerals, Joe Govreau, points out that many of the tracked projects are in early exploration stages and may never reach FID or production, due to a variety of factors.

Australia, currently the world's lithium production leader, has languished somewhat in recent years. But this October 23, 2026 Industrial Info Resources news story, Australia's Lithium Comeback Boosted by Pilgangoora Expansion, shows that there are seven Pilgangoora lithium projects worth more than US$1.53 billion in investment.

Currently the U.S. has only one significant producing lithium mine, Albemarle's Silverpeak Lithium Solution Mine in Nevada. Subscribers can learn more from a detailed plant profile.

Mining Alternatives Required

Traditional lithium mining and refining methods have been as slow as watching water evaporate (literally), while also requiring much water and producing thousands of gallons of toxic waste. Hard-rock mining and solar evaporation ponds could take months or years to process each load, with low recovery rates. The process is also very costly.

With lithium's rush to provide clean energy, production methods must get faster and cleaner, and new procedures are providing exactly those results. Direct lithium extraction (DLE), among the most popular currently developing methods, extracts lithium from brines in hours or a few days, with 90-95% recovery rates.

But wait, there's more. In this August 27, 2026 story Assisted by Halliburton, Two Startups Slash Costs of Critical Minerals Refining, Industrial Info's Frankie Vo explains California-based startup Electroflow Technologies' new, streamlined method. "Electroflow has developed an electrochemical process that goes from extracting lithium from brine to refining it into lithium iron phosphate in three steps instead of the traditional 10-step process."

Oil industry service giant Halliburton is assisting Electroflow with its development.

One significant new source of lithium involves brines, both naturally occurring and from wastewater associated with oil and gas production. Many oil companies are investing in the Smackover Formation in southeast Arkansas and east Texas, for its mineral-rich brines that include lithium. For more information on that, see this September 9 Industrial Info Resources story Black Gold to White Gold: U.S. Oil Industry Invests in Lithium.

DLE From Oil and Gas Wells

In the oil field itself, each oil well produces many times more water than it does oil. That water, while rich with other minerals, is also laden with brines, unrecovered oil, and other toxins that have led companies in the past to simply inject it underground, theoretically out of harm's way. That process has led to earthquakes in high production areas such as the Permian Basin of west Texas and southeast New Mexico.

So, finding a way to capture useful minerals, clean the rest, and repurpose that for industrial or other use would help many industries.

To that end, as in this Monday October 19 Industrial Info Resources story, Texas Plant to Extract Lithium from Oil Wastewater, getting lithium from produced oilfield water is also on the horizon. In the story Element3, the system operator, says once it is fully operational, this one project could match half the U.S.'s current lithium production.

The investment and project numbers currently are well below the suggested count, but there are still just over 23 years before 2050. Governments worldwide are investing and otherwise easing the way for new mines, so things could change.

By the Numbers:

134: Number of new mines required by 2050 to meet demand

168: Number of new lithium mining projects tracked by Industrial Info Resources, although many are in early planning stages and may never be completed

Key Takeaways

Lithium mining will have to ramp up greatly to keep up with demand growth from EVs and BESS installations.

text:
Womble Bond Dickinson Partners Kristina Moore and Lee Van Voorhis recently had a podcast discussion about what companies need to know about the U.S. midterm elections. This article is based on that podcast. Click here to listen.

Tuesday, November 3 is Election Day, and Americans will find out which party controls the House and Senate. Historical trends show that the President’s party typically loses Congressional seats in the midterms. With thin margins in both the House and Senate, that may well be enough to flip control of one or both branches to the Democratic Party. Most polling data shows the House is likely to change hands, with control of the Senate still up in the air.

Congressional Democrats have promised to investigate a range of Trump Administration’s practices. Companies that contract with the government, particularly no bid arrangements, and corporate leaders who have advised the Administration or otherwise benefited from a change in Administration policy could find themselves having to answer questions in a Congressional hearing.

What to Know about Congressional Investigations

Moore said a Congressional investigation “is not a litigation, it’s not a courtroom trial, and it’s not an agency enforcement proceeding. The rules and the norms of a congressional investigation are unique to Congress.”

For example, Congress may not accept a common law assertion of privilege, meaning attorney client privilege or work product privilege.

For executives asked to testify, this can be unfamiliar ground. They need to know that political goals drive Congressional inquiries, and no wrongdoing is required to be a subject of inquiry.

So what exactly will Congress want to investigate, should Democrats assume control of either the House or Senate? A few possibilities include:

An alleged pay-to-play culture in which political donors have heightened access to or improper influence over regulatory decisions;

Rising consumer prices, including algorithmic pricing;

The Administration’s regime change in Venezuela – and who may have benefitted;

Data centers and their impact on local communities; and

The dominance of private equity ownership throughout the economy.

“Private parties that have been interacting with the Administration certainly can find themselves in the crosshairs,” Moore said. “A company doesn't have to be accused of any sort of wrongdoing in order to become an important piece of an investigation. It may simply possess communications that Congress believes help explain what has happened.”

Van Voorhis questioned what might happen if control of Congress is split between the two parties. Such a scenario may lead to a heightened environment for Congressional investigations, including the two parties cooperating on areas of bipartisan interest (for example, consumer costs and data centers.)

The Looming Battle Over Executive Privilege

The Department of Justice recently issued an opinion greatly expanding the Executive Branch’s view of the scope of executive privilege protections, in advance of potential Congressional investigations in 2027.

“The DOJ opinion said essentially if you are you speaking with the President or somebody representing the words of the President, and if it is a confidential conversation then that could be considered to be covered by executive privilege.”

However, it’s important to note that this claim of executive privilege sits with the President or his designee within the White House. It cannot be asserted by a private advisor.

Also, it is highly likely that a Democratic Congress will reject this expanded definition of executive privilege, which goes beyond what the courts previously have recognized.

That puts corporate executives in a tough position. They don’t wish to alienate the Administration by cooperating with Congressional investigations, but they may face tremendous pressure, including Contempt of Congress proceedings, to comply with a Congressional subpoena.

Moore said companies should go ahead and conduct an internal investigation to identify which personnel have had conversations with the Administration and who might be called to testify.

“It starts with knowing what your vulnerabilities are and having a strategy,” Moore said.

Van Voorhis asked, “What would be the biggest mistake companies make during the investigation?” Moore said that not answering and engaging with Congress would be a big mistake, should investigators come calling. “You can certainly have a strategy that positions a company to lay low, to not raise any red flags, to not look interesting. But that is different from a strategy of non-engagement.”

Generally, she said cooperating with Congress is the best course of action. The key is finding “that space where cooperation isn’t too painful,” she said.

title: Big polluters get exemptions. Your lungs don't. - EDF Vital Signs
description:
We’ve sketched out that process before,here and here.
Trump’s EPA set up a special email address and invited hundreds of facilities to ask for exemptions for all kinds of pollutants.
One request was sent from an iPhone: “Hello, I am a gas company looking for an exemption.
Even after the supposed deadline came and went, industrial facilities didn’t stop asking, and the Trump administration didn’t stop handing out exemptions, records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by Environmental Defense Fund show.
“Giving companies a pass to delay long-needed, commonsense pollution controls puts more Americans in harm’s way,” Erin Murphy, an attorney at EDF, said.
text:
A new investigation by The New York Times provides the most detailed look to date at how the exemptions came to pass, revealing the process through which the administration maneuvered to allow some of the country’s dirtiest facilities to do their worst, “prioritizing the economic interests of corporations and easing costs for polluting industries” at taxpayers’ expense.

We’ve sketched out that process before,here and here. Trump’s EPA set up a special email address and invited hundreds of facilities to ask for exemptions for all kinds of pollutants. One request was sent from an iPhone: “Hello, I am a gas company looking for an exemption. How do I start?”

It didn’t take much more than that. Companies didn’t even need to make a case, as it turns out, as long as they invoked “national security” or claimed certain technology wasn’t “widely available.” As the Times reports, “The president approved [the exemptions] even though the equipment was readily accessible and the industry’s national security claims had little detail to substantiate them.” So far, 71 coal plants, 71 chemical plants, 40 medical sterilizers, 19 steel-related facilities and one copper smelter have received passes. At least 3.3 million people live within three miles of one of them.

Do you live near a polluter with a free pass? See the map.

And what’s more? Even after the supposed deadline came and went, industrial facilities didn’t stop asking, and the Trump administration didn’t stop handing out exemptions, records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act by Environmental Defense Fund show. “Giving companies a pass to delay long-needed, commonsense pollution controls puts more Americans in harm’s way,” Erin Murphy, an attorney at EDF, said.

The automotive press is practically aflame with rumors that Ford is replacing its Ford Escape crossover SUV with an electric version, also to be named Escape. That has raised quite a ripple across the esoteric field of car-naming. Normally when a model retires, so does the name. The US auto industry is littered with has-beens, wanna-be’s, never-was, and just plain exhausted cars that retired along with their names. Hmmm….perhaps Ford is sending a not so subtle signal about the future of EV sales in the US…

The Future Of EV Sales In The US

By now, everyone knows that EV sales cratered last fall, after US President Donald Trump and his Republican majority in Congress engineered the “OBBA” tax bill to eliminate federal tax credits for EVs.

Still, EV sales did not actually stop in their tracks, let alone reverse course. A fresh wave of off-lease, used EVs helped keep the momentum up earlier this year, and some automakers (looking at you, Subaru) stayed on track with plans for new EVs in the US.

Plug-in hybrids also factored in as a sort of gateway drug, with Audi CEO Gernot Döllner among those looking forward to strong EV sales in that category.

EV stakeholders must smell blood in the water as Election Day 2026 approaches. With polls indicating that Trump will lose his chokehold on federal EV policy, news about EVs has been tumbling through the Intertubes over the past several weeks. Among the examples, Slate Auto opened its first showroom in Chicago, and General Motors unveiled its gen-4 EV platform.

Somewhat bizarrely, the Trump administration also contributed to the news cycle with the launch of the new “BattMan” battery collaboration earlier this week. Under the umbrella of the US Department of Energy, BattMan hooks up federal laboratories with academic and private sector partners to push the envelope on next-gen batteries for transportation applications as well as stationary energy storage.

Ford Waves Goodbye To Another Gasmobile

Of course, Tesla also weighed in with its “flying car” stunt, but that was just a stunt. Over in the world of street legal EVs, Ford has been working the publicity machine to gin up interest in the forthcoming Fathom all-electric pickup truck, which is on track for volume production early next year at an MSRP starting at the affordability benchmark of $28,350 with a built-in inverter that cuts the cost of bidirectional charging, too.

The Fathom illustrates how much blood, sweat, and tears go into naming a new car. It’s a mid-sized pickup like the popular Maverick, but Ford went off in a new direction with the Fathom, considering hundreds of options over a months-long naming journey before settling on a maritime-adjacent reference to deep understanding.

The Fathom will be the first EV to roll off Ford’s new “Universal EV” manufacturing platform, and the automaker has indicated that the next vehicle will be a compact SUV. The consensus has settled on something resembling the Escape crossover SUV, all the more so because Ford has been laying plans to retire the gasmobile…but maybe, not the name.

That’s where the ears of the automotive press have pricked up, drawing attention to the Escape landing page that depicts the rear end of a forlorn, rain-splattered Escape heading off into the dustbin of automotive history along with its dual exhaust system.

And, here’s where things get interesting. The text on the landing page simply notes that the Ford Escape is “tapping the brakes,” which has been interpreted as a pausing message, not a forever message.

However, on the same page Ford provides a good reason why the 2026 Escape will not fly. The car is not for sale in California and several other states.

“The 2026 Ford Escape® is not certified for emissions requirements with the California Air Resources Board,” Ford states in a drop-down link. “Therefore, it is not available for purchase by customers intending to register their vehicle in states that have adopted California’s certification requirements for the 2026 model year, specifically California, Massachusetts, Oregon, New York, Washington, and Vermont.”

Ford goes on to suggest two other gas-powered SUVs that are street legal in California-compliant states, the 2026 Bronco Sport SUV and the 2026 Ford Explorer SUV.

More EV Sales In The USA

So, is Ford really banking on the Escape brand to boost its EV sales in the US? Maybe! In August, the Detroit Free Press summarized a swirl of rumors around the idea of an electric Escape, citing insider sources including a Ford dealer with access to the company’s program codes.

However, in the same report, Reuters cites an inside source who indicated that in 2029, Ford plans to introduce a new entry-level SUV in hybrid and gasoline powertrains.

“At the Las Vegas meeting, the executives, the dealer said, assured dealers that the automaker is committed to hybrid powertrains going forward,” Reuters emphasized.

Hmmmm…so much for an all-electric escape. Back in May, the Canadian Ford dealer MSAFord also raised some questions about an all-electric replacement for the Escape in a blog post (breaks added for readabilty):

“Production of the Ford Escape and Lincoln Corsair ended at the Louisville Assembly plant last December, leaving a giant hole in The Blue Oval’s lineup as it pertains to small crossovers.”

“This is particularly true of the Escape, which disappeared at a time when new vehicle shoppers are increasingly looking for more affordable options, too.

“However, back in December 2022, a report surfaced from AutoForecast Solutions, claiming that the Ford Escape would live on as an all-electric crossover, though it has thus far remained unclear if that plan is intact ever since”

Readers, what do you think? Is half an EV better than none? Full EV sales have yet to surge, but plug-in hybrids have become more popular on the heels of US President Donald Trump’s witless decision to bomb Iran last February.

EREV (extended range EVs) are another halfway-there option that will factor into an uptick in EV sales. The Scout Motors branch of Volkswagen, for example, has stated that EREVs account for the majority of its reservations so far.

Then there’s the pure EV players, including robotaxi stakeholders alongside Slate and Rivian, which is forging ahead with plans to construct a new factory in Georgia.

As for industry leader Tesla, that’s a whole ‘nother can of worms. CEO Elon Musk has earned a fair share of bad publicity in recent years, as depicted in the new “Musk” documentary. However, the film wrapped sometime last year, leaving Musk’s latest hi-jinks for the sequel.
