title: DOE secretary touts Paducah energy projects - WPSD Local 6
description: Tim Walsh, Department of Energy assistant secretary for environmental management, visited Paducah on Thursday to discuss advancements at the Department of Energy Paducah Site, like the Paducah American Energy Hub
text:
With election day just next week, many races are heating up.…

The proposition is set to appear on ballots in Gallatin, Ham…



PADUCAH — Tim Walsh, Department of Energy assistant secretary for environmental management, visited Paducah on Thursday to discuss advancements at the Department of Energy Paducah Site, like the Paducah American Energy Hub data center project.

Walsh was joined by Scott Nolan, CEO and founder of nuclear enrichment start-up General Matter, and Bruce Wilcox, president of Greater Paducah Economic Development. Walsh described projects on the site as crucial to meeting the United States’ future energy needs.

Tim Walsh, Department of Energy assistant secretary for environmental Management, left, speaks at the DOE Paducah Site on Oct. 29, citing it as an important part of the United States' energy future.

“Where there's energy, there's prosperity,” Walsh said. “Under President [Donald] Trump's administration, we are all about driving the cost of electricity down for American consumers. Nuclear power is actually the cheapest and safest form of energy. Just a couple of weeks ago, I was at the Vogtle plant and heard about how that plant now produces the cheapest power in Georgia. So it's really exciting that we have this nuclear renaissance going on that's producing new nuclear reactors. [...] But what really is driving the nuclear renaissance is the need for power. That need is being driven by the digital infrastructure, the superintelligence data centers that are being built right here in America and right here in Paducah.”

Walsh referred to the $100 Billion Paducah American Energy Hub, a partnership with Brookfield, NextEra Energy, Big Rivers Electric Corporation, Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System, announced in July. The project will include both an AI data center and an energy infrastructure specifically built to power it. A media advisory from the DOE prior to the event referred to the project as a $153 billion investment.

WPSD-TV asked Walsh to clarify if the estimated project cost has increased.

Tim Walsh, Department of Energy assistant secretary for environmental Management.

“I think that probably includes some potential expansions that are underway and in discussions right now,” Walsh said. “One of the great things that we're actually doing here is master planning the entire site, and I believe what that probably captures is really what this looks like 10 years from now once the buildings are down and once this whole region is redeveloped based on the master plan that's being put together right now.”

Walsh said the project falls under Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and will not raise electricity and utility costs in the area, while possibly providing excess electricity to the grid. He touted temporary and long term job creation on projects throughout the site.

“We don't force anything on any local community,” Walsh said. “Our job is to clean the past projects up so then the community can come in and engage with us and tell us what they want to see happen here. That's exactly what's happened, and why General Matter was brought in here. So it always starts with the community, and it always looks towards how we can ensure that there's future economic prosperity for this surrounding community and replace the jobs [at the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant] because those jobs were vital to America's security.”

Nolan said the DOE Paducah Site was chosen for General Matter’s enrichment facility both for its history as the last place to enrich uranium in the United States and for Paducah and McCracken County’s community, workforce and values.

Scott Nolan, CEO and co-founder of General Matter.

“We know this is going to be a multi-decade facility,” Nolan said. “We wanted to choose a community that appreciated that and could provide that workforce. This site will bring jobs back to this DOE site. This project will have nearly 200 full-time jobs once we're in operation and up to 1,000 different jobs across the course of construction. [...] This was the year of site preparation. Next year is the year of construction. 2028 is the year of installation and commissioning, and then 2029 is when this site will be fully operational. That's the plan that we have for this location. Here we will take the U.S. from less than 1% of global enrichment to bring enrichment back domestically, not just at some scale, but at a scale that can displace adversarial enrichment from our imports and help get the U.S. on a path to self-sufficiency, both for us and then even supporting our allies.”

General Matter filed their first license application with the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission in late September. Nolan said at the event Thursday that the company expected to hear the acceptance of their application later in the day. A spokesperson for General Matter later confirmed that acceptance to WPSD.

“This license acceptance really marks the official start of our license review, which we expect to take somewhere between 12 and 18 months,” Nolan said. “Our acceptance itself has been in roughly half the normal amount of time, which the NRC has told us is really a sign of the early engagement we did and the quality and completeness of our application. We're excited for that, and excited for that to help us operate as soon as possible to bring U.S. enrichment back to the site where it was once done.”

Bruce Wilcox, president of Greater Paducah Economic Development.

Wilcox discussed the local economic impact of the projects, calling them historical capital investments. He said the Paducah American Energy Hub is the largest capital investment ever in the state of Kentucky.

“General Matter, $1.5 billion, and some other expansions that we hope to accommodate here,” Wilcox said. “We're looking forward to working with General Matter to have them to be one of the largest, if not the largest, employer in Paducah and McCracken County. As a community, we could not be more thankful for our relationships with them, the Department of Energy, and these companies.[...] We're seeing our young people moving home. We're seeing people relocating from out of town. Some of the General Matter people have already bought homes here, so we're already seeing the indirect and induced benefits, the trickle-down effects of things. General Matter’s already spent tens of millions of dollars in our community, utilizing local and regional contractors. So we're already seeing the benefit to assisting families here in our community.”

Multi-Platform Journalist

text:
An increasing number of electric vehicle owners are reportedly considering a hybrid or plug-in hybrid for their next car, according to a recent study.

The 2026 EV Index from HERE Technologies and SBD Automotive, published on September 9, 2026, found that the share of EV drivers planning to purchase a hybrid as their next vehicle rose to 28 percent in 2026, up from 23 percent in 2025.

The report stated that hybrid cars appeal to drivers who want electrification but also flexibility on long trips or in areas where charging is unreliable.

Although about 68 percent of EV owners said the charging experience was better than expected, access, reliability, and confidence remain major concerns.

Access to charging stations is their biggest frustration, with 54 percent admitting they have avoided a trip because they were unsure they could find a charger along the way.

"The next phase of EV adoption will be shaped by what drivers experience in real places and real journeys," Denise Doyle, Chief Product Officer, HERE Technologies said in the report. "Confidence depends on knowing where charging is available, whether it will work, how long it will take and how it fits into the trip. As EV adoption grows, location intelligence and real-time charging information will become essential to making electric mobility easier to plan around and easier to trust."

The study also found that better value for money has become the leading reason drivers consider switching to an EV, cited by 36 percent of respondents.

Lower running costs followed closely at 34 percent, while environmental benefits, which ranked first in 2025, fell to third place at 33 percent. The shift suggests buyers are increasingly prioritizing affordability and everyday practicality over environmental considerations.

The findings in the study are based on responses from more than 4,000 drivers across the United States, Europe, India, and Australia. SBD conducted the online survey in June and July 2026.

text:
EKA Mobility and its group companies inaugurated six manufacturing facilities across Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh on Friday, as part of an investment of more than ₹3,500 crore in an integrated manufacturing ecosystem.

The facilities were inaugurated at an event in Pune attended by Union Minister Nitin Gadkari, Union Minister H.D. Kumaraswamy, Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis and Deputy Chief Minister Sunetra Pawar, among other dignitaries.

The six facilities cover vehicle assembly, automotive engineering, seating, interiors and components. The group operates 11 manufacturing facilities spread across 120 acres, with an annual capacity to produce more than 40,000 electric vehicles.

Advt

Facilities cover vehicle and component manufacturing

The newly inaugurated facilities include EKA's small commercial vehicle plant and bus and truck plant in Pune. Other facilities include the VDL Pinnacle Engineering plant, Instor India plant and Pinnacle Seating and Interiors plant in Pune, along with Pinnacle Interiors' facility in Pithampur, Madhya Pradesh.

The group said it has invested more than ₹600 crore in research and development and holds over 300 intellectual properties. It has a workforce of more than 6,000 employees, including a 1,000-member R&D team.

Dr Sudhir Mehta, Founder and Chairman of EKA Mobility and group companies, said the facilities mark a milestone in building a manufacturing ecosystem rooted in India. He added that the expansion would support indigenous engineering, employment generation and the development of electric commercial mobility.

Growth and order book

EKA reported year-on-year growth of 1,243 per cent in the first half of FY27. The company said it has more than 3,000 vehicles on the road and an order book of over 11,000 buses valued at $1.7 billion.

Its electric small commercial vehicles have recorded more than 1,500 sales across passenger mobility, last-mile delivery and goods transportation.

The company also said its buses are deployed in Zanzibar and its small commercial vehicles in Nepal. Assembly plants are being established in South Africa and Australia.

EKA expects its 11 manufacturing facilities to help create more than 2.5 lakh jobs over the next five years across its operations and wider ecosystem.

title: How a U.N. Report Legitimized Carbon Capture and Skewed Decades of Climate Policy
authors: Katie Worth, Amy Westervelt, Maddie Stone
description:

Benson’s group wrote that the planet offered vast CO2 storage capacity.
Keith, the Canadian physicist, benefited from oil industry interest in a different way: He developed technology to capture CO2.
Their destination: the world’s second major geologic carbon storage experiment, in the Sahara.
As one carbon storage project struggled after another, Benson and other academic researchers continued to insist they could flourish.
text:
In the spring of 2005, the United Nations convened more than 100 of the world’s top scientists in the medieval town of Oviedo, Spain. They were there to finish writing a paradigm-shifting report about a technology that they hoped could help stop climate change.

To celebrate the report’s impending completion, the meeting’s hosts handed out bottles of cava, Spanish sparkling wine, with tongue-in-cheek labels stating that they were to be opened only by those who truly believed it could work.

Belief was necessary because the technology — carbon capture and storage, or CCS — had barely been tested. The idea was simple: strip carbon dioxide from smokestacks before it could flow into the air and warm the planet. Then pump it into a porous part of the Earth’s crust and leave it there. Forever.

The experts in Oviedo had stacks of papers proving that parts of the process worked. But major questions remained about how much space exists inside the Earth to store the CO2, how effectively it could be monitored and whether the poisonous, concentrated gas would reliably stay underground.

Tasked with wrangling roughly three dozen of those scientists toward consensus was Sally Benson, a geoscientist from Lawrence Berkeley National Lab who was co-leading the report’s chapter on underground storage of carbon. After a quarter-century of studying how fluids and gases move beneath Earth’s surface, she was an unimpeachable authority on the subject. She was also a savvy and diplomatic leader, skilled at managing rooms full of big egos and big tempers. It was proving handy in a process that had at times devolved into unruly debate.

The scientists had clashed for years over what the report should say, first at a meeting in Canada, then in Norway, Australia and Brazil. The evidence was scant. Three large-scale experiments were underway, but only one — a Norwegian operation that captured carbon from a natural gas field and pumped it under the bed of the North Sea — had rigorously tested permanent storage. There, the injected CO2 astonished engineers when it floated 700 feet upward through a series of geologic formations. To their relief, it hit a ceiling of shale that kept it underground, and the project was deemed a success. But with so little to go on, the scientists warned in their first draft that any broad statement about leakage risk would be “almost meaningless.”

The researchers were in Oviedo only because Saudi Arabia and other oil-exporting countries had pressured the U.N. to write the report despite the paucity of evidence, according to U.N. officials and records. The oil, gas and coal industries had spent years casting doubt on climate change while quietly fretting that policies to address it would one day put them out of business. The industry, documents show, saw CCS as a way to forestall that outcome, allowing the world to keep burning fossil fuels while simply burying the pollution underground. A U.N. report would bring the technology into the mainstream.

In turn, the U.N. hoped such a report would draw the oil-producing nations into its search for climate solutions. So despite objections from some nations and environmental organizations, which warned that the report would distract from the imperative to phase out fossil fuels, the U.N.’s preeminent climate science authority, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, went ahead. And for the first time, it invited a large contingent of industry researchers to join the scientists in writing the report, as well as several representatives from environmental groups. Benson’s chapter included authors and editors from Shell, Chevron and Saudi Aramco.

The process that followed would make some of the chapter’s scientists uneasy. The IPCC’s procedures stated that reports should assess the existing research on a topic based on peer-reviewed literature and that exceptions must be reviewed and clearly cited.

Bert Metz, one of the highest-ranking U.N. officials at the meeting, was pressing the group to come up with more definitive language about CCS’ potential. The report would be better if it could offer hard numbers, even where none existed in the literature: Precisely how many gigatons of storage capacity did the planet likely have? How long would a well-designed reservoir hold the CO2 injected into it? More than a year? A thousand years?

With so little evidence to work with, David Keith, a Canadian physicist, proposed a workaround: The authors could conduct an “expert elicitation,” taking an anonymous survey about what they expected the evidence to eventually show.

At first, not everyone was willing to go along. Some scientists worried that making what amounted to educated guesses would mislead the public, they told Drilled and ProPublica. Benson and Metz, though, both argued that on such an important matter informed advice was better than nothing.

In the end, the group agreed to take the survey and to keep it off the record — they would “burn it afterward,” Keith recounted, making no mention of it in the official report. When the meeting concluded, some of the scientists popped their bottles of cava in celebration.

“It’s not the hard science that you would prefer, obviously,” Metz would later tell Drilled and ProPublica.

Five months later, the IPCC published its special report, which would help legitimize CCS for a generation.

The 431-page document portrayed CCS as a potential savior for the climate that could enable countries “to continue to include fossil fuels in their energy mix.” It stated that using CCS could lower the cost of stabilizing global CO2 concentrations by at least 30% and that if fully supported by policy, it could account for as much as 55% of the world’s efforts to limit climate change through this century.

It acknowledged that there were still gaps in research and experience with the technology — offering extensive detail deep within its pages about the challenges and uncertainties of piecing together separate but proven steps in the CCS process. But its summary stated that “there are no major technical or knowledge barriers” to storing captured CO2 underground.

All of those assertions, however, rested on the critical determinations made by the scientists handling the storage chapter.

Benson’s group wrote that the planet offered vast CO2 storage capacity. Storage sites that were well selected and well managed, they said, were likely to retain 99% of the carbon pumped into them for at least 1,000 years.

A Consequential Decision

The scientists’ conclusions that day in Spain have had profound, compounding consequences.

The special report has been cited in thousands of academic papers, in legislative testimony and in media coverage validating carbon capture and storage as a realistic solution to global warming.

When climate forecasters built models, their calculations assumed CCS would work. When governments and corporations began making so-called “net zero” pledges, promising to subtract as much CO2 from the atmosphere as they add, they assumed CCS would work. When policymakers gave energy companies billions of dollars in public funds to develop “clean coal,” they assumed CCS would work.

These presumptions shifted the world’s discourse from how to limit carbon pollution to how to remove it from the atmosphere after the fact.

Enthusiasm for the technology has only grown. This spring, California embarked on one of the world’s largest carbon burial endeavors yet. While President Donald Trump eviscerated most programs addressing the climate, he has expanded subsidies for CCS. There are more than 100 applications for storage sites pending in the U.S. alone. U.N. analyses suggest that to achieve environmental goals, a CCS industry the size of the entire global oil production industry would have to be built by 2050.

But 21 years after Oviedo, a staggering gap lies between expectations for the technology and its operational reality. Since 1996, just 12 large-scale geological storage projects have been constructed. Collectively, they bury less CO2 than a single power plant can emit in a year, according to our analysis of sites listed in an International Energy Agency database. Seven of them have faced technical, financial or performance issues. An investigation by Drilled and ProPublica found there’s reason to doubt carbon capture and storage will ever succeed at the scale needed to offer a significant climate solution.

History is full of audacious technological leaps — moments when visionary engineering solved seemingly intractable problems. Scientists told Drilled and ProPublica that they have devoted themselves to studying CCS in that spirit, hoping a grand techno-fix could help the world solve the climate crisis without a painful overhaul of the global energy system.

But that ambition did not exist in isolation. It was bankrolled in large part by companies that stood to profit from its success.

Industry documents show that oil company executives have long seen CCS as a way to hedge against climate regulation, greenwash their brands and preserve their core business. Internal Exxon documents obtained by Drilled and ProPublica show that in 1988, the company determined that any climate research Exxon supported should serve the dual purposes of protecting the value of its oil, gas and coal while preserving the company’s business options; the company would eventually become one of the world’s major funders of CCS research.

Later, the American Petroleum Institute would write in internal communications that the industry’s “license to operate” depended on companies lowering climate pollution, and CCS, it wrote, “enables the use of petroleum and natural gas by providing an opportunity to capture and/or offset emissions.” And at a 2023 prominent oil industry conference in Houston, the CEO of Occidental Petroleum, Vicki Hollub, would explain that a novel form of CCS that sucks carbon directly from the air “is going to be the technology that helps to preserve our industry over time.”

For many university faculty, the rewards for studying the industry’s favored climate solution have been numerous, opening opportunities, funding papers and raising their profiles. Benson is a clear example. When the IPCC was awarded in 2007 with the Nobel Peace Prize for its climate work, she and her co-authors were recognized among the scientists who contributed. When Stanford University sought a new director for its ExxonMobil-funded climate research center, it tapped her. When President Joe Biden prioritized climate policy, he brought Benson into the White House.

Keith, the Canadian physicist, benefited from oil industry interest in a different way: He developed technology to capture CO2. Occidental Petroleum paid more than $1 billion to buy the company he founded.

There is no evidence that Benson, widely described by colleagues as scrupulous, skewed her scientific findings to suit the interests of her industry patrons, and Benson has described CCS’ flaws in her publications.

However, in speeches, presentations and even congressional testimony, she has been a dogged champion of CCS technology, time and again describing it as safe and ready for large-scale deployment, despite having a ringside view to its many setbacks.

She has frequently referenced the most affirmative statements from her group’s work in Oviedo as evidence. But the methodology Benson and her co-authors used to reach those conclusions 21 years ago has not been generally understood. When Drilled and ProPublica told prominent climate researchers about the expert elicitation process, several were disconcerted to learn that there was so little scientific basis for the report’s conclusion that 99% of CO2 was likely to remain underground.

A survey, said Oliver Geden, a vice chair of the IPCC’s forthcoming climate assessment, was “an inappropriate way of assessing the literature.”

Authors “are not supposed to do original research. They’re supposed to just collect what’s out there,” said Roger Cooke, who was a lead author on a subsequent IPCC report. Cooke said expert elicitation, done rigorously, can be valuable, but “just asking a bunch of experts to give their best guess is one of the worst things you can do.”

In a detailed written response, Benson said she did not believe that the survey undertaken in 2005 violated IPCC norms and said the group’s leadership was aware of the process. She disputed that the approach amounted to an informed guess and said that “there was an enormous amount of data” to draw on. The group was trying to agree on the best language to synthesize evidence detailed deeper in the report. She rejected the notion that her research or career were influenced by industry funding, writing that she has worked “tirelessly for 30 years on CCS and other climate solutions” in a sincere effort to combat an escalating planetary crisis. And, she offered, she views CCS as one valuable tool among many needed to address climate change.

Keith said the goal of the expert elicitation was not to seek precision, but to provide a sense of the orders of magnitude of the capacity and risks, “because that’s what’s relevant to public policy.” He said even sites with problems haven’t leaked large amounts of CO2 and that the report’s broad statements “have stood the test of time.” The chapter authors’ confidence in CCS doesn’t suggest “that a bunch of us are tools of the fossil fuel industry.”

The IPCC declined to comment on specific questions about how the report came about. “We are not in a position to comment on individual recollections,” a spokesperson wrote about the expert elicitation. However, they said that the group’s process was in keeping with the organization’s procedures at the time and that it reflected contemporaneous understanding of the technology. The IPCC did not directly respond to the assertion that the authors conducted what amounts to new research during the writing process, and it did not provide requested records that would detail the scientists’ vote. “The IPCC’s role is to assess the full range of available scientific knowledge,” the statement said. Metz referred to the IPCC’s response.

Chevron, Shell and Saudi Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

Drilled and ProPublica spoke with more than 100 experts on carbon capture, climate modeling and influence in academia, including a dozen people who attended the Oviedo meeting. We compiled records of geologic storage tests and surveyed an extensive body of peer-reviewed literature. This investigation is part of a broader examination into how fossil fuel industry funding of climate research has shaped climate policy, solutions and public understanding. It follows our report in June about a BP-funded program at Princeton University and the oil company’s role in crafting one of the program’s most influential climate papers.

Since Benson and her co-authors met in Oviedo, weather catastrophes have multiplied, oceans have acidified and the amount of carbon in the atmosphere has soared. In September, the U.N. released an urgent new report declaring that the race to avert disruptive warming has been all but lost. It concluded that “overshoot” — the notion that temperatures will rise above the world’s adopted goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming — is now a certainty.

Carbon capture and storage, it said, is one of the only ways to bring those temperatures back down.

Looking at a Failure and Calling It Triumph

Just a few days before the meeting in Oviedo, BP put Benson and a handful of other scientists on a chartered flight from London to Algeria. Their destination: the world’s second major geologic carbon storage experiment, in the Sahara.

The British oil giant, along with the state-owned oil companies of Algeria and Norway, had begun to drill for gas at a new field named for a nearby oasis called In Salah. Most natural gas comes out of the ground as a cocktail of methane and CO2. The CO2 must be stripped out and is usually vented into the sky. But at In Salah, the companies saw an opportunity to try out a greener process — one that could become big business.

Earth’s crust is a layer cake of rock. Some layers, like sandstone, contain honeycombed pores capable of holding CO2, while others, like mudstone, can act as impermeable seals, trapping the buoyant gas underground.

That layer cake is impossible to precisely chart from the surface, but engineers sent sound waves into the ground and interpreted what echoed up into rough maps. They learned their target sandstone reservoir sat below a 3,000-foot-thick brick of mudstone they believed would be impermeable. They also learned the sandstone was “tight” — less honeycombed than they had hoped — but still capable of holding gas. So they had begun to inject the CO2.

The plane landed on a sand-strewn strip circled by jeep tracks and rocky plateaus. A photograph shows Benson, medium height, her blond bob tucked beneath a hard hat, standing in the desert alongside a BP-funded physicist from Princeton named Robert Socolow and seven other men in front of a well that was pushing CO2 under the desert. In Salah had been operating for less than a year but seemed to be going smoothly.

Afterward, Benson traveled to Oviedo to finish drafting the special report, which listed In Salah among key sites that “indicate that it is feasible to store CO2” underground at significant scale.

That assessment has not held up.

Energy companies had first begun pumping CO2 into the ground commercially in the 1970s, when they realized it would loosen up stubborn crude oil, sometimes doubling an oil field’s output. They called it “enhanced oil recovery,” and though they didn’t try to lock the CO2 in place, much of it seemed to stay underground.

The idea to use carbon injection as a climate fix came a few years later from an Italian physicist named Cesare Marchetti, who suggested disposing of carbon deep in the ocean or underground. In the 1980s Exxon tried, and gave up on, efforts to develop the idea. And it wasn’t until 1996 when the first large-scale CCS project — the operation in the North Sea — began.

In a recent interview inside her narrow, fluorescent-lit office at Stanford University’s earth sciences building, Benson said it was shortly after that that she first heard of CCS. A colleague at the Department of Energy had sent her a slide deck by Princeton’s Socolow about the technology. “I was like, ‘I think this is nuts,’” she told Drilled and ProPublica.

“I just couldn’t really picture it working at scale.”

But, as both an idealist and a pragmatist, she was drawn to the potential for science to solve difficult environmental problems. She made a crude calculation of how much CO2 might fit beneath California and was surprised by the answer: a lot. At least in theory. And it changed her mind.

As Benson became one of CCS’ leading experts and champions, she increasingly found herself in rooms full of oil industry veterans. In 2000, she helped establish a partnership between the Department of Energy and companies including Chevron, Texaco and BP. That program had a focused mission: make large-scale geological storage an operational reality by 2015.

In 2002, Benson was asked to sit on the advisory council of a new BP and Ford Motor Co.-funded climate research center at Princeton University. At a summit there the following year, Benson expressed concern that focusing on leaks could undermine public support for CCS, according to meeting records and the account of another person in attendance.

“Need to present optimistic estimates,” the minutes recapping her presentation say.

By 2007, Benson was helping to run her own industry-funded research center. A few years earlier, ExxonMobil CEO Lee Raymond, a thunderous voice of climate denial, had put up $100 million of the company’s money to fund climate and energy work at Stanford University. With another $125 million from three other companies, Stanford’s Global Climate and Energy Project became one of the best-funded climate research centers in America.

The donation came with strings: ExxonMobil and the other sponsors had veto power over which research projects received funding.

Students and activists protested the funding structure, accusing ExxonMobil of retracing the path of tobacco companies, which paid for scientific work on obscure causes of cancer as a distraction from their culpability.

Benson defended the arrangement ardently and often. ExxonMobil and the other sponsors approved every grant that Stanford recommended, never exercising their veto power, she said. Reporting by Drilled and ProPublica did not contradict that assertion. Benson also pointed to the fact that the program funded an array of research, including on renewable energy.

In an interview and written response, Benson said researchers who take funding from oil companies are motivated not by corporate agendas, but by genuine interest in the work. The funding underwrites the inquiry, she said, not its conclusions. Where there’s “alignment,” she added, the industry support can be “amazingly catalytic and helpful.”

In response to a request for comment, Stanford University directed Drilled and ProPublica to former law school dean Paul Brest, who led a committee that reviewed energy research funding at the school. Brest said that faculty have a right to seek any funding they choose, so long as sponsors cannot direct the work.

Most important to Benson was that scientists and their students have the opportunity to research matters of great consequence. She has published more than 50 papers on geologic carbon storage since joining Stanford, most of them highly technical evaluations of CCS that reiterated its importance to reducing emissions, and many underwritten by ExxonMobil and other industry sources. “I don’t know anybody else,” she told Drilled and ProPublica, “who would eventually provide, you know, $225 million of funding” to study climate solutions.

But whether researchers intended to serve their funders’ agenda on CCS or not, some say the effect has been undeniable. “It seems like a credible solution because you have credible people at credible institutions working on it,” said Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard historian of science and an expert in corporate influence.

Benson was still getting settled into her new job at Stanford when the project in Algeria ran into major problems.

On a 118-degree day in 2007, In Salah’s inspectors heard CO2 whistling through the top of an abandoned oil well nearly a mile from the nearest injection site. Engineers had believed it would take years before the CO2 plume could spread so far underground, but the gas had cracked through the sandstone and found a new path.

To stop the leak, workers poured cement into the well, plugging it permanently. But soon a second problem arose: Satellite data revealed the desert floor above the injection sites had bulged. When project engineers again used sound waves and other tools to map the layers underground, they arrived at an alarming discovery: Pressurized CO2 had sent cracks a quarter of the way up through the 3000-foot-thick layer of mudstone. If it breached the rest, it could leach into the pan-Saharan aquifer, acidifying a source of drinking water millions of people depend on.

BP and its partners eventually summoned Benson and the other science advisers to London. The dangerous gas, they could now see, was moving in ways they had predicted it could not. Nonetheless, the advisers suggested that injection proceed temporarily to see whether it could safely be done under lower pressure and with careful monitoring.

But the Algerians had had enough. In 2011 BP and its partners stopped injection, and in 2012 they quietly scrapped the project.

Benson would later describe In Salah as a technical failure but a triumph of detection. “It was monitored and people found a problem,” she told Drilled and ProPublica.

“Then,” she added, they “learned from it.”

More Problems, More Dependence

As she did in Oviedo, Benson still maintains that the fundamental mechanics of CCS are well enough understood to know that it can work.

As proof that geologic formations can handle high-pressure gas, she points to the natural gas industry, which injects large amounts of its product back underground for temporary storage.

She also points to enhanced oil recovery. Over the last 40 years, American companies have injected 100 times more CO2 into drilling fields as a way to extract more oil than they have into what CCS industry insiders call “dedicated” CO2 storage reservoirs. There are few reports of accidents or leaks at these sites.

Unlike dedicated CO2 storage, though, enhanced oil recovery is less likely to cause pressure to build up underground, because the CO2 pumped in fills space left by the oil that’s forced out. (These sites also can result in a net addition of CO2 in the atmosphere, since they wind up producing still more oil.)

The record of the industry’s largest CCS sites — ones designed solely to help the climate — has been far more troubled.

Around the time In Salah shut down, the world’s third large project — a Norwegian site named Snøhvit several hundred miles north of the Arctic Circle — also met critical obstacles. When injection began in 2008, engineers had calculated the site would have an 18-year capacity. But they had radically overestimated how much CO2 it could absorb and had to relocate the project after just three years.

In the U.S., a decadelong effort to build a “clean coal” power plant outfitted with CCS proved impossible within a reasonable budget and was abandoned in 2015 — but not before the government had spent $378 million in taxpayer money. Benson was on the project’s advisory board for part of that time.

That year in Canada, Shell opened a $1 billion carbon capture and storage facility — also largely paid for by the country’s taxpayers — connected to open-pit oil sands mines. The industry routinely promises that plants like this one, called Quest, capture at least 90% of emissions. But at Quest, once the energy required for the capture process itself is accounted for, the capture rate instead has hovered around 68%, according to a report by the research group Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. It has also caused hundreds of microearthquakes.

Shell did not respond to a request for comment.

As one carbon storage project struggled after another, Benson and other academic researchers continued to insist they could flourish.

In a keynote speech at a 2018 conference in Sweden, Benson showed a slide with a map of CCS facilities across the world, most of which were enhanced oil recovery sites. Her map included In Salah, which had shuttered. And it included another project, in Australia, which had yet to open. “The operations have been very good at all of these projects. And they’ve gone well in terms of safety,” she said.

She also showed a slide pointing to the 2005 U.N. special report’s statement that an “appropriately selected,” well-managed reservoir would likely retain 99% of its carbon for more than 1,000 years. “This was an expression that if you find the right site, the CO2 should be permanently stored,” she said.

In a written response, she said she continues to cite the 21-year-old special report’s conclusions on leakage because “the methodology was sound then and remains so.” Benson said that she is careful to qualify her characterizations and show evidence in her presentations, and that during her presentation in Sweden she did so. She did not directly address the status of projects portrayed in her map.

When the Australian project, called Gorgon, did open the following year, it turned out to be the biggest CCS fiasco yet. Australia had allowed Chevron, ExxonMobil and Shell to drill a major new natural gas field there with the requirement that the companies buried at least 80% of the CO2 that came out of the ground with it. It was billed as the world’s largest CCS operation.

Instead, it has been plagued by clogged injection wells and underground pressure spikes. In their operating year ending in 2025, the companies were able to inject just a quarter of the CO2 collected there. Since they vent the remainder, Gorgon, once billed as a model for climate solutions, became the largest single source of industrial carbon pollution on the continent.

“Like any pioneering endeavour, it takes time to optimise a new system to ensure it performs reliably over 40-plus years of operation,” a Chevron spokesperson wrote in an emailed response. “We realise that people refer to the challenges at Gorgon in an attempt to discredit CCS, however, as we have shown, we can capture and store greenhouse gas at scale.” Shell and ExxonMobil did not respond to requests for comment.

An Idea Takes Root

While operators struggled to prove CCS could be viable, the world became dependent on it working.

As soon as the IPCC published the 2005 report, climate modelers that help assess the most economic ways to limit global warming began folding CCS into their calculations.

They projected not only that CCS could stop billions of tons of emissions from reaching the sky, but that it could suck old carbon pollution out of the atmosphere. They adopted a theory that supposed vast fields of switchgrass or fast-growing willow could absorb carbon into their stalks and leaves, and when those plants were harvested and burned for electricity, their emissions, too, would be captured and buried.

The modelers incorporated this subtractive approach so prodigiously that, on paper, they could reverse climate change. Global temperatures could overshoot targets in the short term, so long as enough carbon was eventually sucked back out of the air to bring those temperatures back down.

World leaders embraced the wiggle room this theory provided them. When they signed the U.N. Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, pledging to keep warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, they counted on these so-called negative emissions among the key tools that could make it possible. In 2018, when the IPCC published a special report on how to reach that goal, 89 out of its 90 scenarios included using large-scale CCS.

Now, in its latest report, the U.N. says that it is virtually impossible to still get to a 1.5 C future — or anything close — without removing carbon from the atmosphere. There are several ways to do that — reforestation and the use of minerals spread on fields to absorb carbon, for instance. But these methods are either small scale or even less proven than CCS.

By 2015, the tantalizing idea of “negative emissions” was showing up in new, mainstream ways. “Net zero” pledges to one day offset carbon emissions began rolling in from most of the world’s nations, as well as cities like Omaha, Nebraska; the band Coldplay; ice cream chains; funeral homes; and even ExxonMobil.

But real-world CCS projects have not met the moment.

To scale the technology as much as U.N. analyses suggest is needed to limit warming to 2 C would require not only a technological feat but almost unimaginable resources, Drilled and ProPublica found. Carbon dioxide injection would have to almost immediately increase by more than 400 times. That would require more than 2,000 new geological waste sites to be established — a new large-scale CCS project put into operation every four days, on average, for the next 25 years.

To move the CO2 to those sites would require 68,000 miles of specialized pipeline in the U.S. alone. Globally, at least 85 custom-built tankers would be needed to carry the high-pressure gas safely across oceans. Just four exist.

And if all of that were accomplished, the effort would come at an almost inconceivable cost: tens of trillions of dollars.

“Fuck, OK, It’s Harder Than We Thought”

At Benson’s office at Stanford, in a building where rocks painstakingly collected from field sites fill cabinets in the halls, the Society of Petroleum Engineers hosts Friday socials — beer and snacks provided — and the adjacent courtyard is named after the oil company Arco.

Inside, propped on a stack of boxes, is a framed copy of Biden’s keystone climate legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act. On it, national climate adviser Ali Zaidi scrawled in blue sharpie, “Thank you, Sally, for helping truly transform our energy & climate future!”

Benson returned to Stanford after a nearly two-year stint in Biden’s White House as the head of the energy division of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, where she says she provided periodic scientific advice as the act was being pushed through Congress. One of the most ambitious climate policy efforts in history, it offered a large set of incentives for CCS, which the fossil fuel industry had lobbied for intensely.

But even while oil industry leaders have pushed the world to embrace CCS, behind closed doors, they have remained skeptical of its potential as a climate solution.

In 2007, as ExxonMobil funded Benson’s center at Stanford, its former CEO Raymond told a room full of industry leaders that carbon storage might be considered “kind of the Holy Grail.” Executing it, though, would be “a whole different animal” than injecting carbon underground for enhanced oil recovery. “You can’t assume that’s going to happen. And the cost is going to be very, very significant.”

A 2011 internal slide deck from BP stated that while carbon storage would allow fossil fuels to remain the world’s dominant source of energy, “the pace of CCS development has been slow and the future pace remains uncertain.” And in a 2018 internal presentation, ExxonMobil predicted hardly any CCS would be deployed by 2050, even as it modeled that global CO2 emissions from energy production would continue to skyrocket.

Yet the industry saw brand value in encouraging CCS anyway. An ExxonMobil document from 2021 describes a public relations campaign to persuade the political and financial “elites” to “believe ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change,” in part by proving its efforts on CCS will “play an indispensable role” in a greener economy.

For her part, Benson still has faith in the technology’s viability, despite the failures. “These are big projects, right? The idea that everything goes exactly according to plan, especially for these first-of-a-kind projects — it’s unrealistic.”

As proof that CCS is on the rise, she pointed to 77 operating CCS projects identified in a report by the industry group the Global CCS Institute and said that another report demonstrated a tenfold growth in CO2 injected underground since 2005.

When ProPublica and Drilled reviewed that same data, however, and excluded the enhanced oil recovery projects, we found just eight operating large-scale carbon burial projects on that list (10 using the group’s more recent data), and half the increase in annual injections that Benson stated.

Experts interviewed for this story insisted — often in an anguished timbre — that CCS simply must work because decades of delay have foreclosed other paths to a stable climatic future.

But just because the world now needs CCS to work doesn’t mean it can.

“It’s always some issue,” said Glen Peters, a senior researcher at the Cicero Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “I think there’s been a lack of willingness for the community to say, ‘Fuck, OK, it’s harder than we thought.’”

The latest CCS effort got underway this spring, in California, when the oil company California Resources Corp. began injecting CO2 beneath the state’s Central Valley.

California — long a vanguard of environmental policy — has embraced the technology. In 2021, as it was formulating a plan for how the state should reach its climate targets, the California Air Resources Board invited Benson to give a presentation on the role CCS could play.

“The fraction of CO2 retained underground is likely to be very high,” she told the board, again pointing to the 2005 special report: “This study said 99% over 1,000 years.”

The board set the ambitious goal of burying more than 100 million tons of CO2 a year by 2045, more than all the carbon that has ever been geologically stored around the world combined. Since it opened in May, the new project has injected just 7% of its advertised capacity, but California Resources Corp. is now seeking permits for eight more CCS projects across California, and other oil and gas companies have proposed four more, including two that Stanford is directly involved with.

California Resources Corp., in a written response, said the company is injecting the amount it had planned for early operations and will increase to capacity as the project develops.

Could California truly be burying 100 million tons of CO2 a year by 2045? For the first time, in an interview, Benson was hesitant to commit. “I think it’s very challenging,” she said. “That’s a lot of infrastructure, a lot of money, a lot of projects.”

Asked a second time, she once again demurred. “Oh gosh. If we really set our mind to it. If we could wave a wand.”

Fargo, ND — Congresswoman Julie Fedorchak (R-ND) welcomed the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposal to revise the Biden administration’s oil and natural gas methane regulations, restoring flexibility for producers and addressing mandates that threatened to shut down wells and discourage new development. EPA estimates the proposed revisions(link is external) would save consumers and businesses $45 billion and enable production of an additional 210 million barrels of oil and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.

“North Dakota producers know how to develop our resources responsibly. They’ve invested in capturing more natural gas and reducing flaring while producing the energy our country needs,” Fedorchak said. “Federal rulesand regulations should support that progress. The Biden administration instead imposed unworkable mandates that threatened to shut down productive wells, eliminate jobs, and raise costs for families. I appreciate Administrator Zeldin listening to our concerns and proposing a more practical approach. Affordable energy starts with giving American producers the ability to produce.”

North Dakota’s congressional delegation urged EPA to withdraw the rule in 2023, warning that its requirements would undermine domestic production and undermine North Dakota’s successful approach to gas capture. Under the North Dakota Industrial Commission’s framework, operators achieved a 95% gas capture rate while natural gas production reached record levels.

In 2024, the Biden EPA finalized one-size-fits-all, burdensome regulations that were estimated at the time to cost $18 billion. However, the Biden EPA underestimated the costs and refused to acknowledge their regulations would force many wells to close and stop new wells from opening. Overall, the Biden administration’s rule threatened domestic production and drove up the cost of living for Americans—from heating bills to prices at the grocery store and the pump.

“Behind every barrel of oil and every cubic foot of natural gas produced in the U.S. are millions of workers, businesses, and the heartbeat of this nation’s economy. The Biden EPA destructively targeted all this. President Trump promised to end the war on oil and natural gas, and I vowed to do my part, while protecting our environment,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. “We have listened to Americans’ concerns and are taking our biggest step yet to fix it. When owners and operators can produce, America benefits with lower prices. That is common sense, and it’s what we’re delivering with this proposal.”

SEG Solar, a global solar manufacturer, has signed a land agreement for a planned $950 million, 4-GW heterojunction (HJT) solar cell plant at the Tomball Industrial Campus in the greater Houston area.

The facility is expected to create more than 700 local jobs and is planned to come online in two 2 GW phases scheduled for 2028 and 2029. SEG reportedly plans to manufacture HJT cells, modules and other key components are made in one place.

The facility will be located adjacent to SEG’s existing 4 GW Tomball #1 module manufacturing facility and its 4.6 GW Tomball #2 module manufacturing facility, which is currently under construction. The company hopes to produce modules with HJT technology to help solar projects meet domestic content requirments.

“Bringing HJT cell manufacturing to the U.S. will give customers a more domestic supply chain with clearer sourcing and a single company standing behind the product,” said Jim Wood, CEO of SEG Solar. “As the only U.S. company dedicated to integrated domestic vertical manufacturing, SEG will continue to strengthen our U.S. operations and innovation. American-made cells, American-made modules, one company accountable.”

SEG opened its second Texas plant in August, and began assembling HJT modules from it the following month.

text:
TOPEKA, KAN. (Firm to Farm) — For decades, federal agencies have repeatedly attempted to expand their regulatory authority beyond the boundaries established by Congress. Few areas demonstrate this tendency more clearly than the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) interpretation of the phrase “waters of the United States” (WOTUS) under the Clean Water Act (CWA).

For farmers, ranchers, and rural landowners, the consequences have been substantial. Ordinary agricultural activities involving drainage, land clearing, construction, and improvements to farmland have sometimes triggered federal permitting requirements carrying significant compliance costs and potential civil and criminal penalties.

The Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency,[1] substantially curtailed this regulatory expansion. But the litigation and regulatory maneuvering have continued. Recent developments in 2026 suggest that federal wetlands regulation may finally be moving toward a more predictable framework grounded in statutory text, the constitutional division of authority between the federal government and the states, and respect for private property rights.

The Supreme Court’s Decision in Sackett

Michael and Chantell Sackett purchased a residential lot near Priest Lake, Idaho, intending to construct a home. The EPA asserted that their property contained federally regulated wetlands and ordered them to stop construction and restore the property. The agency’s position rested on an expansive interpretation of federal jurisdiction that treated wetlands as regulated waters when they possessed a sufficiently significant ecological connection to traditional navigable waters. The Supreme Court rejected that approach.

Writing for the Court, Justice Alito explained that the CWA’s reference to waters of the United States encompasses relatively permanent bodies of water, such as streams, rivers, lakes, and oceans. Wetlands fall within federal jurisdiction when they have a continuous surface connection to an otherwise covered water, making the wetland practically indistinguishable from that water. The Court rejected the controversial “significant nexus” test, which had permitted federal regulators to assert jurisdiction based on ecological or hydrological relationships that were not necessarily apparent to a property owner.

The significance of Sackett extends beyond wetlands regulation. The decision reaffirmed an important principle of statutory interpretation that administrative agencies cannot enlarge their authority merely because doing so might advance a desirable regulatory objective. Congress writes the law. Administrative agencies implement it. That distinction is essential to the constitutional separation of powers.

The November 2025 Regulatory Proposal

On November 20, 2025, the EPA and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers published a proposed rule intended to bring the regulatory definition of “waters of the United States” (WOTUS) into closer conformity with Sackett.[2] The proposal represented an effort to establish clearer jurisdictional boundaries and reduce uncertainty concerning the treatment of wetlands, tributaries, and other water features. It also attempts to distinguish federally regulated waters from features that should remain subject primarily to state and local authority.

The position of the proposed rule is that the CWA does not establish a general federal land-use regulatory system. Nor does it authorize federal agencies to regulate every location where water occasionally accumulates or flows. Rather, the statute regulates particular categories of waters within the scope of Congress’s legislative authority.[3]

September 2026 Supplemental Notice

An important development occurred in early September when the EPA and the Department of the Army announced a supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking seeking comments on additional alternatives for defining jurisdictional waters and wetlands.[4]

The proposal addresses three particularly important concepts: perennial waters, relatively permanent waters, and continuous surface connections as follows:

Alternatives for defining “perennial” waters, including a definition requiring standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year under ordinary conditions;

A consideration of defining “relatively permanent” waters by reference to perennial water bodies, while recognizing limited interruptions resulting from drought or other circumstances. One alternative would permit certain temporary interruptions lasting no more than 30 consecutive days during a year.

A more specific interpretation of the continuous surface connection necessary for wetlands to qualify as federally jurisdictional. Under one alternative, the connection generally would require perennial surface water linking the wetland to an otherwise jurisdictional water, subject to limited exceptions for temporary interruptions. Another alternative would confine jurisdiction over adjacent wetlands to those that are practically indistinguishable from a jurisdictional water.

These proposals are significant because they attempt to translate Sackett‘s judicial standards into administrable regulatory criteria.

Observation: From a rule-of-law perspective, the effort is overdue. Landowners should not have to retain environmental consultants and attorneys simply to determine whether an ordinary drainage feature on their property falls within federal jurisdiction.

The Inland Empire Case

On September 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit issued an amended opinion in Inland Empire Waterkeeper v. Corona Clay Co.[5] The litigation involved alleged Clean Water Act violations associated with discharges into Temescal Creek in California. Following the Supreme Court’s decision in Sackett, the defendant challenged whether the creek qualified as a water of the United States.

The Ninth Circuit addressed whether the question of whether a waterbody qualifies as WOTUS under the CWA concerns the merits of a claim or the federal court’s subject-matter jurisdiction.[6] The court treated the issue as one of the merits rather than jurisdiction. It also recognized that Sackett materially changed the governing legal framework. Accordingly, the court concluded that a new trial was necessary to determine whether Temescal Creek qualified as a jurisdictional water under the standards established in Sackett. The court did not, however, decide whether Temescal Creek is subject to federal regulation.

The decision illustrates the continuing impact of Sackett on previously litigated disputes. It also highlights the difficulties associated with applying older judicial precedents concerning intermittent and seasonal streams after the Supreme Court’s rejection of expansive jurisdictional theories.

Note: For farmers and ranchers (and rural landowners), the lesson is important: earlier agency determinations and judicial assumptions about federal jurisdiction may require reconsideration under current law.

Federalism and the Proper Role of the States

One persistent misconception in the wetlands debate is that limiting federal jurisdiction necessarily eliminates environmental protection. That proposition misunderstands our constitutional structure. The United States operates under a system of dual sovereignty. The federal government possesses enumerated powers, while states retain substantial authority over land use, water resources, and environmental protection.

The Clean Water Act itself recognizes this arrangement. 33 U.S.C. §1251(b), expressly acknowledges the primary responsibilities and rights of states to prevent, reduce, and eliminate pollution and to plan the development and use of land and water resources. Consequently, a wetland that falls outside federal jurisdiction is not necessarily beyond regulation. State wetlands statutes, drainage laws, water-quality requirements, and local land-use restrictions may continue to apply. The distinction is not between environmental protection and environmental destruction. It is between regulation authorized by Congress and regulation imposed without sufficient statutory authority. From a constitutional perspective, that distinction is indispensable.

What Farmers and Ranchers Need to Know

The practical consequences of these developments deserve particular attention.

The presence of wetlands does not automatically establish federal jurisdiction. The analysis must consider whether the feature satisfies the governing legal standards for waters of the United States.

Ordinary agricultural exemptions remain important. Section 404(f) of the CWA,[7] contains exemptions for specified normal farming, ranching, and silvicultural activities. However, these exemptions are subject to statutory limitations, including the recapture provision in §404(f)(2).

Landowners should carefully document drainage patterns and surface-water connections. Photographs, historical aerial imagery, topographic information, and hydrological evidence may become important when jurisdiction is disputed.

Jurisdictional determinations remain valuable. When substantial construction, drainage, or land improvement is contemplated, obtaining an appropriate determination from the Corps may reduce regulatory uncertainty.

State law cannot be ignored. A successful argument against federal jurisdiction does not necessarily eliminate permitting requirements imposed by state or local law.

Landowners must recognize that the applicable federal regulatory framework remains unsettled.

Because of ongoing litigation, the EPA continues to apply different regulatory frameworks in different states, subject to the Supreme Court’s decision in Sackett. Currently, the amended 2023 rule applies in 24 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories, while the remaining 26 states operate under the pre-2015 regulatory framework as constrained by Sackett.[8]

Conclusion

The recent developments in wetlands regulation represent an important test of whether federal administrative agencies will adhere to the limits imposed by Congress and the Supreme Court.

The September 2026 supplemental proposal offers the possibility of greater regulatory clarity. The Ninth Circuit’s decision in Inland Empire shows that courts continue to grapple with the consequences of Sackett.

But regulatory certainty requires more than replacing one administration’s interpretation with another’s. It requires fidelity to statutory text, respect for private property rights, and recognition that the federal government does not possess unlimited authority over land and water merely because environmental concerns are involved. Farmers and ranchers should be able to understand the legal restrictions applicable to their property without confronting an unpredictable federal permitting system.

The Supreme Court established important boundaries in Sackett. The challenge now is ensuring that federal regulators respect them. In addition, farmers, ranchers, and rural landowners (and their legal counsel) should remain alert to legal theories that elevate concepts such as “dignity,” “climate justice,” and “environmental equity” over traditional property rights and statutory limits on government power. Whatever their packaging, such theories can provide cover for expanding government control over privately owned land without clear legislative authorization and threaten the independence of agricultural producers and the constitutional protections upon which private property ownership rests

text:
The Palisades nuclear plant in Michigan might be restarted before the end of this year, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said, despite a string of safety incidents at the site.

Mr Wright visited the reactor owned by Holtec International that was shut down in 2022, but is now in the process of restarting. The plant has become a symbol for the nuclear energy sector in the US, which is experiencing something of a renaissance due in part to the heavy electricity needs of data centres.

On Thursday, Mr Wright said Palisades "would be back running before the end of this year", while speaking with reporters during a tour of the reactor. "It will be 800MW of additional, reliable and secure energy," he added.

He concluded by taking shots at the Democratic Party. "This is a reversal of the stuff Democrats did for years, doing everything they can to stand in the way of energy production and the contrast could not be more stark."

But the restart plan has faced criticism. Kevin Kamps, executive director for environmental advocacy group Don't Waste Michigan, hit back shortly after Mr Wright's visit to Palisades.

"Once they restart this zombie reactor, all bets are off," Mr Kamps said, calling the reactor by a name used by critics of restarting decommissioned nuclear plants.

"They are playing radioactive Russian roulette on the Lake Michigan shore, wasting billions of dollars of state and federal taxpayer money to do so, and they are risking a Chernobyl or Fukushima-scale catastrophe, putting in peril the Great Lakes, the Great Lakes State and beyond."

Michael Keegan, another director of Don’t Waste Michigan, said the "public relations slathering of icing on this rancid cake is a whitewash".

Mr Wright's visit follows an incident that increased the concerns of those who have voiced opposition to the restart plan. In September, a nuclear fuel assembly was tipped during a refuelling process at the plant. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission said no radiation had been released.

Shortly after workers successfully retrieved the tipped nuclear fuel assembly, Holtec described the recovery as a "remarkable demonstration of technical ingenuity and precision manufacturing".

It was yet another blemish on the plant's record.

In 2012, an NRC report raised concerns about the work culture at the plant, where it said safety concerns were routinely dismissed. In 2016, when the plant was owned by Entergy, security staff were placed on leave for failing to properly follow fire prevention protocols.

In October 2025, a worker at Palisades fell off a refuelling bridge into a pool of water, but was not seriously injured.

The NRC sent a letter to Holtec this month after an inspection that determined that, although Palisades maintained a safety-conscious work environment overall, “a chilled work environment” existed in the supply chain and quality assurance departments.

“Employees in these two work departments are hesitant to raise safety concerns using all available avenues without fear of retaliation,” the NRC said.

Patrick O’Brien, Holtec's director of government affairs and communications, previously told The National that the company was “taking actions to address these issues and will continue our work to maintain and strengthen a healthy safety-conscious work environment”.

He also said the reactor would "return to service when all required work is complete and all federal requirements and industry standards are met".

title: European Commission Proposes Targeted Delays to EU Methane Regulation Requirements
authors: Latham & Watkins LLP, Latham & Watkins LLP
description:
On 14 October 2026, the European Commission (Commission) adopted a proposal to postpone specific provisions of the EU Methane Regulation.
Background Building on the EU Methane Strategy adopted in October 2020 under the European Green Deal, the EU Methane Regulation entered into force on 4 August 2024.
A notable feature of the Methane Regulation is the extension of its scope to methane emissions from imported fossil fuels.
The Commission proposal states that the amendment does not introduce new requirements and is not aimed at changing the regulatory objectives of the Methane Regulation.
EU Methane Regulation compliance and reporting will therefore remain relevant in offtake negotiations, lender due diligence, and financial models.
text:
The proposal postpones certain importer obligations and methane intensity provisions, citing rising costs and strained energy supply.

By Alexander Buckeridge-Hocking, Michael D. Green, John-Patrick Sweny, James Bee, Toon Dictus, and James Thompson

Key Points:

Proposed amendments to the EU Methane Regulation are progressing through the EU legislative process, with both the Commission and the Parliament having now adopted their positions.

The Commission proposed that the importers’ obligation to demonstrate that supply contracts are subject to equivalent MRV measures would first need to be reported by 31 May 2029 (in respect of 2028 supplies) rather than applying from 1 January 2027.

Under the Commission’s proposal, methane-intensity reporting for importers and EU producers would move to 5 August 2029 (from 2028), and demonstration of compliance with maximum methane-intensity values to 5 August 2031 (from 2030).

The European Parliament has since adopted its position supporting an extended, three-year postponement, with the importer MRV deadline moved to 31 May 2031 and first methane-intensity reporting to 5 August 2031.

The Parliament would exclude imports from countries subject to EU sanctions restricting fossil fuel imports from the extended timeline.

On 14 October 2026, the European Commission (Commission) adopted a proposal to postpone specific provisions of the EU Methane Regulation. The targeted amendment concerns the monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) obligations for importers of natural gas, oil, and coal, as well as the methane-intensity reporting requirements for both importers and EU producers. The Commission frames the proposal as a measure to relieve pressure on European industry and national administrations amid increased energy prices as a result of global energy supply disruption, especially in relation to liquefied natural gas (LNG) and oil.

On 22 October 2026, the European Parliament (Parliament) adopted its position on the proposal, endorsing the need for a postponement but supporting a longer, three-year delay and introducing additional conditions.

Background

Building on the EU Methane Strategy adopted in October 2020 under the European Green Deal, the EU Methane Regulation entered into force on 4 August 2024. It targets methane emissions from the energy sector, covering crude oil, natural gas, and coal, as well as biomethane once injected into the gas network. It introduces mandatory MRV requirements, requires operators to conduct regular leak detection and repair (LDAR) surveys, and bans routine venting and flaring except in emergencies or unavoidable circumstances.

A notable feature of the Methane Regulation is the extension of its scope to methane emissions from imported fossil fuels. Since 5 May 2025, importers have been required to provide competent authorities with information on the methane emissions of crude oil, natural gas, and coal placed on the EU market.

Under the current text, from 1 January 2027, importers would be required under Article 28 to demonstrate that contracts concluded or renewed after 4 August 2024 are subject to MRV measures equivalent to those applying to EU producers. Further, under Article 29, by 5 August 2028 and every year thereafter, EU producers and importers must report on the methane intensity of their production and, by 5 August 2030 and every year thereafter, demonstrate that methane intensity is below maximum values established by the Commission by delegated act.

The Commission’s proposal is said to respond to concerns about the implementation timeline raised by several Member States, third countries, and the oil, gas, and coal sectors. The additional year is intended to allow Member States to complete their national penalty regimes, national accreditation bodies to accredit verifiers, and competent authorities to assess and recognise compliance-solution providers.

The Commission proposal states that the amendment does not introduce new requirements and is not aimed at changing the regulatory objectives of the Methane Regulation.

Proposed Timeline

The Commission’s proposal, which amends Articles 28 and 29 of the Methane Regulation, would push back each of these obligations by one year. The table below sets out the current position alongside the timelines proposed under each of the Commission and the Parliament’s adopted proposals.

Notably, under the Parliament’s position, energy imports from countries the EU has sanctioned would not benefit from the extended timeline. Importers would be required to report these volumes separately, including in mixed cargoes, and the Commission would publish and update an indicative list of the countries concerned.

Impact of the Parliament’s Position

If retained, the Parliament’s position would give importers, producers, and operators significantly more time to prepare for compliance. However, the sanctions carve-out would in practice create a two-tier regime: volumes from sanctioned countries would face earlier deadlines and would need to be reported separately.

The Parliament also wants the Commission to report by 1 July 2029 on how importer and methane intensity provisions are being implemented, with the possibility of proposing future changes if implementation problems continue, or security of supply is threatened. However, similar concepts and discussions that have been introduced in recent years, such as the controversial “kill switch” for the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) — which would have allowed the Commission to exempt certain imported goods from CBAM during serious and unforeseen market disruption — have resulted in significant controversy and ultimately been rejected. The broader scope of the Parliament’s amendments also diverges from the Commission’s stated intention to confine the proposal to a targeted one-year delay, and will likely be a topic of discussion in upcoming negotiations.

Potential Impacts for Exporters, Offtakers, and Project Financings

For producers and LNG exporters selling into Europe, the proposal postpones the compliance timetable but leaves the substance of the obligations unchanged. While the importer obligations apply to EU importers, in practice they are passed upstream through supply contracts. Sellers should therefore expect EU buyers to continue to seek MRV-related representations, data-sharing undertakings, cooperation covenants, and cost-allocation or price-adjustment provisions in new and renewed sale and purchase agreements, particularly because contracts concluded or renewed on or after 4 August 2024 remain within scope.

The proposed delays provide importers and Member States with additional preparation time. EU Methane Regulation compliance and reporting will therefore remain relevant in offtake negotiations, lender due diligence, and financial models.

Next Steps

The Parliament is now ready to start negotiations with the Council on the final shape of the law. Once the Council has adopted its own negotiating mandate, interinstitutional negotiations between the Parliament, the Council, and the Commission can begin. Any provisional agreement would then require formal adoption by both co-legislators before publication in the Official Journal. Given the 1 January 2027 application date of the current importer obligations, the co-legislators will need to reach agreement and complete adoption within a compressed timeframe for the postponement to take effect before that date.

The Commission emphasised at the time of its original proposal that further amendments fall outside the scope of the proposal and has called for swift agreement to maintain regulatory certainty. The Parliament’s position, which extends both the length and the scope of the postponement, will therefore be a central point of discussion in trilogue negotiations. During the postponement, the Commission will monitor implementation and security of supply, with any issues to be considered in the Methane Regulation’s periodic review under Article 36, due by 1 January 2028.

This article was prepared with the assistance of Samantha Banfield at Latham & Watkins.

Latham & Watkins will continue to monitor developments relating to EU sustainability regulation and the broader energy efficiency and ESG landscape.
