text:
Korea, 30 October 2026 – Africa Finance Corporation (AFC), the continent’s leading infrastructure solutions provider, and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) today launched the Africa Sovereign Climate Facility (ASCF) at a signing ceremony in Korea, marking a significant step towards scaling up climate finance and accelerating low-carbon, climate-resilient development across Africa.

With total financing of US$690 million, the ASCF is designed to help African countries address the growing impacts of climate change while advancing their economic development priorities. By combining technical assistance, capacity building and large-scale blended finance, the programme will support governments in integrating climate considerations into national development planning and accelerating the implementation of their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

The programme’s first phase will focus on Angola, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Nigeria, countries facing significant climate vulnerabilities, infrastructure deficits and rising greenhouse gas emissions. Through an integrated, country-led approach, the ASCF will support interventions across critical sectors, including clean energy, health and well-being, food and water security, and climate-resilient infrastructure and the built environment.

Samaila Zubairu, President and Chief Executive Officer of AFC, said: “The infrastructure we build today must both power Africa’s growth and withstand the climate pressures of tomorrow. Through this partnership with GCF, we are combining concessional finance with AFC’s project development expertise and capital to help governments turn national priorities into reliable energy, stronger food and water systems, and resilient infrastructure. Success will be measured in businesses that keep producing, communities better protected and jobs sustained. That is how climate finance becomes an investment in Africa’s lasting prosperity.”

Catherine Koffman, GCF Regional Director for Africa, said: “The Africa Sovereign Climate Facility will help Angola, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Nigeria turn national climate priorities into investable projects in clean energy, resilient infrastructure, food systems and water security. GCF’s USD 280 million is designed to work alongside substantial co-financing, reaching an estimated 4.5 million people and avoiding 3.4 million tonnes of emissions. This partnership shows how blended finance can strengthen sovereign investment systems and deliver climate capital at scale.”

The launch builds on AFC’s longstanding partnership with GCF to mobilise climate finance and advance sustainable infrastructure development across Africa. In 2023, GCF committed US$253 million to AFC Capital Partners’ Infrastructure Climate Resilient Fund (ICRF), supporting the development of climate-resilient infrastructure as an investable asset class and helping catalyse additional investment from institutional and private-sector investors. The collaboration reflects a shared commitment to using innovative financing structures to address Africa’s infrastructure needs while strengthening resilience to climate change.

As part of its participation in the ASCF, AFC will arrange and fully fund a parallel commercial facility of up to US$260 million, with a tenor of up to 10 years, for Angola, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Nigeria through their respective Ministries of Finance. The facility will complement concessional climate financing, expanding the capital available to support eligible investments while helping participating governments integrate climate resilience and low-carbon development into national planning.

Over its lifetime, the ASCF is expected to reduce, avoid, remove or sequester approximately 5.78 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO₂e) in greenhouse gas emissions — roughly equivalent to removing 1.3 million cars from the road for one year. The programme is also expected to reach 5.2 million beneficiaries through climate adaptation interventions, equivalent to the current estimated population of Cape Town, South Africa.

Africa remains particularly exposed to the effects of climate change, with rising temperatures, increasingly unpredictable rainfall and more frequent extreme weather events threatening livelihoods, food and water security, infrastructure and economic productivity. Rapid population growth and urbanisation are adding further pressure on public services and infrastructure systems, reinforcing the urgency of embedding climate resilience into the continent’s development trajectory.

The ASCF aims to strengthen the link between national climate priorities and investable infrastructure opportunities, helping participating countries move beyond incremental responses towards more coordinated and transformational climate action. Its integrated financing model is designed to mobilise additional concessional and commercial capital alongside technical assistance and capacity building, addressing barriers to investment and supporting projects capable of delivering climate and development benefits at scale.

The launch reinforces AFC’s commitment to mobilising capital and deploying innovative financing solutions to address Africa’s infrastructure needs while supporting sustainable, inclusive and climate-resilient economic growth. Through its partnership with the Green Climate Fund, AFC aims to help bridge the gap between Africa’s climate ambitions and the financing required to translate those ambitions into tangible development outcomes.

About AFC

AFC was established in 2007 to be the catalyst for pragmatic infrastructure and industrial investments across Africa. AFC’s approach combines specialist industry expertise with a focus on financial and technical advisory, project structuring, project development, and risk capital to address Africa’s infrastructure development needs and drive sustainable economic growth.

Nineteen years on, AFC has developed a track record as the partner of choice in Africa for investing and delivering on instrumental, high-quality infrastructure assets that provide essential services in the core infrastructure sectors of power, natural resources, heavy industry, transport, and telecommunications. AFC has 49 member countries and has invested over US$20 billion in 36 African countries since its inception.

title: No false choices: We can improve infrastructure permitting AND protect rivers
description:
Every community needs reliable infrastructure and clean water, and a permitting process that helps balance these needs.
Sign up to get the most important news affecting your water and rivers delivered right to your inbox.
New threats could emerge after approval, when fewer options remain to protect water.
Fish and wildlife (§§1301 and 1304-1305): The bill would let states take over some federal wildlife reviews.
The bill would weaken protections for national forests and Tribal reservations by narrowing federal agencies’ authority to require measures that protect these lands and resources.
text:
It’s common sense that before building a road, pipeline, mine, data center, or dam, developers should have appropriate permits to make sure they are meeting basic standards to safeguard rivers, drinking water, wildlife, and communities. Every community needs reliable infrastructure and clean water, and a permitting process that helps balance these needs.

American Rivers supports making permitting faster, clearer, and easier to navigate. We implement river restoration projects that require permits, and we know that better agency coordination and adequate agency staffing can help projects move forward while protecting rivers.

The Senate’s recently introduced Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) would help speed up energy and infrastructure development, and it includes some useful provisions for online project tracking, agency capacity, and coastal restoration (§§1132, 1133, and 1308).

Let's Stay In Touch!

We’re hard at work for rivers and clean water. Sign up to get the most important news affecting your water and rivers delivered right to your inbox.

But these benefits do not outweigh our concerns about the bill’s overall effects on rivers and freshwater. Here are some of the provisions that we are concerned about:

State and Tribal water protections (§1202): The bill would limit states’ and Tribes’ ability to protect water quality by making it harder to set and defend protective conditions and narrowing the review of potential harm. For certain infrastructure projects such as dams, interstate power lines, and gas pipelines, this could leave warmer water, lower river flows, and other harmful changes unaddressed, even when agencies identify a need for protection.

Streams and wetlands (§1204): Small wetlands filter pollution and hold floodwater. Yet the bill would treat filling wetlands up to two acres for development as causing only minor harm for certain permitting decisions. Size alone cannot measure damage, especially when repeated stream crossings affect an entire watershed.

Responding to problems (§§1203–1205 and 1401): The bill would limit when federal agencies can restrict dumping fill into rivers, lakes and streams, extend some permit terms, and make it harder for courts and agencies to stop or correct harmful work. New threats could emerge after approval, when fewer options remain to protect water.

River reviews and public input (§§1101–1110): Most rivers depend on everyday permitting safeguards. Narrower reviews and limits on legal challenges could leave communities with fewer adaptive ways to protect drinking water and fisheries and to reduce flood risks.

Fish and wildlife (§§1301 and 1304-1305): The bill would let states take over some federal wildlife reviews. Federal standards would remain, but differences in state commitment to protecting imperiled species, staffing, and expertise could complicate protection across state lines. A new science definition would also create disputes over which evidence agencies may consider. Limits would be set on our ability to challenge projects harmful to fish and wildlife.

Hydropower (§§2232–2233): Dams affect river flows, water quality, fish, and Tribal resources. The bill would weaken protections for national forests and Tribal reservations by narrowing federal agencies’ authority to require measures that protect these lands and resources. Routine maintenance should preserve existing river protections.

Right now, Congress has an opportunity to address these concerns. American Rivers is committed to working with Congress to secure practical, bipartisan improvements to the bill—from preserving states’ and Tribes’ power to protect their streams, wetlands, and fish to maintaining federal protections to safeguard clean water.

Congress should keep decisions grounded in science, give communities a meaningful voice, and ensure agencies and courts can act before river damage becomes permanent. Partnering together, we can ensure that this bill preserves basic safeguards for waters while making permitting work better for people, projects, and the rivers we all depend on.

title: Toyota Expands Its Woodland Vision with New Adventure-Ready Concepts at SEMA
description:
Across the lineup, CALTY Design Research established a cohesive visual and functional identity for the Woodland concepts, built around exploration with everyday usability.
The RAV4 Woodland Plug-in Hybrid Concept and Sienna Woodland Concept show how Toyota’s electrified and family-focused vehicles can take on a more adventurous role.
The Woodland bZ Concept extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery-electric future.
The Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Toyota Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct interpretations of refinement and versatility to the lineup.
Together, the Woodland concept family broadens Toyota’s vision for modern adventure by showing how capability can take many forms—plug-in hybrid, hybrid, and battery electric; compact, spacious, and premium.
text:
PLANO, Texas (Oct. 30, 2026) – At the 2026 SEMA Show, Toyota is exploring a broader vision of everyday adventure with a new family of Woodland concepts that reimagine how a variety of electrified and family-focused vehicles can be equipped for life beyond the pavement.

With versions of the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, bZ, and Crown Signia in the showcase, the Woodland concept lineup is designed for drivers who see adventure not as a destination, but as a way of life. From city streets to trailheads and campsites, each concept reflects Toyota’s approach to blending utility, efficiency, comfort, and capability in ways that support getting out, staying longer, and carrying more of what matters.

Across the lineup, CALTY Design Research established a cohesive visual and functional identity for the Woodland concepts, built around exploration with everyday usability. Common design and equipment themes include lift kits, large over-fenders, rugged satin-black wheels, All-Terrain tires, two-tone paint on the roofs and hoods, roof racks, and cross bars.

Each model is adorned with Horizon Blue paint, inspired by Toyota’s color palette used in the 1960’s on models like the Stout, Crown, and Corona. Together, these elements create a consistent Woodland expression that emphasizes confidence, versatility, and a readiness to follow the route that looks a little more interesting.

The RAV4 Woodland Plug-in Hybrid Concept and Sienna Woodland Concept show how Toyota’s electrified and family-focused vehicles can take on a more adventurous role.

The Woodland bZ Concept extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery-electric future. The Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Toyota Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct interpretations of refinement and versatility to the lineup.

Together, the Woodland concept family broadens Toyota’s vision for modern adventure by showing how capability can take many forms—plug-in hybrid, hybrid, and battery electric; compact, spacious, and premium. United by a shared design language and a common spirit of exploration, the Woodland concepts imagine a future where more vehicles are ready to leave the pavement behind and make the journey itself part of the story.

title: Used EVs Are Selling Faster Than Gas Cars or Hybrids - Car and Driver
description:
Despite being more expensive, used EVs are selling nearly two weeks faster than gas cars.
Compared with September 2025, used EVs sold 10.1 percent faster, while gas cars saw a 19.9 percent longer sales window.
However, gas-powered cars take up the top two spots on the overall fastest-selling cars list.
Gas-powered cars may have dominated the top two spots, but EVs still managed to sell faster overall than the gas-powered herd.
As gas prices continue to soar in the United States, it appears more people are interested in going electric.
text:
Used-car shoppers are reportedly leaning toward EVs and luxury models, according to a study from iSeeCars.

Despite being more expensive, used EVs are selling nearly two weeks faster than gas cars.

Last month, used EVs sold for an average of $32,533, while gas vehicles averaged $31,954 and hybrids averaged $34,476.

Shoppers in the market for a used car are reportedly shifting toward electric powertrains. A report from iSeeCars claims that EVs are the quickest-moving cars in the used-car market compared with their gas and hybrid counterparts, despite a higher price point than last year.

The report studied over 1.5 million cars between one and five years old to find trends in the current used-car market. Between September 2025 and September 2026, used EVs saw a 9.8 percent price increase, while hybrid prices rose 4.9 percent and gas-powered prices rose less than half a percent. EVs sold for an average of $32,533 in September 2026, landing right in the middle of the more expensive hybrids at $34,476 and less expensive gas-powered vehicles at $31,954.

Though EV prices are increasing, they’re moving off sales floors a lot faster than gasoline models that have stayed relatively the same price. In September 2026, used EVs averaged 41.9 days on the market, which is 13 days less than gas-powered cars. Hybrids find themselves in the middle with about 48.6 days on the market. Compared with September 2025, used EVs sold 10.1 percent faster, while gas cars saw a 19.9 percent longer sales window.

However, gas-powered cars take up the top two spots on the overall fastest-selling cars list. The Lexus IS500, which saw its last production year in 2025, took the top spot, followed by the Audi A4 Allroad, another gasoline model. The Audi Q4 e-tron Sportback sits in third place as the first EV on the list, spending an average of 29.8 days on the market. Gas-powered cars may have dominated the top two spots, but EVs still managed to sell faster overall than the gas-powered herd.

The fastest-selling EVs recorded were the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron, followed by the Toyota bZ4X, and the Lexus RZ 300e. Though not on the top-10 fastest-selling list at all, Teslas saw some of the highest price increases this year, with the Model S averaging $10,636 higher than in September 2025 and the Model X gaining $9336. The Model 3’s price increased by about $3870.

EV prices started rising in April 2026 and have steadily increased since then, reaching a peak in August. As gas prices continue to soar in the United States, it appears more people are interested in going electric. When used-car shoppers aren’t looking at electric models, luxury brands tend to sell better than more mainstream models.

text:
Passing the 100 GW milestone for cumulative U.S. module production marks a historic turning point, but the domestic solar industry’s long-term survival hinges on moving past celebratory groundbreakings and confronting everyday manufacturing realities . During the opening day panel at pv magazine USA Week 2026, industry executives and market analysts discussed how U.S. manufacturing is tackling workforce bottlenecks, equipment sourcing hurdles, and the complex path toward a self-sustaining supply chain .

Reaching the first 100 GW required an estimated $21 billion in capital expenditure over five decades . With billions more flowing in under the Inflation Reduction Act, the conversation has shifted squarely from raising capital to achieving sustained factory utilization and profitability .

“The big question is: can the level of investment now provide a manufacturing landscape that is sustainable?” asked Finlay Colville, founder and head of Terawatt PV Research . “Having manufacturing that’s profitable and having a policy framework where the certainty level can be a few years—I think that’s the biggest issue now .”

While institutional investors continue backing the sector, operational execution on the ground remains an uphill climb. Training enough skilled operators to run complex, automated lines is a major bottleneck . Qcells Global Chief Technology Officer Danielle Merfeld emphasized that managing an integrated facility under one roof requires extraordinary coordination across distinct production stages, moving far beyond assembling finished components from disparate parts .

“The hardest part isn’t any one of the single processes that we have,” Merfeld explained . “It’s orchestrating the ingot, wafer, cell, and module—each of which is a factory within its own technology and materials that just happens to be under one roof .”

Beyond managing internal factory orchestration, companies are actively rethinking how physical campus layouts impact project economics. For SEG Solar, scaling up production in Houston involved partnering closely with community colleges, local universities like Texas A&M, and drawing on the region’s existing manufacturing base . By strategically co-locating subcomponents such as backsheets and junction boxes right on the corporate campus, SEG has been able to trim transportation expenses and protect internal margins . Elaborating on this vertically integrated strategy, SEG CEO and President Jim Wood noted that operational efficiency allows the business to thrive independently of federal incentive structures .

“As we integrate each one of those components into our business, we’re able to hold onto that margin,” Wood said . “Even without the 45X tax credits, we’re a profitable business with or without those tax credits .”

Quality control and independent testing are also taking center stage as developers and financiers demand rigorous proof of long-term field reliability . Zennia Villanueva, Vice President of Quality at RETC, noted that new domestic manufacturers are flooding testing labs with prototypes and batch-testing requests to catch process variations early before modules reach commercial deployment .

“They are pretty conscious and want to make sure the quality is there, so we receive a lot of prototypes to be tested and requests for batch testing to make sure there’s consistency across different lots,” Villanueva observed .

Looking ahead, panelists debated whether a 100% self-sustaining domestic supply chain is realistic or even strategically sound . Colville argued that attempting to build every upstream material from scratch within a tight timeframe risks creating expensive, low-quality products that cannot compete globally . Instead, he advocates for identifying targeted domestic priorities while maintaining pragmatic trade relationships for specialized upstream materials . Highing the risk of forced isolationism, Colville warned against unrealistic expectations for complete self-reliance .

“The idea that within a few years it’s going to be 100% silicon-based is absolutely not going to happen—or if it does, you’ll get a lot of low-quality, expensive product that’s not as good as what you can buy falling off the back of a lorry in Shanghai for pennies,” Colville warned .

Ultimately, bridging the gap between ambitious manufacturing announcements and commercial execution will require a pragmatic balancing act. As the U.S. solar sector digests evolving trade policies, navigates impending Section 232 import guidelines, and scales up regional workforces, the ultimate measure of success will not be headline-grabbing capex figures, but long-term asset bankability and sustained manufacturing profitability .

title: President Trump Unveils EPA's New Contradictory Methane Proposal at Campaign Rally
description:
“Tonight I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations,” Trump announced to the crowd, located near the oil-rich Permian Basin.
On the one hand, the agency says it lacks the legal authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from cars, trucks, power plants, and industrial sources under the Clean Air Act.
On the other, the latest EPA proposal relies on, in some cases in the same section of, the Clean Air Act to regulate methane, a greenhouse gas, from the oil and gas industry.
(The EPA is accepting public comments on its proposed repeal of its authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions for fossil fuel-fired power plants until Nov.
“Under crooked Joe Biden, ‘Dumocrats’ crushed the small oil and gas operators,” Trump said during the rally Tuesday.
text:
At a Tuesday campaign rally for Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Lubbock, Texas, President Trump announced the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposal to roll back a Biden-era methane rule, setting up a likely future showdown in how the agency oversees climate pollution under the Clean Air Act.

The proposal marks a break from the agency’s previous approaches to greenhouse gas regulation by maintaining that — for now — the EPA still has the authority to regulate climate pollution from the oil and gas industry, though it might revisit this decision later. With affordability top of mind for many midterm voters, however, the President framed the move in economic terms.

“Tonight I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations,” Trump announced to the crowd, located near the oil-rich Permian Basin. The new plan would loosen federal requirements for oil and gas operators to detect and repair leaks, ease restrictions on gas flaring, and eliminate the Super Emitter Program, a third-party monitoring and reporting system designed to identify major releases of methane, known as a climate super pollutant.

Trump said the proposal, which addressed a 2024 rule known as OOOOb/c, would “save consumers and energy producers $45 billion in costs, unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas, and produce 210 million barrels of oil.” Under President Biden, the EPA estimated the rule would prevent the release of 58 million tons of methane and 16 million tons of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), leading to major public health and climate benefits. Climate change already is raising costs for American households by an estimated $400 to $900 annually, according to a 2025 Brookings report.

Trump’s Lubbock announcement follows a series of sweeping deregulatory moves by the EPA in which the agency has stated it does not have the authority to regulate the greenhouse gas emissions that cause climate change under the Clean Air Act. EPA’s most notable decision came in February when the agency rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding, the U.S. government’s scientific finding that greenhouse gases harm human health and the environment and the legal basis for its rules addressing climate change. More recently, the EPA stated in September that it would no longer limit climate pollution for power plants, a move which would likely extend the lifespan of coal-fired power plants.

In the wake of these decisions, however, legal experts and environmental advocates say that the EPA is attempting to assert power unevenly. On the one hand, the agency says it lacks the legal authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from cars, trucks, power plants, and industrial sources under the Clean Air Act. On the other, the latest EPA proposal relies on, in some cases in the same section of, the Clean Air Act to regulate methane, a greenhouse gas, from the oil and gas industry.

In its latest proposed rule, the EPA addresses this tension, acknowledging that “stakeholders have also raised concerns” about the agency’s authority to regulate the oil and gas sector’s greenhouse gas emissions under the landmark air pollution law. Depending on the agency’s final handling of the issue with fossil fuel-fired power plants, the EPA states it could then use a “future rulemaking” to resolve the issue in the oil and gas sector. (The EPA is accepting public comments on its proposed repeal of its authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions for fossil fuel-fired power plants until Nov. 2.)

Attacking EPA’s ‘flawed legal basis’

In 1999, the oil and gas industry’s largest trade group, the American Petroleum Institute (API), organized a meeting over whether it should “coordinate a multi-industry, trade group response” to the threat of what it called EPA’s “flawed legal basis” for regulating greenhouse gas pollution, including carbon dioxide and methane, under the Clean Air Act. In 2024, the API filed a legal challenge over the OOOOb/c rule, which was eventually consolidated into a lawsuit with states and other industry trade groups. That suit has been paused while the agency reconsiders the rule.

Parts of the oil and gas industry have flagged this distinction in how the Trump EPA is handling two different greenhouse gases under the same law. Shortly after the EPA repealed the endangerment finding, the Domestic Energy Producers Alliance (DEPA), an oil and gas trade association founded by fracking magnate and Trump donor Harold Hamm, wrote a letter to the EPA, thanking the agency for “restoring the rule of law.” The group called out “methane and other greenhouse gas emission requirements for the oil and gas sector” among its examples of “major regulations based on the Endangerment Finding.”

A few months later, after the agency published an update on its proposed reconsideration of the OOOOb/c methane rule, DEPA wrote in an internal newsletter that EPA “does not explain its legal reasoning for continuing to regulate methane emissions when it has found that it does not have the authority to regulate carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from vehicles and has proposed it does not have the authority to regulate power plants’ CO2 emissions.”

On Tuesday in Corpus Christi, the president called out Hamm by name at another midterms rally shortly before the one announcing the methane rule rollback. “Harold Hamm is here, the great oilman,” said Trump, looking around the audience. “Hi, Harold.”

‘The Very Definition of Arbitary’

Legal experts and environmental advocates say the EPA’s inconsistency leaves unresolved important legal questions about the federal government’s authority to regulate climate pollution, potentially keeping the door open to upend federal methane regulation entirely.

“Treating similar pollutants under the same statute differently, with no stated reason or evidence, is the very definition of arbitrary and capricious decision making,” said Alejandro Camacho, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Camacho argues that if the EPA adopts a broad theory limiting its authority over greenhouse gases, it must explain why that theory doesn’t also undermine its authority to regulate methane. “States have already sued over the power plant repeal, as have health and environmental groups, and they can and should attack this inconsistency too,” he added.

The EPA’s proposal nods to the industry’s questioning of its authority and points to the agency’s history of handling the oil and gas sector separately, “but the agency hasn’t explained how it will navigate it,” said Rosalie Winn, senior director and lead counsel on methane and clean air policy for the Environmental Defense Fund.

Mary Sasso, an attorney for the Clean Air Task Force, said the agency’s decision to defer the question could leave the future of methane regulation uncertain. “I think that there’s very real concerns that we could see changes to EPA’s interpretation of its own authority finalized in some type of regulation that would be really damaging for public health and the environment,” she said.

Camacho agrees, and warned that the deferral could foreshadow future agency backtracking. “The deferral is less a reasoned distinction than a placeholder for the next rollback,” he said.

The administration also argues that the proposed changes will reduce regulatory costs, encourage domestic energy production, and help lower prices for consumers. “Since day one, President Trump has been putting real money back into the hands of American people by putting American energy back in the hands of the American workers, businesses, and communities,” said Interior Secretary Doug Burgum in a press statement about the proposal.

Consumer savings uncertain

Although the EPA estimates that the proposed rollback to the methane rule would save consumers tens of billions of dollars, the relationship between domestic production and consumer prices is more complicated, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In an emailed response to DeSmog, the EPA said its estimate reflected the anticipated cost oil and gas operators would save by not having to comply with regulations, their excess profits, and consumer savings. The proposed rule reflects this calculation in its Regulatory Impact Analysis section, but does not provide further details on how the agency determined these figures. These figures are not independently established consumer savings.

“As much as it would be easy to paint oil executives as cartoonish villains hiking prices while families suffer, individuals have little to no control over benchmark oil prices,” said Kelly Mitchell, the executive director of the oil and gas watchdog Fieldnotes.

“The administration may claim that new rules will incentivize new production, bringing online supply to counter the barrels trapped behind the Strait of Hormuz,” Mitchell said. “However, these new rules are primarily designed to help operators of marginal wells — wells that produce fewer than 15 barrels per day.”

Mitchell questioned whether the benefits of the rollback would reach consumers, arguing that changes would primarily reduce costs for oil and gas operators without guaranteeing lower prices at the pump. “We’re left with an outcome where oil companies get to war profiteer, avoid using any of those profits to clean up a major pollution source, and fail to reduce prices. Now they have the gall to look us in the eyes and tell us this is a gift to the American consumer.”

Since rescinding the endangerment finding, the EPA no longer accounts for the cost of harms from additional climate pollution — only the economic harms — which does not figure into the new rule’s estimated savings. Meanwhile, in a study recapping the last decade of climate-induced health harms, the Lancet reported a record high of 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 — and almost 72 percent of them caused by climate change.

The proposed rule places particular emphasis on a class of low-producing facilities known as marginal wells, which typically produce relatively small amounts of oil and gas. The Trump administration alleges that regulations established under the previous administration stymied these wells. “Under crooked Joe Biden, ‘Dumocrats’ crushed the small oil and gas operators,” Trump said during the rally Tuesday. “There are small operators, they’re great operators too, I know so many of them — with crippling regulations and methane that caused prices to skyrocket.”

The EPA says many of these wells are family-owned operations that struggle with the costs of complying with Biden-era standards, but an Environmental Defense analysis found that nearly half of all marginal wells are owned by just 93 corporations.

The proposed methane rule reconsideration is the latest development in a broader campaign to weaken federal methane protections under the purview of Aaron Szabo, a former registered lobbyist for a member of a major trade group pushing for these rollbacks. Earlier this month, Szabo stepped down as the head of the EPA Office of Air and Radiation. Last month, DeSmog reported that members of the oil and gas industry had simultaneously voiced public support for federal methane rules while covertly working to “eviscerate”them during the second Trump administration, according to an investigation published by Fieldnotes.

text:
DANBURY, Conn.-- FuelCell Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: FCEL) today announced the completion of the second tranche of its previously announced $49 million financing supported by the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM). The approximately $24.7 million balance (before closing and transaction fees) completes the financing package approved by EXIM in June 2026.

The financing supports FuelCell Energy’s delivery of five 2.8-megawatt (MW) FuelCell Energy Blocks to Gyeonggi Green Energy (GGE) in South Korea. With nearly 60 MW of installed capacity, the GGE site is among the largest fuel cell installations in the world, has been in continuous operations for 13 years, and demonstrates FuelCell Energy’s long-standing experience delivering distributed, utility-scale power solutions.

The transaction builds on EXIM-supported financing completed by FuelCell Energy in 2024 and 2025 and further connects the company’s U.S. manufacturing base with international demand for reliable power. FuelCell Energy manufactures its fuel cell platforms in Torrington, Conn., and more than 90% of its supply chain is sourced from the United States.

“EXIM can be an important strategic bridge between American manufacturing capacity and global demand,” said Matt Latino, Chief Financial Officer of FuelCell Energy. “For FuelCell Energy, this transaction is another proof point in our broader capital strategy: matching the right source of capital to the right opportunity and building diversified financing capacity to support disciplined growth in both U.S. and international markets. Access to well-structured capital can strengthen our competitiveness, expand the reach of our U.S. manufacturing platform, and help us pursue attractive growth opportunities while maintaining discipline around our balance sheet and return on invested capital.”

FuelCell Energy’s commercially proven platforms are designed to provide continuous power at the point of use and can serve applications ranging from utility and industrial facilities to the growing power requirements of data centers and AI infrastructure. The company’s global installed base is approaching one gigawatt.

“EXIM’s ability to support U.S. companies across the export lifecycle can help American manufacturers compete more effectively in global infrastructure markets,” Latino added. We value the role EXIM can play alongside commercial banks, private capital and other financing partners as we build the capital capacity to support our growth. Technology manufactured in Connecticut is delivering utility-scale power internationally today, and we believe that same manufacturing platform can serve growing demand for dependable power around the world.” The transaction was structured under EXIM’s loan guarantee program and arranged with Private Export Funding Corporation and supported by AF Capital.

title: Speed to power: solutions to US data centres' challenges | Wood Mackenzie
description:
It varies by state but in Virginia, a hot spot for data centre location, the wait is 54 months at best.
In Ohio, it’s 84 months – that is, no power supply until 2033 for a project going ahead today.
Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply and the waitlist for the heavy frame gas turbines has stretched out to 278 weeks – roughly early 2032.
Not much use if you want your data centre up and running before 2030 and weren’t early in the queue to order.
What solutions are there for power supply challenges?
text:
How best to measure the breakneck pace of US AI and data centre roll-out? Well, there’s hyperscaler capital expenditure, which has increased four-fold since 2023 and is set to exceed US$750 billion this year, more than either the global spend in renewable power or upstream oil and gas.

Hyperscaler electricity consumption is another metric, skipping along at 23% a year so far this decade – way ahead of total US power demand, which did not grow from 2006 to 2024. Perhaps best is the 201 GW of new data centre capacity that US utilities have committed to connect to their grids, which would increase electricity demand by 30% if it’s all built.

Speed to power is the buzz phrase. All hyperscalers want their data centres plugged into reliable power supply as soon as it is ready to run their large language models and satisfy consumers’ growing reliance on them. The problem is that the US electricity industry, regulators and the entire supply chain alike are not yet capable of moving at the pace, or scale, required.

Chris Seiple, Vice Chair Power and Renewables, and I spent last week in New York talking with power sector investors and financiers about the challenges and opportunities ahead.

What are the biggest challenges for the power sector?

Among multiple challenges there are three big ones. First, the timetable for getting a data centre connected to the grid keeps getting longer. It varies by state but in Virginia, a hot spot for data centre location, the wait is 54 months at best. In Ohio, it’s 84 months – that is, no power supply until 2033 for a project going ahead today.

Second, public opposition to data centre development is growing. Lawmakers have called 400 moratoriums on data centre proposals. One-fifth of projects under development have been delayed by a moratorium, some by more than one.

Third, there’s an acute lack of essential components in the supply chain. Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply and the waitlist for the heavy frame gas turbines has stretched out to 278 weeks – roughly early 2032. Not much use if you want your data centre up and running before 2030 and weren’t early in the queue to order. Wire infrastructure is not much better with waitlists for transformers coming in at 162 weeks and circuit breakers at 137 weeks. Skilled labourers are also emerging as a bottleneck – not an easy problem to solve quickly.

Is it easier to build generation in regulated or unregulated markets?

Unregulated markets are easier in some ways in that the data centres are free to choose their power supplier and often have more flexibility in developing behind-the-meter generation (BTM) solutions. The main challenge is the disconnect between the planning for large loads and the planning for generation interconnections, and connecting the two.

In short, there are numerous independent decisions being made in unregulated markets that can get in the way of building out the grid in the most cost-effective way and that makes sure supply growth keeps up with demand growth. Regulated markets can mitigate some of the planning uncertainty and grid inefficiency.

What’s the timetable to deliver the power?

Realistically, there are no solutions that deliver new supply at any scale in 2027 or 2028 beyond what has already been committed. The task for regulators, the electricity industry and hyperscalers is to ensure that supply is connected by the time that demand ramps up beyond 2028. And the focus should be on delivering the 201 GW capacity already committed – adding more capacity to the pipeline before the current logjam gets moving will only hinder progress.

What solutions are there for power supply challenges?

First, BTM projects – which account for 15% of the pipeline by project count and 40% of planned capacity – skip the need for grid connection and the regulatory hurdles that go with it. Most BTM plans will be gas-fired capacity, backed increasingly by new high-discharge batteries. These projects will be expensive, complicated from an engineering perspective, and few data centres view the BTM solutions as a long-term plan, preferring to connect to the grid at some point.

The ‘ERCOT solution’ could be a pragmatic way forward for unregulated markets. The Texas system operator analyses the planned locations and scale of large load demand in the market, then makes assumptions where developers are likely to build generation. It can then make an ‘80/20’ decision on investment in transmission and connection and hope it all works out.

Interruptibility of demand is emerging as another solution. Data centre developers are trying to figure out how dedicated BTM resources, such as generators or batteries, might offer more flexibility to the grid. At the same ime, regulated utilities are working to communicate to data centre developers what type of flexibility will best optimise getting new load connected faster. Lastly, deregulated market rules are evolving to accommodate flexible interconnect.

Is AI-driven demand changing utilities?

Yes. For one thing, hyperscalers are currently price-insensitive. That’s a new experience for regulated utilities, which can leverage that price insensitivity to deal with affordability concerns and to find innovative ways to get load connected faster or to pursue new generation technologies, such as advanced geothermal or long-duration energy storage.

After operating in a low-growth bubble for decades, utilities are coming up with solutions for a new breed of customers with large loads in grids that are already constrained.

title: A Better Start, Ready for the Day: Green SM Elevates the Urban Mobility Experience in the U.S.
description:
Arrive Ready.”, the message Green SM, a Vietnamese-born all-electric taxi service, has chosen to introduce its experience to the U.S. market.
Through every electric ride, Green SM aims to help passengers begin their day feeling more positive, comfortable and energized.
Across its markets, Green SM builds its service experience around the 5 Good Promises: Good Cars, Good Drivers, Good Price, Good Experience and Good for the Environment.
To celebrate its launch, Green SM is offering special promotions to customers in Los Angeles.
From Vietnam to Los Angeles, Green SM’s global journey represents more than an expansion of its brand footprint.
text:
For commuters, however, this time can be an opportunity: 15 minutes to review a presentation, a few moments to prepare for an important meeting, or a quiet transition from family life to the workday ahead. The key is finding ways to make these moments more meaningful and begin each day in a more positive frame of mind, contributing to overall well-being and happiness.

The in-vehicle experience plays an important role in making that difference. J.D. Power’s 2026 U.S. Automotive Performance, Execution and Layout (APEAL) Study, which evaluates the emotional appeal and ownership experience of 78,514 new-vehicle owners during the first 90 days of ownership across 37 attributes, found that electric vehicles outperformed internal combustion engine vehicles in nearly every category. The largest gap was in the powertrain category, where EVs scored 109 points higher on a 1,000-point scale.

A 2018 study conducted by the University of York in the United Kingdom also reported positive changes among drivers who switched from diesel vehicles to electric vehicles, including improved concentration, greater calmness and a stronger sense of happiness.

Together, these findings highlight how a morning commute can become a more positive start to the day – with less stress, greater comfort and a stronger sense of control. Rather than allowing rush-hour traffic to drain their energy, commuters can turn their journey into an opportunity to prepare, recharge and feel ready for the day ahead.

This is the spirit behind “Start Strong. Arrive Ready.”, the message Green SM, a Vietnamese-born all-electric taxi service, has chosen to introduce its experience to the U.S. market. Through every electric ride, Green SM aims to help passengers begin their day feeling more positive, comfortable and energized.

Making Every Moment Before Work Count: How a Smoother Ride Enhances the Passenger Experience

This experience comes to life through the VinFast VF 8, a D-segment electric SUV in Green SM’s fleet in Los Angeles. Its spacious interior, clean cabin and smooth, quiet performance offer passengers a welcome moment of comfort amid the pace of urban life. Whether heading to the office or an important appointment, passengers can use the journey to finish emails, review key talking points for a meeting, or simply relax and recharge before the day begins.

A pleasant journey is shaped not only by the vehicle, but also by the quality of service. Green Driver partners are carefully selected and trained, with an emphasis on professionalism, courtesy and attentive service throughout every ride.

For customers booking through the Green SM app, available features provide information about drivers, vehicles and routes, helping passengers follow their journeys and stay informed along the way. Fares and promotional offers are also displayed clearly, making it easier for customers to compare options and choose a ride that suits their needs.

Whether it is a morning ride before an important meeting, a transfer from a hotel to an event venue, or a series of journeys packed into a business trip, Green SM aims to make urban mobility more comfortable and convenient. After all, the value of a ride lies not only in getting passengers to their destinations, but also in helping them arrive feeling relaxed, in control and ready for whatever comes next.

From Vietnam to Los Angeles: Bringing Green Mobility to More People Through the Five Green Goodness Pillars

In mid-October, Green SM officially launched its all-electric taxi service in Los Angeles, marking the brand’s first entry into North America and expanding its global footprint to nine markets. Customers can book rides through the Green SM app, contact the call center or hail a vehicle on the street, with options to meet a range of mobility needs, from everyday commutes and longer journeys to airport transfers.

Across its markets, Green SM builds its service experience around the 5 Good Promises: Good Cars, Good Drivers, Good Price, Good Experience and Good for the Environment. In Los Angeles, these principles are reflected in an all-electric VinFast fleet, transparent fares and promotional offers, professional drivers, attentive service and rides with zero tailpipe emissions.

To celebrate its launch, Green SM is offering special promotions to customers in Los Angeles. New users can enjoy 50% off their fares, up to $12 per ride, on their first five trips. Customers can also sign up for Green Pass membership free of charge and receive 10 discount codes each month, with each code offering 30% off a fare, up to $10.

Founded in Vietnam in 2023, Green SM has steadily expanded its operations, bringing all-electric mobility services to markets around the world, including Vietnam, Laos, Indonesia, the Philippines, India, Kazakhstan, Denmark and the Netherlands. The brand has completed approximately 850 million trips covering nearly 6 billion kilometers, helping reduce more than 800,000 metric tons of CO₂ emissions, equivalent to the amount of carbon absorbed by approximately 36 million trees.

In the U.S., Green SM says it will progressively strengthen its local operations and recruit and train drivers from the local community, creating additional employment opportunities while contributing to the transition toward greener transportation in Los Angeles and the surrounding region. Alongside its expansion, the brand will continue investing in its fleet, technology, people and service quality, with the goal of building a sustainable, long-term presence in the U.S. market.

From Vietnam to Los Angeles, Green SM’s global journey represents more than an expansion of its brand footprint. It is also an opportunity to bring a greener, more comfortable mobility experience to people in major cities around the world.

Because a productive day can begin with a better ride. Start Strong. Arrive Ready.

title: Climate Change Suffers Rude Collision With Reality - Yahoo
description:
Democrats' climate change agenda has taken a backseat to politics.
What once were sought and lauded as means to their climate change goal, are now lamented and wielded as a political cudgel.
It has to do with the $368 billion, the single-largest investment in climate change anywhere in the world, anywhere."
Climate change has been increasingly suffering from its rude collision with reality.
The European Union, where the climate change agenda is treated as gospel, and its resulting stagnant economy have hurt.
text:
Democrats' climate change agenda has taken a backseat to politics.

Although this is clear in general, nowhere is it more so than on Democrats' focus on higher fuel prices. What once were sought and lauded as means to their climate change goal, are now lamented and wielded as a political cudgel.

While climate change is still used in conjunction with reporting on every adverse weather event, the unwinding of Democratic Party policies that were ostensibly justified as addressing it has gone comparatively unnoticed. Example One is the misnamed "Inflation Reduction Act," about which President Biden confessed: "It has nothing to do with inflation. It has to do with the $368 billion, the single-largest investment in climate change anywhere in the world, anywhere."

But the IRA's "green" tax credits were ticking fiscal time bombs. Generous and with no cap on how many of these credits could be granted, estimated costs exploded: Initially estimated to cost $270 billion, the estimate doubled to $536 billion, then more than doubled again to $1.2 trillion over ten years. Others, such as an overemphasis on renewable power rather than an emphasis on reliable power, were predestined to fail.

Together, the IRA's costs and failures dovetailed with earlier failures, such as the Biden administration's 2021 $5 billion program to build EV charging stations that resulted in only seven stations being built in three years. Yet despite these earlier reversals, nowhere has Democrats' climate change agenda taken a step back more than in this year's increase in oil and gas prices.

Economically, oil and gas price increases do have a broad impact. Everything that uses them becomes more expensive and most everything uses oil and gas in some capacity. Prices are also readily discernible: Most buy gas regularly and see gas prices displayed constantly - on virtually every street corner.

It is natural, therefore, that Democrats would seize on these increases. These dovetailed with, and accentuated, their "affordability" message. They also could be directly tied to the conflict in Iran begun by President Trump in February. Finally, it distracted attention from the fact that inflation, and with it "affordability," was an issue throughout President Biden's four years in office - after all that's why the "Inflation Reduction Act" was affixed to the aforementioned legislation, much to Biden's own later chagrin.

In short, increased oil and gas prices meant political opportunity and Democrats have taken full advantage.

Overlooked in what seems so straightforward is that today's increased oil and gas prices fulfill Democrats' underlying climate change policy goals. Higher prices reduce demand, and using less fossil fuel is exactly what Democrats' climate change agenda sought … or at least did until this increase in prices.

The liberal Tax Policy Center noted at the time that the IRA failed to live up to its climate change potential. Writing of its generous tax credits, the TPC noted: "By contrast, a carbon tax is designed to achieve only one goal: Raise the price of carbon. There are many ways the tax can be returned to households but in any event the tax still would discourage consumption of carbon-based products by raising their relative prices."

Democrats have backed all manner of ways to restrict the use of fossil fuels and promote "green" alternatives. These include California's ZEV mandate, myriad policies in the Inflation Reduction Act, restricting U.S. production of oil and gas, opposing fracking, stifling pipeline development, onerous CAFÉ requirements, EV incentives, and more.

Climate change has been increasingly suffering from its rude collision with reality. The European Union, where the climate change agenda is treated as gospel, and its resulting stagnant economy have hurt. But nothing has had such a chilling effect in America as the opportunity to make a political issue out of increased oil and gas prices.

Given the choice between policy and politics, there is no choice at all - ironically, even when an outcome advances the policy and the politics Democrats so recently claimed to champion.

name: Clean Energy
title: Five reasons why the US midterms matter for the climate – and your energy bill
description:
“If some of the governor’s offices flip from Republican to Democrat, that could yield a profound change in state climate policy,” Gerrard said.
Trump’s attacks on clean energy have also led to mass job losses, including many in battleground states.
The US’s clean energy workforce lost nearly 37,000 jobs last year – the first annual job loss in America’s clean energy economy since the pandemic, according to a September report from E2, a business advocacy group for the clean economy that analyzed Department of Energy data.
A report from Climate Power puts that number even higher, with 173,000 clean energy jobs either cut or delayed since Trump took office.
The report found that Texas saw the most jobs lost from Trump’s war on clean energy.
text:
1. If Democrats do well, they could gain leverage to oppose Trump’s anti-climate agenda

If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they won’t be able to overturn previous Republican actions like gutting the Inflation Reduction Act, and they can’t pass new legislation that Trump would veto, but they will have more cards to play to oppose Trump’s pro-fossil fuel agenda going forward.

If Democrats take back the House, it will mean the White House has to compromise with Democrats in order to pass budgets. This would give Democrats the power to add climate provisions into appropriations legislation, said Michael Gerrard, founder and director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “Many appropriations begin in the House, and these are huge bills that have to pass, so it’s possible that some pro-climate provisions could be put in some of the appropriations legislation,” he said. “Often presidents sign appropriation bills that have provisions they don’t like because they need to get the budget passed.”

Democrats could also use their power in the House to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses and documents. Dan Farber, a law professor at the University of California, Berkeley, suggested they could investigate possible conflicts of interest or corruption, like the Trump administration intervening in a federal lawsuit to allow Elon Musk to continue using portable gas generators in his Mississippi datacenter, which the suit alleges is a violation of the Clean Air Act.

If Democrats win the Senate, they could oppose further confirmations of federal judges, cabinet officers and sub-cabinet positions. “That gives [Democratic] senators some leverage to stop appointments they don’t want,” Farber said. “But you can also hold appointments hostage in return for other things.”

Preventing appointments of anti-climate judges would leave more vacancies for the next president to fill, he added. “That can have a big long-term effect on the environment.”

Gerrard said a power shift in the House and Senate could change negotiations around the permitting bill which could clear hurdles for both clean energy and fossil fuels projects. The bill would significantly weaken the National Environmental Policy Act, making it impossible for a court to halt a project due to a Nepa violation, he said. “But if the Democrats are in charge of both the House and the Senate, that bill might look different.”

Farber and Gerrard said state climate policy also hangs in the balance this November. The Cook Political Report found that Democrats could gain two-to-four governor’s seats this cycle. “If some of the governor’s offices flip from Republican to Democrat, that could yield a profound change in state climate policy,” Gerrard said.

2. If Republicans do well, expect more environmental rollbacks

If the Republicans buck polling predictions and manage to keep control of the House and Senate, it would embolden Trump to continue his anti-climate agenda.

Trump could continue his favoritism toward polluting companies, because Democrats would lack the investigative and subpoena powers to hold him accountable.

And he could continue appointing conservative justices: “Trump has been packing the lower courts with anti-regulatory, super-conservative judges,” Farber said.

Under this administration, Republican lawmakers have backed Trump on policies that were unfavorable to their constituents – such as voting to repeal clean energy tax credits that created jobs in their districts. If Republicans win in the midterms, Republicans would continue to vote in support of Trump. “Maybe even more so, because I think this would be seen as a big win for him personally,” Farber said.

“They have not just been sitting on the sidelines – they have helped Trump, in terms of repealing the Inflation Reduction Act from Biden, and overturning some specific regulations by Congress. We could see more of that kind of thing coming from them. So it would be another big step backwards,” Farber said.

“I keep thinking, how much worse could they do? But they always find something,” he added.

3. As affordability remains a key issue, voters feel the pinch of Trump’s anti-climate policies

The administration’s constraints on renewables are forcing consumers to spend more on energy. A study by Nera predicted that between 2027 and 2033, economy-wide household energy costs would increase on average by $11.6bn annually from constraining the deployment of solar and wind. The region hardest hit by these constraints is Texas, where rates are forecast to rise as much as 22%, the study found.

Trump’s attacks on clean energy have also led to mass job losses, including many in battleground states. The US’s clean energy workforce lost nearly 37,000 jobs last year – the first annual job loss in America’s clean energy economy since the pandemic, according to a September report from E2, a business advocacy group for the clean economy that analyzed Department of Energy data.

A report from Climate Power puts that number even higher, with 173,000 clean energy jobs either cut or delayed since Trump took office. The report found that Texas saw the most jobs lost from Trump’s war on clean energy.

The Nera report found that increased reliance on natural gas capacity and generation raises reliability risks and increases exposure to price volatility. According to Climate Power, since Trump took office, gas and electric utilities have raised or sought to increase bills by more than $92bn, affecting more than 100 million customers across the country.

Polling shows that Democrats and Republicans in battleground states want candidates to talk more about the climate crisis. And even though one in three US adults have been directly affected by extreme weather, midterm candidates are avoiding talking directly about climate change in what’s known as “climate hushing”.

But researchers from the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability have found that there are three groups of Democratic candidates and officeholders who are talking about the climate crisis in subtle instead of direct ways: energy populists like Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio are using datacenters and utility bills to connect the issues of climate and affordability, climate champions like Arizona Democratic candidate JoAnna Mendoza are promising bold action like investing in clean energy, and candidates who are advocating for an “all-of-the-above” approach to energy, like Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race.

“The one thing that they all have in common is a focus on affordability … and talking about energy issues in the context of affordability,” said Geoffrey Henderson, an assistant environmental policy and planning professor at the University of Michigan.

He noted that a few candidates, like Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa, are emphasizing how extreme weather events worsened by the climate crisis are driving up the cost of insurance.

With various quiet climate messages being tested in battleground states, this election could be a test of how voters respond to these messages. Henderson expects political analysts will study the data after the election to draw lessons from it. “The climate message has in a number of ways been brought into alignment with the affordability question, and so I think this is a test of whether that combination resonates,” he said.

The issue of climate hushing has come up election after election, but Henderson believes it’s a positive thing that candidates are still finding ways to talk about climate, even indirectly. “It’s better that candidates are tying climate to affordability than not mentioning it at all, and I do see how different parts of the country lend themselves to different strategies.”

5. Whatever happens at the polls, some of the big US climate fights ahead will be in the courts

Environmental laws are being tested in US courts like never before. “We’re now at a stage where every significant environmental regulation is challenged in court by one side or the other,” Gerrard said.

The Trump administration has set out to weaken and revoke environmental regulations, triggering a wave of litigation attempting to undo those actions. If a future Democratic president tries to restore those regulations or issue new ones, they would also be challenged in court, Gerrard said.

Gerrard is closely watching the fight over Trump’s repeal of the endangerment finding, which stated that the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere endangers public health, allowing the Environmental Protection Agency to limit greenhouse gas pollution from various sources. “There’s a case before the DC circuit on Trump’s revocation of the endangerment finding – that’s a very big case,” he noted.

Gerrard is also looking ahead to the supreme court’s decision in the Suncor v Boulder case that will decide whether local officials in Boulder, Colorado, can force fossil fuel companies to pay for their share of damages from the climate crisis. If the justices rule against Boulder, it could block future climate damages cases, removing a vital method of accountability.

authors: Patrick Whittle And Robert F. Bukaty, Associated Press

text:
MONTAUK, N.Y. – Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards.

Then, after years of heavy fishing, the big runs of stripers stopped.

“I’m part of the problem, back in the years. I ran party boats, we slayed fish with reckless abandon,” said Jakob, president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association on the easternmost tip of Long Island.

Increasingly, fishermen like Jakob fear the good days of catching striped bass are coming to an end. The fish aren't showing up like they used to, and young stripers are becoming harder to find.

Scientists who study striped bass say anglers on the East Coast are right to be concerned, and they say years of overfishing are just part of the problem. The fish have experienced eight consecutive years of poor reproduction in their most critical habitat in the Chesapeake Bay, regulators said last week, and the population has declined along much of the Atlantic coast.

Factors like years of warming waters — a prime concern cited by many scientists — poor river flow, drought, pollution and possibly increased predation from seals and sharks have left experts and fishermen asking whether tighter fishing limits would even be enough for striped bass to recover. Losing these higher-level predators, which help regulate smaller fish, would threaten an $8 billion fishing industry and tens of thousands of jobs.

___

See a visual essay featuring anglers who were fishing the shores of Long Island earlier this month here.

___

Striped bass fishing is a long-standing East Coast tradition

“Stripers” are prized in part because they put up a fight and can be fished right from shore. From the slippery rocks of Maine's coast to the warmer waters of the St. Johns River in Florida, anglers wearing headlamps can be seen casting into the predawn darkness, hoping for a bite.

Interstate regulators have made changes to the way the migratory fish are managed in recent years, including standardizing the way they're measured against size requirements. But regulators have balked at reducing the level of recreational catch. Some fishermen say the current moves might not go far enough, and stricter action — including possibly a fishing moratorium, a strategy used in the 1980s — is needed to ensure that future generations of anglers can still catch striped bass.

“They are not replacing themselves at a sufficient level. That obviously has everybody concerned,” said Beth Versak, the striped bass program manager for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources. “People all up and down the coast are passionate about striped bass.”

Fishing guides, boat trips, gear, bait, hotel rooms — it all adds up to what members of the industry say is about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs in the U.S. alone.

And it relies on a fish whose future looks grim.

“Striped bass as we know it is going to collapse,” said Patrick Paquette, government affairs coordinator for the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association and a member of an interstate advisory panel about the regulations.

“Sometime around 2029, 2030 it’s going to go off a cliff,” he said, “and it’s going to be ugly.”

Scientists say a variety of factors, including warming waters, have contributed to poor spawning

Striped bass hatch in fresh or brackish water and then spend the early years of their lives in estuaries where the rivers meet the sea. Their ability to reproduce and bring new fish into the population is predicated on environmental conditions that favor them — specifically, cool, wet springs.

Scientists identify four major spawning stocks along the Atlantic. The Chesapeake Bay is where up to 90% of stripers spawn and grow. When freshwater flows are too low, such as in times of drought, or when spring or summer temperatures are too high, the fish suffer and populations can fall, said Toni Kerns, fisheries policy director with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which regulates striped bass.

Conditions have been poor in recent years, and fewer fish have entered the population going back to 2019, said Chris Batsavage, chair of the commission's striped bass management board.

“Low precipitation and waters that warm quickly result in weak year classes,” Batsavage said. “It seems like it's environmentally driven.”

The conditions have led to a “slump of bad years” that have made it especially difficult for the fish to maintain their population in the Chesapeake, Versak said.

Fishermen fear the loss of an iconic species if trends continue

John Skinner, who wrote a book about striped bass fishing and runs a YouTube channel on the subject that has more than 100,000 followers, has been fishing off Long Island for more than 50 years and says once-reliable spots have completely dried up.

“I'm not saying the fishing is bad. I’m saying when you go there in perfect conditions, you catch nothing,” Skinner said. “Absolutely nothing.”

Many other striped bass fishermen across the Northeast shared a recurring story this summer and fall — the fish's once-plentiful schools are dried up, and the individuals that remain are clearly older, meaning years of reproduction failure are starting to take their toll.

Some fishermen said stricter rules or a fishing moratorium could be the only ways to prevent the fish’s population from becoming dangerously low. And they lament what they’re seeing on the waters — smaller schools of fish, many of them older and larger, with few young fish entering the population to provide a future.

They also see more factors than just the warming environment at play. Some see years of heavy fishing on striped bass becoming apparent today in the form of a lower population. Others blame the resurgence of sharks buoyed by years of conservation efforts, as a reintroduction of competition for the fish.

Regulators have taken steps, but some call for a moratorium

The Atlantic States commission considers the stock to be overfished, although it says overfishing is not occurring at the moment. The fish are caught commercially as well as recreationally, but recreational fishing is much larger.

Most of the recreational catch is tossed back into the ocean alive. Still, some fish don't survive the encounter. Regulators have historically expected 9% to die after release, while newer data shows the number could be less than 5%.

Limits on how large a striped bass can be caught and kept are typically in the range of 28 to 31 inches (71 to 79 centimeters), with rules varying by state and location. Striped bass are popular with catch-and-release fishermen, and these days, it’s more common to catch larger bass, many well over 31 inches.

Paquette, the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association coordinator and a longtime angler himself, said that without drastic action he fears the end of striped bass fishing.

“If you’re a guy who thought he was going to retire and striped bass fish, and you’re planning on retiring soon, get a different plan,” Paquette said.

___

Whittle reported from Portland, Maine. Associated Press video journalist Mingson Lau contributed.

GROWMARK, Inc. has made a minority equity investment in Wabash Valley Resources (WVR), facilitating the first advance under WVR’s U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) loan and supporting construction of its fertilizer facility in West Terre Haute.

The facility is designed to produce 500,000 metric tons of anhydrous ammonia annually, creating a major new domestic fertilizer source for farmers across the Eastern Corn Belt. Commercial operations are expected to begin in 2029.

“Our investment in Wabash Valley Resources will bring a new, independent source of ammonia closer to the farmers and cooperatives that depend on it,” said Mark Orr, CEO of GROWMARK. “It’s a long-term investment in reliable domestic supply and the competitiveness of our member-owners.”

GROWMARK’s participation reflects the strategic importance of expanding fertilizer production near the communities it serves. As an agricultural cooperative with extensive crop nutrient and logistics operations, GROWMARK brings a direct understanding of farmers’ needs and the importance of reliable supply throughout the growing season. Its investment in WVR connects those priorities with the development of new domestic manufacturing capacity.

“GROWMARK’s investment is a pivotal milestone for WVR and a strong vote of confidence in independent ammonia production,” said Dan Williams, WVR’s CEO. “With this investment, we move closer to turning years of development into a dependable source of American-made fertilizer. We thank the U.S. Department of Energy and its Office of Energy Dominance Financing for helping bring this transaction to fruition. Our focus now is on building the facility safely and delivering a dependable supply of American-made fertilizer to the farmers who feed our country.”
