By demonstrating that closer economic alignment with the United States brings advantages, the Economic Shield arrangement would incentivize other countries to join.
The Western Hemisphere is the only region that offers the vital combination of proximity, resources, and existing trade relationships.
While the United States stalled, Huawei’s technology spread across the Western Hemisphere, and its presence has been hard to dislodge.
For example, the United States used the ESF to help stabilize Mexico in 1995, and Argentina earlier this year.
text:
No region matters more to the future prosperity and security of the United States than the Western Hemisphere. Deeply integrated supply chains connect the United States with Canada and Mexico, while the wider region possesses the energy, critical minerals, agricultural capacity, and technological and industrial bases that the U.S. economy will require over the coming decades. Over the last twenty-five years, however, the United States has left a vacuum in the hemisphere, and China has moved to fill it. Beijing is now the first- or second-largest trading partner for most of the hemisphere’s economies, as well as the region’s largest bilateral official creditor. Chinese firms have embedded themselves in telecommunications networks, invested in dozens of ports and logistics facilities, and occupied increasingly important positions in critical-mineral supply chains. Unless the United States takes action, even governments friendly to Washington will become dependent on China.

Washington should forge an integrated regional economy, offering U.S. public- and private-sector economic resources in return for collaboration and reform, while helping participating countries become more prosperous and not reliant on Beijing. This effort should be implemented through an Economic Shield of the Americas partnership, which would start with like-minded governments that meet a common set of business-climate and trusted-collaborator standards and are aligned with U.S. concerns about China. By demonstrating that closer economic alignment with the United States brings advantages, the Economic Shield arrangement would incentivize other countries to join. The partnership should aim to concentrate U.S. diplomatic, financial, and commercial tools in these willing partners and on strategically important sectors for at least a decade.

The United States, if it is to be strong, prosperous, and secure in the coming decades, will require full access to the Western Hemisphere’s energy, food, minerals, and technology. If those assets and resources can be secured, the benefits will be immense. American jobs can be created, migration pressures reduced, technological progress ensured, and security enhanced. To grasp those opportunities, Washington should develop an economic partnership with countries in the region, offering U.S. public- and private-sector economic resources in return for collaboration and reform. The objective should be to make the hemisphere the world’s most attractive place to do business.

The Western Hemisphere is fundamental to U.S. prosperity. But over the last twenty-five years, the United States has left a vacuum in the hemisphere, and China has moved to fill it. Beijing, formerly so absent, is now the first- or second-largest trading partner for most of the hemisphere’s economies, as well as the region’s largest bilateral official creditor. Chinese firms have embedded themselves in telecommunications networks, invested in dozens of ports and logistics facilities, financed and invested in oil and gas, and occupy increasingly important positions in critical-mineral supply chains.

Despite Beijing’s advances, Washington still has great advantages in the region: proximity, trade relationships, educational and familial ties, and the largest consumer market in the world. Yet the United States has never fused those advantages into a coherent hemispheric commercial strategy, one that mobilizes American business to secure leading positions in the sectors on which economic growth, technological capacity, and national security depend. The time is ripe for a change, and there are, at present, an unusually large number of pro-American, pro-business, reform-minded governments in the hemisphere. Now is the time to build a partnership with this coalition of the willing and, through its success, encourage others to join. Washington should not seek to own the hemisphere’s resources through this partnership. Its objective should be to forge a regional economy in which American and trusted-partner companies provide the capital, technology, infrastructure, and commercial relationships that help participating countries become more prosperous and not reliant upon China.

This effort should be organized around an Economic Shield of the Americas, a framework for cooperation on investment, strategic infrastructure, supply chains, energy, critical minerals, and technology. Like the Trump administration’s Shield of the Americas security partnership, the first members should be like-minded governments—like-minded in their support for economic reform and aligned with U.S. concerns about China. There will be substantial overlap between that group and countries already participating in the security-focused Shield of the Americas. But a close political relationship should not guarantee participation; countries that align with the United States politically but have not undertaken economic reforms may not be the best partners for viable projects, while countries that undertake reforms without safeguards for sensitive infrastructure will not advance the initiative’s strategic purpose. Over time, additional countries should be encouraged to join if they have demonstrated progress on economic governance, openness to American investment, procurement transparency, and the protection of critical systems.

If countries meet those standards, they should receive priority access to U.S.-backed financing, project preparation, trade and investment missions, technical assistance, and senior-level commercial engagement. This kind of sustained and concentrated application of U.S. financial and commercial tools on willing partners, along with measurable country and sector targets and a statutory framework capable of enduring across administrations, has the capacity to generate unprecedented growth.

The current situation in the Western Hemisphere has become unacceptable. The United States is dependent on supply chains and infrastructure that a competitor can monitor, disrupt, or block. Meanwhile, China is free to influence commercial rules, technology choices, and port alignments. The combination of those factors, as well as the lack of a unified strategy, is costly for American companies, depriving them of markets, projects, and opportunities.

In some countries, the United States has succeeded, albeit after a slow start, in responding to the China challenge in the region. In 2021, Paraguay came close to switching diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to mainland China in return for access to vaccines. Paraguay ultimately decided to maintain its relationship with Taiwan, in part because the Taiwanese government worked with India and other democratic partners to help Paraguay obtain vaccines. But the pressure from Beijing was enormous, and Washington initially had no answer or competing offer.

That same year, Panama renewed the concession for the Balboa and Cristóbal ports at both entrances to the Panama Canal. The ports were managed by Hutchison, a Hong Kong‒based company subject to pressure from Beijing. During peacetime, control of those ports allows surveillance of commercial and military traffic. In a crisis, these ports could be used to delay or complicate U.S. military access. Only after U.S. President Donald Trump’s inauguration in 2025 did Washington act with the necessary urgency. Under U.S. pressure, Panama withdrew from the Belt and Road Initiative, subjected the port concessions to greater scrutiny, and ultimately reclaimed control of the ports after its Supreme Court invalidated the concession. Making those changes after the fact was far harder than it would have been to prevent Chinese access in the first place. But the United States succeeded in securing a critical channel.

Washington has, at times, failed in its dealings with Buenos Aires. Despite the fact that Argentine President Javier Milei is a close ally of Trump’s, the country has occasionally disregarded U.S. concerns. Argentina’s economic dependence on China limits Milei’s room to maneuver: Beijing is one of the country’s largest trading partners, a major investor in mining and infrastructure, and an important source of financial support. But China’s influence in the region is a phenomenon of the last twenty-five years. In the 1990s, China was neither a serious trading partner nor a major creditor to Argentina. But in August 2026, Argentina renewed a roughly $19 billion currency-swap agreement with China, including $5 billion already activated to support financial stability, giving Beijing considerable leverage over a country still struggling with currency and financing pressures. The limits of U.S. influence in Argentina are demonstrated by the Espacio Lejano radio station, in the west of the country. The station is operated without adequate Argentine oversight by an organization linked to the Chinese military and has dual-use capabilities. Washington has raised these concerns repeatedly, but Buenos Aires has declined to terminate the fifty-year agreement.

Unless the United States takes action, Chinese influence will expand across the Western Hemisphere, and its dominance of mining, telecommunications infrastructure, strategic ports, and artificial intelligence (AI) stacks will grow. Beijing could remain the indispensable buyer of the region’s commodities and become the lender of last resort. If this were to happen, even governments friendly to the United States would become dependent on China. They would feel obliged to support Chinese positions, back Chinese candidates for leadership positions in international institutions, and adopt Chinese technical standards in areas including electric vehicles and AI. Without a permanent change in course, when U.S. and Chinese interests diverge, Washington will not be able to count on its neighbors’ support.

Not only is action needed, but there is now an opening in which such action would be welcomed. Two decades ago, a swath of the hemisphere was governed by instinctively anti-American administrations. Today, however, there is a sizable cohort of center-to-right governments that are pro-American: in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, and Peru. These countries want greater investment from the United States, as well as alternatives to excessive dependence on China. Many are also willing to undertake reforms that their predecessors postponed. The United States should take advantage of this opportunity, and target governments that want closer strategic relations with Washington, as well as with American companies. Washington should demonstrate that closer economic alignment with the United States brings advantages, including greater access to development financing, more American investment, faster project development, and participation in initiatives on energy, critical minerals, food and fertilizer, water, and digital infrastructure. The success of that effort should lead other countries to join. Membership should remain open to governments willing to meet high standards on business climate, treatment of U.S. investors, transparency, and trusted strategic infrastructure.

The United States needs a secure supply of energy, critical minerals, food, fertilizer, manufactured inputs, and digital infrastructure in the Western Hemisphere. Events since 2020—including the COVID-19 pandemic, wars in Europe and the Middle East, shipping disruptions, and long-term competition with China—have demonstrated the risks of depending on fragile, distant supply chains. The Western Hemisphere is the only region that offers the vital combination of proximity, resources, and existing trade relationships. Canadian and Mexican energy and manufacturing supply chains are already deeply integrated, while Latin America and the Caribbean offer energy, critical minerals, agricultural capacity, labor, manufacturing potential, and growing technology markets.

The Economic Shield partnership will require the type of sustained commitment that the United States has not brought to the region in decades. It would concentrate U.S. diplomatic, financial, and commercial tools on a limited number of willing partners and strategically important sectors for at least a decade. Agreements would link preferential access to U.S.-backed support with measurable targets. Rather than another regional assistance program, the Economic Shield of the Americas would be a long-term commercial strategy, led by private investment and supported by the full weight of the U.S. government.

The first countries to join should be aligned with U.S. concerns about China, as well as united in their willingness to undertake economic reforms. The countries that meet this threshold should receive access to U.S. financing and commercial support for high-quality projects, in return for measurable economic reforms. Canada and Mexico should be engaged from the outset, due to their energy, manufacturing, agricultural, mineral, and technology strengths. Similarly, Brazil, due its economic and productive heft, must be included. Likely early partners would also include Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, and Peru. A center-left government such as Uruguay’s could qualify by maintaining predictable rules, welcoming U.S. investment, and protecting critical systems.

Although the initial coalition will not be able to achieve every hemisphere-wide production objective, it could lay the groundwork for future success by bringing together a critical mass of energy and mineral producers, agricultural exporters, manufacturing centers, technology markets, and strategic transportation hubs. Working together, this group could establish trusted supply corridors, complete a first batch of major projects, and demonstrate the commercial value of closer alignment with the United States. Visible success could incentivize additional governments to join the initiative.

To create more investable projects in the sectors most important to the United States, Washington should fully mobilize its economic toolkit: the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, the Export-Import Bank of the United States, the U.S. Trade and Development Agency, and its large shareholdings in the Inter-American Development Bank and IDB Invest. To signal that the U.S. commitment is serious and long-term, Congress should provide an initial ten-year pledge of approximately $10 billion, which would seed new projects through feasibility studies, project preparation, geological and technical assessments, permitting and regulatory assistance, workforce development, transaction support, and limited equity or first-loss capital to reduce early-stage risk. To finance commercially viable projects that are ready to proceed, Congress should also authorize another $50 billion in lending, loan-guarantee, export-credit, and political-risk capacity.

The members of the Economic Shield should expand the capital base of the North American Development Bank and extend it to cover Southern Mexico and Central America. Projects relating to water, energy, logistics, nearshoring, and strategic infrastructure should receive support. The United States should join the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF) as a large shareholder to shape infrastructure finance across the region. Washington should also pursue membership of the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB) while immediately creating a dedicated cofinancing and guarantee facility with the CDB.

The Economic Shield would concentrate U.S. commercial and financial public resources, target them to willing partners that meet a common set of business-climate and trusted-collaborator standards and commitments, and by doing so aim to mobilize at least $250 billion in private capital over the next ten years. Private capital should come from American companies, partner governments, development banks, pension funds, infrastructure funds, and other private investors. In addition, countries receiving concentrated support would be expected to contribute their own resources, undertake agreed reforms, and create the conditions required for commercially sustainable projects.

The Western Hemisphere possesses extraordinary energy resources, but too many countries lack the power required for sustained economic growth. This must change. The Western Hemisphere should become the battery, gas station, and oil derrick of the world. Over the next decade, the United States and its partners should seek to increase Western Hemisphere oil and natural-gas production by as much as 50 percent. They should expand electricity generation, transmission capacity, pipelines, LNG facilities, and the other infrastructure required to deliver reliable power to industry and consumers.

Several countries are already moving to develop this infrastructure, although at different speeds. Argentina has introduced major investment incentives and is expanding the pipelines, oil-export capacity, and proposed LNG facilities needed to unlock the colossal oil and gas reserves on the Vaca Muerta site. Meanwhile, Ecuador is seeking new investment in oil but is struggling with regulatory uncertainty, infrastructure limitations, and opaque project development. Colombia’s new government has pledged to reverse the previous administration’s restrictions on hydrocarbon development and resume exploration. Those efforts are needed. Latin American and Caribbean producers could replace a meaningful portion of Russian gas exports to Europe and Asia, thereby reducing Russia’s revenues and geopolitical leverage. Washington should also help these countries create a pipeline of commercially and technically viable nuclear energy projects, including through the provision of U.S. small modular reactors.

There are around sixty critical minerals essential to energy, defense, manufacturing, and advanced technology. The Western Hemisphere possesses large quantities of roughly two-thirds of them. Developing secure hemispheric supply chains will not solve every critical minerals problem, but it would address many of the United States’ most pressing vulnerabilities. Yet much of this immense mineral wealth remains undeveloped or is exported for processing to China. The long-term goal should be complete hemispheric supply chains for every strategic mineral possible: from exploration and extraction through processing, recycling, supporting infrastructure, and purchase by an end user. Every link in the supply chain should be located either in the United States or in trusted countries within the hemisphere. Over the next ten years, the region should become not only a leading global source of minerals but also a major center for processing, refining, and mineral-based manufacturing. American companies and trusted partners, rather than Chinese state-owned or state-backed firms, should become the leading international investors, operators, technology providers, and purchasers supporting that transformation.

Project Vault—an independently governed public-private partnership to protect American manufacturers from critical-mineral supply disruptions—should be replicated. It is backed by up to $10 billion in long-term Export-Import Bank of the United States financing and nearly $2 billion in private investment, and will purchase and store essential raw materials in secure facilities across the United States. It will then be able to give participating manufacturers access during market disruptions while creating a large, creditworthy source of demand for mineral suppliers.

The Western Hemisphere is one of the world’s great bread baskets, feeding more than a billion people. The United States and Canada have highly productive farms, while Mexico has extensive manufacturing capacity. South America and the Caribbean possess additional agricultural land, freshwater, and energy, and the potential for substantial productivity gains. The long-term goal should be to move the hemisphere from agricultural strength to agricultural abundance, increasing current output by 50 percent within twenty years while protecting water supplies, soil quality, forests, and other natural resources. Over the next decade, the United States should lead an effort to increase combined Western Hemispheric agricultural output by at least 25 percent. This would require sustained annual growth of more than 2 percent. It is an ambitious target, but it is achievable.

Fertilizer will be essential to increased agricultural production, but Brazil and other Latin American producers are highly dependent on imported fertilizer, including from Russia. Preventing Russia or any other external supplier from disrupting agricultural production will require sufficient hemispheric capacity and diversified supply. Fortuitously, the essential inputs to fertilizer are already present in the hemisphere. Canada possesses world-leading potash resources, while the United States and several regional partners possess natural gas, phosphate, industrial capacity, and fertilizer expertise. Further, the hemisphere’s research institutions and companies are working to generate alternatives to these conventional inputs.

Water is also essential to agricultural production. The hemisphere possesses enormous freshwater resources, but they are unevenly distributed and frequently disconnected from the farms, cities, and industrial centers where water is most needed. Further, aging systems, leakage, groundwater depletion, drought, and inadequate storage limit the amount of available water. Participating countries should establish national water-productivity targets and invest in efficient irrigation, wastewater reuse, desalination, reservoirs, leakage reduction, and modern water-conveyance systems. Over the next twenty years, the hemisphere should seek to improve agricultural water productivity by at least 50 percent, allowing output to increase without a corresponding decline in freshwater levels.

Whoever builds the hemisphere’s telecommunications networks, cloud systems, data centers, and AI infrastructure will shape its technical standards, gain access to critical data, and acquire lasting commercial and political influence. The experience with 5G should be a warning for Washington. While the United States stalled, Huawei’s technology spread across the Western Hemisphere, and its presence has been hard to dislodge. Once supplied, a country’s telecommunications backbone is expensive and politically difficult to replace. The same danger now exists across subsea cables, cloud computing, data centers, digital payments, satellite systems, cybersecurity, smart infrastructure, and AI. If American companies do not build these systems, Chinese companies will.

The United States should not aim to eliminate all Chinese technology from the hemisphere, but rather to supplant China as the preferred partner for the next generation of strategic infrastructure and to prevent participating countries from becoming dependent on Chinese-controlled technology. American and trusted-partner companies should compete to win new projects involving sensitive government communications, subsea cables, cloud infrastructure, data centers, advanced telecommunications, energy networks, cybersecurity, and AI. Participating governments should remove untrusted equipment from the most sensitive parts of existing networks as fast as is technically and commercially feasible.

Successive American administrations have begun this effort. The first Trump administration sounded the alarm about Huawei, and the Biden administration used the CHIPS Act, international semiconductor partnerships, and support for the Open Radio Access Network technology to strengthen trusted supply chains and encourage alternatives to Chinese equipment. The second Trump administration has established the American AI Exports Program and supported the export of complete American AI technology packages. The Economic Shield would concentrate and sustain these efforts in the Western Hemisphere, aiming to make the secure American and trusted-partner technology stack—the full collection of infrastructure and capabilities required to develop and use AI—the preferred platform for the hemisphere.

Countries such as Brazil and Mexico would not have to end every commercial relationship with China to participate in the Economic Shield. They should, however, protect their most sensitive infrastructure through secure and interoperable systems, transparent procurement, effective cybersecurity, and safeguards preventing any foreign supplier from controlling critical data or communications. Rather than a rigid hemispheric mandate, individual technology roadmaps should identify the energy, telecommunications, data center, and other investments required to expand trusted technology in that country. In return for the tech policy commitments of participating governments, the United States should help assemble industry-led packages combining hardware, services, and long-term financing.

There are numerous, serious constraints. There will always be a crisis in Europe, Asia, or the Middle East to pull Washington’s attention away. And, in the longer term, inadequate power and digital infrastructure, political turnover, and attractive Chinese offers are all substantial challenges. Many countries in the Western Hemisphere have suffered from chronic underinvestment, unpredictable regulation, slow permitting, and inadequate pipelines and transmission systems. And, in the United States, financing, technology, and diplomatic support have often been insufficient to enable U.S. companies to compete. Consequently, resources remain undeveloped, electricity remains expensive and unreliable, and Chinese firms gain opportunities to finance, build, and influence strategically important energy infrastructure.

Potential partners’ vulnerability to sovereign-debt crises is another constraint. When governments lose access to capital markets, servicing debt becomes the priority and economic reforms become politically unsustainable; in that environment, China can present itself as the lender of last resort. Given the deficiencies of the international debt architecture in meeting this challenge, the United States should use its leadership in the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Group of Seven, and the Group of Twenty to require full disclosure of sovereign obligations, establish firm timetables for creditor negotiations, enforce comparable treatment among creditors, and extend an expedited restructuring process to vulnerable middle-income countries in the Western Hemisphere. IMF assistance should provide temporary liquidity and support serious economic reforms, but it cannot restructure debts that are genuinely unsustainable.

In addition, the Treasury Department’s Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF) gives Washington the capacity to respond rapidly when a friendly government pursuing difficult reforms confronts a short-term currency or liquidity crisis. Although it should not become a permanent bailout facility or a substitute for the IMF, temporary currency swaps, loans, or guarantees can be a bridge to an IMF program. For example, the United States used the ESF to help stabilize Mexico in 1995, and Argentina earlier this year. When used properly, the ESF can prevent a temporary financial shock from destroying reforms or from forcing an important hemispheric partner into China’s arms.

The Trump administration has restored the Western Hemisphere to the center of American national security and economic policy. Turning that renewed focus into a strategy capable of operating for multiple decades, and across multiple administrations, will require congressional authorization, multiyear financing, common targets across federal agencies, and long-term agreements with participating governments. Future administrations can build on these foundations.

The United States is uniquely positioned to offer Western Hemisphere countries a powerful combination of private capital, technology, government finance, energy, and market access, in return for cooperation. It can knit the hemisphere together into a mighty grouping and establish the Economic Shield as a lasting framework for hemispheric prosperity and security.

title: Ford Execs Stick to 2029 EV Breakeven Target - IndustryWeek
description:
Customers will be able to start pre-ordering Fathoms, the first vehicle to be built on Ford’s Universal EV platform, early next year but CFO Sherry House said Ford will still be investing heavily throughout 2027.
Also calling for lots of capital—about $1.3 billion next year—is Ford Energy, the battery-storage venture housed inside Model e and building a 4 million-square-foot plant in Kentucky that will produce lithium iron phosphate systems.
That, House said, means progress toward the 2029 breakeven target won’t be linear.
Shares of Ford (Ticker: F) were up nearly 4% to $12.43 in midday trading on Oct. 29.
Over the past six months, they’re essentially flat and the company now has a market capitalization of nearly $50 billion.
text:
Heading into a year in which they will launch the Fathom pickup truck and invest more in a new energy-store business, the leaders of Ford Motor Co. still expect the company’s electric-vehicle division to break even in 2029.

After Ford reported its third-quarter profits of nearly $2.1 billion on revenues of $49.5 billion, CEO Jim Farley and his team told analysts and investors that they are confident the midsized Fathom, which is being priced at about $28,000, can gain traction in an EV market where prices have risen of late. Ford is ramping up operations at its Louisville, Kentucky, plant, where COO Kumar Galhotra said teams have completed 90% of validation testing and cranked out 5,000 unicastings, which are a big part of the company’s strategy to lower costs by reducing vehicles’ number of parts.

Ford’s Model e group posted a loss of $1.1 billion before interest and taxes during the third quarter, which was an improvement from $1.4 billion in the same period of 2025 but slightly worse than Q2’s $919 million EBIT loss. Revenues from the division were down more than 30% year over year to about $1.2 billion as Ford, like its peer General Motors Corp., has cut production to reflect a fall in demand after the expiration last year of certain tax credits for EVs.

Customers will be able to start pre-ordering Fathoms, the first vehicle to be built on Ford’s Universal EV platform, early next year but CFO Sherry House said Ford will still be investing heavily throughout 2027. Also calling for lots of capital—about $1.3 billion next year—is Ford Energy, the battery-storage venture housed inside Model e and building a 4 million-square-foot plant in Kentucky that will produce lithium iron phosphate systems. That, House said, means progress toward the 2029 breakeven target won’t be linear.

“We’re now expecting higher expenses in 2027 as the plant’s coming into focus,” House said on an Oct. 28 conference call. “We think that the next step-function change in profitability is going to happen in the first half of 2028 as UEV and Ford Energy both ramp with revenue […] You’re going to see Fathom launching towards the end of [2027] with the first derivative of the platform. Then you’re going to have that full year of production in 2028. Then we’re going to be escalating the Ford Energy business with investment [and have] full-year production also by 2028.”

Ford’s goal of making money (or at least not losing much) from EVs by late this decade has it on a similar path to GM, whose CFO Paul Jacobson said last month that it will be 2028 before GM’s EV financials start to turn a corner in earnest. A key in that forecast is GM’s battery platform of choice, a lithium manganese-rich chemistry it is working on with LG Energy Solution that has a higher energy density than LFP cells such as Ford’s.

Shares of Ford (Ticker: F) were up nearly 4% to $12.43 in midday trading on Oct. 29. Over the past six months, they’re essentially flat and the company now has a market capitalization of nearly $50 billion.

title: Alliant Energy secures USD5.1bn to develop new power generation assets (US) | Enerdata
description:
US energy utility Alliant Energy has secured a USD5.1bn loan guarantee from the US Department of Energy (DOE) to support power generation, energy storage and transmission projects across Iowa and Wisconsin (United States) (Alliant Energy press release, 28/10/2026).
The financing package will support the development of new generation assets, including 1.8 GW of natural gas-fired generation (1.6 GW of greenfield projects and 240 MW of expansions at existing gas-fired power plants), 1 GW of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and transmission infrastructure.
It will also help finance 2 bcf (56 mcm) of LNG storage.
According to Alliant Energy, the loan package is expected to generate up to USD1.2bn in customer savings over its lifetime through lower financing costs.
The DOE financing supports projects included in Alliant Energy's long-term investment programme and is intended to improve system reliability while accommodating growing electricity demand.

The irony is that the Republican Party I joined—and the Republican Party I still believe in—was never supposed to be about division and retribution.

text: Bryan Mayor Pro Tem James Edge has issued a response to the Brazos County Republican Party Executive Commission’s Resolution of Condemnation released yesterday. The resolution was in response to Edge publicly endorsing Democratic candidate James Talarico in the race for Senate and can be read by clicking HERE. Edge issued the following response via Facebook which you can read below: The Brazos County Republican Party Executive Committee, under the leadership of Russ Ford, has voted to publicly “condemn” me because I endorsed James Talarico for the United States Senate. I have to admit, I’m a little flattered. A month before a consequential election, with plenty of important things for a political organization to be doing, they decided that James Edge is the problem that requires their attention. I suppose everyone eventually gets their moment in the sun. Seriously, I think their decision to attempt to retaliate against me (for exercising my 1st Amendment rights) demonstrates just the type of destructive, divisive, hyper-partisanship that I, along with many others, want to get away from. And I am certainly in good company. The Brazos County Republican Party has developed something of a tradition of attacking Republicans who don’t conform sufficiently to their prevailing orthodoxy. John Cornyn. John Raney. Kyle Kacal. Dade Phelan. Joe Straus. And others who, at various times, have been deemed insufficiently conservative—or insufficiently willing to follow their extreme positions, have all been attacked by these same people. The irony is that the Republican Party I joined—and the Republican Party I still believe in—was never supposed to be about division and retribution. It was supposed to be about principles. Limited government. Fiscal responsibility. Individual liberty. The rule of law. A strong national defense. Free markets. Constitutional government. A few weeks ago, I proudly endorsed James Talarico for the United States Senate. I did so knowing full well that some Republicans would disagree with me. That is their right. But I made my decision based on what I believe is best for Texas and for our country. I don’t regret it, and I am not going to apologize for it. Since making that endorsement, I have received an extraordinary amount of encouragement from friends, neighbors, elected officials, former colleagues and others across our community. Much of it has been private—which I completely understand in today’s political environment—but it has been remarkably consistent. And that tells me something. There are a lot more people in this community who are tired of the politics of division, corruption, intimidation, purity tests and personal attacks than some people in the local Republican Party seem to realize. The Brazos County GOP appears to believe that political success comes from subtraction and division—identifying Republicans who aren’t sufficiently “right-wing,” pushing them out, and then congratulating themselves for having a more ideologically pure party. I believe the opposite. You don’t build a majority by continually shrinking the tent. For years, I have watched good Republicans—people who knocked on doors, made phone calls, raised money, worked elections and devoted countless hours to the party—walk away from the local organization. Many of them still consider themselves Republicans. They simply don’t recognize the Republican Party they once worked so hard to build. I haven’t walked away. I haven’t changed my principles. And I haven’t changed parties. I have simply exercised my right—and my responsibility—to make my own judgment about who I believe should represent Texas in the United States Senate. If the Brazos County Republican Party wants to “condemn” me for doing that, they are certainly entitled to do so. But they should understand something: A public condemnation doesn’t intimidate me. It doesn’t silence me. And it certainly doesn’t make me regret my decision. If anything, it has given me one more opportunity to explain why I made it. I remain a Republican because I still believe in the principles that brought me to the party in the first place. And I intend to keep fighting for those principles—with or without the approval of the Brazos County Republican Executive Committee. After all, I didn’t get into public service to be told what to think. I got into it to think for myself. Edge appeared on The Infomaniacs in September after making his endorsement. You can hear that conversation by clicking HERE.

title: The chemicals that keep us cool leave something behind - North Carolina Health News
authors: Will Atwater, KFF Health News, Michelle Crouch, Rose Hoban, Charlotte Ledger, Ashley Fredde
description:
As of April 2026, the utility had spent $91 million addressing PFAS contamination in its drinking water supply, WilmingtonBiz reported.
Finding chemicals to do the job safely, efficiently and without harming the environment has driven successive changes in refrigerants.
By the 1980s, scientists had linked ozone layer depletion to chemicals common in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol cans.
The EPA is starting to take steps to learn more about TFA in drinking water.
In a proposed rule published in July, the agency included TFA among 30 unregulated chemicals that public water systems would monitor between 2028 and 2030.
text:
By Will Atwater

Driving in a North Carolina summer can be miserable without reliable air conditioning.

Nonetheless, checking for a refrigerant leak isn’t part of a routine check under the hood, said “Crazy” Charlie Thompson, owner of C and C Automotive in northeast Durham. By the time a driver notices a problem, some refrigerant may already have escaped.

“When angel breath quits blowing on them, that’s when they are like, ‘Huh, we need some more Freon,’” Thompson said.

Drivers often buy small cans of refrigerant to recharge their systems themselves. Some products contain only refrigerant; others include sealants intended to stop leaks. Thompson said those sealants can clog his shop’s refrigerant-recovery equipment.

“When they introduce that to their system, it stops up our $25,000 reclaimer, and they don’t want to pay us for that,” he said.

Familiar refrigerants, such as Freon, have evolved to address environmental concerns. But some of the newer alternatives come with a trade-off: Chemicals used to reduce coolant’s climate impact end up breaking down in the atmosphere into trifluoroacetic acid, or TFA, a pollutant that persists in the environment.

Many researchers classify TFA as an ultrashort-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance presenting yet another challenge for North Carolina communities already grappling with how to remove PFAS from drinking water — and how to pay for that removal.

Cape Fear Public Utility Authority draws much of its drinking water from the Cape Fear River, which has been contaminated by decades of PFAS releases from an upstream chemical plant operated by Chemours and its predecessor, DuPont.

As of April 2026, the utility had spent $91 million addressing PFAS contamination in its drinking water supply, WilmingtonBiz reported. But all that money hasn’t been able to stop TFA, according to the agency. Even as their granular activated carbon filters have reduced most of the PFAS it monitors to levels at or near nondetection, some ultrashort-chain compounds, like TFA, are harder to capture.

Researchers have detected TFA in tap water served by CFPUA’s Sweeney Water Treatment Plant. Those detections do not establish where the TFA came from, but they illustrate the challenge: Treatment is an imperfect solution to the PFAS problem.

“There isn’t really a silver bullet,” said Richie Kaur, senior superpollutant reduction advocate for climate and energy for the Natural Resources Defense Council. “There’s not a perfect refrigerant in the world. If we had it, we would have used it.”

A history of trade-offs

Refrigerants perform a basic job in refrigerators and air conditioners: moving heat.

“When you’re cooling something, the refrigerant is transferring heat from, say, inside the house and throwing it outside, and your house is cooled,” Kaur said.

Finding chemicals to do the job safely, efficiently and without harming the environment has driven successive changes in refrigerants.

Early refrigerants, used beginning in the 1800s, included ammonia, sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide. Some posed toxicity or flammability hazards. By the 1930s, synthetic alternatives had begun to enter commercial use.

Those alternatives brought environmental problems. By the 1980s, scientists had linked ozone layer depletion to chemicals common in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol cans. The Montreal Protocol, adopted in 1987 and strengthened through subsequent amendments, set in motion their phaseout.

Hydrofluorocarbons became widely used replacements. They spared the ozone layer but were potent greenhouse gases. In 2016, countries adopted the Kigali Amendment, another internationally negotiated settlement, to phase down their production and consumption, with the first reductions beginning in 2019.

The search for alternatives helped usher in a newer generation of refrigerants that break down faster in the atmosphere and have a much smaller direct warming effect.

One of them, HFO-1234yf, is a compound made of hydrogen, carbon and fluorine, now used in most light-duty vehicles, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA says its global warming potential is hundreds of times less than predecessor compounds, and it breaks down easily.

But when HFO-1234yf escapes into the air, it breaks down into TFA.

Chronic exposure

Scientists are still working out what widespread TFA escape means for people and the environment. A 2024 review documented its presence in rain, soil, drinking water and other parts of the environment, warning that its extreme persistence and continued releases are driving its accumulation.

Ultrashort-chain PFAS such as TFA pass through the body more quickly than some longer-chain PFAS, which can persist for a long time in human tissue. Nonetheless, humans are chronically exposed to these quickly moving chemicals because they’re highly present and persistent in the environment, said Anna Reade, director of PFAS advocacy and environmental health for the Natural Resources Defense Council.

Reade also noted that “health research has lagged behind the emergence of these chemicals.

“We’re kind of at a very early stage of understanding the impacts that TFA can have on human health,” she said. “But already in that early stage, we are seeing some health effects that are also shared with other PFAS, like reproductive harm and thyroid disruption.”

U.S. research on these chemicals is lagging behind work being done in Europe, where regulators use a different definition of harm, said Lee Ferguson, a Duke University professor of civil and environmental engineering. He said that may be why there’s been more focus on the effects of TFA across the Atlantic.

The EPA is starting to take steps to learn more about TFA in drinking water. In a proposed rule published in July, the agency included TFA among 30 unregulated chemicals that public water systems would monitor between 2028 and 2030. The findings would help inform future decisions about whether to regulate the contaminants.

The proposal would not set a drinking water limit for TFA.

What’s next for refrigerants?

Nearly 300 million light-duty vehicles were registered in the United States in 2025, including about 9 million in North Carolina, according to U.S. Department of Energy data. Those numbers illustrate the enormous scale of automotive cooling and its potential to contribute to TFA pollution — even though not every vehicle uses a refrigerant that breaks down into TFA.

Many vehicles will lose refrigerant at some point, but the EPA does not require leak repairs before a vehicle’s air conditioning system is recharged, although state or local requirements may differ.

A fully charged vehicle air conditioning system can hold about two pounds of refrigerant, estimated Jeremy Arling, a senior fellow specializing in super pollutants at the Natural Resources Defense Council. Those systems are exposed to heat and vibration, and the refrigerants end up escaping through tiny gaps in the rubber seals.

“Over the life of a car, you probably will lose your whole charge,” he said.

Reducing leaks is one challenge. Choosing what goes into cooling systems is another.

The Kigali Amendment was intended to push countries to reduce production and consumption of older refrigerants that affected the environment, but it does not dictate which refrigerants replace them.

Across refrigeration and air conditioning, alternatives include carbon dioxide, ammonia and propane, said Kaur, a senior scientist for the National Resources Defense Council. Carbon dioxide can be less efficient in hot climates, propane is highly flammable, and ammonia is toxic and mildly flammable.

The EPA already allows carbon dioxide in air conditioning systems in new vehicles, subject to safety requirements, but it does not permit propane for that use.

“But now the question is, what do we want to go to?” Kaur said.

text:
Kingsport, Tennessee-based polymers producer Eastman Chemical Co. has announced the reinstatement of a previously allocated United States Department of Energy (DOE) grant designed to support its efforts to divert plastic from landfills using chemical recycling processes.

Eastman’s announcement refers to a $375 million allocation (the firm uses the word “award) that matches the amount of one that was announced in 2024 and then terminated in 2025.

Those previous announcements indicated the chemical recycling investment would take place in Longview, Texas, where Eastman has existing chemicals and polymers production capacity.

Now, however, Eastman says “the project scope has been adapted” and indicates the funds will go toward “expanding proven U.S. advanced manufacturing technology by increasing output from Eastman’s commercial-scale methanolysis facility in Kingsport, Tennessee, by approximately 30 percent through debottlenecking and technology advancements.”

According to Eastman, the planned investment in Tennessee will be “supporting the reindustrialization of a strategically important domestic recycled plastics supply chain” in a way that “restores underutilized American recycling assets and increases domestic capacity to transform difficult-to-recycle polyester waste into virgin-quality recycled materials.”

The company says the reinstated DOE award is $375 million minus “approximately $35 million Eastman has [under] the previous agreement.”

Eastman says the project will result in “reindustrializing existing American recycling assets and strengthening the critical recycled polyethylene terephthalate (PET) supply chain by restarting and repurposing underutilized U.S. recycling infrastructure.”

The company indicates the funds may also help it plan a second U.S. methanolysis facility, offering it “flexibility in the location and timing” for that potential facility.

“This partnership represents an opportunity to strengthen American manufacturing by building a more resilient domestic supply chain for recycled materials,” says Mark Costa, Eastman’s board chair and CEO.

“Eastman is demonstrating that methanolysis technology can transform difficult-to-recycle polyester waste into virgin-quality materials at a commercial scale,” he adds.

“The DOE is proud to support this strategic investment in American ingenuity, industrial competitiveness and the future of U.S. manufacturing,” says Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “By expanding its proven, American-made recycling technology and putting underutilized assets back to work, Eastman is demonstrating how innovation can strengthen domestic manufacturing, revitalize existing industrial infrastructure and build more resilient supply chains.”

Eastman says it is prepared to build on its U.S.-developed methanolysis technology and the performance of its commercial-scale facility in Kingsport. The Science Direct website describes methanolysis as involving the treatment of PET scrap with methanol and catalysts in a range from 350 to 530 degrees Fahrenheit.

The company says it expects up to $100 million of incremental revenue growth in 2026 compared with 2025 from the Kingsport facility and more than $100 million of incremental revenue growth again in 2027.

“For our customers, this creates an opportunity to act now,” says Costa. “By partnering with Eastman, they can secure reliable domestic sources of high-quality recycled content while helping build responsible recycling end markets that convert more hard-to-recycle waste into valuable materials. Customer commitments are what will translate this proven technology into a stronger, more resilient U.S. circular economy.”

EP.9 – The Global High Tea Series | India-GCC Cooperation in Critical Minerals: Building Resilient Supply Chains for a Clean Energy Transition

Introduction

Critical minerals are becoming increasingly important to global economic competitiveness, energy security and technological advancement. Minerals such as lithium, cobalt, copper, nickel and rare earth elements are essential for renewable energy technologies, electric vehicles, battery storage and advanced manufacturing. As countries accelerate their energy transitions and seek to diversify their supply chains, access to these resources has emerged as a strategic priority. For India and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, this presents an opportunity to expand a longstanding partnership centred on hydrocarbons, trade, investment and energy security towards cooperation in critical minerals and clean energy technologies.

India’s growing demand for critical minerals is closely linked to its renewable energy ambitions, electric mobility, advanced manufacturing and broader objectives of technological self-reliance. The National Critical Minerals Mission, launched in January 2025 with an outlay of ₹34,300 crore over seven years, identifies international partnerships as an important mechanism for securing reliable and diversified mineral supply chains. GCC countries, meanwhile, are pursuing economic diversification strategies that increasingly emphasise mining, mineral processing, international resource investments and the development of downstream industries. Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 identifies mining as a key pillar of economic diversification, while the UAE is leveraging its financial and logistical capabilities to strengthen its position in global critical minerals supply chains.

Recent developments indicate growing momentum in India-GCC cooperation in this sector. India signed an agreement with the UAE in September 2024 to strengthen critical minerals supply chains and an agreement with Saudi Arabia in February 2025 covering joint exploration and technology transfer. Partnerships involving Indian companies and GCC-based investors also offer opportunities in battery recycling, mineral processing and investments in overseas mining projects. These initiatives reflect the potential to combine India’s technical expertise, industrial capabilities and mineral-processing requirements with GCC capital, international investment networks and emerging mining ecosystems.

Beyond bilateral cooperation, India and GCC countries could explore opportunities for joint investments in mineral-rich third countries, particularly in Africa, where access to resources can support diversified supply chains. Such partnerships could combine GCC investment capacity with India’s technical and industrial capabilities while supporting local value addition in resource-producing countries. Regional connectivity initiatives, including the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), may also provide opportunities to strengthen logistics, trade facilitation and the movement of critical minerals across international markets.

However, building reliable critical minerals partnerships requires more than securing access to raw materials. Cooperation must also address mineral processing, recycling, technology transfer, investment risks, regulatory coordination and responsible sourcing. Environmental sustainability, social safeguards, transparent supply chains and community engagement will be essential to ensuring that these partnerships deliver long-term benefits. India and the GCC can therefore explore a broader framework that connects resource access with research, industrial development, sustainable mining and the development of resilient mineral value chains.

The webinar will examine how India and GCC countries can deepen cooperation in critical minerals as part of their evolving economic and strategic partnership. It will explore the role of bilateral agreements, investment partnerships, technology transfer, third-country collaboration and regulatory coordination in strengthening supply chain resilience and supporting the clean energy transition.

Key Takeaways

Critical Minerals Complement Rather Than Replace Hydrocarbons: The global energy transition is adding critical minerals to the traditional energy-security agenda, not replacing oil and gas. India continues to depend heavily on crude oil imports, while critical minerals such as lithium, copper, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths are essential for its clean energy, electric mobility, battery storage and advanced manufacturing ambitions.

Converging Economic Diversification Priorities: India’s National Critical Minerals Mission and the GCC countries’ economic diversification strategies create opportunities for cooperation. Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 identifies mining as a third pillar of its economy, the UAE is leveraging its strengths in logistics and advanced manufacturing, Oman is developing its copper sector, and Qatar is exploring overseas investment opportunities.

Hydrocarbon Wealth Is Financing the Energy Transition: GCC sovereign wealth funds, state-owned enterprises and private investors are using capital generated from hydrocarbons to support investments in critical minerals, renewable energy and emerging industries. This creates opportunities to connect Gulf capital with India’s industrial and technological capabilities.

From Energy Cooperation to Industrial Partnerships: India–GCC cooperation should extend beyond resource access and conventional energy trade towards joint exploration, mineral processing, refining, recycling, logistics and advanced manufacturing. Greater attention to midstream and downstream activities is essential to capture value across the mineral supply chain.

Complementary Strengths Can Drive Joint Investments: India can contribute market demand, engineering expertise, industrial capabilities and skilled professionals, while GCC countries can provide patient capital, investment networks and access to overseas mineral assets. Joint ventures and special investment vehicles could help combine these strengths, including through partnerships in third countries.

Commercial Viability and Long-Term Investment Are Essential: Critical mineral projects involve significant exploration risks, infrastructure requirements and long gestation periods. Sovereign wealth funds can absorb some investment risks, but financing alone cannot guarantee success. Strong project economics, transparent governance and long-term commercial viability are essential to attract broader private-sector participation.

Value Addition Matters More Than Extraction Alone: A major opportunity lies in developing domestic capabilities in mineral processing, metallurgy, refining, permanent magnets and advanced materials. Reducing dependence on a limited number of countries for processing and distribution will require India and the GCC to invest across the entire value chain.

Skills, Research and Technology Partnerships Are Critical: Building local industrial capabilities requires investment in geology, mining engineering, metallurgy, exploration technologies and workforce development. Joint research, specialised training, university partnerships and AI-enabled exploration can accelerate technological learning and strengthen operational capabilities in both regions.

Recycling and Sustainable Mining Must Be Prioritised: Critical mineral extraction and processing are energy-, water- and resource-intensive activities with significant environmental implications. Cooperation in recycling, resource efficiency and sustainable processing can improve mineral life-cycle management and reduce environmental pressures.

Practical Standards and Institutional Coordination Are Necessary: India and the GCC have an opportunity to develop compatible standards for sustainable sourcing, environmental governance and responsible mineral development. These frameworks should be practical and commercially workable, supported by regulatory coordination, research partnerships and effective implementation mechanisms.

Speaker

Dr Ramu C. M.

Senior Analyst (Geopolitics & Threat Intelligence)

Cyber Security Foundation, Bayer

Dr. Ramu C. M. is a Senior Cyber Threat Intelligence Analyst at Bayer, with expertise spanning cyber threat intelligence, geopolitical risk, energy security and critical minerals. He holds a Ph.D. in Geopolitics and International Relations from Manipal Academy of Higher Education, where his doctoral research examined hydrocarbon-based energy linkages across the Persian Gulf and Caspian Basin. Before joining Bayer, he advised corporate, financial, humanitarian and energy-sector clients on geopolitical developments and security risks across the Indo-Pacific, Europe, West Asia and Africa. He is a paid geopolitical commentator for Sky News Arabia and Asharq-Bloomberg and writes on energy security, critical minerals, green hydrogen, maritime geopolitics and Eurasian energy corridors. He has also contributed to strategic policy and defence dialogues on corporate resilience, energy security and critical-mineral supply chains. His work examines how geopolitical competition, cyber security and economic statecraft shape corporate resilience and the security of strategic resource supply chains.

Moderator

Dr Dhritishree Bordalai

Senior Research Associate, International Relations

Centre for Public Policy Research

Dr Dhritishree Bordalai is a Senior Research Associate (International Relations) at the Centre for Public Policy Research (CPPR), Kochi, India. She holds a PhD from the Centre for European Studies (CES), School of International Studies (SIS), Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), New Delhi. She completed her MPhil in European Studies from SIS, JNU. Dhritishree has completed her Master’s in Politics with Specialisation in International Relations from SIS, JNU. She graduated from St. Stephen’s College, University of Delhi with History as her key discipline. She has a Certificate in Public Policy and Management from the Indian Institute of Management, Kozhikode (IIM-K). She has interned at the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) in New Delhi and was previously working as a Mahatma Gandhi National Fellow under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE, GoI).

Dhritishree has been awarded the UGC-DAAD Short-Term Scholarship during her PhD at the Otto-Suhr-Institut für Politikwissenschaft (OSI), Freie Universität Berlin, Germany. She has attended several national and international conferences on her area of research and presented a paper at the Young Researchers Conference in JNU. Her core areas of research are migration, security and refugee studies.

text:
The DOE’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation has unveiled a new strategy and initiative to strengthen American battery leadership

The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) today announced DOE’s national battery strategy and a new partnership to strengthen American leadership in advanced battery technologies, expand domestic manufacturing capabilities, and secure domestic supply chains. These efforts will support American innovation, create new opportunities for American jobs, and advance President Trump’s reindustrialisation agenda.

DOE’s Strategy for American Leadership in Batteries establishes the Department’s priorities to build a fully integrated domestic battery supply chain by 2030, achieve U.S. leadership in battery technology and manufacturing by 2035, and accelerate the commercialisation of safe, affordable, and reliable energy-storage solutions.

“From transportation and power grids to medical devices and consumer electronics, batteries are essential to modern life,” said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “DOE’s national strategy demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to accelerating American battery innovation, onshoring manufacturing, and securing the supply chains we need to power our economy and maintain American energy dominance.”

U.S. battery demand across transportation and energy-storage applications is projected to nearly quadruple, increasing from 179 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2025 to 707 GWh in 2035. Meeting this demand presents a significant opportunity to expand domestic manufacturing, strengthen America’s industrial base, and create new workforce opportunities.

DOE’s strategy identifies six strategic pillars:

targeting investments in the upstream and midstream supply chain steps;

accelerating commercial deployment of laboratory discoveries;

prioritising manufacturing process innovation;

targeting mission-driven deployment for grid modernisation;

coordinating on the national strategy with international partners;

and investing in American talent.

Launch of Battery Manufacturing Accelerator Consortium

To advance DOE’s battery manufacturing priorities, CMEI has launched the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator (BattMan), a national consortium of DOE National Laboratories, industry partners, and academic institutions focused on addressing critical barriers in scaling new battery technologies.

The accelerator will focus on lowering manufacturing costs, speeding the transition of novel battery technologies from laboratory discovery to manufacturing deployment, and boosting U.S. leadership in energy storage manufacturing. BattMan‘s work will harness Super Intelligence (SI) and advanced manufacturing capabilities to identify challenges earlier and improve production processes.

The accelerator will also strengthen critical mineral supply chains by advancing battery materials made from more abundant domestic elements. This will reduce battery production costs, shorten commercialisation timelines, and fortify America’s battery manufacturing sector.

The Battery Manufacturing Accelerator consortium is supported by CMEI’s Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office and led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory.

This is driving demand for local battery supply and energy infrastructure, it said.

Inpow plans to work with EGAT and other partners in areas including new energy vehicles, energy storage and energy equipment, with battery manufacturing at the core of the cooperation.

Inpow's 300,000th power battery pack rolled off the production line on October 15. Its batteries are used in models including the Aion i60, Aion N60 and Aion UT. The 2027 Aion i60 equipped with Inpow batteries offers a range of 700 kilometers.

SAN ANTONIO — Today, the San Antonio City Council voted to approve development restrictions to protect communities from data centers, making the fast-growing city the latest to act as state leaders in Austin do little to help.

District 6 Council Member Ric Galvan’s proposal passed with an amendment to include a setback from UNESCO heritage sites.

San Antonio has one of Texas’ largest concentrations of data centers. Nearly three dozen already operate in the city, and the municipally-owned electric utility expects another 59 to open in the coming years.

DeeDee Belmares, Public Citizen’s San Antonio-based organizer and clean energy advocate, issued the following statement:

“Across the state, Texans have been demanding that public officials side with their communities instead of Big Tech. The San Antonio City Council heard the call and listened to the people.

“The new specific use zoning permit will allow the public to weigh in on a project before it is voted on by city council, helping residents protect their neighborhoods from the rush to build these facilities. Still, community members who have relentlessly pushed for local action know that the work is far from over. Every existing data center and future development must be carefully scrutinized to ensure a profit-driven developer’s cost of doing business doesn’t come at the expense of public health or the quality of life for thousands of San Antonians. Now, this movement will maintain vigilance over data centers while pressing legislators in Austin to build on what the council achieved today.”

title: Why the Erasure of Factory's Fossil Fuel Emissions is a Mistake - TATLER
description:

text:
Introduction

Ever since the Environmental Protection Agency was established in 1970, it has had the central mission to ensure “Americans have clean air, land, and water.” But recently, that narrative has taken a significant turn. When EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin took office, he quickly announced his plans to “power the Great American Comeback,” declaring that “we are driving a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion to drive down cost of living for American families, unleash American energy, bring auto jobs back to the U.S. and more.”

Since then, much of the EPA’s work has involved toppling regulations and climate commitments made by previous administrations. And on Sept. 14, the EPA made one of its final moves to completely erase one of the most consequential climate policies from the Biden administration by removing limits on climate pollution from power plants.

The limits have existed since 2024 and impose regulations on coal plants in operation and future gas-burning plants. By 2039, coal plants would have been required to install carbon capture technology that would reduce their emissions by 90% or be shut down. Additionally, gas plants constructed after 2039 generating at least 40% of their maximum capacity would need to reduce their emissions by 90% before 2032.

The repeal of this regulation would revert the rule to Obama’s weaker 2015 standard, which aimed to reduce carbon pollution from power plants but recognized fossil fuels as a “critical component of America’s energy future.” However, the EPA has recently proposed another deregulation that would eliminate all greenhouse gas emission standards for all power plants.

According to the EPA’s estimation under the Biden administration, the original regulation would cost businesses $19 billion to comply, though in its recent repeal the EPA changed the figure to $310 billion without explanation. Though these figures are drastically different, they’re both smaller than the estimated $370 billion the regulations would bring in public health benefits over the next two decades. These benefits include prevention of up to 1,200 premature deaths, 870 hospital visits, 360,000 asthma attacks, and prevent school and work absences.

In the repeal’s fact sheet, the EPA explained how the technology the old regulations relied on wasn’t available at scale and that the repeal would lead to economic relief for many families. However, at the time of the Biden-era ruling, the Department of Energy planned to appropriate money to make the technology more feasible.

The EPA’s fact sheet also states that “GHG [greenhouse gas] emissions from fossil fuel-fired EGUs [electric generating units] have no material impact on global climate change” and that “even if you complete[ly] eliminated all CO2 emissions from all new and existing EGUs in the U.S., there would be no meaningful effect.” The EPA also described that the ruling would allow coal production to increase more than 10 times.

This statement directly contradicts scientific understanding of climate change, including that the U.S. power sector contributes to around 24% of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions. To put that percentage into perspective, if the U.S. power sector were its own country, it would be the fifth most polluting country globally.

Even as climate change has taken a political backseat, it has created extreme weather disasters such as Hurricane Isaias and the landslides in Nepal. NOAA estimates that natural disasters caused by climate change have cost $182.7 billion in 2024 alone.

The new ruling is expected to go into effect on Nov. 16, though the EPA has opened the docket to comments from the public. The EPA closes the comments on Nov. 2 to review them and make changes to their original ruling. The comments are meant to highlight potential research gaps the EPA missed in its original ruling and to amplify voices of specific demographics that the EPA potentially overlooked.

As of Oct. 29, the docket only had 96 comments from various individuals and organizations. Submitting a comment can amplify the American public’s needs to focus on the climate crisis. Though unique comments have more impact than repeated ones, repeated comments can also draw attention to specific issues. Comments can be submitted with names or anonymously, and there is no age restriction on commenting. text:
Graphics AI Assisted
SEOUL, October 30 (AJP) - Orders for the batteries that keep AI data centers running are still pouring into South Korea's battery makers, even as investors question whether the artificial intelligence (AI) boom has swollen into a bubble.
Samsung SDI on Thursday reported a third-quarter operating profit of 407.8 billion won (US$308 million), reversing a 591.3 billion won loss a year earlier.
The result, its largest in 12 quarters, came on climbing sales of energy storage systems (ESS) and battery backup units for AI data centers.
LG Energy Solution, the country's largest battery maker, posted record quarterly revenue of 9.64 trillion won, up 59 percent, in preliminary results released Oct. 8. Operating profit rose 25.7 percent to 756 billion won.
Stripped of 416.9 billion won in U.S. production tax credits, LG's operating profit came to 339.1 billion won, helped by rising ESS shipments in North America and compensation from some electric vehicle customers.
SK On, the battery unit of SK Innovation, was the only one of the three in the red. It swung to an operating loss of 80.5 billion won as battery sales fell and one-off gains from the previous quarter fell away.
An ESS banks electricity in large arrays of batteries and releases it on demand, working as both a shock absorber and an insurance policy for data centers that cannot afford a second of downtime.
Global data center electricity consumption is set to more than double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.
South Korean manufacturers once dominated the field, holding about 70 percent of the global ESS market in 2017. A string of fires at storage sites in Korea then pushed them into retreat, and Chinese rivals moved in with cheaper lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells.
Chinese companies still held 76 percent of North American ESS battery shipments in the first half of the year, according to SNE Research. North America took in 75.9 gigawatt-hours (GWh), about a sixth of global shipments.
Edited and compiled by AJP. Graphics AI Assisted
The tides changed as U.S. President Donald Trump on Aug. 26 signed Executive Order 14420, declaring a national emergency over foreign-made power grid equipment. The order lets the Energy Department bar battery storage systems from foreign entities deemed a national security risk.
"Since the Trump administration tightened restrictions on China and pushed to reshape supply chains, interest in securing non-Chinese cells and stable suppliers has been rising, mainly among U.S. ESS operators and system integrators that had used Chinese cells," said Kim Young-kwang, SK On's head of financial management, on SK Innovation's earnings call.
South Korean battery makers have spent the electric vehicle slowdown retooling underused American EV lines to make LFP storage cells. LG Energy Solution now makes storage cells at five North American sites, aiming for more than 50 GWh of capacity by year-end.
Samsung SDI began mass-producing LFP storage cells in early October at StarPlus Energy, its Indiana joint venture with Stellantis. Its ESS orders this year topped 60 GWh through October, enough to run its storage lines in Indiana and Ulsan at full tilt through 2028.
SK On, a later entrant, is still converting lines at its Seosan plant in Korea and its Georgia factory, where cells are due to ship to U.S. firm NeoVolta from next year.
Samsung SDI said it has also signed leading global customers for cylindrical batteries used in humanoid robots and aerospace.
"Humanoids and aerospace are markets with very large growth potential over the mid to long term," Cho Han-je, Samsung SDI’s executive vice president for strategy and marketing, said on the call.
"By 2028, their share of revenue within our cylindrical battery business is expected to exceed 10 percent, contributing meaningfully to earnings."
LG Energy Solution's ESS products. Courtesy of LG Energy Solution
The AI-driven ESS boom has also trickled down to other suppliers, including builders of ESS facilities. HD Hyundai Electric, a power equipment maker, booked record quarterly revenue of 1.18 trillion won in the third quarter.
"Our biggest concern right now is capacity. There are so many orders from the United States that profitability keeps climbing, with margins rising every quarter," an HD Hyundai Electric official said at an energy industry exhibition in Seoul this week.
"It is so much a seller's market that even if we add capacity, I don't think margins will fall," the official said.
The official said worries over a possible slowdown in AI investment had drawn frequent questions this quarter. "But that is not what our sales teams are feeling. There is still a lot left."
Talk of an AI bubble, and of chipmakers priced beyond their earnings, has hung over markets this month. Battery and power equipment makers share some of that unease, but are still adding lines and signing contracts that run years ahead.
Whatever becomes of the AI trade, the data centers already rising will still need to keep their lights on.
Edited and compiled by AJP. Graphics AI Assisted
AJP Takeaways
- Samsung SDI reported a third-quarter 2026 operating profit of 407.8 billion won on Oct. 29, its largest in 12 quarters, on higher sales of energy storage systems and battery backup units for AI data centers.
- LG Energy Solution posted record third-quarter 2026 revenue of 9.64 trillion won and operating profit of 756 billion won, while SK On swung to an operating loss of 80.5 billion won.
- Chinese companies held 76 percent of North American ESS battery shipments in the first half of 2026, according to SNE Research. U.S. Executive Order 14420, signed Aug. 26, 2026, lets the Energy Department restrict foreign-made grid battery storage.
- Samsung SDI said its ESS orders exceeded 60 GWh through October 2026, filling its Indiana and Ulsan lines through 2028. It expects humanoid and aerospace batteries to exceed 10 percent of its cylindrical battery revenue in 2028.
